MESSAGE OF GRAND MASTER
The Grand Master then delivered his Message, as
follows:
"Masonry is the activity of closely united men
who, employing symbolical forms borrowed principally
from the mason's trade and from architecture work
for the welfare of mankind." . . •
'
Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
Under our Constitution it is the duty of the Grand Master "to
present at each Annual Communication a wri'tten message therein
setting forth all his official acts during the year, exhibi~ing the
general condition of Masonry within the jurisdiction, and recommending such legislation as he may deem necessary or expedient
for the welfare of the Craft."
It is in accordance with that requirement, and not with the.
intent or purpose that it should take the form of an address 1 that
I present this Message to Grand Lodge-including herein some
suggestions, without recommending any legislation thereon.
In this connection I may say that such recommendations as
I make with reference to legislation are due to the fact that it
is the policy of our jurisdiction to reduce our entire jurisprudence
to hard and fast rules incorporated in the Constitution or in
Regulations possessing the same force and authority. We now
have 232 Constitutional Provisions and 492 Regulations.
My experience as Grand Master has confirmed the opinion
I have long entertained, that we have entirely. too much legislation.
Instead of confining our Constitution to the basic Jaw we have
included therein not only rules, regulations and stat11t~s, but in

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

some instances even approved decisions of Grand Masters
construing the law.
I can not but believe that this has been unwise-particularly
_with reference to the decisions made by Grand Masters. It is of
course entirely meet a nd proper that decisions of Grand Masters
which have been approved by Grand Lodge sho uld be collated and
printed ; I believe, however, that these should be deemed precedents by which a Grand Master would be guided, rather than
decrees by which he will be bound; because every decision, even
in our Courts, is made with reference to only the particular case
in which it is rendered. Not only is a Court not bound by the
decisions of another Court of co-ordinate jurisdiction, but it not
infrequently happens that a .Court of Last Resort will modify or
even overrule one of its own decisions.
Now the Grand Master is invested with all the functions of
Grand Lodge when that body is not in session. It does not,
therefore, seem to be proper that in the discharge of his duties
he should be bound by a decision of a predecessor, even where it
has been approved by Grand Lodge, except as to matters which
properly constitute the basic law of the Institution.
As it is, he is bo und by a decision perhaps inadvertently made
a nd which was approved by Grand Lodge only because it was
included in an "omnibus" recommendation of the Committee on
Jurisprudence whose attention was not called to the effect thereof;
and there results the peculiar anomaly that I have this year as
Grand Master made a decision which is not only justified but
required by our law, but which I neve rtheless believe to be
absolutely wrong.
.
.
It was in connection with the withholding of my approval of.
an amendment to its By-Laws adopted by Jewel Lodge. It appeared that at the stated meeting held on February 5th there was
an amendment presented changing the time of meeting from 1 :30
p. m. to 10:30 a. m.; that that amendment was presented in writing
and duly noted in the minutes of the Lodge and a ll requirements
in connection therewith were strictly obse rved ; that at the next
stated meeting, held on March 4th, 1920, the amendment proposed
was amended by changing the time from 10:30 a. m. to 12:00
o'clock noon; and after being so amended it was adopted by
unanimous 'vote of the members present.
I was compelled t o withhold my approval of this amendment
because one of my predecessors had made a decision, which had
been approved by Grand 'Lodge, to the effect that written notice
of the amendment actually adopted must have been given at the
preceding stated meeting and that it was not competent for the
Lodge to amend the proposed amendment.

Now the purpose of requiring notice to be given is of course
to inform the L odge that it is proposed to cha nge the existing
law; and that the proposed amendm ent will be considered at a
certain time. Whe n that time arrives the purpose of the n otice
has been fulfilled and the proposed amendment may then be
considered and acted upon exactly as any other amendment of
which no notice is required. In other words, it is subject to an
amendment which is germane to the o riginal amendment.
That this is a reasonable view must be apparent; and while
this Grand Lodge is of course not b ound by parliamentary law,
it is the rule announced in Roberts' Rules of Order, where (in
considering the question of Amendments to the Constitution
req uiring previous notice) it is said:
"The object of this notice is to inform the Society
that the subject matter of the amendment will be up for
consideration and action at a certain time. It is not to be
inferred that notice is required to amend this amendment;
if this were the case it would be almost impossible to
properly amend by-laws, etc., but this last amendment
must be germane to the original amendment; no o ther
amendmen t is in order or can delay action on the original
amendment."

8

9

Notwithstanding all this, however, I was compelled to withhold my approval of· the amendment adopted. T his made it
necessary for J ewe I Lodge to go through the entire proceeding
a new. Although the members of the Lodge were unanimously in
favor of meeting at noon, this could not be done until a new
amendment was submitted, which could not be acted upon until ·
th e following stated meeting. If, at that meeting, two-t hirds of
the members present had been in favo r of meeting at 12 :30 instead
of at 12·:00 it would have been necessary to defeat the am endment
presented and propose another amendment whic h would go over
for another mo nth. Incidentally it may be said that it would be
impossible to determine whether or not two-thirds of t hose present
preferred to meet at 12 :30 rather than at 12 :00, because under our
law no such amendment could be made to the amendment proposed ; and therefore of course no vote thereon be taken.
A decision which would so result must have been inadvertently
made. Nevertheless that is the law as announced by t his Grand
Lodge. Of course, if Grand Lodge sustains the views I entertain,
it may reverse its previous action by disapproving t he decision
I made. I was, however, bound by a decision of one of my
predecessors which had been approved by Grand Lodge; and m y
decision should therefore be apJlroved. Had I n ot been bound by
that decision I would have approved the amendment; and if m y

10

action had been sustained by Grand Lodge that wou ld establish
the law until changed by some later decision which Grand Lodge
would approve. As it is, if Grand Lodge believes I am correct
in the views I entertain, it will be necessary to change the law
by specific legislation.
Entertaining the views I do, I am therefore compelled to
recommend that A'.rticle XII( of the By-Laws be amended by inserting after the words "provided that written notice of such amendment" the words "or of an amendment to which such amendment
was made."
In addition to the foregoing, and for reasons in each case
stated I make the followingRecommendations for New Legislation
Minutes-It has come to my knowledge that in several Lodges
the minutes are not transcribed into .t he Record Book and presented
to the Master for his approval until long after they have been
approved by the Lodge.
I can see no good reason for keeping a Minute ,Book and a
Record Book. A rough draft of the minutes could be made by
the Secretary in any convenient form. These minutes could then
be transcribed into the Record Book and presented at the next
stated meeting for approval. Any objection or correction could be
noted on the minutes which, when approved by the Lodge, could
be signed by the Master at the close of the meeting at which
they were approved. As it is no w there is nothing to show that
the minutes signed by the Master are the ones which were really
approved by the Lodge.
I therefore recommend that the first and second subdivisions
of Section 1 SO of A rticle V of the Constitution be so amended as
to require the Secretary to record all proceedings at each meeting
and to transcribe the same into the Record Book, and at the next
stated meeting to present the minutes so transcribed to the Lodge
for approval or correction; and after being so approved and
corrected to the Master for his signature.
Remission of Dues-Under the provisions of the 3rd subdivision of Section 41 of the Constitution, unless remission of dues of
a member is made at the stated meeting in July for the preceding
twelve months, a Lodge is not exempt from Grand Lodge dues on
account of such member.
I have had my attention called to the fact that some Lodges,
on account of local conditions, and principally on account of the
weather, never have a quorum at the stated meeting in July, and
therefore no stated meeting is held. Not heing able to remi• the

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

11

dues in July, they are compelled to include in their contributions
to Grand Lodge the per capita tax on members whose dues have
been remitted by the Lodge because of their inability to pay the
same.
T his is certainly inequitable; and no good reason appearing
why the dues should be remitted in the month of July rather than
at a stated meeting held in any other month, I recommend that
the 3rd subdivision of Section 41 of the Constitution be so amended
as to relieve the subordinate Lodge from paying the per capita
tax on any Mason whose dues may have been remitted at any
stated meeting during the year.
Bi-monthly Report-Th e Grand Secretary is now required by
the 10th subdivision of Section SO of the Constitution to not only
keep in his office a full and complete list ~nd record of all expul&ions, suspensions and restorations of which he shall be notified
by the several Lodges, but to transmit that list to every Lodge,
and to include therein, which is of course proper, a list of
rejections. The custom has been to issue this list bi-monthly.
From the investigation I have had made, I am satisfied that
this entails a useless expenditure of time and mo ney. I n most
Lodges the Secretary simply announces the receipt of the notice.
In some, the names of those within that particular jurisdiction are
r.ead; while in others not even the fact of the receipt of the list is
announced. This situation could be of course cured by requiring
the list to be read. In my opinion, however, no good purpose
would be thereby. served.
A petitioner for the degrees is required to state in his petition
that he has not been rejected within . a year. Visitors are either
vouched for, or if examined are required to present documentary
evidence of. their standing. If anyone desires to know whether
any particular individual has been suspended, expelled or rejected,
that information can always be obtained by communicatng with
th e Grand Secretary.
I therefore recommend that Section SO of the Constitution
be so amended as to relieve the Grand Secretary of the necessity
of transmitting the list to the Lodges, but to re quire him to include
in the list kept by him a record of all rejectio ns.
Veterans-On several occasions while visiting Lodges, particularly in the mountain districts, I have hear d the desire expressed
that some provision be made in our law to authorize Lodges by
resolution to provide that a member who has held membership over
a long period of years, or who has reached an advanced age, may
be relieved from the payment of dues.

In another instance the _suggestion was made·that Grand Lodge
should provide some form of certificate to be issued to a Mason
who had been a member of the fraternity for fifty years.
I make no recommendation for legislation as to any of these
matters, but suggest they receive the consideration of Grand LodRe.

considered the personal privilege of those who were most
vociferous in their condemnation of the practice.
Having primarily in mind, however, the. inhibition against the
Lodges communicating with each other concerning legislation, I
recommend that the entire provision I have quoted be repealed.

Communication Between Lodges-In Section 127 of the Constitution it is provided among other things: "Nor shall any Lodge
send out any circular or other communication to Lodges or Masons
concerning legislation to be brought before the Grand Lodge or
the election of officers therein."
It will be noted that the inhibition goes only to Lodges and
not to individuals. I can. conceive of no good reason why a Lodge
should not be permitted to communicate with another Lodge with
reference to legislation to be brought before Grand Lodge.
Theoretical)y at least the Lodges through their representatives
enact the legislation in Grand Lodge. Why should they be
precluded from· communicating with each other concerning any
proposed measure?
Insofar as the question concerns the election of officers, it
takes on a different aspect; although here again it i-s to be noted
that it is only the Lodge against which the inhibition lies. Furthermore, there is really nothing ethically wrong in seeking office either
for oneself or for another. It is purely a question of propriety;
and one concerning which men may properly differ. Of course
the office should seek the man and not the man the office; but
he goes far who contents himself with a willingness to accept the
office his friends seek for him.

Balloting in Groups-It has become obtrusively apparent that
the condition existing today necessitates a change in the methods
\"~ich prevailed fifty years ago. When the Lodges were small
and the petitioners few, · no reasonable objection could be urged
to the law which requires that a separate ballot be taken on every
petition, and that every member present shall vote. Under the
co nditions which have existed during the past two years, this has
been rendered impracticable, if not indeed impossible. For instance, in one case which has been called to my attention, at a
meeting of a Lodge there were present ninety members. Eighteen
petitions were to be acted upon. Disregarding entirely the requirement of our law that the reports of the investigating committee
shall be read to the Lodge (a law, by the way, which I have found
is "more honored in the breach than in the observance") it would
require at least twelve minutes to ballot upon each of the candidates, and the balloting alone would therefore consume three and
one-half hours.
Now there is of course good reason for requ'iring that every
member present shall vote, and that no one shall be excused;
otherwise it might happen that by a preconceived arrangement
the number actually voting would be so small as would make it
possible to determine who, if anyone, deposited. a blackball; and
the secrecy of the ballot would be thereby impaired. I can, however, see no good reason. why a ballot should not be taken on all
the petitions at one time. If no cube appeared there would be
no necessity for another ballot; and all the candidates would be
declared elected. If there was an unfavorable ballot it would indicate that there was objection to at least one of the candidates.
The petitions could then be divided into two groups and a ballot
taken upon each of these groups just as in the first instance it was
taken on all . . If a cube appeared in either of these ballots, that
group could be again divided or a separate ballot could be taken
on each of the petitions included in that group, depending upon
the number of petitions and the number of brethren present. It
need not be made obligatory, but it could be left optional with
the Lodge at the discretion of the Master.
I therefore recommend that the Constitution be so amended
as will permit Lodges in their discretion to ballot upon more than
one candidate at the same time.

If there has ever been an officer elected in the Grand Lodge
of California without having had some letter "or other communication" sent out in his behalf, it must have been before my advent
in Grand Lodge. It happens that because of my personal views
concerning such matters, I have never even indirectly, or. by
insinuation or suggestion, asked any man to vote for me for any
Masonic o'ffice; but if what the Lodges are precluded by this
section from doing had not been done in my behalf by those who·
desired to see me elected Junior Grand Warden, I wouf<l not now
be addressing this message to Grand Lodge.

Of course the practice may have ceased with niy election.
I have reason to believe, however, that it did not have its inception
at that time, because I distinctly recall hearing the question di.•·
cussed during the first year I attended Grand Lodge; and my
impression at that time was that the real complaint was that
someone else had . done, or was doing, that which seemed to be

Return of Fees-There appears to be some confusion concerning the disposition to be made of fees paid by petitioners who are.
elected but who do not receive any of, or all, the degrees. I have
made a decision (VI) covering the question presented in the
event of the death of the candidate; but in view of the fact that
we have specific legislation covering certain contingencies, I am
of the opinion that it would be advisable to include therein the
entire question; and that all the legislation with reference to the
matter should be either in the Constitution or in the Uniform Code
of By-Laws; but not in both, as is now the case.
I therefore so recommend.
Withdrawal-In connection with the matter last referred to
I here call the attention of Grand Lodge to a case which arose
during the administration of my predecessor and which can not
be disposed of to the satisfaction of either the Lodge or the
brother concerned without some legislation by Grand Lodge.
One of our Lodges initiated a candidate who subsequently
wrote the Lodge that because of an unfavorable opinion of the
fraternity he had conceived he did not desire to advance any
further.
The Lodge prefers not to carry him upon the records as an
Entered Apprentice; and the only alternative under our present
law is to prefer. charges against him. This would be perhaps
law is to prefer charges against him. This would be perhaps
warranted by a decision rendered by Past Grand Master Foshay
to the effect that no brother will be permitted to resign from
Masonry or renounce . the Order; and that an attempt to renounce
Masonry is an offense and should be punished. This action, however, the Lodge does not desire to take. They believe that it
would be an injustice to place upon this brother the stigma of
having been expelled from a Masonic Lodge. They take the
position that having come into the Lodge of his own free will
and accord, he should now be permitted of his own free will and
accord to quietly retire therefrom. I feel constrained to say that
I am inclined to the views entertained by the Lodge.
If he were a Master Mason he could take his demit without
question. His motive might be the same as that which impels
the action of this Entered Apprentice; but no question would be
raised. I am of course not unmindful of the purpose with which
a d.emit was originally issued. In this jurisdiction, however, we
recognize the right of a member of a Lodge in good standing and
whose dues are paid to withdraw at any time by giving notice of
his intention; and his membership in the fraternity thereby ceases.
In other words we do not seek to compel a Master Mason to

retain his membership. Wherein is the difference in principle in
the case of an Entered Apprentice?
Here is a man who has been guilty of no infraction of the
moral law and whose only offense against the fraternity, if that
indeed be an offense, is that because of something that has occurred, . he has changed the favorable opinion he had formed of
it when he presented his petition. He makes no charge. against
the fraternity, or against the Lodge, or against any of its members. For reasons best known to himself he simply desires to
sever all connection with the fraternity. The Lodge under the
circumstances does not desire to carry him as an Entered Apprentice. On the other hand, those who know him best, the members
of his Lodge, his neighbors and associates, are unwilling to cast
upon him the stigma of having been expelled from a Masonic
Lodge. They Believe that it would be an injustice; and I may
frankly say that I share that belief.
I am not prepared to make any recommendation as to just
what legislation should be enacted to permit the Lodge to do that
which it desires in this case. I can not, however, forbear saying
that it does seem to me that some method should be provided
whereby any Mason who so desires may be permitted to voluntarily sever his connection with the fraternity; but to be subject of
course, as is a demitted Master Mason, to its discipline.

III.
Quorum-The question propounded was whether unde1 Section
78 of the Constitution seve n members of the Lodge are rquired
to do business, or if seven Maste r Masons being present one o r
more may be visitors.
At first blush it seems strange that such a question could
ever arise. It would be naturally supposed that all seven must·
be members of the Lodge. The doubt, I learned, however, has
arisen because of the peculiar phraseology of our law-the provision of which with reference to this particular question is
as follows:
"No Lodge shall transact any business with a less number
than seven present except th e conferring of degrees."
It is, of course, not necessary that the number requisite to
confer degrees shall be members of the Lodge; and it is, therefore, perhaps not so strange that the question has been raised.
It will be noted that the number necessary for the conferring of degrees is not stated. In deciding the specific question
I, therefore, deem it not improper to cove r the entire matter,
and here report in full the opinion upon which I based my
decision.
The old Constitution and Regulations are silent as to the
number of brethren necessary to make a quorum for the transaction of business. Indeed, there appears to be considerable
confusion with reference to the entire matter-independent of
the question of whether or not the number necessary to constitute a quorum should be members of the Lodge.
· At one time the opinion was very generally entertained that
five Masons were sufficient to open a Lodge and carry on business other than initiation ; but that fo r the latter purpose seven
were necessary. The question apparent'.y was not as to the
membership of those present, but as to the number of brethren
r equisite to constitute a legal lodge with competent powers to
perform the rite of initiation and transact business. Mackey
was of the opinion that in the absence of all written laws on
the subject· we were compelled to refer to the ritual for authority; and that, according to the ritualistic rule, seven constituted a quorum for work or business in an Entered Apprentice's
Lodge, fiv e in a Fellow Craft's and three in a Master Mason's.
It will be noted that he made no distinction between a
Lodge "at work" and "transacting business" ; at least with
reference to the question of the number necessary to constitute
a quorum. He· did, however, in fact recognize that a distinction
exists, because he states that the Pa r:iam entary law which provides that a deliberative body shall not proceed to business until
a quorum of its members is present is applicable to Masonry,
" e.x cept that in con'stituting a quorum for opening and working
a . L odge it is not necessary that the requisite number shall be
actual members of the Codge ; for the proper officers of the
Lodge being present, the quorum may be completed with any
brethren of the craft."
That a distinction is to be observed between "work" and
"business" in determining the n.umber r equired to be present

20

GRAND LODG!a OF CALIFORNIA

is recognized by our Grand Lodge in the provision of Section
78 of our Constitution; and the uncertainty with reference to
the number required for the transaction of business is there
disposed of; but there is nothing in that section to indicate
whether or not the number necessary to transact business shall
be members of the Lodge; nor have I been able to find any
other provision of our Constitution which throws any light on
the matter. The question must, therefore, be answered by a
consideration of the principle involved.
The evident purpose of the ru!e requiring a quorum is
· that no business shall be transacted in the absence of a sufficient number interested in what is done. Visitors have no
interest in the business that concerns only the particular
Lodge; and they have no right to vote upon any question
"which may properly come before it." There would, therefore, be no reason why they should be counted to make up
the "quorum" required to transact business.
Furthermore, if all seven need not be members of the
Lodge, no one of the seven (except, of course, the Master)
need be ; and there might then be presented the extraordinary
spectacle of a meeting with fifty Masons present, no one of
whom (with the exception of the Master) would be entitled
to vote upon a question cominl! before the Lodge.
I am, therefore, of the ooinion that it was clearly intended
by Section 78 of the Constitution to provide that no business
shall be transacted by any Lodge unless there are present at
the time at least seven members of that Lodge. And I so
hold and decide.

The purposes for which the funds of a Lodge may be
used are specifically set forth in Section 88; and "the Lodge
can not by amendment to its by-laws or otherwise use or permit the use of its funds or property or any part' of them for
any other thing whatsoever."
I, of course, need not remmd you that personally I am
inclined to doubt the wisdom, to say nothing of the justice,
of our law upon this subject. I, of course, realize that the
enactment of the law was apparently made necessary by the
conditions which gave rise to it. Nevertheless, my own idea
has always been that so !ong as any individual Lodge was
able to pay the contributions levied by Grand Lodge and
to promptly and generously respond to calls for relief made
upon it, the disposition and disbursement of its funds was its
concern and not that of Grand Lodge. That, however, is
only my own individual opinion; and while my personal views
would, of course, influence any opinion I might be called upon
to render in construing the law, they do not justify me in
ignoring or controverting its plain provisions. However worthy
may be its purpose and however commendable the motives of
the brethren, the proposed assessment is not "'for the payment
of necessary expenses of the Lodge and for the special calls
for charity for ':"hich it was instituted"; and it is, therefore,
clearly unauthorized and consequently illegal.

From the figures furnished by you it is evident that the
expenditure o_f $200.00 for a Past Master's jewel would not
be an extravagance. Indeed, your Lodge can far better afford
to expend the sum of $200.00 for a jewel than could some of

question not of the amount of money, but of the purpose for
which it is to be expended. Your resolution is based on the
assumed existence of a "social fund." It is true that that term
is frequently used with reference to the money authorized to
be expended for social purposes No such fund, however, is
authorized by our law.
"The Lodge may expend in each Masonic year twenty per
cent of its total revenue for the preceding year for purpose
of refreshment and the promotion of fraternal intercourse."
The amount which may be expended during any one year
is not, however, increased by reason of the fact that during
the preceding year less than twenty per cent of the revenue
was expended. In other words, the difference between the
amount actually expended and the amount which might have
been expended is not carried over to the succe.:ding year and
made available during that year; and no fund is created.
You will, of course, note that the authorized expenditure
is for purposes of refreshment and the promotion of fraternal
intercourse; i. e., for the benefit of the members of the . Lodge.
It is not contemp'.ated that . the money, or any part of it, shall
be expended for the benefit of any individual, either in the
purchase of a Past Master's jewel or for a life membership.
* * * From what I have written you will, of course
understand that the provision for the purchase of a life mem~
bership should be eliminated from your resolution.

fees paid by him must be returned (Cons. 108b). T his would
indicate that it is not the e'. ection to membership which warrants a Lodge in retaining the fees.
If, however, the candidate refuses to p~ocee d fu rther he

to retain it. The alternative is to return it to the one from
whom it was received, or, in the event of his death, to his
personal representative.
There would be, of course, no difference between an elected
candidate dying before receiving his first degree and one who
had died after receiving his first and before the second, or
after receiving the second and before the third-except with
regard to the $20.00 contribution fo r the benefit of the Homes.
That amount is payable on all initiates. The moment a candidate is initiated the Lodge becomes liable to Grand Lodge for
the payment of that amount ; and even though it is retained
by the subordinate Lodge until with its other contributions it
is paid to Grand Lodge, it remains the property of Grand
Lodge, and the subordinate Lodge has no control over it.
The Lodge would be, therefore, unautkoriied to include that
amount with the fee it might elect to return.

Dispensations
With few exceptions the requests for dispensati_o ns which have
been made were either to reballot upon rejected petitioners, or to
receive petitions from those _w ho are without the prescribed qualification of residence.
There is apparently a growing practice upon the part of Lodges
to make requests for · dispensation to reballot upon rejected petitions where the facts do not justify such a procedure. Indeed,
there is an apparent misconception of the entire subject of dispensations and of the purpose of the law authorizing the issuance
thereof.
I am of the opinion that the power vested in the Grand Master
to issue dispensations is to be exercised only on extraordinary
occasions. I therefore adopted the policy of not issuing any dispensation without being fully advised of all the facts and circumstances prompting the request. In other words, I was not disposed
to issue a dispensation to reballot merely because a request therefor was made, or to issue a dispensation waiving the qualification
of residence merely because the petitioner is in the army or navy.
To Reballot-With reference to requests for · dispensations to
reballot I concur unreservedly in the views expressed by Past
Grand Master Bledsoe in his report thereon to Grand Lodge. It is
unfortunately true that it occasionally happens that a petitioner for
the degrees is rejected by a member actuated by unworthy motives.
It is, however, assumed of course that no Mason will deposit a
cube without reasons which to him at least appear to be good and
sufficient. He is not required, nor even permitted, to disclose the
reasons nor even the fact that he did deposit a cube. Neither is it
permissible to make any effort to ascertain who is responsible
for the rejection of a petitioner.
·
Requests for dispensations to reballot are nevertheless fre.quently made upon the ground that some particular individual has
voted to reject a petitioner who should have been elected; and
that the brother who deposited the cube was not . justified in so
doing. I have been in all instances careful to explain that the
mere fact that it was generally believed that the petitioner should
have been elected,· and that the Lodge subsequently by unanimous
vote requested a dispensation, would ·not of itself in my judgment
warrant the issuance thereof. It might well happen that the member who deposited the cube was not present at the meeting at
which the unanimous request for a dispensation was made; and

committee in making that strict examination into the qualifications
of the petitioner which is required by our law. Even where the
petitioner has resided for years in the community, it is frequently
difficult to find those who have had a real opportunity to form an
opinion as to his character. I believe it would be practically impossible to do this in the majority of instances in which requests
for dispensation have been made.
It will be, of course, understood that I am not intimating for
a moment that there was a single one of these petitioners against
whose character the slightest possible objection could have been
made. Indeed, I am not unmindful of the fact that the course I
have pursued may have had the result of keeping out of the fraternity many splendid men who would have reflected credit upon
it. I am, however,"one of those who believe that it is better that
we be denied the fellowship of one hundred men who are worthy
and well qualified than that a single one who is not be admitted
to our number.
It is also to be remembered that our law authorizing the Grand
Master to dispense with the prescribed qualification of residence
in the case of petitioners in the army or navy is a departure from
the principle upon which is based our claim of jurisdiction; and
that there are Grand Lodges which do not look with favor upon
our law as to jurisdiction, believing that it is a violation of that
comity which should exist among the several jurisdictions.
Our theory of jurisdiction is that one who has come from
another St;te and has resided here for one year with a bona fide
intention of remaining, .l oses the residence formerly held by him
and acquires one in this State. We, however, recognize the principle that a person shall not be deemed to have gained or lost a
residence by reason of his presence or absence while employed •
in the service of the United States. It would thus appear that in
receiving the pe.tition of one who is not a resident of California,
we invade the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge or' the State in
which the petitioner resided at the time of his enlistment.
In some instanc.es I have refused a dispensation where the
facts might have warranted its issuance. I did this in the exercise
of the discretion vested in me, because I believed it to be for the
best interests of the fraternity, and for this reason: It had become

Of course it would be desirable to establish a rule defining
the conditions under which the Grand Master would as a matter
of course issue a dispensation to receive a petition from one who
was without the necessary qualification of residence. That, however, is impossible. If any rule could be established it would be
incorporated in the Constitution. It is because this is not possible
that the matter has been left to the discretion of the Grand Master.
The rule is that no Lodge shall receive a petition for the degrees of Masonry unless the applicant shall have been a resident
of this jurisdiction for the statutory time. There is, however, one
exception to this rule. The petition of a person belonging to the
army or navy who has not the qualification of residence may be
received if the Grand Master will dispense with that requirement.
It is only in the case of one in the army or navy that the qualification of residence may be dispensed with; but it does not follow
that it will be, merely because· a request is made; otherwise it
would be an idle act to require the Lodge to make the request.
I am not at all certain that it would not be advisable either
to dispense entirely with the qualification of residence in the case
of one in the army or navy, or to repeal the provision under which
his petition may be now received by a dispensation from the Grand
Master. I make no recommendation with reference thereto; but
suggest that this matter receive the earnest consideration of Grand
Lodge.

To Transact Business-A request was made by Selma Lodge

This would clearly contemplate that the Grand Master is
authorized to issue such a dispensation-not by virtue of any
inherent rights by him possessed, but by virtue of the authority
in him vested by Section 43 to exercise all the executive powers
of Grand Lodge during the interval between its Communications.
Indeed I think it may· be fairly inferred from the whole
scheme of our legislation that its real purpose was not to. restrict
the power of the Grand Master, but to have it clearly appear that
he exercised that power not by virtue of any inherent right as
Grand Master, but by authority specifically ·vested in him by
Grand Lodge.
Charges Preferred at Direction of Grand Master
Entertaining the opinion I do that Grand Lodges in many of
our American jurisdictions have unduly interfered with the autonomy of their subordinate Lodges, I have not been inclined to
exercise the authority vested in the Grand Master, except where
I believed that the act or omission of any particular Lodge would
affect the entire craft in tliis jurisdiction-or result in irreparable
injury to the Lodge itself.
In three instances, I directed that charges of un-Masonic
conduct be preferred in Lodges in which it appeared that no
cognizance was to be taken of offenses which had come to my
knowledge.
One was a case in which complaint had been made through
the Grand· Secretary that one of our Lodges had elected a petitioner who had been rejected by a Lodge in Pennsylvania. It
appeared that the petitioner had concealed the fa~t that he had
been rejected in Pennsylvania, and had falsely stated that he had
never been rejected by a Masonic Lodge. The Grand Master of
Pennsylvania was advised that while we do not concede the claim
of that State to perpetual jurisdiction over rejected candidates who
subsequently acquire a bona fide residence in this State for the
statutory period, we will not countenance the election to membership in any of our Lodges of a petitioner who conceals material
facts which he is required to disclose, or who falsely answers the
questions propounded to him; and that we would deal with this
case on that basis alone.
In addition to the fact that the petitioner had returned false
answers to the questions asked, it was charged that his character
was such as would debar him from admissiort to any regular Lodge
in Pennsylvania; and specific instances of his transgressions were
called to my attention.
The Master of the Lodge having been advised of the facts
before the matter was called to my attention, and no action having

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

31

been taken, I directed that charges be preferred against the mem.t>er referred to for un-Masonic conduct. I explained t o the Master
that because of the fact that we do not recognize the claim of
perpetual jurisdiction over rejected candidates, we are especially
careful in the investigation we make in such cases, and that I had
no doubt that if the petitioner had djsclosed t he fact that he had
been previously rejected, the efforts which would have been made
to ascertain if there were good reasons for such action would have
resulted in an unfavorable report from the investigating committee.
I further explained t hat I exceedingly regretted the necessity
for the action I felt compelled to take in this case; that I was in
wtire and absolute accord with him in his belief that the man
who by living a straight life makes an earnest effort to retrieve
an early indiscretion should receive encouragement; and that we
should not be too prone to refuse forgiveness even for an offense
which could not be extenuated; but that to condone this offense
would not only justify the claim which Pennsylvania makes for
perpetual jurisdiction over rejected candidates, but would convey
the false impression to Masons in that State that we are le!s
careful in the selection of our material than are tltey.
I had hoped to be able in this message to report the result of
that trial; but I have been precluded from so doing because of
what I want to believe was an excusable delay in carrying out
my instructions. Charges we re, however, finally preferred by the
Junior Warden at the direction of the Master; and the case was
by me transferred to another Lodge for trial.
Assuming the facts to be as herein set forth, the member
refe rred to will be expelled from the rights and privileges of
Masonry, not because he had been rejected by a Lodge in Pennsylvania before he acquired a bona fide residence in this State,
but because he has been guilty of un-Masonic conduct in failing
to disclose the fact of his rejection.

In the third case in which charges were preferred at my
direction, the accused had been tried in the Superior Court on a
criminal charge and acquitted-but under such circumstances as
gave rise to a very general belief in the community that there had
been a gross miscarriage of justice.
Certain happenings in connection with that trial and the subsequent comment thereon rendered it imperative, in my judgment,
that such action should be taken by the fraternity as would
emphasize the fact that there is nothing in the Masonic relation
that requires any brother to aid and assist another to escape the
consequences of a criminal act, or that even justifies him in so
doing; and that any suspicion to the contrary is without any
foundation.
In this, as in the other cases, the charges were preferred by
the Junior Warden at the direction of the Master and were by my
order transferred to another Lodge for trial. The accused was
convicted; and the punishment fixed at expulsion.

Our Foreign Language Lodges
It will be remembered that at our communication last year
my predecessor, Grand Master Webster, recommended that either
Acacia Lodge be permitted to revive the use of the German language or that we should require all our Lodges to adopt and use
the English language in their work.
On the recommendation of the Committee on Jurisprudence
no action was taken on the recommendation made by the Grand
Master. The result, therefore, was that for the time being Acacia
Lodge was required to continue the use of the English language
while Hermann Lodge was permitted to use German, Speranza
Italiana, Italian, and Vallee de France and La Parfaite Union,
French.
The recommenadtion of the Committee on Jurisprudence was
due to the existence of certain conditions in Acacia Lodge to
which it is unnecessary to here particularly refer, and was influenced to a great extent by the opinion of Brother Fischer, the
Inspector of Acacia Lodge. Since that time Brother Fischer has
become convinced that there has been a material change in the
condition which then prevailed and that the circumstances warrant
a reconsideration of the action taken last year. I was by him
informed that Acacia Lodge would be very grateful for an opportunity to again present its petition to Grand Lodge for permission
to revive the use of the German language, but was disinclined to
do so without a recommendation from the Grand Master that the
petition be granted.

34

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The situation was somewhat embarrassing. With the change
in the conditions which influenced the action of Grand Lodge at
its communication in 1919, there would appear to be no good reason
why Acacia Lodge should not be permitted to work in the German
language if the continued use of foreign languages was to be permitted in this jurisdiction. If there was no valid reason why a
Lodge should not be permitted to work in a foreign language, it
would seem to follow as a matter of simple justice that no discrimination should be made against any particular Lodge; and
while Grand Lodge had very properly refused to allow itself to
be "dragooned". into taking the action a few recalcitrant members
of Acacia Lodge desired, it now appeared that there was a practically unanimous desire on the part of the members of Acacia
Lodge to be permitted to work in the German language. There
was now no sign of discord in that Lodge and the utmost harmony
prevailed-the only discouraging feature being the particularly
small attendance due . to the fact that the work is being carried
on in a language with which the great majority of the members
are unfamiliar.
I was, however, disinclined to recommend that the petition
of Acacia Lodge be granted, because I then entertained the belief
that Grand Master Webster was absolutely correct when he stated
that the necessity for foreign-speaking languages had gone by, if
it ever existed.
While I have never been o~ the opinion that it would be
advisable to ~ompel the foreign language speaking Lodges to work
in English, it had been my hope that they might be persuaded to
do this. With this idea in mind l at various times conferred with
the representatives of Speranza Italiana and La Parfaite Union,
with whom the question might be discussed without the interjection
of any matters which were not essential to the principle involved.
In every instance the question was discussed fairly and dispassionately; and it is pleasing to be able to report that while it was
evident from the arguments they urged that they were not convinced of the wisdom of my judgment, there was apparent a
willingness to respect the opinion of the Grand Master. As an
evidence of this I was assured by the Master of Speranza Italiana
Lodge that an effort would be made to confer at least one degree
in English before the expiration of my term of office; and it was
with extreme pleasure that upon the occasion o f my official visit
to that Lodge I witnessed the third degree conferred in E nglish.
At the banquet which followed the meeting I expressed the views
I entertained, and this gave rise to a very interesting discussion
which I purposely encouraged. A doubt as to the correctness of
my views was there raised in my mind- not alone by what was

35

said, but by the evidence of a spirit among these Masons of
foreign birth which needed no language for interpretation. What
had been theretofore to me a cold, concrete, academic question
took on a new aspect.
This doubt. was strengthened and confirmed on the occasion
of m y visit to Hermann Lodge where, bot h in the Lodge room
a?d at the banquet table, at my specific request the question was
discussed. From what was. there said, as well as from what I had
heard at Speranza I taliana (and this was likewise the unanimous
opinion of the brethren expressed on my visit to La Parfaite
Union) I became convinced that even a change to the English
language would not (as I had supposed) result in making these
Lodges a ttractive to the native born of foreign parentage. The
me~bership in these Lodges is recruited almost entirely fro.m the
foreign born; and they are no t visited to any great extent by even
those of the native born who are thoroughly familiar with the
language in which the work is conducted,
.
Now I am one of those people who believe that most of our
troubles arise from trying to make ourselves believe tha t our mistakes were right. Therefore instead of endeavoring ·to find arguments io res?lve the doubts which had arisen in my mind, my
efforts w~re directed toward a n endeavor to ascertain if the opinion
I entertained was nqt really the result of a confusion of thought.
I have long entertained the belief that with the retenti~n by
gro.ups. of foreign born citizens of the language of the country of

of our own. I believed that. it would be not only to the benefit of

birth, because it would tend to Americanize them. For the same
reason I have advocated· the exclusive use of the English language
as a medium o~ instruction in our elementary schools; and I have
even deprecated the prevalence of foreign language newspapers.
Entertaining these views, my desire to have all our Lodg es

consideration the peculiar conditions which differentiate a Masonic

qualified Gf our foreign born citizens are to be imbued with the

On mature reflection I became convinced that insofar at least
as Masonic Lodges are concerned, adherence to the ideas I had

Relief for Austrian Masons
It is our proud boast in California that no Mason in distress
ever appeals to us in vain. There came to us an appeal for food
from what purported to be the recently organized Grand Lodge
of Vienna. Theoretically we are still at war with Austria and
these are an enemy people; but if they were Masons in distress
we had a duty to perform.
I was not ignorant of the condition described. From the' letters of a personal friend engaged with Hoover in the work of the ·
American Relief Association I had learned something of the pitiable plight into which these people in Central Europe had been
plunged by their misguided rulers. .I knew that women and
children were suffering for the necessities of life; that not only
was there no fresh milk for the little ones, but that canned milk
was a rarity; that butter was unknown and lard was a luxury;
and that their meat supply was so limited as to be practically un-

37

attainable except by those who could afford to eat at high price
hotels and restaurants.
I had been informed that the general suffering was weighing
most heavily on that great middle class which, having had the
least to do with; the causes which led to the war, had made the
greatest sacdfices for it. I surmised that it was from this class
that there, as everywhere, the fraternity in great part had been
recruited; and that among those bearing the greatest privations
were M_asons who, .perhaps tc;>o proud to accept public charity
unless literally starving, would gratefully receive aid extended by
their American brethren.
·
·

Although the dictates of humanity, no less than the tenets of
our profession, would warrant our relieving the distress of a
starving people, yet it was from the funds of the fraternity that
I purposed making the necessary expenditure. I therefore
requested the Grand Secretary to ascertain if there was indeed a
Grand Lodge in Vienna; and if those from whom the appeal had
come were its constituted officers. As a result of the investigation
~e made we learned that the Grand Lodge of Vienna was organtz~d on December 8th, 1918, and at that time (July) had 14 Lodges
with about 1100 members; and that Dr. Richard Schlesinger from
whom the appeal had come, was the Grand Master.
'

Wi~h this assurance I directed the Grand Secretary to expend
$500.00 in _the pur~hase of food drafts which would be honored by
th~ Amencan Relief Association in Vienna on presentation. For
this amount we were ab!e to provide for the distribution of 1400
pounds of flour, 500 pounds of beans, 160 pounds of bacon, J 50
pounds of lard, 120 pounds of corned beef and 480 cans of milk.
On August 26th, 1920, the following letter was received from
Dr. Richard Schles~nger as Grand Master, under the seal of the
Grand Lodge of Vienna:
"We were most agreeably surprised to receive today
from your hand a Food ·Draft for ten packages Lit B

"Poli ticks"
As is of course known to most of the brethren in Grand
Lodge, I have long been of the opinion, which I have not hesitated
to publicly express, that Masonry as an Institution would not
continue to justify the esteem in wh ich it is held unless the craft
were a~~kened ·to a realization of t he duties which devolve upon
us as c1t1zens.
It is just ten years ago today when in Grand Lodge I proclaimed the belief that there is no higher duty devolving upon
us as Masons than the duty we owe the Stllte as citizens; and

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

qne of the highest duties devolving upon an American citizen is
that which requires him to concern himself with, and take a part
in politics-not politics in that sense of artful 0 r dishonest efforts
to secure the success of party schemes, or even that less objectionable but still restricted sense of the management of a political
party or the advancement of the interest of any particular candidate for public office, but politics in that broader and larger sense
in which it is defined as a branch of ethics-that which concerns
the regulation of a Nation, State or Community and the preservation of its safety, peace and prosperity.
Of ·course it was never my purpose to make Masonry a
political organization in any sense of the word; and nothing is
further from my desire; but it has alway51 seemed to me that as
Masons we might with perfect propriety concern ourselves in our
Lodges with those great public questions which so vitally affect
us as c1t1zens-even though we are as firmly resolved as were
the Fathers' "against all 'politicks' as what never yet conduced
to the welfare of the Lodge, nor ever will." Indeed I believe that
this is not merely our privilege but our duty; and that it is likewise our duty as Masons to assist in the formation and crystallization o.f that enlightened public opinion upon which depend the
strength .and perpetuity of a democracy.
This, however, it is to be remembered, does not contemplate
an organized "Masonic vote" in support of, or in opposition to,
any public measure-or (much less) any individual candidate,
Mason or non-Mason. "Masonry does not vote nor command
votes." All that is contemplated is that an honest attempt shall
be made to solve the problem presented by the question at issue;
that it shall be fairly and frankly discussed; the proofs presented
and the arguments analyzed; but the individual Mason is to be
left free to follow the dictates of his own conscience and to consider his own political preference. Above all, it does not carry
with it' even the suggestion that because a man is a Mason he is
expected to vote for or against any particular candidate. What
may be called "the new program" stresses the importance of the
duty_of a Mason as a citizen; and good citizenship precludes the
consideration of a candidate for public office except with reference
to his indivit:!ual worth and his fitness for the office to. which he
aspires.
ln emphasizing these views I have repeatedly s·aid publicly
as well as privately (and I mention this as illustrative of my purpose and desire in my persistent advocacy of the depar.ture of 'the
craft from its traditional policy) that I will not vote for any man
merely because he is a Mason, nor against another . because he is
not. Indeed, paradoxical as it may seem, I believe it is un-Masonic ·

to do so-un-Masonic not only because it is un-American, · but
because it is in contravention of the principles upon which our
Institution is based.
I subscribe unqualifiedly to the views expressed by Brother
Theodore Roosevelt, for whom there were but two classes of
citizens--good citizens and bad citizens; and I will not exclu de
any man from the first, nor include him in the last, either on
account cif his fraternal relations or because of his race ot creed.
Other things being equal, and only then, I will give the preference
to a Mason-not because he and I happen to belong to the same
fraternal organization, but with the hope that he has become
imbued with the spirit of Masonry which incites us to greater
fidelity in the discharge of every duty.
From one point. of view it was perhaps unfortunate that the
program emphasizing the potentialities of Masonry in the relation
of the individual to the State was launched in the year in which
elections will be held. There would have been less likelihood of
a mistake being made if there had been time to have the craft
become thoroughly imbued with the purpose of the movement
before the temptation was presented to seize upon it as an opportunity to further the political ambitions of certain individuals.
A few mistakes have been made. That was natural if not inevitable. I have never been oblivious to the fact that there is a
certain hazard attendant upon our undertaking. It is, however,
to be remembered that if there was no danger in the "traditional
policy of the craft" it was only because it was in itself innocuous
and inutile insofar as its direct influence on the nation was concerned. Of course no mistake would be made where nothing was
attempted to be done. So long as the time of our Lodges was
devoted exclusively to the conferring of degrees and the elucidation of the symbolism which illustrates a "system of morality
veiled in allegory" we were absolutely safe-if not sane.
Conscious, howeve.r, as I was of the danger of mist;kes being
made, I felt that we might confidently rely upon the discretion
and good judgment of those to whom was entrusted the administration of the affairs of our Lodges; and it is pleasing and gratifying to be able to report that this confidence was not misplaced.
There have been called to iny attention only two instances in
which the Master of a Lodge has failed to· observe the distinction
sought to be impressed upon the craft between the discussion of
public questions and "doing politics" in the ordinary acceptation
of that term.
In one there was a notice in the Lodge Bulletin headed
"Masonic Judiciary" in which certain members of the craft were
commended to 'the brethren for their suffrages.

The other was a notice in a Lodge Bulletin calling attention

on election day.
In each instance I wrote the Master of the Lodge calling his
attention to the impropriety of using the Lodge Bulletin for such
a purpose. I likewise reminded him that while an individual is
of course free to support any candidate for whatever reasons may
seem to him good and sufficient, it is not the . duty of a Mason
to support a candidate for the office of Judge of the Superior
Court merely because he is a member of the craft; and that an
intimation to the contrary from the Master of a Lodge to his
members was not only unwarranted, but was a violation of the
fundamentals of good citizenship and would subject us to deserved
criticism.
These, as I have said, were the only instances called to my
attention in which there occurred in any Lodge anything which
might be subject to criticism. There was, however, another matter in which I felt called upon to take a decided s.tand. I received

was Masonry to be made a political organization,· and that the
moment it was so regarded, its power would vanish.

head I purpo,,e speaking further concerning this; and I here refer
to only one aspect of the situation.
Craft Masonry has not provided in the Lodge that which
many of our brethren desire. They therefore seek it not only in
the so-called "higher degrees" but in organizations composed
exclusively of Master Masons where their good intentions may be
possibly misdirected.
·
I have no great fear of mistakes that may be made in a
Lodge, however "advanced" may be its program; because it is
always subject to the direction and control of constituted Masonic
authority. When, however, Masons organize outside the Lodge,
a different situation is presented;. and there is today ~on­
fronting us a condition which I believe is fraught with danget to
the fraternity and with which it will be difficult to deal.
·
There are certain organizations which, although composed
exclusively of Masons, are not under the direct control of
Grand Lodge. Nevertheless, because no one who is not a regular
Mason is eligible to membership therein, they are known as
"Masonic" organizations; and for their actions our fraternity is
by the public held amenable. Some of the activities in which
they are engaged are extremely commendable in their nature;
and they foster a fellowship which is to be greatly desired, provided that it be not misused. Not infrequently, however, their"
actions are such as should not be countenanced in any Masonic
organization.
While, as I bave said, these organizations as such are not
subject to the control or supervision of the Grand Master, or
even of Grand Lodge, membership in them does not relieve the
individual from the obedience he as a Mason owes to the supreme
Masonic power and authority in this State. It has therefore
seemed to me entirely proper to call the attention of Grand
Lodge to a matter concerning which complaint was made to me.

"OUR D UTY TO OUR OWN MEMBERS · IS TO
SUPPORT THEM LOYALLY AND ENTHUSIASTICALLY."
A pecu:iarly illuminating postscript announced that " The expen.se of
sending out this announcement was paid by friends of the candidates
without any cost to Jinistan Grotto."
It will be of course understood that my reference to the
matter is without regard . to the particular individuals for whom
the support of the members of Jinistan Grotto was sought.
Indeed, it happens that some of them are my personal friends;
and were I a voter in Los Angeles I would esteem it a privilege
to be able to vote for them. My objection is without regard to
the individuality of the candidates and is two-fold in its nature.
In the first place the issuance of such a circular, paid for by
friends of the candidates, is a prostitution of the principles of
Masonry. It is reducing what purports to be a Masonic organization to the level of a '. 'piece club." It is directly engaging
· in "politics" a s that term is generally understood, and will be
certain to invite disaster. Indeed, it has already brought discord
into the organization itself as well as into the ranks of Mason ry
in general in the city · of Los Angeles.
It is open not only to the objection to which I have hereinbefore referred in considering the notices in the Lodge Bulletins,
insofar as there is an intimation that it is the duty of Masons
to su.pport their brethren for public office, but also to the further
objection that the members of Jinistan Grotto are advised that
their dwty to their own members requires their political support.
Here lies the vice of qrganizations of this sort. Superimposed
upon their obligations as Masons is apparently a superior duty
to give preference to those of their own number even as against
other Masons no less worthy of the support of all good citizens,
including those who happen· to be members of this particular
organization.
I can not but believe that this is subversive of the basic
principles of our Institution; and I have deemed it my duty to
call the matter to the attention of Grand Lodge, not with the idea
that any definite action shall be taken, but with the hope that there
will be such a plain expression of views as will define the policy
of Grand Lodge.

Grand Lodge. Indeed their aims, purposes and activities are

not only to all Masons but to all undergraduates who are the
sons or daughters of Masons. This feature alone should make a
very strong appeal to all Masons, and particularly to those who
have sons or daughters who are now at the University or who
expect to enter in the future. There will be here an influence
of a sort too often needed by young men and women at college,
and particularly during their freshman year. There is now a.
sorority at the University composed of women who are members of the Eastern Star; and with the co-operation which will
be received from that sorority and Acacia Fraternity, the University Masonic Club could be made a great factor for good in
the stll.dent life.
At our Communication in 1914 Grand Lodge adopted a resolution approving the desire of the Chapters of Acacia Fraternity
at the University of California and Stanford University to erect
Homes and commending the project. Kind words, however, will
not buy building material nor pay ·carpenters. That resolution,
it is true, was with reference to the Acacia Fraternity and not
to such a project as that to which I now refer, the benefits of
w~ich will not be confined to members of Acacia Fraternity, but
will embrace all Masons at college and also students who are
the sons or daughters of Masons. It would seem that in the
furtherance of so commendable a project Grand Lodge might
well make a contribution to the fund which is now being raised
to provide the urgently needed clubhouse.
Committee on Masonic Education
The report which will be presented by this Committee will
fully advise Grand Lodge of what has been done. Generally speakini", I may say that the results have exceeded our most sanguine
expectations; and I avail myself of this opportunity to warmly
commend Bro. Irving J. Mitchell and his associates on the Committee, and to express to them my personal appreciation of their
efforts and my 1gratitude for the endeavors they have made to
successfully carry out the ideas I have so long entertained and
which constitute the dominant note of my administration. The
work this year was in its nature an experiment; and it has become
apparent that to achieve complete success there must be a change
in, or perhaps I would better say an extension of, the plan of
organization.

At the Communication last year Grand Lodge authorized the

Malcolm Mcintyre and Wallace R. Farrington. In passing, and
as illustrative of the personnel of the men who are willing ·to give
their time to forward this movement, I may s~y that one of the
brothers named is the President of the Chamber of Commerce,
another is the Manager of a large Life Insurance Company, and
.the third is the publisher of the Honolulu Bulletin. Grand Lodge
is already advised of the appointments originally made to the four
Local Units. I appointed Brother Andrew L Johnston in place
of Brother John Clute, who resigned to accept an appointment as
Inspector; and I have recently appointed William V. Cowan as
Chairman of the Northern California Unit, vice J. Fontaine Johnson, resigned. The Fresno Unit is at present without a Chairman.
The work of the San Francisco and Los Angeles Units has
been particularly efficient and too much credit can not be given
them. · The Fraternity is also greatly indebted to those brethren
who responded to the requests for· speakers and who thus contributed to the success of what was .the distinctive feature of our
work this year.
At the suggestio·n· of Brother Mitchell, Officers' Associations
~ave been formed in all the larger cities and towns and in many
of the Districts. It was our hope that every district in the Jurisdiction would either organize an Officers' Association or arrange
for at least one district meeting each month at which all the Lodges
would be represented, and at which some public question would
be discussed; but in this we have been disappointed. In some districts the f~ilure has been due to conditions which it will be difficult to overcome;-the Lodges are small and widely separated
and th~ roads are poor. In other districts, however, where nothing has been · done, it was not because of unpreventable conditions
--<>r on account of a lack of desire on the part of the brethren;
but it was due solely and simply to an absence of the proper initiative. This indicates the necessity for an extension of the plan
formulated last year.
The Local Units should be, .of course, retained; but the CommiHee should have a representative in every district. This could
be accomplished by providing for District Deputy Grand Masters
as is elsewhere herein suggested. Of course the most efficacious
way of carrying on the work would be to place it under the supervision and direction of some competent person who would be able

to devote a considerable portion of his time to it, and who would
be able to visit those districts where his presence was evidently
needed.
Indeed, if the right man could be found, it might be advisable
to have him devote his entire time to the work-or at least so
much thereof as might be necessary. He could be made Chairman of the Committee on Masonic Education and would of course
receive his expenses and such compensation as might be agreed
upon. The Committee will no doubt in its report make some suggestions and I therefore make no recommendation with reference
to the matter.

A report by that Committee will be presented at t his communication, wherein will be set forth in detail the plans of the
Masonic Service Association with, I assume, a recommendation
of the action to be taken · by Grand Lodge. It will be therefore
unnecessary for me to here refer in detail t o the plans, or to the"
organization through which it is proposed to carry t hem out.
While it is not my purpose to anticipate the reco mmendation
to be made by the Committee on General Policy and Purposes,
nor my desire to attempt to influence the action to be taken
by Grand Lodge, I do not deem it improper to state the opinion
at which I have arrived as a result of some little attention and
consideration I have given the quest ion.
Early in the year I obtained a transcript of the· stenographic
report of the proceedings of the first triennial meeting of the
Association, held on November 11th, 12th and 13th at Cedar
Rapids, which I have carefully examined (and which has been
transmitted to the. Committee · on General Policy and Purposes).
I have also had some correspondence with Brother Schoonover,
the Chairman of the Executive Commission; and have likewise
had an opportunity to personally discuss the matter with him
and also with Brother Randell and Brother Wherry, who are
members of the Executive Commission. I have also had some

correspondence with certain Grand Masters of other jurisdictions.
On being advised that Brother Schoonover desired to hold
a meeting in San Francisco for the purpose of conferring with
the Grand Master and with the representatives of the jurisdictions comprising the South Pacific Division of the Association,
I arranged for a luncheon at which the attendance was requested of all our Past Grand Masters, the elective officers of
Grand Lodge and the Chairmen of the various Committees,
together with all the members of the Committee on Masonic
Education. The luncheon was held on August 7th; and in addition to Brothers Schoonover, Randell and Wherry and a very
creditable representation from our own jurisdiction, there were
present, among others, Grand Master Cattron of Utah, Grand
Master Atkinson of Nevada and Past Grand Master Fredricks
of Arizona. After addresses made by Brothers Schoonover, Randell and Wherry, there was a general discussion of the entire
question.
It was a very delightful occasion, and there was no one
present who apparently did not appreciate the opportunity offered
to personally meet these brethren of national prominence from
other jurisdictions who are so zealously and unselfishly devoting
their time and talents to the fraternity, actuated by no other
desire than to be of service to their fellow man. Candor, however, compels the statement that nothing that was developed
there, or in the private conversations I had with the brethren
referred to, converted me to the opinion they entertain, o r mate'rially influenced the views with which I had been theretofore
imbued as a result of the study I had given the subject. Those
views I may say are not influenced to any great extent by what
appears to be the primary objection generally made by those
jurisdictions which have either refused to become members of,
or which have withdrawn from membership in, the Association:

My disinclination to encourage such an o rganization is due
solely to my belief that it is thoroughly impracticable. I do
not mean by this merely that the pfan proposed is impracticable;
because the plan of course is subject to change and amendment.
I mean that it will be impracticable, if not indeed impossible,
to effectuate the purp-oses desired through any national organization. I have in mind now the only activity· of the Masonic
Service Association which (with one exception, to which I shall
refer under the head of " Recognition") particularly appeals to
me-the educational program ; because I am thoroughly satisfied that the Grand Lodge of California would never consent to
the adoption of any plan whereby its relief to another jurisdiction, in the event of a great disaster, would be made to depend
upon a survey and report of any commission of representatives
of any other Grand body. We will, I feel certain, be content to
rely upon the assurance of the Grand Master of t he particular
jurisdiction in which the disaster occurs that th~ condition warrants the acceptance of the relief which we will have offered.
The measure of that relief ·will be only their necessities and our
resources.
The program outlined by the Association for t he education
of the craft is, however, particularly alluring to those of us who
are already engaged here in California along similar lines; but
I believe it can be carried out only by the individual jurisdictions.
Our visitors were kind enough to concede that we had already
progressed far in this direction ; and that we in California were
even now doing what they· propose. In this connection the
suggestion was made that by becoming a member of the Association, the Grand Lodge of California might be of service to
other jurisdictions in helping th em to· do what we have done
even though we ourselves might not believe any great benefi;
would come to us. If there were merit to this suggestion, it
should of course appeal· very strongly to us ; and it w ould furnish
a reason why we should become thus associated with the other
member jurisdictions. I can not, however concur in the belief
which prompts that suggestion. I say ;his with . the utmost
respect for the opinion of the distinguished brother making it,
and on!~ because the statement is prompted by an intimate
knowledge of our own experience.
I believe that such progress as we have made is the result
of efforts which can not be successfully undertaken by a national
organization. Our own experience warrants the belief that no
matter how ambitiou·s may be the program which emanates from
Grand Lodge, nothing will be accomplished unless thete comes
an ·urge therefor from the subordinate L odges.

I am not greatly impressed with the fear expressed that
the sovereig~ty of our Grand Lodges will be imperiled by the
existence of such an or ganization. Indeed, so far as I am
pe'rsonally concerned, I would be erttirely willing to concede
some of 'the attributes of our individual sovereignty if convinced
that · it would redound to the interest of the fraternity as an
Institution, and in a consequent benefit to the nation. Furthermore, I h ave no apprehension that the Masonic Service Association will ever develop into a national Grand Lodge ; because I
believe that some of those who are now its most zealous advocates would be among the first to sever their connection ·with
it if there was ever any likelihood of such a development.

In other words, to speak in business terms, the real problem
is to create the demand and not to supply it; and still· speaking
in the terms of. business, and to use a much hackneyed phrase,
the idea must be "sold" · to the Lodges. It can not be sold
through catalogues or form letters, or even by personal correspondence. We must send salesmen, in the person of speakers
into the territory of each Lodge.
'
If a speaker could be · sent periodically into every Lodge in .
every .iurisdiction the promised land would be in sight. This,
however, we have even here in our own jurisdiction found not
merely impracticable, but virtually impossible, even with four
local units of the Committee on Masonic Education. How much
less likelihood is there then of expecting that what we have
n~t . succeeded in doing, concentrating our effort in one Jurisd1ct10n, can be done by an organization two thousand miles away
from us.

. In the last analysis, whatever is accomplished along these
Imes must be by the individual jurisdictions. It is not therefore
a question of being willi'ng through. membership in the Association to assist another jurisdiction, even though we may not
be benefited ; because what applies to · this jurisdiction applies
to each.
I believe that the most that can be done by a national
organization is to furnish encouragement and support for those
who are working in their own individual jurisdictions. I do not
underestimate the value of this, IlDr am I insensible to the
benefit; but I can not forbear saying that 1· do not believe it is
commensurate with the effort which must be made and the
expense in time and money involved. In business terms again,
the "overhead" of such an organization is too large. Further~o~e, no plan w~ich could be devised by any central organ1zat1on would satisfy 1the requirements of all the jurisdictions.
This was the mistake made by certain national organizations
engaged in war work. Some of us here in California found it
extremely difficult to convince the national organization that a
plan admirable for Connecticut was worthless in California.
I have said nothing concerning the expense inv<>lved in
membership in the Association, because I am certain that that
would not be a material factor in determining our action. If we
entertained the belief held by Brother Schoonover and his associates and by the brethren of those jurisdictions which are members of the Association, I am sure that the fact that it might
cost us four or five thousand dollars annually would not preclude
us from becoming a member of the Association. Twice that

57

amount (}udic1ously expended, of course) might be well devoted
to effect the desired end.
Impressed as I am with the importance of the aims and purposes of the Masonic Service Association, insofar as its educational program is concerned, and because I am in such absolute
and ent_ire consonance with the views which gave rise t o it, it is
with great reluctance that I find myself unable as Grand Master
to recommend that Grand Lodge become a member thereof.
