Sister Jurisdictions
As was of course only right and proper, I have been particularly careful ·to permit nothing to be done that could possibly
imperil the extremely friendly relations which exist with all our
sister jurisdictions.
It has been a great pleasure to comply with such requests
as have been made by Grand Masters of other jurisdictions to
have degrees conferred in our jurisdiction for their Lodges; and
the same courtesy has been extended us whenever requested.
The only definite complaint made against us by a sister
jurisdiction was satisfactorily adjusted.
Nevada-Complaint was made by the Grand Master of Nevada that our Golden State Lodge No. 358 had elected to membership R. W. Robinson, a petitioner claimed to be the material
of Montezuma Lodge No. 30 of Nevada. The matter was brought
to the attention of the latter Lodge by a request made by Golden
State Lodge to confer the Fellow Craft and Master Mason degrees
upon the candidate in question.
I immediately caused an investigation to be made and arrived
at the conclusion that while our Golden State Lodge was without
fault in the matter, there was justification for the claim made
by the Grand Master of Nevada.
At the time Robinson presented his petition to G.o lden State
Lodge he stated he had been a resident of California for over
ten years, but had spent much of his time in other States; that
he had been transferred · by his employer from Los Angeles to
Goldfield, Nevada, and after remaining there about t wo years
had returned to Los Angeles, " this being my home."

61

•

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA
PROCEEDINGS OF '!'HE

It further appeared, however, that at the time his petition
was presented he had actually resided in Los Angeles for only
six months. In taking the matter up with the Grand Master
of Nevada I explained to him that this was one of those embarrassing cases which occasionally arise as a result of our construing the question of residence with reference to "the union
of act and intent." Although I had no doubt that Golden State
Lodge had acted honestly and conscientiously in the matter, I
was compelled to admit that if Robinson while in Goldfield had
petitioned for the degrees in Nevada, claiming that place as his
residence, no one of our Lodges would have just cause for complaint; and that under the circumstances, and particularly in view
.of the fact that Robinson had resided in Los Angeles for
only six months at the time his petition was presented, and that
for more than two years prior thereto he had been continuously
in Nevada, I was disposed to adopt any suggestion he might
make.
Some delay ensued, owing to the fact that the Grand Master
of Nevada had been unable, it appears, to confer with his
brethren of Montezuma Lodge, but I was subsequently advised
of his belief that Montezuma Lodge No. 30 might "rightfully
claim Robinson as their material and also the total amount of
fees as usual." This information was communicated to our Golden
State Lodge, the Master of which had previously informed me
that such a settlement would be entirely satisfactory to his
Lodge; and in acknowledging the receipt of the letter of Grand
Master Parks I 's uggested that further correspondence be between
our respective Lodges, and that the matter be adjusted by them to
their mutual satisfaction.
•
Having had no further word concerning the matter and desiring to know the result thereof to report to Grand Lodg.e, I
communicated with the Master of Golden State Lodge. He replied that he had received no answer to a letter he had written
Montezuma Lodge, and that Robinson had returned to Los Angeles, intending to reside there permanently. I instructed him
that he should nevertheless remit to Montezuma Lodge the total
fee which Montezuma Lodge would have received had Robinson
been elected to membership in that Lodge; and that the candidate should not be given his degrees until the consent of Nevada
had been received.
Illinois-A sense .of propriety necessitates a reference in
this Message to a matter which was presumably closed at our
communication in 1918, the report of which, on page 228 of our
Proceedings of that year, has placed the Grand Lodge of Illinois
in a falje position.

63

The matter came to my knowledge with the receipt by the
Grand Secretary from the Grand Master of Illinois of a check
for $252.20, together with a letter conveying a very plain intimation that an injustice had been done the Grand Lodge of Illinois.
On examining the proceedings I found that the Grand Master
of Illinois was not without some justification for his feelings
in the matter. A fair inference from the statement in our Pro!
ceedings would be that the Grand Lodge of Illinois did not
purpose compelling its Gothic 'Lodge to reimburse our El Centro
Lodge for expenses incurred in the relief of one of its members,
Brother Todd, and had ignored a communication from Brother
Whicher to the Grand Secretary of Illinois.
The facts appear to be substantially as follows: A controversy had arisen between . Gothic Lodge of Illinois and our El
Centro Lodge as to the amount which had been· expended for
the relief of Brother Todd, due to a misapprehension upon the
part of Gothic Lodge. Not being able to obtain reimbursement
from Gothic Lodge, our El Centro Lodge had taken the matter
up with our Grand Secretary. He wrote not to the Grand Secretary of Illinois, but to Grand Master Scro gin. No acknowledgment of the receipt of that letter was made; but it appears that
the matter was taken up by Grand Master Scrogin with Gothic
Lodge; and an investigation was being made while our Grand
Lodge was in session. The matter was referred by the Grand
Master to Deputy Grand Master Fitzgerrell, now Grand Master,
who thereafter referred it back to the Grand Master because he
believed it necessary for the correspondence to come through
his office. Shortly thereafter Brother Scrogin died, and in cleaning up the papers which had come to him from his predecessor,
Grand Master Fitzgerrell found this, with other matters. He
immediately communicated with with the Master of Gothic Lodge
to ascertain if the case had ever been adjusted. Learning it
had not, he gave the matter his attention, and after "a long and
extended investigation of this case" advised Gothic Lodge to pay
the bill. This was done and the result thereof was the sending
of the check first referred to.
When the check was received I was out of the city; and
Brother Whicher, because of the circumstances under which it
had been sent, in acknowledging the receipt of the check suggested that with the consent of the · Grand Master it would be
returned. I was, however, unable to concur with that suggestion
because as I stated in my letter to Grand Master Fitzgerrell I did
not believe that the Grand Lodge of Illinois would be willing
to accept it except upon the theory which would preclude me
from offering it-and th;1t was that the claim of El Centro Lodge.

64

GRAND LODGE OF °CALIFORNIA

was not a just one; and that I did not believe that the Grand Lodge
of Illinois would permit the Grand Lodge of California, however
willing it might be to do so, to bear a burden which should be
assumed by Gothic Lodge.
In my letter I expressed my very great regret . that any
warrant · was even inadvertently given for the idea that the Grand
Lodge of California ever believed that the Grand Lodge of Illinois
was derelict in any of its duties or delinquent in any of its obligations; and I explained that I personally knew the converse to ·
be true, because as one of the Trustees for many years of the
Masonic Board of Relief of San Francisco I had personal knowledge of the fact that there was no jurisdiction in the United States
more willing and ready than Illinois to comply in spirit as well
as in letter with its obligations.
It is also proper to say in justice to Gothic Lodge that the
entire correspondence not only with our El Centro Lodge but as
well between that Lodge and the Grand Master of Illinois· (with
which I was furnished) makes it evident that the position that
Lodge took was due to a misapprehension of the facts. On
the othet hand, El Centro Lodge had just cause for complaint and
for its suspicions in the matter, because of certain criticisms
made of its actions by Gothic Lodge, to which I ·called the attention of Grand Master Fitzgerrell.
It happened that I had just returned from a visit to the
Imperial Valley; and speaking of the brethren of El Centro Lodge
whom I had had the pleasure of meeting, I was able to assure
the Grand Master of Illinois that nowhere are there to be found
better men, or Masons more thoroughly imbued with the teachings of our fraternity and more ready and willing to discharge
the duties and responsibilities ·devolving upon them.
I had a splendid letter from Grand Master Fitzgerrell in
reply to my letter to him, in which, among other things, h.e
stated that in the letter written me he had no intention of criticizing our El Centro Lodge, but, borrowing an expression I had
used, he was rather writing in defense of his own brethren than for
the purpose of ~riticizing our El Centro l.odge.
I make this extended explanation not merely to justify the
Grand Lodge of Illinois to the Grand Lodge of California, but
as well that other jurisdictions to which knowledge of this matter
may co.me, may understan'd that not only does Illinois not permit any of its Lodges to evade payment of any of its obligations,
but that California understands this to be the fact.

While I am convinced of the good faith of Brother Forbes, you
will observe that I do not attempt to justify his action; and had he
been brought to trial and disciplined upon charges preferred against
him while he was resident in your jurisdiction I would have feh
constrained to take cognizance of the verdict and judgment.
The Grand Lodge of California claims penal jurisdiction over all
Masons residing in our territory; and we of course concede the
corresponding right to any Grand Lodge which we recognize as regular
to discipline any of our members residing in its jurisdiction. It is to
be noted, however, that the offending Mason must be "resident in such
jurisdiction." I am not prepared to say that we would take any action
upon a judgment rendered in a foreign jurisdiction upon a trial of
charges preferred against one of our members who did not at the
time the charges were preferred reside in that jurisdiction for acts
committed while sojourning therein. That would depend, I apprehend, upon the circumstances of the particular case. In this connection
it is to be noted that you do not say at which time the acts complained
of were committed. It does appear, however, from the edict issued
by M. W . Stephen Motta that it must have been prior to the first
day of December, because that was the date upon which Forbes was
suspended; and in the remarks of the Grand Master in Toltec Lodge
he stated (in addressing Forbes) : "You have been busy now for
several months in this jur~sdiction, but tonight you will stop."
Your communication to my predecessor is dated April 21, 1920;
and I am informed by Brother Forbes that he did not leave your
jurisdiction until April 18-three days before the date of your letter.
If this be the fact it appears that Brother Forbes was in your jurisdiction for nearly five months (four months and twenty-one days)
after the edict against him was issued by Grand Master Motta, in
which edict it is stated:
"A committee will be appointed, and when the evidence
is in form you will be summoned to appear before them to
show cause why you should not be forever expelled from
further participating in the rights and privileges of Free
Masonry."
If during the time he was residing in your jurisdiction charges
had been preferred against Brother Forbes, and after trial he had been
suspended or expelled for un-Masonic conduct, it would be the duty
of the Junior Warden of his Lodge under our law to prefer charges
against him for the acts and conduct alleged in the charges preferred
in your jurisdiction and of which he was there convicted. Of course
our law is predicated upon the assumption that the Grand Lodge
claiming penal jurisdiction is regular in its organization and was so
recognized by us. The question of its regularity, validity, legitimacy
and recognition would therefore be open to inquiry as a part of the
defense made by the accused.
It appears, however, that during the · time Brother Forbes was a
resident in your jurisdiction, your proceeding against him was limited
to the issuance of an edict of the Grand Master suspending him with
certain other brethren named without trial; and you now desire to
know "before taking final action in the matter, whether the trial of
this brother should be conducted by California Lodge or by a Lodge
in this (your) jurisdiction."

It was with that idea in mind, and not because I was influenced by the "hysteria of war," that in 1917 I introduced th~
resolution providing for the appointment of a committee to repe>rt
some plan whereby the breach between French and Anglo-Saxon
Masonry might be healed, and which resulted in the action taken
by Grand Lodge the following year.
We have now materially modified the principles enunciated
by Grand Lodge in 1913 as a test for recognition, by restricting
the applicati.o n thereof to Grand Lodges of English-speaking
countries. We have adopted a policy which we believe is in
consonance with the spirit of the age, which looks to substance
rather than to form; and every application from a Grand Body
in any other than an English-speaking country will now be considered upon its merits w.i th relation to the situation of the
applicant and with a view of doing full and complete Masonic
justice. That we have done so much makes it necessary that we
shall do more-not merely that we may not withhold recognition
. where it should be granted, but as well (and which is certainly
not less important) that we shall not unwittingly grant it where
it should be withheld.
As a result of the investigation I felt compelled to make
before answering the complaint of the York Grand Lodge of
Mexico, I am convinced that it will be extremely difficult, if not
indeed impossible, to arrive at a proper understanding of the real
condition of Masonry in Mexico, and therefore to do "full and
complete Masonic justice."
·
In considering the question of the recognition of the Grand
Bodies in France, Belgium and Italy we could proceed intelligently. That queittion had been discussed for years. The facts
which had been collated and the arguments which had been made
pro and con were easily accessible. It was only necessary to
formulate our co.nclusion. Here, however, is a controversy between
tw.o contending bodies, each claiming recognition as against the
other, and each basing its claim on a disputed contention, and
with reference to a condition not generally known.
Insofar as the action to be taken by Grand Lodge is concerned,
the situation would not be materially better, if indeed it would not
be worse, if an application were made by a Grand Body in one of
the South American States where there was no controversy. In
that case the statements upon which our action would be predicated would be purely ex-flaYte ,· and we might accept them as true
only to find later that we had been misled, intentionally or unintentio.nally, as to the real condition.
We ought to know the condition o(Masonry in every country
-not merely that we can act intelligently upon any claim for

Our Inspectors
The service that is being rendered by some of our Inspec~ors
is of such inestimable value that too much. credit can not be given
th
Realizing that they possess special kno~ledge of local
of which the Grand Master is naturally .ignorant, I have
ver gratefully availed myself of every opportunity ~resented to
Y. sugg est'ions from them·' and I have been especially pleased
receive
f
rom
1"th the annotations made by some of them on the reports
Lodges · which were transmitted through them.
The Inspectors constitute the link between Grand Lodge and
the Lodges of their respective districts; and those to whom I refer

co~~ltions
~ eir

71

are not unmindful of the fact that they represent the Grand
Master as well as the Grand Lecturer. They realize that their
duty is not fully performed by merely teaching th.e esoteric work;
but that upon them devolves the responsibility of seeing that the
Constitution and Edicts of Grand Lodge are maintained and supported and that the plans promulgated by the Grand Master are
carried out so far as the circumstances will permit. · If any of
those I have in mind have failed to do all that they would like to
do,· I am quite certain it has not been for lack of an earnest effort.
It has, however, become apparent that with the growth of the
jurisdiction, and particularly since the adoption of our plan of
Masonic education, to fully and properly discharge all the functions of an Inspector is more than can be reasonably expected
of any one individual.
The natural and inevitable result has been that those Inspectors
to whom the ritual seems of supreme importance are inclined to
give to that all, or at least the greater part of, the time they are
able to devote to the discharge of their duties ; while on the other
hand those who recognize the real potentialities of the office of
Inspector are sometimes inclined to begrudge the amount of theit
time which is consumed in teaching the esoteric work.
In a report from one of the. most capable of our Inspectors
the opinion is expressed that " not only the educational movement
but also the standing of the Order could be improved here (in
his District) and possibly elsewhere in the State if the Inspector
were relieved of the duty of instructing in the ritual and holding
schools of instruction by having that work apportioned to some
other officer, or to an assistant who would be responsible to the
Grand Master."
This opinion, which is shared by other Inspectors with w.h om
I have discussed the matter in my visits throughout the Jurisdiction, warrants my suggesting to Grand Lodge an idea which had
occurred to me but which I hesitated to express because it involves
a radical change in our entire system.
I believe, however, that the change I have in mind would not
only be of material assistance in our educational movement and
furnish further evidence to the community of the worth o.f our
Ins.t itution (as was suggested by the Inspector referred to), but
would result in an increased proficiency in the esoteric work.
I have discovered that on account of physical conditions it is
practically impossible in some districts for even the most indefatigable Inspector to -give to all the officers of his Lodges the
time which is required to make them proficient in the work; and
that in many Lodges the officers are compelled to rely upon such
assistance as they receive from their Past Masters. The same

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

reasons which preclude the Inspector from visiting the Lodges as
often as he would like to do, likewise render it impracticable, if
not impossible, for all the officers of the Lodge to attend such
schools of instruction as are held by the Inspector. In many of
our Districts the vocation of the officers is such that during the
summer it is extremely difficult for them to devote any considerable portion of their time to Masonry; while in winter the condition
of the roads and the inclemency of the weather practically isolate
their Lodges. Considering all these things, it has occurred · to
me that not only should the duties now incumbent upon the
Inspectors be divided, but that the office itself would be better
abolished; and that in lieu thereof we provide for Deputy Grand
Lecturers and District Deputy Grand Masters.
The Deputy Grand Lecturers could be appointed by the Grand
Lecturer, and might include any Master or Past Master. who could
attain such proficiency in the work as would entitle him to a
certificate from the Grand Lecturer; it being understood of course
that there would not be more than one Deputy Grand Lecturer
in any Lodge.
This would make it possible to have in every community,
however small, some one thoroughly proficient in the r itual and
able to instruct · the officers. It would likewise relieve the Grand
Lecturer of a part of the constantly increasing burden under
which he is now staggering. Instead of being compelled to visit
every remote hamlet, he could confine his work to holding district schools of instruction at' which the presence of all the Deputy
Grand Lecturers in that District would be required. While the
officers of any Lodge would be of course privileged to attend,
the primary purpose would be to afford the Deputy Grand Lecturers an opportunity of "checking up" with the. Grand Lecturer;
and a failure of any Deputy Grand Lecturer to attend the meeting
held in his District without a satisfactory excuse would be warrant for the withdrawal. of his certificate, and the appointment of
another in his place.

would make available the service of some of the ablest and most
influential Masons in the State for w hom there is no plac.e under
our . present system. They are leaders in the civic life of their
communities ; but the very reaso ns wh ich make them such preclude
th.em fro m g iving to the esoteric work (even were they so inclined) the time which it requires. They served as Masters of
the~r Lodg~s in their youth, and before larger affairs engaged
the~r attention. They are vitally in terested in the problems with
wh1c? the world today is pregnant and are eagerly seeking their
solution. If they have not devoted to Masonry the t im e a nd effort
they are willing to expend in that search, it is only because
the way has not been pointed out t o them. This will be their
opportunity.

The District Deputy Grand Master would have no concern
with the esoteric work; but would discharge the other duties now
devolving up on the Inspectors. H e would be appointed by the
Grand Master, report to him and be his special representative.
Unless other provision were made therefor, the work of the Committee on Masonic Education in his District would be carried on
through him.
'
While many of those now serving as Inspectors would naturally be appointed District Deputy Grand Masters (unless they had
a preference for the esoteric work) the creation of t hat office

should .receive immediaote cn·nsiderat io n ; and I t herefore sug~est
the entire matte~ be referred to the Committee on General Policy

Public Schools Week
The crisis co nfronting the Public Schools of America furnished
an opportunity for a practical application of the views I have so
often expressed concerning the duty devolving upon the Fraternity.
A g~eat danger was threatening an I nstitution in which we are
all vitally interest ed as citizens o f t he Commonwealt h and which
has always been t he especial concern of the Masonic' F raternity.
T hat danger would be averted if· the A merican people were aroused
from. ~he apathy due solely to a lack of knowledge of existing
conditions. Here was a concret e inst ance o f the good which could
be ~ccomplished by having our brethren in formed and advised in
their Lodges co ncerning a matt er which might not be otherwise
brought . to the ir a ttention.
. · I therefor.e issued a Pr~clamation (a copy of w hich appears
m the appendi x hereto) setting aside the week commencing Septe~ ber ~7t.h .as P ublic Schools W eek in the Masonic L odges in
this Jurisdiction and expressing the desire of the Grand Master
that some phase. of the ques~ions affect ing the Public School Sys.tern would be discussed durmg that week in every L odge in the
Jurisdiction.
·
·
The result was extremely gr atifying. I h ave received repor ts
from all over the State and there was apparently an almost universal compliance with the desire expressed in the P roclamat ion.

In the large majority of instances joint meetings· were held to
which the families of the brethren were invited. Public educators
everywhere gave their earnest co-operation. Incidentally I m~y
say that they have been loud in their praise of what the · Masomc
Fraternity in California has accomplished for the public schools
of the Nation and of this State in awakening the public generally
no less than the Craft itself to a realization of existing conditions.
We must now be extremely careful to permit nothing to be
done which may possibly militate against the great good which
has been accomplished. There are in the Fraternity as well as
out of it earnest, zealous, loyal friends of the Public School. S~s­
tem whose views do not in their erttirety find support in the principles upon which our Institution is based; and it must be clearly
understood that they do not, and 'can not, speak for the Craft.
The position of Masonry with reference to the Public Schools
is unambiguous, certain and definite.. It was admirably stated by
Brother Theodore Roosevelt when he said:

to Masonry. He is no fri~nd of either the Fraternity or the Public Schools who attempts to create an impression to the contrary;
and no thought ful and well informed Mason will say or do anything which will lend support to such an attempt. It was no doubt
with some such thought in mind that Theodore Roosevelt in speaking' of the members of a society of the sort to which I have referred said: "They are the worst foes of our public .school system
because they strengthen the hands ·o f its ultramontane enemies."
It was Brother Roosevelt's sterling Americanism which made him
such a zealous Mason. He was s.peaking of Americanism as . he
understood it; but in expressing his views as an American he was
enunciating Masonry's position with relation to the Public Schools.

Condition of the Craft
Our Growth.-This has been an extraordinary year. W het.l ier
or not it has been attended with success it is too soon yet to determine. Our growth has been phenomenal. Twenty new Lodges
have been formed and over eleve-n thousand new members have
been added to our rolls. The loss haSI been ,comparatively small
and our net gain has been nearly nine thousand. These figures
are quoted without any personal exultation-not merely because
the\ growth of the Fraternity in any one year is in n o sense· attrib11table to the administration of the particular Grand Master
in office ; but as well because of the fact that I am not altogether
certain that the condition warrants any exultation.

I do not mean to imply by this that there has been a · disposition upon the part of the Lodges, to consider quantity rather than
quality; but there is an ever recurring doubt in my mind as to
the healthfulness of such a growth. I know that our new members have not this year received the instruction they ought to have
received, and whicb they would have received had the time of the
officers not been so fully occupied in conferring" degrees. I fear
that not many have had sufficiently impressed upon them th~ ·fact
that with their admission to the Fraterrtity there devolved" upon
them duties ana responsibilities which they' mus't• faithfully . discharge · to justify the · confidence ·we have reposed in them;' that
·they must be better fathers, sons, husbands and brothers-and better citizens; that in their· business transactions they must deal

absohitely "on the square"-not merely with the' Craft but with
all with whom they do business; that they must in short make
their Masonry a part of their every day lives. O f cpurse those
are the lessons the ritual and the charges . teach; and perhaps ·they
"heard with understanding" and gave due heed to the words pronounced by the officers "trippingly on the tongue."

Generally speaking, the increase in membership has been in
the large centers of population and in the growing communities.
There arc, however, districts in the Jurisdiction where the Lodge~
are continually growing weaker. Some of our mining districts
where Masonry in earlier days flourished so vigorously ar~ being
gradually depopulated and the Lodges are in a moribund condition. I was at one time in accord with the opinion which has
been expressed by some of niy predecessors that unless a number
of consolidations were effected the more drastic measure of arresting the charters of some of these Lodges would become necessary;
but after having visited with these brethren, and observed the spirit
with which they are animated I would be loath to suggest the
withdrawal of their charters even though a desired consolidation
were not effected. In many of these Lodges there is a fellowship
of which any Body of Masons might well be proud. Their brethren
are indeed "linked together by an indissoluble chain of sincere
affection." They need and they deserve the encouragement of
Grand Lodge-not merely for what they have been, but for what
they are.
In this connectfon, without any suggestion from the Lodge,
or, any of its members, and even without the knowledge of any
of them of my purpose so to do, I here call attention of Grand
Lodge to a condition more or less typical of many of these little
Lodges. The particular Lodge to which I refer was chartered in
1855. The membership on August 1st, 1920, is exactly what it
was on August 1st, 1915. The average attendance is eight. There
have been only three initiations in the last two years. Its total
resources amount to $444.00 (of which amount, by the way, $150.00
is in Liberty Bonds). There was a liability incurred to one of
our Boards of Relief in the sum of $650.00 for the expense of the
last illness and funerals of two of its members. In one case (where
an operation was necessary) the expense was over $500.00. Principally from contributions made by its members, $400.00 of this
amount has been paid; and out of its meager resources this little
Lodge has paid to Grand Lodge its contribution of $113.40. I(
a request for a remission of its Grand Lodge contribution had
been made, there is no doubt it would have been granted. It
would be a gracious thing, and an acknowledgment of that spirit
of Masonry to which I have referred, if Grand Lodge would, without a request therefor, return to this Lodge the amount of the
contribution received from it.
Attendance.-Whatever may be the problem in any particular
Lodge, oq in any particular district, there is one common to all.
It is that of attendance. It might be perhaps more appropriately

referred to as that of "non-attendance." The other form 1 however
is purposely used because of the fact that there has bee n a mate~
rial increase in attendance in those Lodges in which an earnest

In the questionnaire which I sent to the Masters of the Lodges,
I asked for specific information as to whether or not there had
been provided for the members something in addition to the degree
work either in the way of talks or special features; and if there
had been, if there was a noticeable increase in the attendance. I
also desired to know if refreshments were provided at any of the
meetings; and if so, how often and upon what occasions. If evidence were needed of the correctness of the views expressed under
this head, it is furnished by the answers received to these questions. In this connection, by the way, I desire to make acknowledgment of the special effort made by some of the Masters to
have their reports comprehensive. One of them (Brother Marshall
of Alta Vista Lodge) · attached to his report a chart in the form
of a "graph" which shows at a glance not only the attendance at
every meeting during 1920, as compared with the corresponding
meetings during 1919, but as well whether or not there were special features provided. I regret exceedingly that it was received
too late to be reproduced and included in the appendix as a part
of this Message. It graphically illustrates a condition typical of
that in most of our. Lodges, as shown by the reports I have
received.

Wherever Lodges had provided special features, there was a
material increase in the attendance; and almost universally the
attendance was larger at the meetings at which there was no degree
work. Where the attendance was larger at the meetings at which
degrees were conferred, refreshments were provided at those meetings and not at the others. In many instances where a Lodge had
. introduced the discussion of public questions as a part of its regular program the attendance had been more than doubled.
This is peculiarly significant in view of the fact that it will
be r~membered that in all instances I asked for the . average number m attendance at all meetings, stated and called; and that in
most of the Lodges even where the new program has been adopted,
the change has been made in only one meeting in the month. The
attendance at those meetings was so large that it brought up the
average to the figures given, even where there had been no material increase in the attendance at the other meetings.

. The complaint we make with reference to the lack_ ~f atte~d­
ance is not peculiar to our jurisdiction. The same condition exists
in all the American jurisdictions. It has been said that less than
10% of our American Masons attend Lodge. I am personally
inclined to the belief that the percentage is very much smaller;
and that there are few jurisdictions in the country where more
than 5% of the members in the entire jurisdiction are c:ven irregularly in attendance at their Lodges.
Startling as the statement may seem, I believe that the nonattendance which is so generally deplored is evidence of the worth
of our membership. That our members generally do not attend
Lodge is, I think, due solely to the fact that in t?e av~rage Lodge
there is not provided the sort of program which will naturally
attract the kind of men of whose membership we have a right to
be proud.
The Ritual.-If a remedy is to be found for the ills of which
we complain we must first ascertain the cause. I can not but
believe that it is due primarily to the fact that there is too much
ritual. I do not mean by this merely that there are too many
repetitions of the esoteric work> due to the increase in the number
of candidates. That repetition can be avoided by the adoption
of the so-called "group plan" which has always obtained in many
of our Eastern jurisdictions, and which will be exemplified at this
Communication. This, however, will not entirely remed_y the
condition.
I believe that the ritual itself is too long and should be materially abridged. There is no reason why the degree of Master
Mason could not be conferred in its entirety without the elimination of a single essential feature and retaining all the beauties of
the symbolism in perhaps a little more than one-half the time
now consumed. Forty minutes, orr at the most one hour, should
be sufficient for the purpose.
The fact ·of the matter is that we have unduly magnifie~ the
importance of the esoteric work. The ritual was certainly never
intended as anything more than the means to an end. With us
it has become apparently the end we have in view. Everything
revolves around it; all else is made subservient to it. Proficiency
in the ritual is the test of efficiency in the Master. Apparently
the most important thing in Masonry is for the Master of a Lodge
to know when to say "on" and when "upon" and to remember
that on one occasion a certain distinguished personage "exclaimed"
while on another he merely " remarked."
I hope I will not be misunderstood as intimating that I do
not regard it as essential that the "work" should be correctly

79

given. I of course recognize the fact that communicated as it is
from mouth to ear its preservation depends upon the exactitude
with which it is communicated; and whenever I have r eferred to
the subject I have been careful to explain that I want to see the
work given as nearly "letter perfect" as is possible, and of course
as impressively as it can be. The undue importance we have
attached to the ritual, however, and the. time which is consumed
in conferring degrees have not only resulted in the lack of attendance of which we complain, but are responsible for the condition
Past Grand Master Hervey had in mind when in his admirable
address · to Grand Lodge he said: " By failing to respond to the
intellectual and spiritual demands of their members som~ of our
Lodges are ·l osing the interest and active support of many of the
best Masons in California and are in danger of becoming the
patrons of the me~iocre."
This condition is to be particularly deplored when we remember that the Masters of our Lodges are selected through the system of "rotation in office ;" and that generally speaking (and eliminating the exceptions which prove the rule) the men who could
do the most for Masonry as Masters of their Lodges will not serve
for seven years where practically the entire time of the L o dge is
devoted to the conferring of degrees. Of course the system of
rotation in office is in itself objectionable. We select our Masters
not for what they are, but for what we expect they will be in seven
years from the day they receive their first appointment "in the
line;" but even the abandonment of that system would not result
in attracting the service of the ablest of our number if we continued to subordinate everything else to the ritual.
Social Side of Masonry.-N ot t he least of the ills attributable
to a Lodge which is so "busy" that it can not find tim e for anything but the conferring of degrees is the lack of that fellowship
through which men become closely united. To promote that fellowship, the social side of Masonry must be developed. Here
again I must not be misunderstood. I do not seek to make the
Lodge a "playground of Masonry." We can not, however, close
our eyes to the fact that not infrequently the great attraction of
these "playgrounds" is the fellowship men have failed to find in
the Lodge. There will always be, of course, Masons who simply
want to "belong;" that is not the sort I have in mind. There are,
however, initiated in every Lodge, earnest, sincere men who knock
at our doors with a real desire to be helpful to their fellow men
and who are quite content to remain worthy Master Masons; but
who are lured to some co-ordinate Body of Masonry because they
have failed to find in the Lodge that which they sought.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The precepts of Masonry must be illustrated by its practices.
It is .virtually impossible to entertain a sincere affection for a man
whom you do not know even by sight and whose name you have
never heard. ''True friendship" can not exist among strangers;
and if the members of a Lodge are not to "remain at a perpetual
distance" an opportunity of becoming acquainted with each other
must be afforded them. Whatever will accomplish this purpose
is to be desired; but experience has shown that there is · nothing
so conducive to sociability and real fellowship as gathering around
the refreshment table·s. The reports show that those meetings_
were best attended where refreshments were provided; but he
would be a careless observer who concluded from this that the
increased attendance was due to the opportunity to enjoy what is
popularly termed a "free feed." That was but an incident; the
real attraction was the sociability attendant upon such occasions.
If proof of this were needed it would be supplied by the experience of one of the most energetic and capable of our Masters.
One of the most attractive of the many social features provided
by him for the members 0£ his Lodge was the "dollar dinner" for
which the members themselves paid.
There is, ~f course, some excuse, if not good reason, for the
failure to do more along this line than was done during the year
just past. The Lodges were simply swamped with petitions; the
friends of the candidates were insistent that they should receive
their degrees at the earliest possible time; and the officers of the
Lodges were overburdened with the work devolving upon them.
Let us, however, hope that the "rush" is now over; and that all
the Masters will now do what I am pleased to say many of them
did and give more thought to the members they already have than
to obtaining new ones. I would like to here refer specifically to
several Masters throughout the Jurisdiction whose work has been
especially noteworthy. This, however, is of course impracticable.

issued there are at least six more now being organized, two of
which will apply for Dispensations this month.
If in my reference to the condition of the Craft I have seemed
to unduly stress those things wherein I believe we have failed
rather than those wherein I know we have succeeded, it has not
been in a spirit of fault finding; but with the hope that if there are
indeed faults in our system they will thus be made more evident
and therefore more likely be corrected. I believe that Masonry
has done a good work in California during the past year; and I
am intensely proud of what has been accomplished by the Craft.

responsible for the number of new Lodges formed during the past

As have been all Grand Masters, I am especially indebted to
the Grand Secretary and Grand Lecturer. The intimate relation
which should exist between the Grand Master and Grand Secretary, and which it has been my pleasure to enjoy, has but increased
my pride in the friendship of John Whicher. His conception of
the office of Grand Secretary in its relation to that of Grand
Master is ideal. He relieves the Grand Master of the necessity of
giving his ·attention to matte.rs of pure routine, but is punctilious
in referring to him those which should receive his personal attention, including even inquiries which might be answered by the

he seems especially desirous of doing nothing which even the

of the Grand Master. He has been to me a tower of strength.
Indeed I may frankly say that without his aid and assistance, no

Conclusion
The year just past has been in many ways one of the happiest
of all the years of my life. I have believed, perhaps fatuously, that
an opportunity was afforded me as Grand Master of Masons to
perform a service not merely to the Craft, but to the Commonwealth. I could not hope to measure up to that opportunity as
I viewed it; but the effort I have made has been commensurate
with my ability. I have left undone many things I would have
liked to do; but I hope I have done nothing that would have been
better left undone.
A few days more and" I shall be no longer "the first among
my equals;" but I have learned the lesson I have sought to teach
-that the inestimable privilege of "service" is not peculiar to any
rank or station. I shall be quite content to be one of those "closely
united men working for the welfare of mankind" and for the safety,
peace and prosperity of the Nation.
CHAS. ALBAAT ADAMS,

Grand Master.

APPENDIX
October 31 , 1919.
To the Master of Each Lodge in the Jurisdiction:
Worshipful Sir:
At the request of the United States Treasury Department I
am specifically calling your attention to the resolutions adopted
by Grand Lodge at its latest Communication, pledging the Fraternity to co-operate with the Government in its campaign for
the promotion of thrift as a national policy.
In compliance with that resolution you are requested to immediately name a member of your Lodge as a Thrift Agent to
cooperate with the Government in the sale of Thrift and War
Savings Stamps, War Savings Certificates and Treasury Savings
Certificates.
·
You. are also requested to provide the agent named with an
adequate revolving fund to enable him to carry on hand for the
convenience of the members of your Lodge a sufficient supply of
such securities of the United States Government.
It is suggested that these securities furnish a particularly
appropriate form of investment for the interest which accrues on
the Government Bonds held by your Lodges. It is of ·course
unnecessary to state that any available funds in the Lodge Treasury
may be invested in these securities.

84

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

It is hoped that you will not be content to comply merely
with the strict letter of the resolution, but that you will endeavor
to carry out its spirit as well by making every effort to instill
and encourage a spirit of thrift and saving among the members
of your Lodge. This can best be done by inducing them to form
the habit of making regular purchases of Thrift and War Savings
Stamps.
During the war the appeal for the purchase of Thrift Stamps
and War Savings Stamps was made to the patriotism of the people.
The most enthusiastic proponents of the plan, however, were those
who realized that it was not, strictly speaking, a purely war time
measure; and that the necessities of the hour simply furnished
the opportunity for the institution of a Nation-wide m ovement
for the inculcation of a spirit of thrift and economy in the American people. The vision presented to them was that of better
citizenship. They recognized the fact that good government ·cannot exist without the basis of g ood citizenship, and that good
citizenship implies that the individual citiZen shall be honest,
industrious and thrifty.
Never was there greater need than now (not even during the
war) for that good citizenship which is the boast of our Fraternity. It is therefore suggested that the members of your Lodge
be notified either through your ·Lodge Bulletin, or by special
notice sent to them, or otherwise, that this is a part of the program
adopted by the Grand Lodge to enable the Fraternity to bear its
part in the movement for the development of a higher and better
American citizenship.
Fraternally yours,
CHAS. ALBERT ADAMS,

Grand Master.
PROCLAMATION
Public Schools Week in the Masonic Lodges in California
To the Masters, Wardens and Brethren of the Several. Lodges
in this Jurisdiction:
As Masons we unqualifiedly subscribe to the belief that an
educated and enlightened citizenship is the first great care of a
progressive State; and that upon our Public Schools depends the
hope for the perpetuity of a free and untrammeled democracy.
The professions we make as Masons demand that as citizens
· of the Commonwealth we take an active and intelligent interest
in all matters affecting 'OUr Public Schools.

85

A crisis is now confronting the Public School System in
America. There is a dearth of competent teachers, schools are ,
being closed, children, particularly in the rural communities, are
being de nied the education to which they are entitled and there
is apparently a deplorable apathy concerning remedial measures
which have been proposed.
To focus the attention of the Craft on existing conditions, I
as Grand Master of Masons in the Jurisdiction of California, do
now proclaim the week commencing Monday, September 27th,
1920, as "Public Schools Week" in the Masonic Lodges in this
Jurisdiction ; and I do earnestly request that during that week,
in every Lodge in this Jurisdiction some phase of the questions
affecting the Public Schools be brought to the attention of the
members present by speakers appointed for that purpose.
A tentative program and suggestions for the appointment of
speq.kers appear on the following pages.
Dated at San Francisco this 30th day o f August, 1920.
CHAS. ALBl!RT ADAMS,

(Seal)

Grand Master.

Attest:
JOHN WHICH'f:R,

Meetings
It is suggested that wherever it can be conveniently done
several Lodges unite in holding a joint meeting. In the smaller
communities, particularly, it is suggested that the meetings · be
open ones to which the families of Masons may be invited.
In the large cities where two or more Lodges meet on the
same evening it is suggested that a joint meeting of all those
Lodges be held. The occasion will be such an important one
that no Master should hesitate in giving up the entire evening for
the purpose.
Special notices should be sent by every Lodge to all its
members and every meeting should be well advertised.
In every community the cooperation of the County Superintendent of Schools should be secured. He has been already advised
by the State Superintendent of Schools of the proposed program
in our Lodges.
Immediately upon receipt of this announcement the Master
of the Lodge should either arrange to have his Lodge join with
some other in a meeting, or make it his special business to secure
one or more speakers to address his own Lodge.

In this co nnection, however, it is to be particularly remembered
that these discussions are not intended as propaganda for the

PROCEF.OINGS OF 'l'HE

GRAND LOOOE OF CALIFORNIA

support of any particular measure-National, State or Local. They
are intended to be informative and instructive with the idea that
there shall be a fair and full discussion of every subject presented.
Any member present should not only be permitted, but encouraged,
to express any views he may entertain in opposition to those
presented by the speaker.

· To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Pursuant to the provisions of the Constitution I present herewith a report oE the transactions of the Grand Secretary's office
for the fiscal year ended July 31, 1920, together with a detailed
statement of all moneys received within the year, and an itemized
statement of the disbursements of Grand Lodge. I also append
an account of receipts since the close of business July 31 to and
including October 7, 1920, and all unfinished business of Grand
Lodge.
The experiment of taxing petitioners for the degrees $20 each
for the benefit of the Masonic Homes appears to have been a success, and ought to materially reduce the per capita tax on the members. A special form of receipt for the $20 contribution has been
printed, and copies will be sent to Lodges, to be delivered to contributors immediately after the conferring of the first degree. Masters should instruct their Secretaries that the moneys derived from
this $20 fee are no part of Lodge funds, and should be deposited
in a special account-and so far as may be, where some interest
may accrue for the benefit of the Lodge. A good plan would be'
to accept two checks from the petitioner, one for the fee required
by the by-laws and one for the Home fee.
All Lodges have reported with the single exception of Loyalton No. 359.

Special Communications of Grand Lodge
7. Grand Lodge was convened by order of the Grand Master,
for the purpose and at the times and places following:
October 17, 1919, Victory Lodge No. 474 was duly constituted
and the officers installed by the Grand Master.
October 25, Grand Lodge was convened by R. W. Samuel E.
Burke, Senior Grand ·Warden, who constituted Blythe Lodge No.
473 in ancient form.
·
November 22, Brother Burke repaired to National City and
convened Grand Lodge for the purpose of dedicating the new
Masonic hall at that city.
December 9, at San Francisco, funeral of Past Grand Master
Stevens, conducted by the Grand Master.
The Grand Master corivened Grand Lodge and dedicated the
new Masoniq hall at Fillmore on the 14th of February; the new
Masonic hall at San Jacinto, February 16, and the new Masonic
hall at Buena Park, February 17.
February 25, Grand Lodge was convened at Maricopa, and
the Grand Master dedicated the new Masonic hall at that city.
March 6, Grand Lodge was opened at Yreka, and the Grand
Master on that day laid the cornerstone of the Yreka Grammar
School.
April 6, at Masonic Temple, San Francisco, funeral of George
P. Adams, Grand Tiler.
May 15, Grand Lodge convened at Sacramento, where the
Grand Master, in the presence of a large gathering of brethren,
solemnly dedicated the new Masonic Temple.
June 25, Grand Lodge was convened a.t Whitt.ier and th~ Grand
Master laid the cornerstone of the pubhc hospital, the gift of a
brother to the city.
August 19, Grand Lodge convened at Salinas, where th.e Grand
Master laid the cornerstone of the high school at that city.

Unfinished Business
8. The following business, unfinished at the last annual communication, was referred to the Committee on General Policy and
Purposes:
The resolution of Past Grand Master Henderson, to consider
whether Lodges should not return to the ancient practice of conducting business while open in the first degree; and
The resolution of Past Grand Master Hervey, providing that
this Grand Lodge approve the constitution of the Masonic Service
Association of the United States and accept membership therein.

GRAND LODGE OF CALil!'ORNIA

Courtesy Work
10. An unhealthy practice has grown up, possibly a relic of
conditions existing during the world-war, whereby Lodges of this
jurisdiction as well as of sister jurisdictions, request that degrees
be conferred upon candidates as courtesy to the requesting Lodge.
As a matter of fact, the requests are made to favor candidates who
might better receive their degrees in the Lodge of their election.
One grand jurisdiction, Pennsylvania, requires that petitioners must
receive their degrees in the Lodge of their election, and I heartily
commend that practice, notwithstanding it may occasionally work
a real hardship on some worthy candidates. Within the year our
Lodges have asked Lodges of other jurisdictions to confer 312
degrees, and we have extended like courtesies, without fee, to the
extent of conferring 1188 degrees. ·

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON GRAND MASTER'S
MESSAGE
To the M.".W.".Grand Lodge of California..
Brethren:
Your committee to which was referred the Message of the
Grand Master and the Annual Report of the Grand Secretary,
has had the same under consideration, and now reports as follows:
Grand Master's Message
After a careful consideration of the substance as well as the
text of this important document, your committee is persuaded
that it will be accepted not only at this time, but also in the years
to come, as one of the most notable addresses ever presented to
this Grand Body. Charming in it.s textual style, it may well be
considered a distinctive contribution to Masonic literature; and
in that respect alone, your committee is confident that it will be
read and re-read, not only by those here present, but by the
members of the Craft throughout this and sister jurisdictions, with
ever increasing pleasure and delight.
But the outstanding merit of the message is attached not to
its literary excellence but rather to the clear, lucid and inspiring
presentation of the Grand Master's conclusions, recommendatio ns
a nd suggestions touching subjects intimately associated with the
welfare of the F raternity.
As indicated by the Message of the Grand Master and the
Report of the Grand Secretary, the Fraternity, during the year
now closing, has experienced an unprecedented growth in number
of new. Lodges, and also in the numbe r of those who have been
accepted as worthy to become members of the Craft. The rapid
augmentation of our membership and the steady increase in the

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND L ODGE OF CALIFORNIA

number of .Lodges promote, of course, a steady expansion of the
influence of Free Masonry. As the influence of our Fraternity
increases, its responsibilities niultiply. It follows, therefore, from
year to year, that the duties of our succeeding Grand Masters
become more trying and exacting.

or particular measures. The Grand Master has spoken in terms
so clear and explicit that uisconception would appear to be
well-nigh impossible ; and yet, perhaps, the thought of some
brethren has experienced confusion.

112

It might be deemed appropriate for this committee to exercise
only the simple ' f.atiction of referring to the . several standing committees of Grand Lodge those sections of the Message which will
properly go to them for extended consideration; but it has been
suggested that it may without impropriety point out, for purposes
of emphasis, certain sections which would appear to be of special
importance. It is in accordance with the spirit of the suggestion
thus referred to that the following matters are here m entioned:
Politics.-Under the caption "Politicks,'' the Grand Master
calls to the attention of Grand Lodge matters which, in the opinion
of your committee, are of such weight. as to merit the most serious
consideration of the Craft. . Our Institution, in this jurisdiction,
has attained to a great membership and an excellent organization.
It possesses, therefore, a tremendous though peculiar power,_ the
nature of which, we fear, is all too frequently misunderstood. It
is not surprising, therefore, that some Masons, actuated by sincere
motives, should mistake the tangible organization of Masonry for
its intangible power to promote unity among its votaries, and
attach themselves to the false belief that Masonry can remain
Masonry and yet, as an .organizatio.n, function in the determination
of political, civic, social, industrial and religious questions. To
brethren ~f this erroneous opinion we would commend the language
in the old Charges of 1722:
No· private piques or quarrels must be brought
within the door of the Lodge, far less any quarrels
about religion, or nations, or State policy. * * * We
are of all nations, tongues, kindreds and languages,
and are resolved against all politics, as what never yet
conduced to the welfare of the Lodge, nor ever will.
The Grand Master has sought to impress upon Mason&
throughout the jurisdiction the importance of informing themselves, as individuals, with reference to .public affairs. He has
urged them to a quicker interest in the duties of citizenship. He
has commended to them certain specific subjects as especially
deserving of their attention. The facilities of the Institution have
been employed to impart inspiration and enlightenment to the
individual, but w ith no intent that any individual should in turn
seek to commit the Institution to· the formal support. of persons

113

Instances of ill-advised ·action on the part of Lodges, or
officers of Lodges, have been rare indeed. Your committee is confident that insofar as Craft Masonry is concerned, the sound
judgment of the great body of our membership, and its attachment to the true ideals and purposes of Masonry, will stand as sure
·defenses against impropriety of action .o r rashness of counsel.
T_here is perceiv~ble, however, the operation of a certain spirit
which. is manifesting itself occasionally in ill-considered measures
and · proposals by organizations restricting their' membership to
Mas,t er Ma~ons, and representing t hemselves to be Masonic, or
"branches of Masonry." The . Grand Master has specifically
pointed out the regrettable political propaganda recently promoted
in . the name of Jinnistan Grotto in Los Angeles, and has also
stated his reasons for disapproving of the proposed organization
of a particular "Masonic" industrial association in Humboldt
county. Your committee agrees unreservedly with the observations
of his Message with respect to these matters, and therefore recommends that, by the adoption of this report, his attitude toward
·both these cases, and his action in one, be approve&.
Crafts Councils.-In this connection, the Grand Master has
this committee, with a request that it report thereon,
.the matter of the so-called "Government Crafts Councils," which
are under the jurisdiction. of the "Supreme Council of Craftsmen."
T h e Craftsmen represent their institution as an "operative branch
of · Masonry."
ref~rr.ed to

Your committee · has not been acquainted with the details of
the history appertaining to the Governing Crafts Councils and the
Supreme Council of Craftsmen,· but understands that they are
outgrowths of a movement which originated in the Electrical
Crafts in San Francisco. It appears t hat a number of our brethren,
employed in the electrical trades, felt it would be to their advantage
to form an organization having for its purpose mutual protection.
It was their desire .to see that th e Masons belo nging to these
trades were regularly employed, and to guard against discrimination, which in some instances, is said to have been practiced against
them. To objects such as these, commendable in themselves,
there could be no objection whatever. It appears, h owever, that
those connected with the original m ovement beca~ e imbued with
a vision of larger . accomplishments, and with a hope of attaining

PHOCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

thereto, they established the Governing Crafts Councils as secret
societies subordinate to a Supreme Council of Craftsmen, which
was organized in December, 1916, in San Francisco. The brethren
made the mistake of sehing themselves up, without the shadow of
sanction, as the founders of an "operative branch of Masonry,"
and then adopted principles which, in some respects, are insupportable from the Masonic point of view. A ritual was formulated
covering two degrees in the Governing Crafts Councils and one
degree in the Supreme Council of Craftsmen. This ritual is a
strange jumble of inconsistencies and conflicts between teachings
which on the one hand might be approved by Masons, and which
on the other hand are deeply tinged with semi-radicalism. Considered as a whole, it appears to be an amateurish work, ill-considered, poorly balanced and, indeed, very objectionable.

which will almost certainly result in bripging serious discredit upon
the Institution of Free Masonry. In the opinion of your committee. Grand Lodge should not hesitate to take such action as is
calculated to free the Fraternity from a menace of this kind. We
say this without desire to injure the se~sibilities of the brethren
who may be associated with the Craftsmen. We believe that in
the exuberance of zeal they have failed to consider · the dangers
attendant upon their course.

114

Active membership in this organization is definitely restricted
to Blue Lodge Masons who "are actually employed at some trade
or calling whereby they earn their living." Associate membership
is granted to Blue Lodge Masons who are-we quote-"indirectly
connected or employed at some trade or calling whereby they
earn their living." This does not include the professions, financiers or speculators, but includes those who are directly connected
with industrial production. The laws of the organization ·also
provide that no Mason is eligible to membership "who is opposed
to, or who is antagonistic to organized labor, or who in any
manner lends his aid, moral or financial , to accomplish its destruction." It is an · announced principle of the organiza!ion that its
members are actively to co-operate and assist one another not
only in connection with securing positions of profit, but also in
connection with political affairs. They are also to co-operate
actively in the politics of labor unions in which they may hold
membership, and initiates are admonished that "no sluggards, no
drones, nor any incompetent craftsmen can expect to remain
among them." Any member whose sympathies depart from this
sort of program is to be led out of the Lodge publicly and de!lied
all further communication. The organization, which asserts, evidently with respect to this country, that "a J>retense of democracy
now prevails," pledges its members to "aid and assist all nations
and peoples to govern themselves under a free democracy of
the people."
Your committee has sketched these points briefly. There are
many others that might well be mentioned; but for the purpose
of brevity we believe these are sufficient to indicate most clearly
that an institution of this sort, advertising and representing itself
as "Masonic" or "a branch of Masonry" is destined to a career

\15

Your committee therefore recommends that Grand Lodge
enact such legislation as will result -;n · making it a Masonic offense
for brethren of this jurisdiction to become members of or to
retain membership in said Governing Crafts Councils . and said
·supreme Council of Craftsmen , so long as said organizations continue in any manner whatsoever, either in their ritual or otherwise,
to represent said organizations as a branch of Masonry. Your
committee also recommends that the matter ·be referred to the
Committee on Jurisprudence to prepare suitable legislation in
accordance with the foregoing recommendations.
Public Schools.-That Masons are supporters and defenders of
the public schools goes without saying, During the year, due to
the efforts of the Grand Master and other Grand Officers, the
Committee on Masonic Education, the Inspectors and the officei;s
of Lodges, there has been a notable revival of Masonic interest in
the subject of public education. The general developments in this
connection have been adequately presented in the Grand Master's
Message, and it is to be presumed will receive further attention in
the report of the Committee on Masonic Education . Your committee takes this opportunity. most heartily to applaud the
accomplishments recorded. It believes that great good will result.
At this point we des.ire, however, to offer, one or two suggestions.
Masonry in this jurisdiction is committed to the suppoi:-t ancl
defense of the public school system; but it is not and should not
be committed, as an Institution, to the support of particular
measures merely because they purport to be for the benefit of the
public schools. We can be unitedly for the public schools and
yet divide as to the merit or advisability of particular measures
relative thereto, just as we can be unitedly for the United States
Government and yet divide on measures respecting its welfare.
It would be unfortunate, if not calamitous, if Masonry were to
conceive itself bound to prosecute propaganda in behalf of all
measures and proposals advertised as "for the benefit of the
schools;" for , it is not of record that proposed school legislation,
or any other sort of proposed legislation, proceeds from the Fount
of Divine Wisdom. Your committee believes with the Grand

FROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Master, that it is the duty of a Mason not to accept ready-made
opinions in regard· to such matters, but rather to give each proposal
careful, painstaking study and investigation, and to cast his vote
or govern his actions in accordance with his unprejudiced
convictions.
Secondly, it is of supreme importance that in our advocacy of
public education we should guard carefully, lest by an unregulated
zeal we fall into false conceptions of the real issues involved.
The Grand Master, we believe, has clearly and convincingly treated
this delicate subject, and he has brought to it, also, the illuminating observations of our late Brother _Theodore Roosevelt. You~
committee is in heartiest accord with the Message of the Grand
Master as to this matter, and commends his enlightened policy
to the full approval of the Craft for its guidan~e. .

We note with satisfaction the granting of twenty dispensations for the formation of new Lodges. Of these new Lodges,
five are located in or contiguous to the city of Los Angeles, five
in the densely populated cities of Alameda, o'akland and Berkeley,
one in San Francisco and one in San Jose. The others are located
in cities 'of smaller population. In other words, twelve of the
twenty new Lodges have been formed in the most populous centers
of the jurisdiction. They represent, in the opinion of your committee, not only a logical ·movement to relieve the pressure o n
previously existing Lodges, due to the great amount of . degree
work shown by the Report, but also a commendable and growing
tendency to strengthen the Institution by enlisting more of its
members in the active' work of Masonry, through the organization
of a greater number of Lodges.
Your committee believes that the recommendation of the
Grand Secretary with reference to courtesy work is most timely,
and that steps should be taken to correct a practice w hich is
becoming burdensome to many of our Lodges.

In submitting · my annual report as Grand Treasurer I beg to
direct your attention to the fact that seven years ago the Grand
Treasurer reported the invested funds of the Grand Lodge and
the Masonic Homes to be about sixty-one thousand dollars.

At the present time the securities held by those institutions
amount to about three hundred and fifty thousand dollars.
The constantly increasing work in the office of the Grand
Treasurer, made necessary by the care of these bonds and the
further fact that it is the opinion of your Grand Treasure·r that
invested funds in such large amount should be placed in the
custody of a trust company, caused your Grand Treasurer to
recommend to th!! Grand Master and to the Trustees of the
Homes that such action be taken.
The Grand Master and Trustees concurred in the recommendation; the Anglo-California Trust Company was selected and all of
the securities, with the exception of a few bonds of small
denomination, are now in the custody of that institution.
WILLIAJ\1'. P. FILM:ER,

Grand Treasurer.

REPORT OF TRUSTEES MASONIC HOMES
The following report was read, and adopted as presented:
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California
herewith submits its report for the year ending August 31, 1920.
Immediately after the close of the last annual communication of
Grand Lodge the Board met, and. in accordance with our by-laws,
proceeded to elect officers for the ensuing year. All officers were reelected.
During the year the Board held monthly meetings, alternatin~ between San Francisco and Los Angeles, and weekly conferences of the
members residing in these two cities have been regularly held, to the
advantage of the business of the Homes.
At the November meeting the Grand Master notified the Board
that he had appointed Brother James B. Gist of Los Ange!cs as
Trustee for the term of four years, vice Oscar Lawler, term expired.
SALE OF OUTSIDE PROPERTIES

The Home has been the owner of many small pieces of property,
obtained for the most vart by deed from residents of the Home. These
properties arc of little value, many being small homes and not readily
salable, but through old ·association have great value in the minds of
the donors. During the year your Trustees have sold five pieces, at
full market va1uc, realizing the sum of $6Hl8.48. Of this sum, $2649.30
has been placed to the credit of the residents at the Home who owned
the properties, under the provisions of Rule 16. The sum of $3459.18,
being proceeds of sales of properties of deceased residents, was placed
in the Endowment Fund.
SALE m· SAN GABRIEL

We are pleased to report a cash sale of this property for the sum
of $30,814.56. This amount coven the cost of the property. adjustment
of the Covina purchase, plus all expenses of taxes, insurance and UlJ ·
keep and a profit of approximately $2500. The funds obtained from
this sale have been credited to the Building Fund.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

123

present time we are installing an automatic sprinkler fire system
throughout the main building and annex. This will reduce the fire
hazard and no longer list this building in the opinion of the under·
writers as a "fire trap."
CEMETERY AT DECOTO

The Home "cemetery plot" at Decoto has been replotted and
properly ornamented. Uniform marble markers have been set for
each grave, curbing and walks constructed and the plot inclosed by an
ornamental iron fence. Through the generosity of Brother Max Hornlein, the beautiful statue of "Grief," formerly resting in the grounds of
Stanford University, now occupies the center of the Home cemetery, as
a memorial to our departed.
COVINA IMPROVEMENTS

No improvements have been made at Covina, except the grading of
the playgrounds and new orchard. Some repairing, repainting and re·
placements are the only building expenditures made.
THE FARM AT DECOTO

Labor conditions made it again necessary to work the ground on
shares, and the shortage of rain materially reduced the crops. The
prune and apricot crops were not sufficient to warrant the sale of any
fruit, and it was all dried and retained for use at the Home. The
Home garden has produced bountifully, and all the various vegetables
are liberally served to the residents.
·
THE FARM AT COVINA

The young lemon grove this year produced about $477, and the
trees are in good condition. The orange trees show the best progress
of any in the neighborhood, arid are very promising. Not a single
tree was lost or damaged. New deciduous trees were set out this year,
most of which are doing nicely. An unusual season and some poor
stock will necessitate some resetting. Our garden is very productive,
but a change in grading to meet water conditions will give us' an increased area. Owing to unsatisfactory labor conditions we have suffered from a lack of proper care of the vegetable garden at t"imes. We
now have four good grade Holstein cows, furnishing us an abundance
of milk. Our poultry is in poor condition because of inexperienced
care. This will be remedied at once.

IMPROVEMENTS AT DECOTO

BUILDING PROGRAM AT DECOTO

During the year the various buildings at Decoto have been painted,
but due to the difficulty in getting labor, there is still considerab'e
carpenter work to be done. This is now being taken care of. At the

The time is approaching when it will be necessary to replace the
six wooden cottages, now housing some fifty men residents, with a
modern sanitary fi re-proof building. T his should be done as soon as

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

conditions of labor and material will warrant. The funds for this
purpose will be available in the near future, and we ask authority at
this time to develop a building program, providing for construction to
begin, when, in the judgment of the Trustees, conditions justify it.
More hospital accommodations are urgently needed to care for . residents who become ill. There is now available the sum of $21,000, the
gift of our late Brother John R. Daggett of California Lodge No. 1,
which may be applied to the construction of an annex to the hospital.

Our regulations provide that "An applicant suffering from any
disease or ailment necessitating hospital treatment will not be received."
As pointed out elsewhere, our hospital is overcrowded with those
who become ill after their admission to the Home. The Grand Lodge
should give this regulation most careful consideration. Are we fair to
the brother, a Mason in good standing for many years, who becomes
incapacitated through paralysis or other ailments, spends his savings in
attempted cure, and after years of Masonic fraternalism, when he
needs help and wishes to end his days among his brethren, is refused
admission to the Home?
It is true his Lodge cares for him in a public or semi-public institution, but what is the obligation of Grand Lodge in such a case?
Experience has taught us the difficulty of securing capable and necessary help even for our small hospital at Decoto. This difficulty would
be increased with a larger hospital. Would it not be the part of wisdom
for the Grand Lodge to endow a ward, or otherwise maintain, in an
existing institution in a large city, equipped for the proper care of an
unfortunate brother who is now ineligible fo the Home.

124

BUILDING AT COVINA

The present buildings at Covina are adequate for present demands,
unless Grand Lodge should make radical changes relative to eligibility
for the admission of children.
The Grand Chapter R. A. M. has provided $8500 now invested in
Liberty bonds, for the construction of a vocational building for boys, and
the Grand Council R. & S. M. has provided $4000 in cash and bonds for
the construction of a domestic science bungalow for girls. The
domestic science building should be of sufficient size to accommodate the
high school girls, in addition to providing the facilities for domestic
science education.
Experience in institutions similar to ours, where educational
features are emphasized, has proven it desirable and practical to
domicile high school girls in a separate building. Their libraries, their
studies and their hours are different, and it meets the features of club
cottages. Such a building would provide housing space that would
later become a necessity with increased numbers in the Home. These
two buildings are much needed, and should be constructed as soon as
building conditions warrant.
FINANC£

We are pleased to be able to report to Grand Lodge a better
financial condition than in any previous year. The transfer from the
war fund of $55,000 to the Home funds, and the sale of the San
Gabriel properties, have met all deficits, and we now have the nu.deus
of a working capital for emergency or improvement.
Due t~ the success of the plan of collecting $20 from each initiate
for the benefit of the Homes, it is apparent that the per capita tax from
the members may be materially reduced this year, and your Trustees
make such recommendation.
ADMISSION OF TH£ INCAPACITATED

The Trustees are frequently compelled to refuse admission to an
applicant who has all the necessary qualifications of eligibility, but who
is physically disqualified.

ADMISSION M

125

CHILDREN WHOSE FATH£RS AR£ LIVING

During the year the Trustees have received applications from
Lodges in behalf of children whose fathers were living, but whose
wage, or environment, was such that the Lodge felt the father could not
properly care for the child. Your Trustees have adopted no general
policy, in regard to these cases, but have handled each case upon its own
merits, remembering that the Home was not intended for the purpose
of enabling a father to shift the responsibility of the care of a child to
other shoulders, nor to enable him to obtain a convenient boarding
school for the child. Permission to send a child to the Home has only
been give~ when the case was, in the judgment of the Trustees, one in
which the Lodge should properly render assistance to the parent.
SUP£RINT£ND£NT FOR TH£ COVIN A HOM£

Since the completion of the new buildings and the increase in the
number of children at Covina, the need of a Resident Superintendent
has become more and more apparent to the Board. With the system
of health regulation and mental development recommended by the
Department of Pediatrics of Stanford University and adopted by this
Board, the presence of a competent Superintendent is necessary. We
must provide for the proper guidance of both children and employes
to meet the standard of personal and individual care the fraternity
desires to extend to each child whose preparation for future usefulness
is left to us. The economical purchase of supplies and the efficient
direction of the farm, garden, and dairy, are duties not to be expected
of a Matron. The local Trustees have generously and without com-

· 126

pensation given their time to this wo.rk, but the demands are growing
far beyond what should be expected of them to meet. The addu1 instruction in the proposed vocational and domestic science building the
direction of the gymnasium and playground work, and the develop:i.ient
of a practical interest in all outdoor activities for the children, require
continuous supervisioi;i.
Your Trustees recommend the appointment of a Superintendent at
the Covina Home an~ the construction of a suitable residence therefor.
