Through the scholarship donated last year by the San ·Francisco
Sciots, one young woman from the Home has been given a practical
business training and is now employed and self-supporting.
An eighteen-year-old graduate of the Home, who was endeavoring
to earn sufficient to procure a mining · engineering degree, is now being
given the benefit of the scholarship provided by the San Francisco
Bodies of the Scottish Rite, and is now attending Cogswell Polytechnic
College. Several of the children are now about to be graduated from
the Home and are looking forward to the advantages of the scholar·
ships.
RECOM MENDATJONS

1st-That a building program be authorized, as herein suggested.
2d-That the Board be authorized to place in pub'ic or semi-r,ublk
institutions, under such r egulations as the Board of T rustees may
adopt, such applicants for admission who, except for their physical disabilities, would be admitted to the Home.
3d-That the Trustees be authorized to employ a Superintendent at
the Covina Home and provide necessary quarters for him.
4th-That the per capita tax for the support of the H omes IJC'
reduced from one dollar to thirty-five cents.

Since our last annual report, 27 residents have been admitted, 17
being men and 10 women. Two have voluntarily departed, and 18 have
passed to their last reward. There are now at the Home 84 men and
54 women.
The health of the residents has been good, with the exception of
those who by reason of age have become infirm . and helpless. The
Coleman hospital is now housing 16 members of the Home, and every
attention possible is being provided for them.
Many of the brethren have <;ontributed to the welfare of the Home
by their labors in the carpenter, tailor, shoe and barber shops, picking
fruit and berries, watering the lawns and flower gardens, in the garage,
library, kitchen, pantry and dining room, and doing light chores.
The women residents attend to all the maki~g, ·mending and marking of the household linen, and have taken charge not only of their
own rooms, but as well the halls, stairways, wash rooms and other
parts of the main building. They also attend to the changing of all
table linen, and assist at times in work connected with the dining room
and the hospital.
Every day, immediately following lunch, the blind residents repair
to the library, where a good reader imparts the current news of the day.
The social features are not neglected, and all the residents are
afforded all the diversion necessary.
From time to time arrangements are made so that the brethren and
lad ies of the Home have opportunity to visit Lodges and Chapters of
the Eastern Star, and automobile trips are made often to Oakland and
other nearby cities.
Many entertainments have been given for the pleasure and benefit
of the fami!y by Lodges, members of Lodges and their ladies. Following is a summary of such entertainments;

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

THE COVINA HOME
The happy, healthful and appreciative family of exceptionally
trained children at Covina, make their best report to the fraternity by
their cheerful appearance and hearty voices. To the readers of these
reports who have no opportunity to see. the children Pyrsonally, we feel
is due some description of the method of care, and results attained,
"
with these deserving children of the fraternity. .
A consistent adherence to the recom1Tlendaticins of the Department
of Pediatrics of Stanford University, gives the children a strong physical
and mental advantage. Followi'ng the annual examination, each child
is charted in such manner that a steady correction of all weaker
tendencies is made, with pleasing results. The system of individual
care instead of group or mass training, brings out the latent value of
the child in special traits or features. The proper: selection of diet, the
regulation of exercise suited to the physical needs of the individual
child, and providing indoor and outdoor diversions that promote a
mental and physical progress, are features of training made with a
systematic effort that ·develops a marked increased efficiency.
The mental development of the children is evidenced by the high
percentage of promotions in school work, and their music and memory
work at home. Their physical training shows results in hiking trips
near the Home, and in swimming at their beach camp. At Easter time
forty children averaged seven miles per day on mountain trails for
four days . . A good portion of the trip was in the deep snows of Mt.
Ba'dy, at an elevation of more than COOO feet. At Camp Tucker at
Balboa, all but five of the children learned to swim well. Forty-six of
the seventy children swam across Newport Bay, a distance of a quarter
of a mile, and twenty-one swam from the Palisades to Balboa, a distance of 1.7 miles. They are almost expert in fancy diving and feature
swimming.
With no desire to boast, but to give the fraternity a true knowledge
of th_e person~! training of the children, we must .state for them tha t
their courteous and pleasing mannerisms excite the most favorable
comment at school and among visitors. They are ch.osen for · class
officers, committee work and contests at all times. Our young folks
make every effort to be a credit to the Home, and this mention is
properly due them. When we consider that a large percentage o f the
.c hildren coming to the Home are from shipwrecked families, in some
cases without proper health or moral attention, it reflects much · credit
both upon the persevering child and its patient instructors.
An unconscious and very beautiful example of the practice of the
tenets of Masonry, is displayed in the quick assimilation of the newly
admitted child into the fu:J family spirit by the children. They intui-

.. ..
1,)L

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

tively extend a fellowship that cheers and gratifies. They are exceptionally kind to each other. They sympathize with the lonesome. They
are patient with the slow. They are tolerant with the unruly beginner,
and forgiving to those who have erred or wronged. At the same time
they are keen in contests, active in sports, and most energetic to disp'.ay
a superior skill in all their Home activities.
!n this connection let us state that these industrious boys and gir.l s
are most impatient for the construction of the Vocational Training
building for boys, and the Domestic Science building for girls. As they
excel in athletic sports and school work, so should they excel in the
prai;tical work these bui!dings will provide.
Because of an unusual number of withdrawals from the Hom.e, our
number is about the same. Our last report showed sixty-six children.
We have admitted twenty-one and dismissed seventeen during the year,
totaling at this time seventy--one. A greater number of dismissals were
among the older ones, and our average age is growing lower. Norwithstanding the lower age average, we have but four children under
school age.
Our health record has been splendid. Our cares have not been
great. When a shortage of help occurred our children met the
emergency nice!y. Our inc'rease in per capita cost is remarkably less
than the increase of market prices. We attribute this to careful buying,
guarding against waste, and the watchfulness and thoughtfulness of the
children in cooperating at all times by saving clothing and supplies.
We deeply appr_e ciate the assistance and cooperation of dealers
among the craft, who render us a valuable service in timely purchases.
The teachers of our schools work with us like members of our famil y,
and our neighbors are cordial and friendly.
That the Trustees might know the compa rative sta ndard of the
schools our children attend, they requested Brother E. E. Knepper,
assistant County Superintendent o{ Schools, to make an unprejudiced
survey for their information. We are pleased to present his report:
"Los Angeles, April 5, 1920.
"Trustees Masonic Home, C9vina, California.
"D ear Brethren:
"In accordance with your request, I visited the Charter Oak Gramma r School and the Covina High School, devoting one day to a careful
examination of both schools. In making the definite inspection and
comparison you desired, I gave particular attention to the following
points :
"Organization of the teaching force.
"Amount and nature of supervision.
"Quality of instruction.
·

153

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALil''ORNIA

"Cooperation and team work on part of teachers.
"School atmosphere and attitude of pupils.
"Special subjects taught .in addition to the County Course nf Study.
"Material equipment, buildings, furnishings and school gt'oands.
"THE C_HARTER OAK GRAMMAR SCHOOL.-This school is situated in an
intelligent and progressive community, whose people insist upon and are
willing to provide the best possible school facilities for their children.
Until recently the building and grounds were adequate for the accommodation of the pupils in attendance, but the rapid growth of the
school will make it necessary in the near future to provide a larger and
more modern school buildiiig and an extension of the school grounds.
Happening to meet the Clerk of the School Board of this District, I
called his attention to these approaching needs and recommended that
he take up the matter with his Board, with a view of getting plans
under way for a bond issue. The district has an assessed valuation of
$1,509,225, and is amply able to bond itself for needed building purposes.
"The present school is a four-room building, with principal's office,
an excellent library, and a liberal equipment of all the accessories and
practical aids to instruction that belong to an up-to-date school. The
instructional part of the school work is in the hands of four teachers of
regular grades and five teachers of special subjects, the latter including
art, music, physical education, domestic science and manual training.
These special subjects are included in the County Course of Study, but
in this school are given an emphasis and attention that is generally
found only in the larger schools.
"In addition to this exceptionally liberal provision of instructors for
a school of this size, a certificated nurse pays a weekly visit to the
school, looking after the pupils' welfare, visiting their homes when
desired, and giving the girls of the upper grades regular instruction in
nursing and the care of children.
"The school is in charge of Miss Clara Thompson, who is recognized as one of the most capable grammar school principals in this large
county. She has her school and teaching force well organized, and the
teachers and pupils are all working in complete harmony and along the
lines of a carefully formulated plan. .This harmonious working ha5 its
reflection in the cheerful attitude of the pupils toward the school and
their work. They show a marked degree of · interest and application
and are making the most of their opportunities. I spent some time
listening to the recitations of the Seventh and Eighth. grades, and can
candidly say that, out of the thousands of young people whose class
room work I observe each year, I have not seen any who excel these
Charter Oak pupils in the sincerity of their endeavor and the intelligent
interest they take in their work. It is apparent that they are being
trained along right lines and are recei_ving the kind of instruction that
enables them not only to learn and memoriz.e, but also to think,

"The school is under the general supervision of the· County Superintendent, and a representative of this office keeps in touch with it by
paying two or more visits each year. Locally, the school has its own
principal to direct it, and is under the further supervision of District
Superintendent B. S. Mil!ikan, who is also Principal of the Covina High
and Grammar schools. As Charter Oak is a district tributary to this
union high school, its pupils are given advantages along the line of
instruction in the special branches referred to above. The ~pecial
teachers of art, music and physical education from the Covina schools
visit the school regularly and give the same instruction that is given to
the Covina schools. On certain days of the week, the large auto busses
of the Covina Union High school. take the Charter Oak boys and gir!s
of the upper grades to Covina . for instruction in manual training and
domestic science, in this way givirig them the advantage of the excellent
equipment of the larger school system.
"Viewing it from every angle, I can safely say that the Charter Oak
school, in its present excellent condition and with the possibilities for
still further material improvements, offers a complete and satisfactory
grammar school education, giving ample attention to all that pertains to
the mental, moral and physical welfare of its young people.
"COVINA UNION HIGH SCHOOL.-This High school is approximately
a mile and a half distant from both the Masonic H ome and the Charter
Oak School and its auto busses take the children of the Home to and
from their respective schools each school day. It has a teaching force
of twenty and enrollment of about four hundred. In organization,
material equipment and quality of instruction, the school is fully up
to modern requirements, and, being accredited by the University of
California, its graduates are admitted without examination to all the
institutions of higher learning.
"The buildings and grounds have the advantage of a very sightly
location in the town of Covina, and present a well kept and attractive
appearance. While the grounds are extensive and afford plenty of room
for athletics and outdoor activities, the buildings are at present feeling
the increasing pressure of a rapidly growing student body, and additional
buildings will before long have to be considered, especially in view of
the recent law raising the age of compulsory attendance, so ·that practically all eighth grade graduates will be required t~ go on for at least
a year or two in High school. The erection and equipment of more
buildings, which must of necessity come, will afford opportuniti •!~ for
adding larger additional facilities to the present equipment.
"The teaching force of the H igh school is made up of instructors
of experience and ability, and the various departments are equipped
with everythin~ that is needed to make the instruction effective. 'the
recitation rooms are large and well lighted, and in the furnishing of

152

154

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

the science laboratories, woodshops and departments of Art, Music,
Commerce, and Home Economics, no expense or pains have been spared
in providing liberally for all the educational needs of the young people
in attendance.
"A careful observation of the school advantages offered to the
children of the Masonic Home who complete the grammar course at
the Charter Oak school and enter the Covina Union High school convinces me that it would be difficult to find a place where better provisions could be made for this phase of their education and preparation
for lives of future usefulness.
"Very sincerely yours,
(Signed)
"E. E. KNEPPER,
"Assistant Supt. of Schools,
"Los Angeles County, Cal."

DONATIONS TO THE COVINA HOM:E

Donations are not regarded as a mere assistance in maintenance.
The value lies in the desire to give to the children something unusual
in supplies, c'.othing or visits. A professional or individual service
rendered is of much greater value than money could buy, because of
the personal and sincere desire of the donor to benefit the Home by
the service.
·
·
.
A much appreciated and very valuable service this year was that
of Drs. Arthur J . Ritter and Harold K. Faber in making the physical
and mental survey for the Department of Pediatrics of Stan·f~rd University. Aside from the great value of the work of the University,
the personal interest of the doctors individually in the children, with
whom they now feel acquainted., is of great assistance to those working
at the Home. The fraternity and the children owe much to these
good men.
Pursuant to the recommendations made in the annual surveys, the
most skilled physicians are secured to give special treatments and
~nake necessary physical corrections. The past year we are particularly
indebted to Dr. J . M. Dunsmoor, Dr. Nannie C. Dunsmoor, Dr. Geo.
P. Waller, Dr. C. H . Criley, Dr. L. R. Linhart, Dr. Robt. M. Dunsmoor,
Dr. Walter R. Crane, Dr. Eleanor Seymour and Dr. Chas. S. Young.
The operations were largely for removal of adenoids, tonsilectomies
and circumcisions. Treatments for corrective measures were all skillfully handled.
The dental care of children is an important factor.. The teeth
are kept in splendid condition, but more attention must be given to
orthodontal work. Among the dentists who have contributed their
services to the children are Dr. I. D. Nokes, Dr. H. E. Ransom, Dr.
.
S. E. Burke and Dr. W . T. Stover.
Among the steady, a'.1-the-year-round friends of the Home are Bro.
P. G. M. Hervey and his good wife, who' are always thoughtful 'of the
needs and pleas·ures of the children. Brother Hervey is always ready
with his time and good counsel, and Mrs. Hervey has a well' organized
army of good ladies who see that the children are not overlooked during
the fruit-canning season.

From the Department of Pediatrics of the
Stanford University Medical School
1920
The present report embodies the results of a survey of the
Masonic Home for Children at Covina, made June 24-27, 1920.
This survey included a mental and physical examination of all the
children :and a further brief study of the sanit ary conditions of
the Home and its surroundings. The report therefore deals with
the various conditions affecting the welfare of the children under
the guardianship of the Masonic fraternity at the Home in Covina.

PHYSICAL STATUS
The physical examination included, in addition to the usual
ro utine, measurements of height, weight, sitting height, nutrition,
systolic and diastolic blood pressures and pulse; a vision test with
Snellen types and a rough hearing rest with the watch. A special
examination for flat feet was also made and revealed a number
of cases of this defect. Sixty~s even examinations were made in
all, thirty-four of girls, and thirty-three of boys. Fourt~n of the
children had been, at the time of the examination, less than one
year at the Home, and . consequently had not obtained ihe full
benefits of th e Home. In general, these benefits have resulted
from a well ordered life in favorable surroundings with good food,
a sufficiency of outdoor activity and in addition the remedying
of physical defects. The nutrition of the children was found to

Our Annual Appeal
Don't send your invalids to California unless they have suffic ient means to maintain themselves, or your Lodge is able and
willing to support them.
By sending them without sufficient means, you wrong your
invalid brother and practice an imposition upon the Craft in
California.
Remember-it is just as expensive to live here as anywhere,
and burial expenses are higher.
Rem.ember-a sick man can't get by the Examining Physician
fo r the larger corporations, and it is of no use to try.
I herewith present a compact statement of the work performed since September 1, 1919:
More than 536 investigations.
More "than 307 telegrams.
More than 10,641 letters sent out.
And arranged fo r the disposition of 134 deaths, besides other
miscellaneous matters attended to on the spot in the office.

Ten applications cancelled during the year, for failure to repo rt
fo r duty, for inattention to duty, insubordination and failure to
make good.
Through the able management of Brother Fred Purdy, we are
pleased t o report one of the most successful years of our particular branch of Masonic endeavor. We feel that the Employment
Bureau is now on a basis where it can actually carry out and
perfect the purpose for V.:hich it was organized. More . and more
members of our Fraternity are corning to know and under stand
the workings of this Bureau, and by this knowledge they are
benefiting us, their deserving brother, and themselves.
For all this aid from whatever source we are sincerely grateful,
and we hope that those who have helped to make the report
this year so encouraging will continue to do so in the future. And
we hope, too, that the employer who has not assisted us in the
placing of our applicants in the past, will not ·forget to call upon
us and give us a chance to make good. And this, with alh our
might, we will strive · to do.
And, after all, the only practical help that one man may give
to another is by placing him in a position to help himself. T he
handing out of a paltry dollar may tide over the needs of an hour,
but that is all. It is not the truest charity, nor, in fact, is it vhat
the man himself usually desires. What he really wa nts is a job,
a chance to work, establish himself, and thereby better his condition. This is the work that the Masonic Employment Bureau is
doing. Will you not give your support?
All of 'which is respectfully submitted.
DR. S. E. BURKE, President.
]. M. DUNSMOOR, S ecretary.

PETITION OF ACACIA LODGE TO WORK IN
GERMAN
To the M .'.W.'.Grand Lodge of California:
The petition of Acacia Lodge No. 438, F . & A. M., of Los
Angeles, California, respectfully shows:
That Acacia Lodge No. 438, F. & A. M., was o rganized under
the name of Germania Lodge No. 438, and was granted its charter
October 14, 1913. That at the time said charter was granted the
right to use the German language in its meetings and in conferring the degrees was also granted to the then Germania Lodge.
That its original membership was twenty-four and that o n
Octob er 7, 1918, it had about eighty members.
That in the stated meeting held by the then Germania Lodge
on September 2, 1918, two motions were presented for adoption :
one, that the name of the Lodge be chan ged, and the other, that
the language used by the Lodge in its meetings and in conferring
the degrees should, for the time being, be the English language.
That both of said motions were then and there defeated.
That at t he stated meeting held October 7, 1918, said motioris
were taken into reconsideration and finally unanimously adopted,
the name of the Lodge being changed to "Acacia Lodge No. 438,
F. & A. M."
That said changes were made on account of the war then
raging between the United States and Germany and because strong
pressure was brought upon your petitioners by members of the
Masonic Fraternity other than those belonging to the then
Germania Lodge.

228

PROCEEDINGS OJ;' THE

That your petitioner desires to again us'e the German language
in its meetings and in conferring the degrees for the following
reasons: ·
I. The Lodge was originally organized by people of German
birth or origin. They in turn initiated, passed and raised men of
German birth or origin, who became members of the then Germania Lodge solely for the reason that they could then be taught
Masonic principles and have Masonic intercourse in the language
with which they were most familiar. Since your petitioners have
adopted the exclusive use of the English language the attendance
has fallen off, because most of the members do not sufficiently
master the language to freely converse in the same, and, what is
more disastrous, to properly work and give the degrees in the
same. As a consequence it has been extremely difficult to persuade
members to take offices and assist in the work and the work itself
is not performed as it should be.
2. The change was made under an extreme pressure from
the outside and under the belief that in case the change was not
made voluntarily, this Worshipful Body would force us to take
the same.
3. It would be inequitable to refuse the request of Acacia
Lodge and to permit other foreign-speaking Lodges to continue
to hold their meetings and give the degrees and lectures in their
respective lang.uages.
4. When the change was made from German to English, it
. was in the mind of all members of Acacia Lodge that said change
was to be temporary only, and not permanent.
5. That such a change would not only benefit Acacia Lodge
alone, but the Fraternity at large, for its doctrines and principles
could then be thought in a language which the members of the
former thoroughly understand; thereby making them better
Masons and more contented than they have been heretofore. For,
after all, contented people make good citizens, something this great
_commonwealth sorely needs at the present time. And the exclusive
use of the English language does not necessarily make ·one a
contented American. It is more a question of fundamentals, such
as economies, and, in our case, tolerance, because in ninety-nine
cases out of one hundred we of German birth came to this country
and became citizens thereof on account of either unfavorable
economic conditions in Germany or on account of intolerance hy
the then imperialistic government of our political tendencies.
Wherefore Acacia Lodge No. 438, your petitioner herein, asl; s
that it be granted the privilege to conduct .all of its meetings and

GitAND LODGE OF CALH'ORNlA

229

to confer all of the degrees ol Masonry in the German language.
Dated September 6, 1920.
Respectfully submitted,
ACACIA LoDGE No. 438, F. & A. M.
By KARL L. RATZJ!R, Master.

Referred to the Committee on General Policy and
Purposes.

PETITION FOR CONCURRENT JURISDICTION·
Eden Lodge No. 113 presented the following petition:
To the M.'.W.'.Grand Lodge of California:
At a stated meeting of Eden L odge No. 113, held on October
4, 1920, it was regularly moved and carried that E den Lodge ask
the Grand L odge to grant Eden Lodge concurrent j urisdiction
with the Lodges of the city of Oakland.
In explanation of this request, we beg to say that at the time
the city of Oakland annexed all of the territory lying between
Fruitvale and San Leandro, E den Lodge auto matically lost jurisdiction over about one-half of its original territory. About onehalf of the petitions now received by Eden Lodge come from this
territory, and the greater number of these petitioners give as their
reasons for applying to Eden Lodge that all of their business and
social relations are with San Leandro.
With out exception these petitioners have been freely granted
waivers of jurisdiction by the Oakland Lodges, as the · fraternal
relations between Eden Lodge and the vario us Oakland Lodges
have always been m ost pleasant and harmonious.
In view of the circumstances, we trust that our application will
meet with y our favorable approval, i}S this will do a way with the
necessity of the continual asking for waivers of 'jurisdiction.
This matter has been taken up with the various Lodges of
Oakland and we are led to believe there is n o · objection on their
part to Eden Lodge making this application.

By order of the Lodge.

GEO. J. HELMS, Secretary.

It appears that a very large majority of the Masonic Fraternity of this jurisdiction have no real idea as to what the Masonic
Homes are and what they are accomplishing, and it is practically
impossible for many of the brethren to visit our Home 'for the
elderly at Decoto, Alameda county, or the Home for the children
at Covina, Los Angeles county. Hence, by and with the consent
of the officers of the Grand Lodge, it was decided to have moving
picture films made of both Homes, and the same to be exhibited
in the Lodge rooms of the subordinate Lodges of this jurisdiction.

The committee laid out a plan, dividing our jurisdiction into
zones, so that the films could pe moved from one Lodge room to
another without any very serious delay. It was anticipated that
when the pictures were shown in the various Lodge rooms, some
one would accompany them who would deliver an address on
the value and function of the Homes. However, acting under the
suggestion of our Grand Master, no action has been taken towards
exhibiting t~ese pictures until the meeting of the Grand Lodge,
when it· was decided that a pre-view of the films would be shown
to the members.
The pictures of the Covina Home were taken under the direction of the Endowment Committee l;>y the Robert Brunton Studios
of Lo·s Angeles, the present officers of which are members of the
Fraternity, and who performed all of the work, making no charge
of any kind for the service rendered. The pictures of the Decoto
Home were taken under the direction of the Trustees of the
Masonic Homes.
Your committee presents this rather unsatisfactory report,
feeling that we have accomplished very little-if anything-during
the year, and firmly of the opinion ' that the Grand Lodge . should
determine if the building-up work of the Endowment Fund should
be continued. The moving pictures are very instructive, and it
seems reasonable, and your committee recommends that these
films be displayed in every Lodge room in our jurisdiction, where
it is possible to do so, in order that the brethren generally will

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON WAR FUND
To the M.'.W.' .Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on War Fund respectfully repo rt that pursuant to the ·order of Grand Lodge in October, 1919, and as
recommended by this committee, the ·sum of $55,000 was transferred to the Masonic Homes of California.
Grand Lodge last year ordered that the balance remaining in
the fund be administered according to the rules and regulations
relative thereto adopted in 1918, and pursuant thereto a number of
soldiers and their families ·r.eceived relief to the amount of
$920.58, and one reimbursement o f $100.00 was received.
The balance in the fund is now $5,619.56.
Your committee is of opinion that no further good can be .
accompli.shed by· any longer keeping this Wa r Fund as such, and
w.e recommend that the entire . balance be transfe1'red to the
Emergency Relief Fund.
WILLIAM RHOD:ES H:ERV:EY,
THOMAS J. BAKER,
.JOHN WHICHER,

Committee.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON RETURNS·
Past Master Harry Wheeler, chairman of the Com~it­
tee on Returns of Lodges, presented the following report,
which, after amendment, was adopted:
To the M.' .W.'.Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Returns has examined the returns of the
subordinate Lodges of this jurisdiction for the fiscal year ending
July 31, 1920.
It is most gratifying to note that the re turns fo r this year
show careful and painstaking work on the part of the officers
entrusted with this important duty.
With one exception they were in the hands of our Grand Secretary on time, and were substantially correct.
The returns of Loyalton Lodge No. 359 have not been received, and up to within a very few days the officers have failed
to respon d to repeated admonitions from o ur Grand Secretary.
On October 6th a letter was received from brother W. H. Duncan,
Master of the Lodg~, which reco unts their difficulties and bears
a promise of better compliance in future.
This condition confronts your committee. The officers of this
Lodge do not seem to have any conception of the responsibiHty
they assumed when they accepted office, nor do they exercise
common courtesy in answering letters from the Grand Secretary.
They show an apathy not to be tolerated. We are mi~dful of
the hard conditions that confront small Lodges situated in thinly
populated districts, but their delinquency is exasperating wlie~ . it
becomes a fixed . habit as it appears to be in this case.
·
However, in view of the difficult situation ·. ~o~fr.onting
Loyalton Lodge and of the promises contained in the letter. fr.om
t~e. Mas~er, we recommend that Loyalton Lodge be given a
limited time to jorward the returns and dues to the G~and
Secretary.

W. Albert E. Boynton, Past Master of Oroville Lodge
No. 103, then delivered his ·a nnual oration, as follows: '
Most Worshipful Grand Master and Brethren of the Grand Lodge :

In keeping with 'our custom, we have gathered to discuss the
principles . and ideals
Masonry, and to learn something of the
history and achievements of our Institution.

of

It is, or' course, impossible within the time allotted to trace the
his't ory of Masonry o'r . even partially enumerate its achievements.
Inste;id of _appealing to your emotions and rejoicing with you this
morning over the past glories and deeds of our Order, I would rather
appeal to your intet ·ect, for this is a time when our thoughts must be
true if our acts are to be right.

The world is in a state of flux ; forms of government are undergoing
radical changes ; the habits and practices of men are being thrown, by
the hurricane of mental turmoil, from their beafen paths. Our future
course must, therefore, b.e guid~d by steady hands, and steered by
the compass of reason.
"Masonry is a permanent ·institution, and although empires and
kingdoms have been overthrown, and changes and revolutions have
taken pla~e in governments and in society since their beginning, yet
Masonry still li.ves-yea, it has today a living, vital existence, and
will continue to exist as long· as time shall be."
The development of }rfasonry is the development of humanity,
for no organization can be greater than the individuals who constitute
'it.·· It was not intended that we should be separate private persons.
but rather parts making up the great body of society. The wonderful
achievements of Masonry in the past are the result of the· cooperation
and united efforts of all its members, and what Masonry achieves in
·the future will · depend almost · entirely' upon the aims and deeds of
individual · members, · acting not as single units, but collectively and
with a common purpose.
·

248

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF CALU.'OHNIA

Therefore, in working for the continued success of our great
Order, I believe that the causes which . will contribute to that success
are the same causes that make possible the deyelopment of the highest
order of individual achievement, the very foun.d ation stones of which
are the hom6, the school, industry and individual character.
As I have said, the wor!d is in flux, and ,if we would come
through tlie h'eat of passion ' and the destroying ' vapors 10{ h'ate' and
venom that have made the world a seething caldron, we must fight
to maintafo the fundamental princip'es of virtue, honesty, industry and
simplicity, which form the basis for all the real developments and
achievements of man. These principles are best incukated in the home
and taught in the school, and they can best be practiced and exemplified in real and honest work, and thereby there will be developed that
character of i;1dividuals that ~i I not only sustain us through the
critical period of our country's history, but will also sustain· and ·
maintain the truest and best ideals of Masonry.
The home is the workshop of character_ If. we take a tiny plant
and twist or bend its stem and maintain this pressure until. that plant
reaches maturity, it will be dwarfed and crooked forever. So it is
with children, for it is mainly in the home that the heart is opened,
the hahits are formed, the intellect is awakened, and character is
mou 'ded for good or for evil.
The social life of a nation reflects that of the home, for it is there
that the individuals who afterward form society, are dealt with m
detail and fashioned one by one.
The · home may be regarded as the most influential school of
civi izatibri, for as the respective members of society are well or badly
trained in' youth, so will the community which they constitute be more
or less civilized. The training of a man, no matter what his natural
views may be, . is inevitably influenced by the moral surroundings of
his early years. Milton says: '"The childhood shows the man as
morning shows the day." It is at the very beginning of growth' that
the germs of good or evil, virtue or vice, are first implanted in man, ·
and largely determine the character of his life.
The home which is the nursery of cJii'.dr.en ·who must grow up
into men and women, will be g-ood or bad, according to the power that
governs it. Where the spirit of love and duty pervades the home, and
where honesty and virtue are always present, and the government is
sensible, kind and loving, there may, we expect the development of
healthy. useful and happy beings, capable as they grow in. strength
of . following in the fo otsteps of their preceptors, walking uprightly
and contributing to the welfare of those about them.
Whi'e the influence of the mother in the home is the strongest in
the development of a child's character, yet we men are not absolved

249

from our responsibility, too. Certain vi·rtues are masculine in chafacter,
and they are best taught and exemplified by man. The qualities of
courage ·and aggressiveness against all forms of deceit and evil should
be exercised by the man; and the hands of the mother should be
.sustained and supported by his strength and endurance. T he father
in his home life can exert a tremendous influence upon his chi'dren,
for by such influence can be taught either a love for that which is
honest, true and wholesome, in all matters that make up their social
and industrial life, or it can create in the mind of the watching child,
ideas that dishonesty is profitable, deceit is cleverness, and falsehood
is more charming than truth. Furthermore, we should · study and
know our own children. Silent'y and unconsciously their individuality
develops and if we would be pals with them we must respond to their
moods and show at all times a sympathy with, and understanding of,
their tasks and trials. It is only when they fail to get sympathy at
home that they turn to strangers.
Next to the influence of the home in the development of the
child, is that of the school..
There is no single remedy that wil'. cure the many ills that afflict
Jur economic life like education. Some men who know better,
deliberately injure their fellow beings, but most of the sufferings and
trials ·that come to us are based on ignorance, narrowness of vision
and prejudice that could be dissipated by the light of understanding.
True education is. not mere book learning, but is the development
of our mental forces through association with the best in tel' ects of
the ages. Through· the .instrumentality of books we come in contact
with the minds of the great intellectual giants of the past, and by an
immediate association with living teachers and students, the growing human mind acquires that breadth of understanding and sympathy that mellows an<;! matures the knowledge acquired from books. In earlier days,
schooling was supposed to be represented by the three R's, and while
reading, 'riting and 'rithmetic are still essential, the true object · of
education should be to enable each student to think and plan and act.
for himself, guided, to be sure, by the experience of others, but primarily exercising that initiative and freedom of decision that is so
representative of Americanism. Our public schools provide the
para phernalia for training the mind just as gymnasium equipment
makes possible the strengthening of the body, but back of it must be
that spirit that teaches each boy and girl to knowingly choose between
the true and the .false, the good and the . bad, and enables each to
deve'op that self-assurance and self-reliance that will withstand the
winds · of adversity, the darkness of deception, a~d the downpours cf
bigotry.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

.We should unceasingly watch and zealously fight to keep our
public schools true and untrammeled avenues o.f education. Above
all, we should demand that the public school _systeni_- ~e. kept free fr~ITI
the contaminating influence of . th<: , professional . poht1c1an. Education
sh0uld a'.ways remain a .part . ·;;£ our, ~ecular governrpent, free from .
all restraints imposed by philosophical or religjous bel,ief~. and opi!Jions.
Children should be taught an absolute adherence to the patriotic
principles of our country, and a clear conception of .the• · rea~. rights
and privileges of man. Unfortunately, too many of the wt.d and
weird doctrines that are prevalent throughout· the world .today, have
been taught by some of the professors in our universities, whose
statements are given added force by reason of the position they hold
in the community.
Let us teach loyalty and patriotism in · our schools, ·in our lodges,
and in our pulpits. Let us preserve and protect those historic spots
which have become dear to the hearts of the American people, for
it is by this means we shall be able to recal! the past and impress upon
the minds of our children the richness of .their heritage.
We are members of a nati~n which gives its citizens the most
of liberty and affords the best .field for its development . .Is it strange,
therefore, that this nation is the one around _which ·the hopes of
humanity cluster? Does it not follow that upon our people rest the
solemn responsibilities of citizenship? Let us pledge ourse'.ves to
- abide by the Constitution and the laws and to seek redress for our
wrongs, real or fancied; only · in the manner therein prescribed.. "It is
a citizen's privilege, his duty, his glory to stand ·firmly_ agamst ~II
movements and efforts to weaken the force of law, to disturb social
order, or to tear down the Stars and Stripes and ·substitute the red
flag of Anarchy."
Let us, therefore, as Masons,· resolve to be better citizens, to do
our share in the great work of carrying on the National, State and
'.ocal government for the benefit1 'of ' all, amf in making that resolution
let us adopt the thoughts of Stevenson :_
···To be honest, to be kind,
To earn a little, to spend a little less,
To make upon the whole a family ha·ppier for his presence,
To renounce when that shall be necessary and not be embittered,
To keep a few friends and these without capitulation,
And above all, on the same grim condition
To keep friends with himself;
Here is a task for all that a· man has of fortitude and delicacy."
The corner-stone of a free government is the intel!igence of its
people.
It is our Masonic duty to raise the standard of our citizenship
to the highest possible plane. What are some of the characteristics

of a good citizen? In brief, he must not be afraid of hard work; he
must be able to fight his own battles and to hoe his own row. Whether
he works for money, · for love, or for ·fame, he must do it with all
his might. In whatever field he labors, he must do his best, bearing
it:i mind that no man whose regard is worth havin.g , will look down
on him. He- must work not only di:igently, but intelligently. Moreover he must be honest. No man can afford to be dishonest either
with' himself or his fellow man. He should follow the advice given
by f>olonius to his son: . "To -thine own self be true, and .it must follow.
as the night the day, thou canst not then be false to any man." ·
He must act upon the square. If he is a manufacturer, let it be
said that his product is built upon hono r. The attorney must be honest
with his client, the engineer must not deceive his emp:oyer.
The American citizen must be honest 'in his dealings with his
country and that country will protect him in the enjoyment of · life,
liberty and the pursuit of happiness. He should cultivate thfift, not
to save money for base or avaricious purposes; but to save it for
economical purposes. · The man who spends all his earnings is ever
standing on the brink of destitution.
One 'of the great needs of the world today is work. Only through
hard, honest toil can we solve many of our pressing prob!ems. ·
We live ' in ·an age of rapid thought and quick action. · It is an
age of constant struggle. No qua'rter is asked, none is given. We
hun·g er after power, riches, glory. We live to conquer, to reach the
goal· in· the mighty race for power and fame. This we call success.
Not so! Death is the victor. Success is but . the glimmer of a
moment, then we, too, pass on to make room for others.
Unfortunately for humanity, our own cares ·chiefly occupy our
minds. Our good purposes are hindered by many obstacles. We live
in -selfish ways, urged thereto by seeming necessity. T oo often do we
achieve success at the expense ·of others. We are competed by needs
that are our masters to lead lives little profitable even to ·ourselves;
too 0ften our motives are misconstrued and our tempers become soured
by ingratitude and injustice, and it is indeed rare that any human soul
keeps whole its U\)selfishness, its generosity, its nobility, amid the
struggles and contentions ·of a busy life. ' Yet what are-

250

251

"Wealth and glory, and place and power ,
What are' they worth for me or you ?
For the lease of life runs in an hour
And death stands ready to claim his due,
Sounding honors or hea ps of gold,
What a re they all · when all is told?"
To those of us who have always been under the necessity of _laboring for. a living, leisure .often a_ppears as a . priceless possession. But

!eisme is often like the mirage that the thirsty n:ian sees on the dese.rt .
when looking across the sun ~parched plains, or hke th~ pot. of gold at .
the end of the rainbow that mov.es on as we approach it.
From the time of Adam man has b~en enjoined to earn his living ·
by the sweat of his brow, and work has, therefore, through al.I the
·centuries been made a part of the price we must pay for happiness.
The busy man is the contented man, and, I might add, the heaith.Y
man. More machinery, both mental and physical, · as. well as. i;ietal, is
destroyed by rust than by work. All the great thmgs of 'life have
been accomplished through work. It is indolence that exhausts, not
action. Nothing is so injurious as unoccupied time. As has been
said, "The human he.art is like a millstone; if you put .w.hea.t under
it, it grinds the .wheat into flour; if. you put no wheat .1t grm<ls o.n.
but then 'tis- itself it . wears ·away."
· ·
· ·
While it is true that some men die of over work, most of th~m
die of selfishness, indulgence · or idleness. The efficient worker i~ hke
a well conducted machine whose wearing surfaces are separated by a
thin film of lubricant so that the power created is tran.smi~ted to the
thing to be accomp'ished without wearing out the machine itself. We
have all seen some individual who can work on day after day fo~ a
long period of time and yet maintain that calm and cheerful maen
that knows no fatigue. Such individuals have learned the art of
lubrication, for they interpose between themselves and the ~ne.rgy they
create a thin but effective film of interest that prevents fnctton, heat
and loss of power.
All great labors have been !abors of love and we should love our
work to do it best.
In the history of the formation of all great nations we fin? that
when every member thereof contributed of his brawn and brain for
its development that nation prospered and advanced, but when through
the development of castes and the belief that labor was fit ' only for
slaves then that nation went into decay. The story of Athens and of
Rome' is the story of too milch leisure for the ruling classes .. and the
development of vices which undermined not on '.y ·the character . of the
people but the very foundation of the State. Let us, therefore, fill
.our minds so full of plans for helpful service not only for ourselves
;ind our loved ones, but also for the good of all .humanity, that '.ike a
field of vigorous growing wheat there will be no room for the weeds
of discontent and the thistles of idleness.
The · forces of dis.i ntegration are at work in this country as well
as throughout the world. The vicious elements must not be permitted
to gain the upper-hand, and now as . never before, my Brethren, must
we develop individual character which shall save us from the
threatened dangers.
·- ·

Character does not mean intellect or learning, for some of the
most influential characters in a community are often men lacking in
literary accomplishments, but possessed of great moral and stabilizing
force. In the affairs of :ife or business, it is not intellect that counts
so much as self-control, patience, discipline and judgment. These are
all moral attributes and have greater weight than scintillating
cleverness.
Jn the light of great examples we are not only justified, but in
duty bound, to aim at reaching the highest standard of character.
This does not mean 'that we should become the richest in material
things, but rather in spirit; not the greatest in world y position, but
in true honor; not the most intellectual, but the most virtuous.
One of the attributes of character is conscientiousness. The man
who is conscientiou!; puts that quality into _his wor~ and his words.
He believes that whatever. is worth doing, is worth doing well, and
unless he has something to say, idle words are superfluous.
Reverence is another attribute of character. The real man shows
reverence for the consecrated things of past generations-for the pure
thoughts and noble aims of others. Without reverence there can be
neither trust, faith nor confidence in man or God, nor can we have
social peace or social progress.
Energy is one of the things necessary in the development of
character. Without it, there is he'plessness and despondency. Says
the old proverb: "The strong man and the waterfall channel their
own path." All great men of history were characterized by tremendous energy. Luther, Cromwell, Washington, Wellington, Napoleon
and other great leaders were tireless when necessity demanded. The
brave man is an inspiration to the weak, and history is full of examp'es
of the tide of battle being turned by the heroic act of a single individual
who would not recognize defeat. The same is true of ordinary life,
for the good and the great draw others after them. Let a man of
energetic and upright character be appointed to a position of trust and
authority, and all who serve under him become conscious of an
increase of responsibility.
Washington's exp:oits in war placed him high upon the pe<lestal
of fame, but the enduring qualities of the "Father of his Country" are
based primarily upon an honest, pure and nob'.e character, a model
for his Masonic brethren.
Each citizen owes to the nation the duty of maintaining in himself
a high, clean, moral character. His personal immorality is a detriment to the nation, yea, it is a part of the nation's immorality.
Teach the youth of our land to honor integrity, for a good character is a man's noblest possession. "It is greater than riches and

The American citizen must have confidence in himself and in

Let ~~ . be optimistic, koking ...ever forward, never backward. Let us

The United States has ever been the land of promise to the peoples
of the world. In the decades that have passed since the signing of
the Declaration of Independence, our country has. held open its arms to
the white races of the world. Our land is broad and although we
still have roon:i fo,r many millions, there is not. a single inch for. the

I do not deny the right of any immigrant, whose family' traditions
penetrate like toots into the past, to bring with him in his heart
remembrances of the· customs and practices of his forefathers, and

.
We must recognize that the question of any foreign subject immigrating to this country is one of privilege, and not of right. T he
United St<!tes of America was made possible by the delegation by
individual States of certain rights and privileges. Except as to those
delegated powers, each individual State is sovereign within its own
borders, and its people have the right, through their elective franchis~,
to do or not to do what seems best to them, as affecting their intercourse with each other, or with neighboring States. We have in the
past announced to the worl.d that the citizens of other nation's might,
under the conditions prescribed, enter into and become part of our
dtizenship. That privilege can at any time, if we so choose, be curtai'ed or entirely termin.a.ted, and no one can just'.y complain ·o f such
action. It is truly said that in the sight of God all ~en are created
equal, but many centuries of h'istory have demonstrated that in the
sight of man all races are not cap11~le of being assimilated. In the
O~ient are people who in recent yea.'rs have developed in the · arts,
sciences and commerce. We have always been glad to assist in their
development, not on:y from the standpoint of trade, but also in the
deve'opment of their minds and souls through the enlightenment of
edt:cation. But God has seen fit to draw a distinction in color between
these races and us, and while we look upon them as friends and
associates in the business world, we may rightly reserve the privilege
of restricting that association in all ~hings that pertain to our social
life, and in that we are like the man who chooses, from among numerous acquaintances, the persons to be guests in his home. The United
States is our home-here we !ive and move and have 01.1r being. Our
children are taught democracy and the thi'ngs that will make them
strong men and noble women when they reach that maturity which
draws them into the active affairs of life. If we choose to invite to
ou r shores only those races whose habits of thought, national traditions
and social characteristics are in conformity with ou r own, why .;houlrl
those of different habits, traditions and characteristics show resentment? What we deny to others, we do not claim for ·ourselves and

REPORT 0.F TH~ GRAND LECTURER
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California :
I herewith submit my report as Grand Lecturer, giving a full
and explicit accou nt of my services during the year just closed.
This has been without doubt the most successful and active
year in the history of the Grand Lodge. There has be.e n a tremendous gain in membership, the largest for any year since its
organization. Many Lodges, however, in spite of the vas t amount
of degree WQrk, have found and taken time to pr ovide entertainment and educational programs for their members. This has not
o nly been instructive and beneficial, but has greatly increased the
attendance, both at degree work and stated meetings. The interest
thus taken has been accomplished in a great measure by the persistent and untiring efforts of ou r Grand Master, and his Committee
on Masonic Education. The Masters' and Wardens' Clubs have
also done much to stimulate interest and make suggestions in this
respect, which I believe will have a beneficial and lasting effect,
and tend to make Masonry a g reater force in the community; as
well as inspire us all to practice o ut of the Lodge the lessons
inculcated therein, thereby making us better Masons and better
c1t1zens. There never was a time in the history of the world,
during this period of reconstruction and social unrest, when there
was greater need for this than at present. Hence now is the time
for ·us as Masons to justify ou·r cause, and practice what we
profess.
I have visited every district in the State, holding schools of

258

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

instruction, both day and night sessions, and have given instruction to Inspectors, officers and brethren in my office and ·at the
Masonic Club, all taking a keen interest in perfecting themselves
in the ritual, I have received reports from most all the Inspectors,
many of these reports giving comprehensive and minute details
of the financial and active doings of the craft in their districts,
and most of them showing large gains in membership.
I desire to express my appreciation and thanks to the Inspectors for their courtesy and valuable assistance rendered to me in
my work, and my congratulations to them for the splendid condition of most of the Lodges un der their supervision. ·
Many new Lodges have been formed during t.he year throughout the State. I believe that there is ample room for many more
new Lodges. ·This will greatly relieve the congested condition of
the degree work in many of the Lodges, and allow more time for
entertainment and educational purposes.
It has been my pleasure to accompany the Grand Master on
many of his visits. He has visited every district in the jurisdiction.
All of these meetings have been well attended and greatly appreciated by the brethren. The addresses of the Grand Master on
these visits have given the brethren a far different conception of
Masonry and the duties oxpected of them as citizens, and his hope
and prayer for all to be more closely united for the benefit of
mankind, and to spread the cement of brotherly love and affection .
My thanks are due the Grand Secretary for many courtesies
extended me in his office during the year.
Thanking the Grand Lodge and brethren for the honors be•
stowed, and the hope that my efforts will be approved.
Fraternally submitted,

Death is as inevitable as the dawn of morning, or t.he sha.dow_s
that thicken as· the sun sinks behind the w estern .horizon; yet it
too often comes suddenly and unexpectedly and brings a throb of
sorrow and anguish.
Life is the commingling of sunshine and shadow; and the
shadow deepens into glo.om for the moment, _when those we love
nd revere a:re laid to rest forever from our sight.
a
When a good man . dies, the people put on the habilaments of
mourning and recount the value of charact~r in the example he
has left to mankind. Our destiny is determined by the character

we build. "The idea of immortality, like the great sea, has ebbed
and flowed in the human heart, beating with its countless waves
against the rocks and sands of fate and · time. We cannot say
whether death is a wall or a door-the beginning or the end of a
<lay; the spreading of pinions to sciar, or the folding forever of

James Baunty Stevens, Past Grand Master of this Grand body,
was born March 27th, 1841, in Miami, Ohio; passed to rest at
Santa Rosa, December 6th, 1919, age 78 years, 8 months and 4 days.
He came across the plains, when a child, with -his father and
family, with an emigrant train, · in 1852. They were six months
on the trip, arriving in California in October, 1852. He was the
eldest of eleven children; five born in Ohio and six in California.
He was married to Martha Gordon, in Jackson, Amador County,
California, November 27th, 1866. He leaves two children, Mrs.
James Newlands, and a son, Harry Gordon Stevens, both Jiving
in San Francisco.
He was made a Master Mason, in Amador Lodge No. 65, at
J.ackson, California, June 20th, 1867. At the time of his death he
was a memher of Yount Lodge No. 12, Napa, California. He was
elected and served as Master of Yount Lodge in 1885, 1886, 1887,
1-888, and 1889. He was made a Royal Arch Mason in Sutter
Chapter, at Sutter Creek, California, June 19, 1874. He was made
a Knight of the Temple, in Sacramento Commandery, No. Z,
March 8th, 1878. He was appointed and served as Grand Marshal of this Grand Lodge during the years 1888, 1889 and 1890.
He · was elected .T unior Grand Warden of this Grand body in 1891;
Senior Grand Warden in 1892; Deputy Grand Master in 1893; anti
Most Worshipful Grand Master. in 1894.
For many years Brother Stevens held an important position
under our National Government, as Assistant U. S. Appraiser of
Merchandise.
His last years were years of illness and suffering, but his
energy met life's vicissitudes with an unfaltering faith in the hope

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA
PROCEEDINGS OF TII~

262

that "the soul of the righteous shall survive the grave, and soar
aloft to realms of life and light eternal."
Brother· Stevens occupied the highest station within the gift
of this Grand body, and his administration was one of ability and
efficiency, and was marked with the greatest degree of fraternal
kindness. Cordial, courteous and refined, a genial companion and
a true gentleman, his nam~ was a synonym of honor and integrity.
His voice is silenced, his place is vacant; he fought the good
fight, he kept the faith, and has been raised by the Supreme Grand
Master to the Lodge above, eternal in the he~vens.
A true Mason, friend and brother, he has gone before, and
will stand ready to welcome the true and faithful when our labors
here are ended. Our Past Grand Master is dead . One of God's
noblemen has gone. "How frail our life, how short its date."
While I would not dry one tear that is shed for him; while
l would not suppress one moan that breathes out the .sorrow of
those who. mourn for him, yet I take heart in the. glad· thought
that •in those things which made our brother beloved, in all these
thing.s he is not dead, and cannot die. May we be influenced ever
by fhe example of those gone before; may we learn lessons of
fidelity to friends, of convictions to duty and truth from those
who are not dead, but simply waiting on the other side the roll
call of the Celestial Grand Lodge, and the gavel sound by the
Supreme Grand Ruler of the Universe.

The first . school given him in charge was the Fairmont Primary; from th.e re he was advanced to the Broadway Gram~ar,
thence to the Valencia street Grammar, and finally to the Sprmg
Valley Grammar. The latter he held from 1876 to 1887.
Being of an energetic and aspiring nature, he felt that. in his
particular profession he was entitled to reach the very pmnacle
of position and influence; consequently in 1886 he stepped out of
the stuffy atmosphere of a principal's office into the open ar~na
of politics, and succeeded in obtaining at his party's convent10n
in 1886 the nomination for City Superintendent of Schools.
His election followed quite as a matter of course, for he had
hundreds of young voter·s who in. their school days had sat at his
feet and felt his prickly rod, interest themselves in his behalf.
He took office in January, 1887, and proved an efficient and zealous
administrator. To confirm this, I will take the liberty of quoting
Mr. George Beanston, the old-time Secretary of the Board of Education and still the acknowledged encyclopedia on city school
affairs. He says, "It was not within his power to introduce
reforms, but he had a right to make recommendations from time
to time for the betterment of the city schools. He made such
recommendations fearlessly, and strongly advocated their adoption. Some of them were adopted and some were not. This was
the experience of all Superintendents."
His restless blood drove him to aspire to still wider prominence. In his opinion he had not yet reached the height to which
he was entitled. Having established a splendid record as City
Superintendent, he could well afford to go before the State Convention of his party in 1890 and bid for the nomination of State
Superintendent of Public Instruction. The coveted prize came to
him easiiy, and at the following election he was triumpha.ntly
elected to preside over the public schools of the State of Cahf.ornia. He took office, and removed his domicile to the State capital
in January, 1891. As State Superintendent he was a member of
the. State Board of Education and its Secretary. As far as known
he acted in harmony with the other members in the preparation
of State text books. He did not, however, favor the assignment
of this work to the Board, which consisted of the Gove~nor, the
Superintendent and the Principals of the three Normal schools.
In his first published report he says, "It will occur to anyone who
takes· the trouble to inform himself that the duties of these several
parties in the positions which they occupy precluded the possibility
of their devoting that attention to the work of compilation which
its importance demanded."

"Personally, I regarded him as an authority on all educational
subjects."
At the end of his term of office he had reached. an advanced

a~e, and ~onsid~red himself entitled to a life of rest, to a dQ/ce far

r~tur.ned to this c.it~ and settled in a comfortable home. A splendid library, , contammg a large section of Masonic works, afforded

EULOGY, George Perrin Adams-Walter P . Johnson, Pa.s t Master.
George ·Perrin Adams born September 12, 1851 ; died April 4,
1920.
The attendants at this seventy-first communication of the
Gra!)d Lodge of Masons of California miss a familiar face. Gecrge
Perrin Adams, during a service of twenty-two years as Tiler,· had
become almo st a traditio n. Grand Masters. came and Grand Masters went ; but the ever faithful Tile r had become, as it were, part
of the eternal round of things. F ew men in the .Fraternity wen
· so generally known to visiting brethren, and his departure henC•!
on last Easter's radiant morn startled, not less than grieved · his
wide circle of friends.
'
Born in Fitchburg, Massachuse tts, September 12th, 1851, he had
tilled out nearly the three sco re years and ten allotted to man.
He came of that old Pilgrim stock which, daring all hardships,
established on this co ntinent institutions of o rderly ·fre.e dbm, and
created a system o f common schools wh ich is one of the foundation stones of our democracy. · He 'belonged to a branch of that
famous Adams family which furnished two Presidents to 'these
United States. and which traced its origin back to o ne of the
Mayflower pilgrims.
As a boy he grew up · in the soeial atniosphere whiCh ' prevailed in ·MasEachusetts when Longfellow, Lowell, Whittier, b 'liver
Wendell Holmes, William Lloyd Garriso n and Werideii ' Phillips
were in their prime: A lad verging on his teeris at tlie · outb'reak
of the Civil w ar, his character began to be mou l'ded by· tlie ci~ter­
mination and elevation of spirit which animated the people of
Massachusetts in the great struggle to rid the Union of the curse
of slavery. And in this' environment he grew toward manhood,
earnest yet fun -loving, persistent · without bluster, kindly but not
complaisant.

268

PHOCEEDHIOS m' 'l'IIF.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

In his twenty-first year he left his natiye State and came by
way of Panama to California, arriving in San Francisco November
13th, 1871. He first entered the postal service and later became
for several years connected with the Land Department of the
Southern Pacific railroad ..
His Masonic career began in 1880, when he became a member
of California Lodge No. 1. In 188'i he was appointed its Tiler and
served until 1892. Then followed an interval of five years until
1897, at which time he was again appointed Tiler and served his
Lodge continuously thereafter in that capacity. for twenty-three
years until his death.
Neat in appearance, gentlemanly and alert in demeanor, genial
in converse, he was a man whom people found lovable. He possessed a fund of quiet humor which enabled him to disarm the
little irritations of life of their sting by .many a quaint quip or
amusing turn of speech. Always conscientious, exact and orderly,
he was a.ttentive and diligent in every labor, and was never a man
to put off until tomorrow a duty which should be done today:
And remembering him as he was, we bare our heads in his
memory, not because of any unusual gifts or accomplishments to
be recorded. He was just one of those plain. thorough-irning.
clean, simple-minded men, who make up the bulk of our beloved
Fraternity. Never would he want to be made to appear what he
was not. He wished only to pass for what he was. He was just
Georll:e Adams, and that meant a personage marked by a sincere
simr>licity-that sort of simplicity, of which the essence is an
uprightness of soul possessing a generous self-forgetfulness. Indeed, I think his distini.tuishing trait was a self-sacrificing loyalty.
He w;is one of the most dependable of men, a worthy citizen, an
exemplary Mason, a faithful friend and a devoted husband.
One of the lessons of life which he had well learned was to
burn his own smoke. There was no petty morhidness ahout him,
and he kept to himself his pains and sorrows. For months before
he died he was in the grip of sore bodily ills, but he continued,
uncomplairting, his daily tasks · till growinl!' weakness forced him
·to desiqt. Then. clear-eyed, s~rene and calmly confident, he waited
·that E;ister Dav when, as with the confiding heart of a little .
chiid. he slipped his hand into that of the Silent Messenger sent
for his release, and went to answer the roll-call in the Celestial
Lodqe which no time can close, and which to those worthy of
admission will remain open during the boundless ages of eternity.
Th,.re let u~ think of him lovingly, amid the spirits of just men
made perfect, known and read of all as one of our Masonic epistles

·for

269

w~itten, as was said by St. Paul in ·his letter to his little band of
fa_1 t?ful Corinthi~ns, "Not. with ink, but with the spirit of the
Livmg God; not m tables of stone, but in the fleshly tables of the
heart."
While now we miss him as the guardian of these fraternal
portals, !e~ us consider whither he has gone and take comfort.
H_e has Jomed the noble company of the righteous, and is vested
with a splendor, excelling that of the buds swelling into beauty
on that Easter morn when his spirit took its flight.
The Lord is good, His mercy is everlasting, and His truth
endureth to all generations. Return unto thy rest, O thou soul,
fo: the Lord hath dealt bountifully with thee. For so He giveth
His beloved sleep.

higher cost of janitor service, materials and supplies, caused the
Board to take action which resulted in an increase of fro m twenty
to twenty-five per cent in the rentals of the "'Masonic Lodges and
other bodies who are tenants of the building.
We are pleased to point to the fact that if the interest charges
on our loan were eliminated a profit of over $1 ,000.00 per month
would have been made this year.
The Board of Directors for the past ten years has held monthly
meetings for the purpose of giving every possible attention to the
business of the Association and the needs of the Temple, and we
feel that our best efforts have been put forth to conserve the
interests of this Grand Lodge and the stockholders of the Temple
Association.
In accordance with the evident desirability of reducing oiir
mortgaged indebtedness at the earliest possible m omen t, we ijµggest t.hat the Grand Lodge again appropriate funds for the , purchase of stock in the Temple Association in such. substantial
amount as it can afford.
Fraternally submitted,
MASONIC TEMPU: ASSOCIATION OF CALIFORNIA.

To the M.".W.".Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Grievances, to whom has been referred

In the opinion of your committee, the charges in this case are
not drawn in conformity with sect ion 190 of the Constitution,
which provides that the charges shall set forth with clearness
and precision (among other th ings) the plate where the offense
was committed. In this case the charge fails to state where the
alleged offense was committed, and due objection was made to
the sufficiency of the charg1e in th is respect and overruled by the
Master, and the trial proceeded and the accused found guilty.
Your committee is of the opinion that some attempt must be
made to follo~ our Constitution in the preparation of charges
against brother Masons, and that the ruling complained of was
reversible error. It therefore becomes unnecessary to pass upon
the other questions. But for the guidance of the Lodge in the
future trial of this case, we would state that we have considered

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON GENERAL POLICY
AN D P U RPOSES
To the M.'.W.'.Grand Lodge of California :
Masonic Service Association.-Y our Committee on General
Policy and Purposes has given careful consideration to the resolution by Past Grand Master William Rhodes Hervey, introduced
at our last Annual Communication, approving the constitution of
the Masonic Service Association of the United States, and recommending that the Grand Lodge of California join su.ch .association. We have also in connection with. and necessary to such
consideration. carefully examined the proceedings of the first
triennial meeting of this association, held at Cedar Rapids, Iowa,
in November of fast year.
Our consideration of the subject and of the aim~ and purposes
· of the Association has been greatly helped by communications
from the distinguished brethren who may justly be said to be the
fathers and sponsors of the idea, and particularly were we enlightened and edified by the opportunity of meeting with these brethren
personally, and learning from them at fi rst hand their views and
their aspirations.
At the outset, wc conceive that it would not be amiss for the
Grand Lodge to know just what this Association is or purports to
be. Generally, it is an Association composed of the representatives of the various Grand Jurisdictions of the United States, intending now to meet annually, and having for its expressed purpose
two main and special aims and other general ambitious aspirations.
The Association had its genesis in the real or fancied needs for
distinctively Masonic relief work which arose out of the emergencies of war, and so impressed Were the brethren who formed this

286

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Association with .the necessity for a nationally-administered relief
work, that they believed the time was ripe for such an organization as this which would have for one of its main purposes a
nati~nal fun,d, and a national organization to distribute _that fund
in situations of dire emergency.
The second main p_urpose is the dissemination of what is
generally termed Masonic knowledge, and this, it is conceived, can
best be done by a national organization.
Your committee has not been able t.o reach a unanimous conclusion as to- the advisability of identifying ourselves with this
organization, or of definitely refusing so to do. It has therefore
seemed better to allow another twelve months for observation of
the organization and its workings, as well as to give the same
opportunity to . further work out our own State plan of Masonic
education.
If such observation of the workings of the Association at first
hand could be obtained we are of the opinion that we could more
inte.llig_ently decide at 'our next Ann~al Communication whether
or -not it is advisable to definitely ally ourselves with the National
Association.
We t.herefore recommend that the decision of this Grand
Jurisdic~ion be held in. abeyance until the next Communication of
Grand Lodge, and that the Grand Master and Grand Secretary
attend the annual meeting of the Masonic Service Association, to
be held in St. Louis on November 9th, 10th and 11th of this year.

amendment, especially as it is the opinion of the Jurisprudence
Committee that other difficulties would be encountered in_ -. the
effort to so amend the Constitution. We therefore m~~e no
recommendation with reference to the propose.cl amendment.

·Report. and recommendation adopted.

to the Lodge; but objections to such decisions may be· laid before

unanimously amended as reported.
Petition of Acacia Lodge.-The recommendations of t he Grand
Master with reference to Acacia Lodge, together with the petition
of said Lodge for the right to return to the use of the German
language in its ritualistic work, have been referred t o this committee, and it is our opinion, both as a matter of policy and of
equity, that no special privileges or immunities should be extended
to any Lodges or individuals under this Grand Jurisdiction, and
inasmuch as the privilege of working in their respective languages
has been extended and continued to another Lodge working in the
German language, and to others working in the French and
Italian languages, respectively, we can see no good purpose in
perpetuating this inequality, and we therefore recommend that
the petition of Acacia Lodge No. 438 for grant of right to use
the German language be approved, and permission given by this
Grand Lodge in accordance w.ith said petition.

Report and . recommendation adopted.
