REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC
EDUCATION
To the Most Wor shipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Masonic Education begs leave to repor t
as follows:
Pursuant to the recommendations made by the Committee on
Masonic Education at the communication of the Grand L odge in
1919, a plan in furtherance of Masonic E ducation was fo rmulated
and aent early in the year by this committee to the Masters an<l
Wardens of all the Lodges of this Grand jurisdiction. In the plan
it was suggested that the officers of the Lodges in each I nspection
district should form themselves into an Association and meet
regularly to consider . ways and means for the advanceme nt of the
educational program approved by this Grand L odge. In ou tlining
the plan it was stated that Officers' Associations would afford
abun dant oppor t unity for a mutual exchange of constructive ideas
among the executives of the several L odges in each district. It
was emphasized that one of our greatest needs is concerted action;
that such gatherings would draw the Lodges in a given district
into a closer relationship, a broader vision of consistent work and
a better understanding of wise a nd efficient methods to be
employed.
It was suggest ed that well-informe d speakers migh t discuss
some broad problem of the day co ncerning good citizenship or
human welfare; that application o f Masonic principles should be

297

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

made thereto in practical .fashion. The thought underlying the
plan was that each officer would carry back to his_ o'."n Lodg~ the
information and inspiration gained at the Associat10n meetmgs.
It was further stated in the plan that the Committee on Masonic
Education in each of the four sections of the State would organize
a corps of the ablest Masonic speakers obtainable to address the
Lodges on evenings devoted to the cause of_ Masonr! and good
citizenship. The necessity was urged for takmg the time to h~ve
addresses given frequently. It was pointed out that no more important work could be done than to give to _the Craf~ the broade~t
and most comprehensive viewpoint concernmg questions of public
interest.
A partial list of topics was ~uggested with the admonition that
particular vigilance should be exercise~ to avoid any quest!on of
a · partisan nature. It was also emphasized that under _no c1rcu_mstances should formal action be taken by a Lodge on any question
presented. It was emphatically stated that talk_s and lectures were
purely educational and should never develop mto a debate upon
which a vote was to be taken.
With this plan in mind the committee proceeded to a further
development of the educational program. It has forwarded the
work under the following heads : First, "Organization of Officers'
Associations;" second, "Forming Speakers' Corps;" third, "Top~cs
for Discussion ;" fourth, "Attractive Meet_ings and How to Bu1l?,
Them·" fifth 1 "Publicity and How to Brmg Out the Members;
sixth '"] oint Meetings of Lodges in Inspection Districts;" seventh,
"Ma~s Meetings of Lodges in Cities." Wherever Officers' Associations have been formed and a consistent effort has been made
to develop that indispensable feature of the work, a marked success has been the inevitable result. Quoting from the report of
the V.".W.'.Grand Lecturer, who has had unusual advantage in
scru1!inizing the situation, he says, "The Masters' and Ward.ens'
Clubs have done much to stimulate interest and make suggest10ns
which I believe will have a benefi.cial and lasting effect and tend
to make Masonry a greater force in the community, as well as
inspire us all to practice out of the Lodge the lesson~ _incul~ ated
1
therein, thereby making us better Masons and better citizens.
Most enthusiastic reports have been received by this committee from Masters and Wardens of different districts concerning the
effectiveness of Officers' Associations.
Lack of time forbids quotations from but a few of the repo,ts
received: An Officers' Association from one of the outside districts reports in part as follows: "Aside from th"e lectures given
us by outside speakers, the meetings are open for _the discussion

of anything pertaining to Masonry in this district. We discuss
ways and means, thresh out problems, debate policies, and as a
result we are all of us carrying into our respective Lodges a
clearer idea of Masonry, a broader conception of its principles and
purposes and a better understanding of what our brother officers
in the other Lodges are doing. Our Wardens and Deacons are
receiving a liberal education in the duties incumbent upon them.
For the first time in years Masonry in each district is thoroughly
united in spirit and in purpose as a result of this Association. We
simply could not do without it. We have talked of meetings every
two weeks instead of once a month."
From an.o ther district come glowing reports of the remarkable influence of the Officers' Association. Once each month the
officers of the Lodges come from a di's tance of thirty to sixty
miles to confer regarqing their needs. The influence of such
meetings has had a marked effect in advancing Masonic enlightenment and understanding in that district.
In this connei:tion it is only fair to state that owing to unfavorable geographical conditions there are some districts in this jurisdiction so located that it will be practically impossible to form an
Officers' Association along the lines designated. It is to be hoped
that no effort will be spared in the districts where an Officers'
Association had not yet been formed to effect their speedy accomplishment at the earliest possible moment.
Regarding the organization of speakers' corps, we are pleased
to state that our brethren have in many cases given most generously of their time and talent. · One of the problems in this work
is to secure a sufficient number of well-informed speakers, men
who are recognized authorities in a particular branch of research.
This is not a period when our members are satisfied with
glittering generalities . This is the day when substantial facts are
apprec'iated by members of the Fraternity as never before, and
the greatest demand appears to be for dependable information
upon questions which are alive and of pressing public importance.
We need to see to it that Masonic speakers thoroughly unders tand · the spirit and the purpose of this Institution.
It has been the experience of this committee that all too
frequently requests for speakers have been mad_e on too short
notice.
It must constantly be borne in mind that the contributions
of our speakers. are purely voluntary and that all demands on the
time of busy men must be made with the utmost consideration.
Arrangements for speakers should be made at least ten days in

299

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

advance to afford them adequate opportunity for preparation and
to insure an attendance which will justify the effort to be put forth.
Regarding topics for discussion, this committee has been
compelled to allow considerable latitude regarding a wise choice
of subjects. Questions of a partisan nature have been referred to
in this report and their undesirability has been emphasized. All
· good citizens, and especially Masons, should be profoundly interested . in all broad questions whose discussion will make for a
higher type of citizenship.
Regarding the arrangement of programs, it is vital that musical
or other forms of entertainment should be in keeping with the
high ideals we are endeavoring to develop. Respecting publicity,
meetings of the character suggested by the committee are of
intense interest to the members of the Fraternity and should be
properly announced and advertised. We deprecate the tendency
of some to give publicity in the news columns of the daily press
of such meetings, and suggest as a Masonic alternative that special
thought and attention be given to printed announcements, to the
end that the form and substance may be interesting and attractive,
hereby attaining the desired purpose.
cannot too strongly
recommend the value of joint meetings of Lodges, that each member may receive full benefit therefrom. In the larger centers mass
meetings have produced remarkable interest and created a fine
spirit among the members of the Craft.
. · This committee desires to acknowledge the wonderful impetus
given to the work this year by the untiring efforts of the Most
Worshipful Grand Master. It is due largely to his zeal and vision
that substantial progress has been made in bringing {nto definite
shape the educational program. The effectiveness of any program
adopted by this Grar.d Lodge will in large measures depend upon
the active support of the Grand Master.
Your committee desires to make the following recommendations:
1. That the present form of organization of this committe.e be ·
continued.
2. That efforts be made to enlist the co-operation of every
Lodge in this Grand Jurisdiction.
3. That Lodges be encouraged to execute constructive programs initiated by themselves, and that each Lodge be requested
to report the details of programs to this committee, that other
Lodges may benefit' by their a·ctivities.
4. That Masters develop the latent talent in their Lodges by
the introduction of short discussions.

5. That a correspondence lecture course be outlined for the
benefit of isolated Lodges.
6. That the committee co-operate with all the Lodges in
suggesting subjects and supplying speakers.
7. That the organization of Officers' Associations be continued throughout the State.
8. That an adequate appropriation be made for the work of
this committee.
Respectfully submitted,

DIRECTIONS TO COMMITTEE ON MASONIC
EDUCATION
Whereas, The work of the Committee on Masonic Education
was re-organized and enlarged at our seventieth annual communication held in October of 1919, and one thousand dollars appropriated for the purpose of its enlarged work, which work was, by
the report of such committee, to be prosecuted with two aims:
first, to create "a better understanding of the basic principles for
which this Institution stands," and second, "the practical application of those principles to the great problems of the day;" and
Whereas, There is absolute need among our Lodges and the
Craft for education that will create a better understanding of its
basic principles for which this Institution stands, as well as education that wil1 inform our brethren on the moral, social and
economic questions of the day; and
Whereas, There has been a tendency in the educational meetings that have been held to dwell too much upon the evils of
anarchy, Bolshevism and socialism, questions that are not necessary to be impressed upon Masons, who are good and true men,
haters of anarchy and lovers of their country; and
Whereas, Our records do not show that after one year of
such speeches and mass meetings there has been an appreciable
increase in attendance at meetings where degrees are conferred,
which was a primary aim of this work; and

,'

300

PROCEEDINGS OF THE .

Whereas, There has not yet been tried, to any ·considerable
l'Xtent, educational wo~k that teaches of the origin, history, traditions, philosophy, ethics and laws of Masonry, which are matters
coming under the first of the two aims of this educational work;
and which if undertaken with equal spirit may arouse a genuine
interest in Masonic study and may increase attendance at Lodge
meetings; now, therefore, it is
Resolved, That the Committee on Masonic Education be requested during the ensuing year to so formulate its work, that at
kast three out of every five speeches delivered through its speakers be on assigned subjects related to education in matters
Masonic, as was stated as the first of the two aims of this
enlarged work, and in accordance with this resolution.

THANKS TO STANFORD UNIVERSITY
The following resolution was unanimously adopted:
Resolved, That the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons
of California, in annual communication assembled, acknowledges

Decisions VI and VII. We approve that portion of Decision
VI which deals with the matter of the return of the whole fee
for the degrees when the petitioner dies after his election and

3U2

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

\
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

before receiving th_e first degree, and with the matter of the return
of the appropriate portion when the death occurs after the first
degree, or first and second degrees have been conferred.
With relation to the $20 fee for the Homes, it is also clear
that the same should be returned where,. before receiving any
degrees, the petitioner dies. A more difficult question is presented
as to the remaining matter discussed in the two decisions, the
solution being in the meaning to be attributed to the word -"initiate" as used in subdivision 1, of section 41 of the Constitution.
The question is one not free from doubt, in vie.w of various meanings that the word "initiate" bears, and the particular conne.c tion
in which it is used. We have concluded that it may fairly be read
as meaning any one coming into one of our Lodges by receiving
a degree or degrees therein as distinguished from one coming in
by affiliation, and as fixing the conferring of the first degree received in the Lodge as the thing which makes the $20 fee · for
the Homes payable to Grand Lodge. In a certain sense of the
word one is "initiated" in a Lodge when he first receives a degree
therein, and we are inclined to the conclusion that this was ·the
understanding of the Grand Lodge in its use · in section 41 of the
Constitution. Under this construction the Grand Master was right
in holding in Decision VI that when a petitioner dies after receiving his first degree and before receiving his · second degree, no
part of the $20 fee for the Homes could be ret1.trned; and also in
holding in Decision VII that an Entered Apprentice from another
jurisdiction coming into one of our Lodges must pay such fee.
We recommend both Decisions VI and VII be approved.

Adopted.

To the M.'.W.".Grand Lodge of California:
Petition of Eden Lodge.-Eden Lodge No. 113 has p.resented
an application for the adoption of a resolution by this body, giving
it concurrent jurisdictio·n with the Lodges of the city of Oakland
over certain territory that it has lost by reason of the annexation
of certain territory by said city. The petitionor may have a case
in this regard meriting relief at the hands of this Grand Lodge,
but in view of certain provisions of our Constitution which have
not been complied with in the matter of application, favorable
action cannot be had.
The whole matter is regulated by section 92A of t he Constitution. In · that section it is provided: "No such resolution shall
be adopted except upon the recommendation of the Grand Master,
and after reference to the Committee on ] urisprudence and report
thereon. Notice of the application for any such reso lution, with a
precise statement of the boundaries of the proposed t errit o ry, shall
be given by the applicant Lodge or Lodges at least thirty iiays
prior to the commencement of the Annual Communication of the
Grand Lo dge, at which the same is to be made, to each Lodge
whose jurisdiction will be affected by the proposed ·resolution."
The application here does not sufficiently describe th e te rritory
to be affected. The resolution of Eden Lodge request ing such
action by the Grand Lodge was adopted Octobe'r 4, 1920, only
eight days prior to the commencement of this communication.
The application is accompanied by th e consent of on ly one of the
Lodges of the city of Oakland, an d it does not appear that any,
such notice as· is required was given to any Lodge in th e city of
Oakland at any time. Certainly no such notice was given thirty
days prior to the commencement of this communication. If we
had evidence of the consent of all the Lodges of the city of Oakland, lawfully expressed at a stated meeting, we might hold that
the required notice was waived, but, as already stated, we have such
evidence only as to one of such Lodges.
We are forced to recommend that the application of Eden
Lodge be ·denied, with the suggestion that a future app lication
m ade in full accord with the re quirements of section 92A of our
Constitution will receive consideration at the hands of th is Body.

.Adopted.

purposed or practices of the organization referred to, to render a
blanket indictment against any of ou·r members who may affiliate
therewith. Neither are we to be understood as in any wise expressing our approval of the organization or of its declared principles
or purposes. Fuller information as to the subject matter involved
is necessary to just action on our part.
.
If any individual Mason, by any sort of conduct or practice
inconsistent with our teachings, by becoming a member of the
organization referre·d to or otherwise, commits a Masonic offense,
there is ample opportunity and provision now, under existing law,
and in accordance with the principles of Masonic jurisprudence,
for his effective discipline.
In the ritualistic ceremony made available to us, the organization is referred to purely in a casual way as "this particular branch
of Masonry." Manifestly · it is no branch of Masonry recognized

• PROCEEDINGS OF THE

He reports that a Lodge requested a dispensation to hold
its stated meeting on January 8 instead of January 9, the date
fixed by its by-laws. Arrangements had been made with the Grand
Master for a joint installation of officers of this and four other
Lodges on January 9. The Grand Master advised the Lodge that
he had no authority to change the date fixed by the by-laws for
its stated meeting. ·Nevertheless, he issued a dispensation to the
Lodge "to transact at a special meeting to be held on June 8, 1920,
of which due notiCe to all members shall be given, such business
as would properly come before the stated meeting in January."
The Lodge had eight petitions and three applications upon which
to ballot, and there was other important business to be transacted.
Authority for this action is claimed under section 78 of our Constitution, whicb provides that no business of any kind (with certain
specified exceptions) shall be done at any other but a stated meeting, unless by dispensation from the Grand Master, as provided
in section 43. The latter section confers authority on the Grand
Master to exercise all the executive powers of Grand Lodge between communications. Executive powers are defined by section
9. The power to change the date of stated meetings of Lodges,
directly or indirectly, is not thereby vested in Grand Lodge or
the Grand Master.
We can see no distinction between the effect of a dispensation
authorizing the holding of a stated meeting at a date other than
that fixed by the by-laws, and one permitting in general terms the
transaction at a special meeting to be holden at another date of
all business that would properly come before such stated meeting.
The only difference would be in the designation of the kind of
meeting. The possW:iility of abuse would be the same in either
case. The members of the Lodge have adopte·d a by-law fixing
the date of stated meeting, and are bound by any action taken by
the Lodge at such meeting. It is their privilege and duty to attend,
or submit to the awards and resolutions of their brethren when
duly convened in accordance with the by-laws. They are not,
however, and should not be, required so to arrange their affairs
as to permit them to be present at any other time which may be
selected by the Grand . Master or anyone else. Occasions may
arise, like the one under consideration, where it would be more
convenient or advisable to hold a stated meeting at some time
other than that fixed, but we are of the opinion that the rights of
the members will be best preserved by adhering strictly to the law.
We, therefore, recommend that the acdon of the Grand Master
in issuing the dispensation be disapproved.

The report and recommendation were adopted.

REPORT OF RITUAL COMMITTEE

Accounts.-In accordance with the annual procedure, your
committee, through its accountant, Brother E. S. Valentine, has
examined the books and records of the Grand Treasurer and Grand
Secretary and has compared corresponding items and totals. Every
item of both receipts and disbursements has been properly entered
and accounted for by each of these two officers of the Grand Lodge,
and their accounts are in excellent shape and kept in an efficient
manner. The securities of the Grand Lodge held by the Grand
Treasurer or by the Anglo California Trust Company for him, have
been checked. All conform to the records and have the proper
coupons attached. The bank balances of the various funds have,
also. been verified and found to conform to the records. The
holding of Grand Lodge securities by a trust company saves the
Grand Treasurer much detail work. This manner of handling the
securities is commended.

To the M:.w:.Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Ritual, to whom, at the last annual communication, was referred the matter of a revision of the ritual, have
had the same under consideration, and beg leave to report as
fqllows:
As we understand the purpose of the reference, it was with the
idea of endeavoring to lessen the time at present consumed in
conferring the degrees, without, however, elim.inating any of the
portions essential to the proper explanation or elucidation of the
lessons sought to be inculcated.
With th.is end in view, we have carefully examined and considered the entire ritual, and have reached the conclusion that if
it is the desire of Grand Lodge to make any change, we believe the
following will reduce the time now necessary for the ritualistic
work, witl'!Out materially affecting its dignity, impressiveness or
continuity.
In the first degree lecture, omit the monitorial portion, as
will be explained by the Grand Lecturer.
In the third degree lecture, eliminate the history, as explained.
DANA R. WELLER,
WM. P. FILMER,
THOMAS }. BAKER,

U. C. Club a t Berkcley.-Your co mmittee has had under consid eratio n that part of the report of the Grand Master deali ng
with the Acacia Fraternity and the proposed Masonic Club at
Berkeley. Representatives fro m .the Fraternity and t he Club
appeared before the committee. an d the situation was gone intr
at length. Undoubtedly the proposed Club is worthy of encouragement and should receive both the m oral and the finan cial support of the Masons of this State. T he proposition, however, is

319

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA
. PROCEEDINGS OF THE

318

not much more than a vision at this time. No concrete idea of
organization has yet been worked out, much less a plan for the
raising of funds, or of even what is actually to be desired in the
way of Club purposes. The brethren who are· attempting this
project, however, are desirous of the assurance of the support of
this Grand Lodge, and this committee is of the opinion that such
support should be assured. We therefore offer the following
resolution and recommend its adoption:

Appropriat'on for Masonic Education.-Y our Committee on
Finance has had under consideration an appropriation in behalf
of Masonic Education, and after a thorough investigation, your
Committee on Finance offers the following resolution and recommends its adoption:
Resolved, That a sum not to exceed $3000 may be expended
by the Committee on Education under the supervision and with
the approval of the Grand Master, on requisitions of said
committee from time to time as needed.

Resolved, That the sum of $2000 be appropriated from the
funds of this Grand Lodge for the purpose of aiding the proposed
.Masonic Club at the University of California, such sum to be
available subject to the following provisions:
That an organization satisfactory to the Grand Master shall
be perfected, and in which organization the Grand Master shall
have at least one representative.
That plans for Club purposes and for the financing and maintenance of the Club shall be perfected satisfactory to the Grand
Master.
··
That a sum shall be raised for Club · purposes which, in the
opinion of the Grand Master, will be sufficient to warrant that
amoui1t appropriated will not be frittered away for useless
purposes.
Roster of Officers.-Your Committee on Finance has considered the advisability of continuing the printing of the roster of
Lodges in its present form. In addition to other information the
roster contains the name and number of each Lodge, its membership, Inspectorial district, when chartered and place and date of
meeting. It also contains the name and address of both the Master
and Secretary, as well as the names of all the other officers of the
Lodge. It is the opinion of the committee that the publication
of the names o.f officers below that of Junior Warden, excepting
the name and address of the Secretary, is not of sufficient value .
to warrant the expense of the publication. The expense of such
publication can be reduced by about one-half by such elimination.
All other information contained in the roste.r is considered pertinent. . The committee therefore recommends that hereafter the
roster be published in its present form, but that the names of the
officers of the Lodges subor?inate to that of Junior Warden,
excepting the name and the address of the Secretary, · be hereafter
eliminated from such roster.

Adopted.

Afternoon Session.

Grand Lodge was called on at 2 o'clock, the Grand
Master presiding.

Election of officers for the ensuing year being now in
order, the Grand Master appointed the following Tellers:
Past Grand Masters Burnett, Keesling, Murphey, Henderson, Hervey, Weller, Webster, Frank W. Mixter and
Jesse M. Whited. The election resulted as follows:

elected Grand Master.

elected Deputy Grand Master.

was elected Senior Grand Warden.

The Grand officers, excepting the Grand Sword Bearer,
Junior Grand Steward and Grand Tiler,. were then installed
in due and ancient form by Past Grand Master Charles
Albert Adams, assisted by Past Grand Master Bradford
Webster as Master of Ceremonies.
Past Grand Master Dana R. Weller, in particularly
happy vein, then presented to the retiring Grand Master
a sterling silver water pitcher and tray.
The retiring Grand Master presented to his newlyinstalled successor a Grand Master's button-badge, to be
worn by him and delivered yearly .to Grand· M~sters in
succession· with the injunction that 1f and when 1t should
not be con~inually worn, it should be returned to the giver.
And it was so accepted.
At 3 :30 o'clock, all business being now completed,
the. seventy-first annual Grand Lodge was closed in Ample
Form.

REPORT
OF THE

Committee on Correspondence
OCTOBER, 1920
By JESSE M. WHITED
To the Most Worshipful Grand Master, Officers, Members of the
Grand Lodge of California, and Brethren of this Jurisdiction:
.I submit my second report on Foreign Correspondence,
Believing, as my predecessor, P. G. M. Murphey did, that the
report of a Correspondence Committee is largely for home consumption, and as the form followed last year seems to have met
with the approval of the Brethren of this Jurisdiction, I am following the same plan in submitting facts and figures to you this
year.
The Proceedings reviewed ·last year dealt largely with the
war period. Those reviewed this year are concerned with that part
that Masonry must or should play in the era of reconstruction
and its duty to itself. It is refreshing to find that we are discarding
some old ideas as to the scope of our activities, and searching for
a means to put into practical effect new ones applicable to the
needs of the present. Perhaps the best evidence that the Craft
generally believe that Masonry should be united for the purpose
of working along the lines that some of us have been preaching,
is the formation of the Masonic Service Association, and the
support given it by thirty-nine Grand Lodges.
Acknowledgment is hereby made of the obligation we are
under to the Secretaries of tho several Grand Bodies of the United
States, to the Grand Secretaries of the various Grand Lodges, the
National Research Society and the Editors of a number of Masonic
publications who furnished· statistics and other interesting data
which are included in the report. One Grand Secretary stated that
some of his correspondents evidently were firm believers in immortality on earth, because he was still awaiting answers to
communications sent months before. The same comment will
apply in a few cases to questionnaires sent to various Grand
Secretaries by me, in an endeavor to compile accurate statistics.
l am pleased to say, however, that these cases are. few and far.
between,

"AFFAIRS OF STATE."
We are of the opinion that the meetings of a Lodge should be
so arranged that at some time there should be an open forum,
wherein could be discussed any questions that vitally concern our
immediate Community, our State or our Nation. "Let there be
light," not only in things Masonic but in all public questions.
While some people are like the Scotchman, "who is open to conviction but would like to see the man who could convince him,"
these are doubtless in the minority.
Our discussions should be along broad educational lines and
noti such as to interest ourselves with or taking part in partisan
politics, in the usual sense of the word.
Idaho:
It has become the fashion to sneer at the "politician." I will
not enlarge upon this. You all know that it is true, and you· all
know why. But let us have the justice to recognize the fact that
the man who aspire& to office and who is elected to it, is just as
good or just as bad as the man who elects him. The American
politician, the American officeholder is the reflection of tRe American people. This may not be a pleasant thing to think about s.ome.
times, but let us be just and honest about it and set ourselves to
remedy it. In so doing we will be good Masons.
· In short, I would have Masonry seek, in a practical way to
apply its teachings towards making good citizens.
He who prophesies in this day is foolhardy. But I will say
this: Great changes are coming as the result of this war.
Iowa:
We have often noted that while Masonry puts a good deal of
time in moralizing and philosophizing about the moral law, yet
when it comes to the matter of acting as a unit in matters affecting the public morality, it suddenly becomes hesitant,. timid, and
holds back for fear that if it took hearty action it might fracture
some 11-ncient landmark or break some · hoary-headed precedent.
Now religion and politics are vital matters of vast importance
in human affairs. One deals with our faiths, our hopes, and our
aspirations, concerning itself not only with this life but with tha.t
to come. The other deals with those rules of human conduct that
ena'ble men of widely differing tastes and temperaments to live
side by side in peace and in order-assuring to each one all the
health and happiness it is possible to give him without hurting his
neighbor.
So that when you say to the members of a vast fraternity that'
they 11hall not concern themselves with religion and politics you
are taking on a big contract-one well nigh impossible of performance. To forbid a great human brotherhood from participation in
such vital matters is like trying to drive out nature with a forkalways she comes running back!
•
In nearly all of our Grand Lodges we have witnessed the adoption of resolutions backing up the President, subscribing liberally
for Liberty bonds, contributing to tbe· Red Cross, accumulation
of war relief funds-all of which were, strictly speaking, political
rather than Masonic-that is unless we are· ready to enlarge our

and peaceable citizens, true to our government and just to our
country. We are not to countenance disloyalty or rebellion but
patiently submit to legal authority and conform with cheerfulness
to the gover.nments of the country in which we live." And so far
as this doctrine is taught and acted upon, even insisted upon, we
are upon an absolutely safe foundation. If the doctrine was carried farther and a thorough examination was made of every candidate for admission and if every violation of this rule were made
a Masonic offense, we would still be within the rules of Masonry
and would be a tremendous support to constitutional government.
Some of the Grand Masters, however, openly advocate state and
national organization for the purposes of regulating the affairs
of state.
Probably we do not sufficiently appreciate the fact that English and American Masonry is a very different thing from Masonry
in many of the Latin countries and in some parts of Europe. W.e
are not sufficiently well informed to be able to speak w,ith authority upon this question but it is certain that many of the insurrections and many of the revolutionary movements in those countries
have been charged upon secret organizations said to have been
either Masonic or quasi-Masonic in their character and so the
Order has from time to time fallen into disrepute and has even
been proscribed in those states.
West Australia:
· The time is undoubtedly fast coming when Masons the world
over must readjust matters and become a little more than a. society
which restricts its benefits of education and thought to its members. Exactly how this is to be arrived at will require very careful handling, but the writer considers that the principles for which
we stand should enable us to enter the field of reorganization, and
strengthened by our bond of brotherhood lend our united ;1;id
towards the solution of the many difficult problems which face
us from day to day, as a result of the upheaval brought about by
the great war.
AFFILIATES
We certainly believe that unaffiliated Masons in a Jurisdiction
are a detriment to the Fraternity locally. While we appreciate the
sentiment that a Brother holds for his Mother Lodge, still it
should not extend so far as to entitle him to all of the benefits
and privileges of the Jurisdiction, wherein he actually resides,
but stop him from assuming any of its burdens or responsibilities.
Canada: ·
There are numbers of non-affiliated Masons in this jurisdiction
which fact is not most creditable to our institution. Many of these
would be helpful members and a little kindly interest shown would
probably result in their becoming actively connected with the
Lodge where they reside. A brother who may have been unfortunate is not necessarily an undesirable.
Maryland:
A demitted brother challenges the consideratiOn of the Fraternity. The general ruling disfranchises a demitted brother; who
has never violated his vows, nor broken his pledges, but simply
has asked to be released from Lodge fellowship, which means really
Lodge dues. There is a weak point here in modern Masonry.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

AMERICANISM
We believe that Masonry should take an active part in the
efforts now being made to Americanize the large number of alien
residents of this country. The need for such service was demonstrated in the composition of the National Army. Of our own
knowledge we know of one Company recruited in California with
a numerical strength of 250 men that had represented in it fiftY·
four racial nationalities. We are "agin" the teaching of foreign
languages in our elementary schools, the publishing of newspapers
in foreign languages, and the colonization of certain sections in
cities or other political subdivisions of our country by any nationality or race. If tlte opportunities offered by our country are
good enough to attract people of other lands, they should be
entitled to enjoy them only by conforming to our laws and customs
and becoming an integral part of the community.
Albert Pike said that one of the highest duties of a Master
towards his brethren was to "Urge them to love one another, to
be devoted to one another, to be faithful to the country, the Government and the laws ; for to serve the country is to pay a dear
and sacred debt."
Alabama:
What does "to lead in enforcing the peace of the world" mean?
It means that the United States must first take the lead in deciding who is right and who is wrong in every controversy that arises
anywhere in the world; she must then assume the heaviest burden
in compelling the party in the wrong (or rather whom .she or
others decide to be in the wrong) to lay aside its arms and return
to the paths of peace, and if it does not, then to furnish more
money, more arms, more ships, more guns, more powder, more
dynamite, more T. N. T., more gas, more men, more blood, more
sorrow than any other nation. We hesitate to accept such a
program.
Let us not deceive ourselves, brethren. There are among us
thousands who, recently coming to our shores, have never contributed one thing of value either to the development or to the
thought of our country; whose ancestors never shed a drop . of
blood for the securing of its safety or independence; to whom we
owe nothing, but who owe us much; yet who like the fabled serpent would strike the breast that has warmed it. They would substitute bloody revolution for the· orderly methods of change provided· by our form of government. The.y would strip the industrious, the provident, the intelligent of the fruits of their labors
and savings and distribute it among the lazy, the vicious, the
indolent and the envio.us. They are by no means confined to the
ignorant, some of them are highly ·educated. Nor is it necessary,
even wise to suppose that they do not sincerely believe that the
methods they propose are the best. This is precisely what makes
them dangerous. A fanatic in an evil cause is the most dangerous
of persons. On the other hand, there is no doubt that many of
those of anarchistic professions are conscious demagogues. Together they make a formidable and threatening combination, which

you w1l!. Masons and .the Masonic F raternity should not and will

Maryland:
We as Masons, however, cannot live upon the past-the future
lies before us. A greater work is in store for us if we conscientiously measure up to our duties than anything the past has presented. Shall we measure up ? We earnestly hope and pray J:hat
we may. If we go forth from our Lodges, old members as well
as new, thoroughly imbued with the beautiful lessons of Freemasonry, convinced of the truth of the teachings, impressed with
the desire to emulate and surpass the record of the past, we shall
be empowered by our united strength to enable our country safely
to ride over the many difficulties, dangers and pitfalls that lie
before us. Masonry teaches loyalty and fealty to flag and country.
We shall, we must, have Americanism in every sense of the word,
for Americanism represents the teachings of Masonry as laid out
by our wise forefathers. Unless we, as a united, determined and
faithful band set our faces firmly against disloyalty, anarchy, bol·
shevism, or whatever the term applied to the foreign growth whose
seed is unfortunately being sown broadcast in this country may
be, a dismal, dark, discouraging future lies before us.

T.he foreign !anguage press, even though it loudly praises
America, nec~ssarily tends to perpetuate immigrant colonies. So
does the foreign language pulp!t and the foreign language Lodge.
f . The language problem facing A~erica is different' from that
lcin!;\' ~ny other country. The question has nothing whatever to
o ';\'It the advantages of knowing more than one language or
the m.herent superiori~y of one language above another. If e~ery
American knew American, then as many other languages might be

I believe the lonesomest man of whom I have ever read or

man in all the world is found. You will remember how Philip
Nolan, for some breach of discipline, was courtmartialed and when
found guilty, upon being asked what he had to say why se1aence •
should not be passed upon him by the United States, cursed the
United States and prayed that he might nevermore hear its name
until the day of his death. The court martial retired to make its
decision, and upon returning, the president of the court martial,
in solemn tones announced to Philip Nolan that the sentence of
the court martial was that his prayer be granted, and from that ·
day until the day of his death he never saw in print nor heard the
name of his country again. How is it with you today, my friend3?
Are you a man without a country? Is this land your home? Is
this flag your flag?

Victoria, 1918:
A Freemason, as a peaceable subject of the civil powers, should
never be concerned in plots and conspiracies against the nation
in which he resides. He should on no account, while taking advantage of the institutions of the country in which he resides, seek
to undermine them by seditious utterances or disloyal actions. He
must uphold the interest of his community and zealously promote
the prosperity of his nation. This present struggle appears to be
a conflict between internal nationalism and loose cosmopolitanism;
and peace of any enduring character can only be realized satisfactorily, when there is complete reconciliation between those two
opposing opinions.

Virginia:
I call upon each Masonic Lodge in Virginia to stand like a
beacon upon a hill, or a light-house upon a shore, shedding light
and luster and pointing the way at all times to liberty, which can
only be maintained by love of country, respect for its institutions
and implicit obedience to its laws.
If you love your country, if you desire that justice, liberty,
equality and prosperity shall dwell therein, remember that it can
only do so when each respects the rights of his neighbor and all .
shall conform cheerfully to the government under which they live.
The duty which I shall call upon you to perform is to make each
Masonic Lodge a center of light, out of which shal1 go an Influence
for cheerful submission to legal and constituted authority.

"On my recent visitation to West Wallsend, I found the supper
spread in the Lodge room, and onl~ consented to sit down when assured by the brethren that the room had not been dedicated. I found
upon inquiry, however, that the Lodge room had been dedicated five or
six years ago, and have written the brethren of the Lodge that other
arrangements must now be made. I learned with surprise that other
Lodges follow the same practice in. their dedicated rooms. The ceremony of dedication must not be regarded as a mere farce, but as a
· setting apart of a room for the solemn purposes of Freemasonry. It
renders the Lodge room forever holy; and brethren should regard such
a room as what it really is, a place of Divine Worship, for once ·they
lose respect for their sacred surroundings, our Freemasonry wi!l assure<lly suffer. To every thoughtful Mason the idea of a festive board
within the hallowed walls of a regularly dedicated Lodge room is most
· repugnant, and I trust no Lodge in this jurisdiction will ever again
offend in this direction."

BANQUETS
Masonry was originally a conv~vial Society, and the "Table
Lodge" and the "Knife and Fork degree" are almost landmarks.
Experience proves that refreshment is still a drawing card in this
present day and age. Unfortunately, in large cities it has had to
give way to the work of the "degree mill." While this may be
desirable from an econom'.c standpoint, still "All work and no
play" is not a desirable thing in any organization.

BIBLE
The place the Holy Bible should occupy in the Lodge, what
it actually is-, and to what extent one must believe it to be the actual
written word of God, still continue to be topics for discussion.
There are some very comforting thoughts in the Koran, the Vedas,
and Book of The Dead. There has been more persecution and
cruelty done under the guise of religion, and attempts to define
or enforce it than in any other movement in the history of the
world. Maso,nry should never put itself in the position of sanctioning or attempting to define for any man his idea of a Supreme
Being or the Divinity of any human document. As we teach by
symbols, so must we regard ALL the Holy Writings of every
religion.

BALLOTING AND THE BLACK-BALL
As there is a demand for efficiency in Lodge work the same
as in every day life, we believe that there can be no serious objection to collective balloting. We have been told there was one
Lodge alone in this Jurisdiction, who voted on seventy-two applications in one evening. While this condition may not prevail in
all Lodges still with the number of petitions now being presented,
some method should be adopted to take care of them expeditiously.
The automobile and a,eroplane are superseding horse and
steam, and Masonry must keep abreast of the times, particularly
when changes· wm violate no fundamental principles.

District of Columbia:
One of the most puzzling subjects for our deliberation seems to
me to be the course now followed in balloting on petitions. Under the
immediately preceding heading, dealing with the bulletin, I commented
on the lateness of the hour frequently reached before the conferring
of degrees. · First impressions are lasting. For the welfare of the
attending brethren as well as the impression on the candidates, degree
work should be attended by as many as can remain throughout the
ceremonies. Late hours for work operate to the disadvantage of the
fraternity, the workers, and the waiting candidates. If, while preserving all those safeguards surrounding the most important matter
of balloting, we can discover some way of saving the time consumed
in, say, eight, .ten or more ballots, it would be a big step in the right
direction. For yo11r thought I offer the proposition that where an
excessive number of petitions are to be balloted on, the Master may
have them all carefully read and then take a test ballot on all of said
petitions collectively. If a brother is · opposed to the admission of any
one of said petitioners, he may indicate his desire for separate ballots
through the medium of the black ball or cube, whereupon the Master
will present each petition for ballot. If, however, the ballot is clear,
the same shall be regarded as effective and applicable to each petitioner,
and the Master shall declare each of them duly elected.
Mary.land:
"Article 23, Section 15, be amended as follows: Balloting upon
proficiency for advancement for the Fellow-Craft and Master Mason's
degree may be taken upon more than one candidate at the same time.
In the event of five (5) negative votes each candidate shall be balloted
on separately."
Owing to the large amount of work before our Lodges, and the
numerous amount of time consumed in balloting, which becomes very
perfunctory, we believe that the adoption of this amendment would
facilitate the work of the Lodges to a great extent without detracting
from the dignity of the work.

THE ROMAN CATHOLIC CHURCH
In our last year report, we treated this under the heading
"Catholics." Our Grand Chaplin inquired; "What do you mean
by Catholics?" so we are using the prefix to show to whom we
are referring.'
Masonry as an organization has no quarrel with the Roman
Catholic Church; popular belief to the contrary, Both organizations contain "radicals," and we do not think that some of the
utterances of part of the Catholic papers are any more an index to
the character and belief of a large part of the American Catholics
than some of the utterances in the Masonic press are of Masonry.
When Masonry as an organization gets behind a proposition,
in order to be successful it must do so on the ground that it is
for that proposition because it is RIGHT, regardless of who is for
or against it. It is usually not good politics or practice to be
obliged to make a defensive campaign. Better let us make the
issue and some one else fight it.

In every country where the Roman Catholic Church holds the
reins of power, Freemasonry does not possess the right to exist.
Masons have been persecuted and tortured by the rack, wheel and
flogging, with the object of compelling them to make known the
secrets which were communicated when initiated. In some countries, not very long since, capital punishment was administered to
individuals who were violating the laws regarding the holding of
Masonic meetings.
Pope Plus IX. in his "Syllabus," denounced and accursed all
Masons, and prohibited all Catholics from associating with members of this institution. The Odd Fellows, Knights o f Pythias,
Sons of Temperance, Junior Order of Mechanics and every other
patriotic o rder, is included in this malediction of the Pope.
Pope Pius X. was in unison with his predecessors from
Clement XII. in 1738, to Pope Leo XIII. in 1890, who condemned
Masons as anti-Christian and immoral, and pronounced excommunication against · Catholics who should become members. One
of the most orthodox 1Catholic papers, and the official organ of
the Archbishop of Chicago, says, "As compared w ith the real
Freemasonry, and the occult degrees of the Blackhand Society of
the Italian Mafia, the Blackhand Bandits are simply robbers and
demand •only money, but the Masons demand that you dethrone
God from the hearts and minds of all." All t he members of the
nameless degrees are atheists. The Catholic Church authorities
have never expressed doubt that the influence of the Masonic
Craft is baneful, and direct antagonism to citizenship.
The Review, another prominent Catholic paper, says, "Why
doesn't somebody in Congress introduce and pass a bill to investigate and destroy these Masonic Orders and other secret societies?"
The probable reason why it is not done is because no such bill
could be passed. Pope Clement XII. prohibited his subjects under
penalty of death fro m becoming affiliated with, or from assisting
at an assembly of Freemasonry, or to render any aid, succor o r
a retreat to one of its members.
In view of the many ii:icidents occurring of recent date, it
must be admitted that there is a bitter enmity between the
Catholic Church and Freemasonry, for though Freemasonry does
not concern itself with Catholicism, the Church of Rome never
loses an opportunity to vilify or malign members of the Masonic
Fraternity.
Iowa:
There is rapidly growing in this country a fraternity which,
while ever protesting it has no political ambitions, is none the less
filling many of our civil offices with its memQers and making its
influence widely felt in public affairs. That fraternity is pledged
to the promo:tion of the interests of one certain church. In its
eyes the state is subordinate to the church, the state is amt should
be merely the vassal servant and instrument of the church. Unlike
the Masonic Fraternity it entertains no scruples whatever about
mixing in politic$. It mixes, and mixes persistently. During the
war it mixed to such good effect that it not only compelled you
and me to c;hoose between contributing to a war relief fund, a
large part of which was to be administered by it to the glory of

24

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

a sectarian church, or of appearing to be a slacker, but it alsc•
persuaded our Government to deny passports to our own war relief
agents until the war was over, so that it might put us before the
world in the light of a charitable organization of vast pretentions
and little or no performance, all the while parading itself as the
only truly patriotic human brotherhood.
Now that peace has come we need look for no cessation of
effort on the part of this fraternity to enable its church to engraft
itself upon the State, to fasten itself there like a leech and fatten
itself upon the lifeblood of our Civil Government.
Shall Masonry still keep her hands out of politics-play no
part in making Democracy safe for the world-have naught to do
with the establishment of a brotherhood of nations?
Perhaps, as an institution, yes.
Nevertheless, thank God, there is no law in Masonry that
prevents us as individuals from doing our duty as men in these
great crises, and that is a privilege that can never be denied us.
While we may be denied the right as an organization to enter
politics for the protection of our country, yet there is no power
on earth that can prevent us from standing shoulder to shoulder
as individuals, and to say to the enemies of our country seeking
to prey either privately or publicly upon her sacred institutions,
even as did the brave poilus to the Prussians marching on Paris
-They shall not pass.
Ireland:
It is an extraordinary thing how common is the opinion that
Freemasonry is opposed to the Roman Catholic religion. We
know that a great many members of that community formerly
belonged to our Order. I had the pleasure of meeting three
Roman Catholic Judges-Judge Keogh, Lord Morris, and Lord
Justice Barry-at Masonic dinners on several occasions, about 40
or 50 years ago, before some of you were born. We know that
the Roman Catholics have seceded from us because they were
obliged to do so by the direction of their church, but many of
them have told me they would like to become Freemasons if they
were permitted to join the Order. There are thousands of Freemasons in purely Roman Catholic countries. Ninety per cent of
the French population are members of the Roman Catholic Church
-nominally, at all events-and still Masonry. flourishes in France,
and also in other Roman Catholic countries. In Ireland, at all
events, we are a non-political body in every sense of the word
and equally non-sectarian.
'
It is a curious circumstance that I am the almoner for the
Masonic Institution for Girls in England in regard to a Roman
Catholic girl who is being educated at the expense of the English
Freemasons in a school kept by nuns in Ballina. The girl's mother
was a Roman Catholic, her father was an English Freemason, and
their children were brought up Roman Catholics. I am sure the
cheque which I get four time~ a year is none the less acceptable
by reason of the source from which it comes, and bearing in mind
the spirit that animates the donors. It is a remarkable example of
the catholicity of Freemasonry to see that it is supporting a
Roman Catholic girl in a Roman Catholic school.

Vermont:
Correspondents from some other states are equally as outspoken and there are many Masons who seem to feel that it is a
special' function of Masonry to oppose the Roman Catholic Church.
The Catholic Encyclopedia, Vol. 9, at pages 786 and 787 and certain
edicts of the church, are cited in justification. No one should
place any great reliance upon these edicts, however, without reading the whole article on Masonry as found in this Catholic Encyclopedia, Vol. 9, at page 771, wherein they will find that Protestant
states were among the first to issue a ban against Masonry and
that at one time this was a very live question even In England.
The wave swept ,over the United States almost within the memory
of our oldest inhabitants and the present ,Vermont statute against
extra judicial oaths was the outgrowth of that controversy. We
carry no brief for the Roman Catholic Church, but any movement
on the part of Masons or any association among Masons which
seeks to get into any controversy with that church is an injury to
Masonry and outside the purposes of the Order. There is probably
something in the confessional of the church and some of the
so-called secrets of Masonry which render it best that a .good
Roman Catholic should not become a member of the Masonic
Fraternity, either from the standpoint .of the church or of Masonry
and there the matter should drop. Masonry is not seeking to make '
recruits from the Roman Catholic Church and the Roman Catholic
Church does not want its members to be Masons. While Masonry
does not solicit members on the one hand, on the other the spirit
of Masonry is deeply religious and we have no quarrel with the
religion of others; neither are we to forget that the Protestant
and the Roman Catholic Churches sprang from a common origin
and are both Christian institutions. There is altogether too much
groundless emotion on this question.
The "Literary Digest" of May .22, gives the religious preferences of all the prominent candidates for the presidency from the
two leading parties. Some of them are Masons. Not one of them
is a member of the Roman Catholic Church and, consequently, if
the nominations are made from these candidates the constituency
of the largest church in the country will be compelled to vote for
a Protestant candidate. If this were changed and the candidate
were to be from the Roman Catholic Church, we suspect that
some of our prominent and enthusiastic Masons who are so alarmed
by the growth of Catholicism and its hostility to Masonry would
foresee the destruction of the country.

Iowa:
For reasons which we have frequently heretofore given, we '
do not believe that a Masonic Lodge should, as a Lodge, attend
the services of any sectarian or denominational church. Nevertheless, there is much more sense in adopting a regulation of this
sort than there is in grinding out everlasting dispensations for
attending divine services. Such attendance is either a Masonic
function, or it is not. If it is, no dispen·sation should be required.
If it is not, it should not be permitted at all. ·
Nevada:
In Nevada the Craft paraded as citizens, loyal and true, and
not "dressed in white gloves and aprons, the usual badges of the
Order of Free Masonry." Today the Masonic parade is seen in
most jurisdictions only in dedication and cornerstone ceremonies,
but in early London Masonry processions of Craftsmen in gloves
and aprons were common, and we are told by Brother Gould that
when the small armory of the Tower of London was finished King
William and his consort Queen dined there in great form, attended
by all warrant workmen, "dressed in white gloves and aprons, the
usual badges of the Order of Free Masonry." If the situations
were reversed, and the days of then · were the days of now, what
,a howl would go up about innovations in the body of Masonry.

South Australia:
A rather suggestive and somewhat original motion ·was introduced by Past Grand Master H . Eugene Stafford (Philippine
Islands) (and duly carried) having for its object the introduction of
a suitable ceremonial wherein Craftsmen could dedicate their sons
to Masonry. In commending his motion, Bro. Stafford observed,
inter alia : "I am satisfied that those of you who have children,
especially boys, would appreciate the opportunity fo dedicate these
sons to Masonry. This is possible, and a ceremony can be devised
whereby a Mason could have his son dedicated, and have it done by
the Lodge of which he is a member in a public function to which the
family .and others can be admitted. The ceremony's influence
would last to the boy's manhood, would teach him who his father's
associates were, and would give him an idea of what Masonry
means which could not be g·iven him any other way." There is,
I think, undoubted value in the ~uggested ceremonial of dedication, even more than appears on the surface. South Australian
Craftsmen might do well to consider the propriety of following the
example of our Philippine .Brethren.

CIPHER RITUALS
One of the charms of Masonry is that its esoteric work is
unwritten, and it has htid a large part in building up the Fraternity.
The printing press and unworthy Brothers, taken in connection
with the action of certain Jurisdictions in adopting ciphers or keys,
cannot have other than a disastrous effect.
The Cipher Ritual is of course a boon to the lazy officer or
member, but this should not be an excuse for its existence or
adoption.
Georgia:
The menace of the cipher still exists. .In the various Proceedings,
from time to ' time, appear efforts to establish the printed key, which
we are compelled to regard as the direct ·violation of Masonic obligations. Some of the more enthusiastic plead for its use as a means for
more uniform ritualism.
We have contended always that Masonry is more than ritualism.
It does not require a cipher to perfect ritualism. If officers and
brethren will take the required time;, work can be learned better than ·
·
from a printed cipher.
Nebraska:
Notwithstanding the efforts heretofore exercised by the Grand
Custodian, and by Grand Masters, the persistent use of spurious keys
and ciphers continues throughout the jurisdiction to a considerable
extent, and it has been very difficult at times to locate them, but the
evil effect of their use is. very apparent.
Nevada :
Then follows a record of lost rituals! To the shame of the Craft
in this progressive jurisdiction. If there must be rituals, let their loss
be a matter between the losers and the Grand Master, and do away
with this lost, strayed or stolen busil!ess in the Master's address.

CLUBS
In the various proceedings reviewed there is not as much
criticism against Masonic Clubs as heretofore. From this we
would judge that they have not had the bad effect · that was
anticipated. When properly directed and managed a Masonic Club,
separate · and apart from the Lodge organization, is a benefit to
the Craft, and experience in California at least is demonstrating it.
Alabama:
Grand Master Woolf oracularly declared that Masonic clubs
'properly conducted are most excellent and can prt>duce most beneficent results, but like many other good things, if not properly
handled, on right principles, may be the source of difficulties.'
Aye; there's the rub. What is 'prope.rly conducted' and what is
'on right principles'? The Lodge should be, in addition to its other
functions, a club where Masonic entertainment and instruction can
be had. Other clubs furnish all the loafing facilities as well as
healthful recreations required.
Massachusetts:
During recent years many clubs have been formed, th~ membership of which has been confined to Freemasons. The primary
object of most of these clubs has been to bring the members into
closer social relations with each other. In some cases quarters have
been rented and in a few instances clubhouses have been bought or
built. I am personally a member of some of these clubs, and I
believe that many of them are well serving an excellent purpose.
There is, however, in my judgment, an element of danger to
the Fraternity in too great a multiplying of these clubs and in the
encouraging of any idea that they are to take over or become the
center of Masonic social relations. If Lodge meetings are likely
to be the mor.e looked upon as occasions only of degree conferring
and Lodges as degree factories, so to speak, then the club idea becomes a distinct menace to the effectuating of the true purpose and
intent of our order. If ~uch club membership prompts a less fre•

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

33

quent attendance at Lodge meetings or a less cordial support of
Lodge work and activities, then it becomes harmful and hot helpful.
There can be no doubt that in recent years due attention to the
social and fraternal relations of the members has been neglected in
many of our L odges and has resulted in a natural turning to club
association as a means of closer fraternal intercourse. The large
number of candidates now being admitted and the time and effort
required of the officers to confer the degrees have fre quently left
all too little time, strength, and inclination on the part of the _officers of the Lodges to properly promote the welfare and happiness
of the Lodge members.
West Virginia :
I have never been able t o understand why everythi ng carried
on in a Club could not be done equally well in a Lodge. If the
Club is engaged in research work, that can and ought to be done in
an open Lodge. If the purpose is to frolic, that ought not to be
allowed anywhere. As I see it Club meetings will weaken, and
ultimately destroy Lodge meetings. As I understand it, nothing is
allowable under the name of Masonry, except Masonry itself. Is
a Masonic Club a Masonic institution? If not, what is it, and
what's it for? If it is for social Masonic purposes, w h y not hold
the meetings at t he regular sessions and pull off the s tunts under
the head "Good of the Order?"
W isconsin:
Most of our lately-built Masonic Temples are provided with
clubrooms for the use of the members. I have been asked this
question: "Where a Lodge has fitted up the lower floor of it s
Masonic Temple as clubrooms, with pool and billiard and card
tables, is it permissible to allow games to be played on Sunday
afternoon?"
I replied to t his inquiry by stating that I could not find anything in our Constitution, Laws and Edicts directly bearing upon
this subject, and added as follows:
"It does n ot seem to be within the power of the Grand Master
to determine the question raised, but I have no hesitancy in giving
you my unofficial opinion on the subject and such as I would rule
were I authorized to decide the point.
"Page 60 of our Masonic Law and Edicts has the following
prohibitive law : 'No communication except for conducting a
Masonic funeral shall be held on Sunday.'
"Our Grand Lodge, therefo re, has taken the position that
Sunday is a Masonic sacred day. It has also declared that 'The
duty devolves upon every Mason • • • to preserve the reputation of the frate rnity unsullied. If the conduct of an individual
member tends to bring Masonry into disrepute or to injq_re the
institution, such conduct is un-Masonic and should not be allowed
to remain unnoticed.'
"I regard as contrary to Masonic tenets and t eachings any
practice by Masons in a building dedicated to Masonic purposes
which would result in desecrating the Sabbath-a day upon which
a Lodge cannot even exemplify our beautiful degrees-and I should
personally condemn as derogatory to Masonry the practice of
permitting games of any kind o n a Sunday in clubrooms owned
by a Lodge, or that are in any way connected or associated with
I .odge activities.''

CORRESPONDENCE
Correspondence Report3, if they serve no other purpose, can
be a "Thing of beauty and a joy forever" to the Correspondence
Committee of a Grand Lodge. They at least must read them.
It s .t o be regretted that the Reports are inaccessible to practically
all of the craft, being found only in the Grand Lodge Libraries.
They could be used more by the Masonic Press as a source of reference. If this was done, perhaps some of the extravagant statements that are given general circulation would be omitted. The
members of a Correspondence Committee by reason of their creation are given a great privilege in' being put in close touch with
the .thought of Masonic world through these reports. This more
than compensates the compilers for the work they must do to prepare them.
Colorado:
Record us as a most strenuous kicker when it is short-sightedly
proposed to confine such writers to bare reporting without com:
ment. Personally we learn more from the Correspondence report
than from business proceedings.
District of Columbia:
One paragraph, quoted from California, says: "In my judgment, the report of the committee on foreign correspondence is
matter for home consumption. Nearly 95 p·er cent of those who
read the report of this committee on correspondence are members
of California Lodges, and it is needless to say they are not vitally
interested in the small details that go to make up a very large proportion of the reports of the several States."
We question his 95 per cent, as well as his wisdom. Our purpose is to tell our "home consumption" in an abridged report what
the Masons in other States are doing. Maybe, if you had a quartet
of high-degree Masons who would whitewash the fourth degree of
the Knights of Columbus, we might wish to keep this dainty
morsel for "home consumption."
Florida:
As we conceive it, the Report on Correspondence is designed
to serve as a sort of postgraduate course in the School of Masonr.y,
and its p_urpose. i~ to. give the in~ividual Masons of one lbcality
accurate mformat1on as to the achievements and accomplishments
in other localities. For many years past, some few of the Correspondence writers have achieved fame as Masonic Jurists, both
interjiJrisdictional and local.
Notwithstanding a firm resolution never to deviate from the
landmarks or suffer them to be infringed, we find that Masonry has
taken many forms in different Jurisdictions; and that no two of the
States of these United States are exactly alike. We believe that
the Correspondence writer should point out the differences between
the various States, and in all matters where interstate law can be
arranged so as to be fraternal and just to all, that it should be the
duty of the Correspondence writer to use his utmost endeavors to
produce such a result.

Wisconsin:
Grand Master Clark · (Missouri} characterizes our brother as
not only the Nestor but the Agamemnon of all correspondence
writers. We believe from reports that Nestor was a "wise old guy"
and so Brother Woods may well feel complimented by the r"eference. We are not so certain, however, as to the allusion to Agamemnon, and fear the Grand Master may have laid himself open
to an action of slander. If we remember mythology aright, Agememnon after the siege of Troy, when the loot was being divided,
took as his share of the spoils a certain comely maiden, a sister
of Paris. Now this might have been excusable if Agememnon had
not been a married man. and would, no doubt, have been very
embarrassing when he presented her to his wife on his return to
Greece. She, however, had anticipated his action by having acquired a second husband while he was fighting his nation's battles,
and on his return, she, together with her soul mate, did what the
Trojans had been unable to ·do; that is, gave this redoubtable general a passage to the other world in short order. In what respect
does Brother Woods resemble Agamemnon? We leave it to the
Grand Master to explain.

prepared a report along the lines of a topical review and pointed
out what he claimed to be a superiority of a topical review over .
the form usually presented. We cannot a~ree with our Brother
Darling as to the method pursued being any improvement over
that usually adopted by other reporters. The method is not at all
new and has been tried by many men of superior ability, who have
been unable to employ it satisfactorily. One of the ablest reviewers
the United States has ever had was Brother Joseph R obbins of
Illinois, who for thirty-one years prepared the Correspondence
Repo rt for that Grand L odge. At the earnest solicitation of the
Grand Master of that Grand Jurisdiction, for two years Brother
Robbins prepared his review along the same lines. He did so with
many misgivings and after two attempts, abandoned it. In speaking of the defects of the system, Brother Robbins said:

concerned, the t opical form of report is very generally disliked,

deal.

Mississippi:
"Does the fact that an applicant for the degrees in Masonry, has
served a term in the State Penitentiary make him ineligible?"
I am unable to conceive of a Lodge in the State of Mississippi
where one coming from the State Penitentiary is able to maintain that
good reputation that is contemp'.ated by this Regulation.
Before a man serves a term in the State Penitentiary there must
first have been a grand jury to pass on his case, and of those at least
twelve members must have voted for a true bill; then he is tried before
twelve men of his own selection, every one o.f whom must say on their
oaths that the evidence shciws him to be guilty beyond every reason· .
able doubt, and to a moral certainty; then his case is reviewed by the
trial judge, and then, if he so desires, the whole matter is passed on
by the Supreme Court. The law gives him the advantage of every reasonable douht, and c'othes him with every presumption of innocence.
This Grand Lodge has always held that a bastard can not be made
a Mason ; and the n1ajority opinion, if adopted, will place the Grand
Lodge in the extremely inconsistent position of holding that being a
bastard (for which the petitioner is in no wise personally or morally
responsible) is a disqua'.ification, while being an ex-convict (for which
he is solely responsible) is not a disqualification.
I certainly think that Masonry would suffer infinitely less from
the few good men (exceedingly few) who might be kept out, than it
would from the reproach that would surely come from opening Its
r!oors to ex-convicts; and therefore I must dissent from the majority
npinion.

41

Our brother's logic is faulty here and this is one of the subiects on which . we expect to see him change his views as time goes
hy and mature reflection takes place. The Constitution of most
Grand Lodges in express terms delegates to the Grand Master the
dispensirig power. It is recognized that a certain rule should be
observed but that exceptional cases occur where someone should
have authority to ·mitigate the strict requirements of the regulation
and so a discretion is by the constitution and by-laws given to the
Grand Master to act in these· emergent and exceptional cas es.
11 ow such action can be deemed a violation of the law, or how any
censure should be attached to a Grand Master for acting in a case
where the Constitution itself says he shall act, we are unable to
conceive.

DUES
We believe that dues should be large enough to take care of
the charities of the Lodge, provide en~ertainment for its members,
and meet its obligations to the Grand Lodge. The tendency in
some Lodges is "to lay up treasures in Heaven" by accumulating
a large surplus, while in others it is just the reverse. Unfortunately
the idea that Masonry is a benevolent association has become quite
common among the unthinking, and too many join with that idea
in mind. They naturally expect to get something for nothing,
which is the true basis of a fraternal order insurance. The
insurance field is dotted with the graves of this class of companies
who have tried to "buck" the law of supply and demand.
Iowa:
lt is . no use for members of individual lodges to complain at
the extra burden of a dollar or two per year in the matter of dues.
The responsibilities of the fraternity must be met. The newcomer
who pet.itions a Masonic lodge in this day and age of the world, is
purchasing a valuable asset. He is becoming a partner in an
already established and highly organized institution, and he should
not complain at being compelled to pay the price which is asked.
But ·the facts do not justify the position that a high fee keeps
men out of the lodge.
Nor will the argument that a reasonably high fee keeps the
man of small means from joining the fraternity hold water. Tt is
not so. ·Human nature again enters into the equation, and while
an increase~ fee may deter. some for a time, yet eventually, ii a
. r eal desire 1s there, the fee 1s saved up, and the satisfaction of the
member in his new affiliation is increased accordingly,

We have always contended that Masonic degrees were worth

New York:
Freemasonry is not a necessity, but a luxury, and any man
who really wants to join the Order will not let an additional ten
do llars or twenty dollars prevent him from making application.

In the light of modern development and the rapid pace a t
which woman has advanced, she has in practically all respects
referred to by that speaker taken her place as the equal of man.
The only remaining accomplishment is that she should be admitted
to membership in th.e Masonic lodge. It is my opinion that her
entrance into our organization would elevate and adorn t he Fraternity, for in all things woman has touched, she has added grace
and charm and goodness. Our Order being devo ted to th e development and cultivation of the highest impulses of the hu man heart
and soul, her assistance would materially aid us in the work we
are trying to perform.

EASTERN ST AR
The Nineteenth Amendment is now a law. Who can tell but
what Masonry will be the next fortress to be stormed? We·understanu there is in one of the large cities in this State an organization
known as "Co-Masonry," which was conceived by Mrs. Anne
Besant. One lady informed a good Brother that she already had
received her third degree, and hoped to get her 32nd shortly.
While Masonry as an inst;tution cannot succumb to the pursuasions of the fair sex to the extent of giving them a full partnership, still as an auxiliary for good the Order of Eastern Star
has a great value. Its interest in the Masonic Homes in thd
various States alone would justify its existence. We believe the
time is fast approaching when Masonry should form its sons into
an organization from which its future members will come. In
such an event the assistance of the Eastern Star would be of
inestimable value.

South Dakota:
Brethren, I am proud of the fact that the Grand Lodge A. F .
and A. M. of South Dakota was the first to recognize a Grand
Chapter of the Order of the Eastern Star and to exchange greetings at the time of their annual session. In the past many Grand
Masters have been opposed to it, mostly because of a lack of
understanding, and many have heen opposed to it because they
have not tried to understand it, but the vast majorit y of well
informed Masons have now been converted to the belief that it is
the best thing that has ever come to Masonry. Times have changed
during this commercial age, "and like all bodies of men the Masonic
Lodge needed some influence other than the symbolic teachings
that are told in their lodge rooms. From a fraternal standpoint it
is an assistance in uniting the entire household in one bond of
sympathy and love for fellow beings." The Order of the Eastern
Star has strengthened Freemasonry with the tender love, charity
and forbearance of our mothers, wives, sisters and daughters. It
has been noted that when chapters of the Order are m ost prosperous th e lodges are most active.
Since the dawn of civilization, Masonry with its principles of
true manhood, has withstood the test of censure and criticism. and
as stated before, stands today the leader among fraternal societies.
By the laws of that ancient institution wome n are not eliQ:ible to
its degrees. It is not difficult to discover why. When Masonry
was founded women occupied a, far different position in the world
from that which they now occupy. They were considered inferior
to man in every sense. They were not admi tted to councils of
church or state. E ven in the home their position was a men ial one.
When the Almillhty created the universe it took Him. so we
are told, only a few days to discover that it was not well for a man
to be alone. It took tho. Masons several thousa nd years to arrive
at the same conclusion. The closing years of last century intro- ···
duced to the world a new era in woman's work, and while she
stands out prominently in other fields of usefulness, she now occupies a position of great helpfuln ess in Masonic circles,

North · Carolina :
Woman has no place in our lodges, no access to our Altars;
and do we deny to her the consolations of religion? The thought
is an absurdity. But why is the lodge closed against woman? For
the reason that the work of the lodge is not suitable to the position
she holds in society. When her nature, and the views ot men are
so changed that woman shall have a place in our legislatures, and
officiate ·:in our courts of law, when she shall wield a trowel on the
builder's scaffold, take part in the sailor's stern strife with wave·
and tempest, or follow the war drum to the field of battle, then
may it be proper to open the lodge for her receptio n. It can not
be that woman is rejected from fea r for the safety of our mysteries,
when we so willingly confide to her keeping our hearts, and our
homes.
