Colorado:
The Committee on Masonic Research reported and the following
practically covers the recommendations adopted :
"Master Masons ·can be divided into three classes: First, the
individual student who has the time and inclination to pursue serious
study, prompted by a sincere desire for more light. Second : The
members who can be aroused to sufficient interest to take part in and
support a study movement. Third: The indifferent member who ,will
listen to what he hears, but will take no part in the plan or evmce
any interest.
"It would seem that, in view of the foregoing, the best plan for .
starting this movement would be to have sets of lectures compiled by
competent writers of our own or other jurisdictions, and that these
lectures be,- so. far as is practicable, illustrated with lantern slides, and
that each lecture be furnished with references to standard and recognized Masonic books, so that any of the brethren desiring may read up
on the subject and a full discussion may be had if desired.

plainl)' .before the candidate the seriousness of his undertaking as a

This plan may work all right, but the chances are that it is more
likely to bring disastrous results than to attain the object desired.
There are so few Masons who really understand the fraternity or have
any knowledge of its history, that there is a large chance of much
false information being panned off on the candidate. Just at the
present time there is an epidemic of symbologists who are disposed to ·
connect Freemasonry with all the ancient symbolisms from time immemorial. Some of the dissertations by these symbol cranks are so
weird and wild that they put the tales of Baron Munchausen in the
shade.
The writer is a firm believer in intelligent discourse in Masonic
Lodges, but the problem is to find speakers who have Masonic sense
enough to properly represent the fraternity.

Indiana:
In this connection also I can not too strongly urge the necessity
of Lodges taking the time to study the fundamentals of Masonry to
the end that the membership may realize that the institution is not a
mere machine for the making of Masons in a formal way, but is a
fraternity that helps to make men better by reason of receiving the
instructions which come to them from the three degrees of symbo'.ic
Masonry. Nor inust we lose sight of the important fact that candidates must be disabused of any impression they may ha.ve that the
Blue Lodge is simply a stepping stone to the so-called higher degrees.
I am in thorough sympathy and accord with both York Rite and
Scottish Rite Masonry, for each Rite teaches beautiful and sublime
lessons, but fundamentally there are no higher degrees than the three
degrees of Ancient Craft Masonry, and we need to impress upon the
brethren the necessity of not only mastering these degrees, but a!so
having them realize their beauty and importance. A brother's obligation
to his Blue Lodge is in no wise minimized by vi~:ue of his membership
in any of the Scottish Rite or Yoke Rite bodies or in the Mystic Shrine.

brethren will become leaders of the collective thought of the Lodge
and the inspiration .of its most beneficent work. Their influence will
appear a'.ike in the ritual work of the officers and in the activities of
the Lodge. And perhaps a Gould will spring out of such. a group and
contribute undying literature to his Masonic home.

jurisdiction, have proved valuable in a number of ways. It is safe· to
say that more has been done during the last three or four years in
stirring up interest that at any time since our establishment was a
Grand Lodge. Scores of members are pursuing the study of Masonry
with great pleasure and profit. This study is carried on not as a matter
of antiquarian curiosity, but in a proper spirit of critical enquiry which
is bound to result in a revaluation of the purposes of Masonry in our
own country and elsewhere. Young men who are now entering Masonry
are in a position to receive definite instruction and to form clear ideas
upon certain phases of Masonry which received but scant attention in
earlier days. This circumstance is likely to have its influence upon tlie
future development and direction of Masonic activity.
Personally I should like to see each candidate be the recipient of
some concise up-to-date treatise on Freemasonry similar to the one so
used in the Grand Lodge of Iowa, compiled by Brother Fort Newton.
The future of Freemasonry is closely connected with and depends much
upon a uniform programme of education, and if we are to keep abreast
of new conditions and new ideals our Masonic thinking must be stimulated and vision enlarged. I trust that for the coming year definite
action in this regard may develop in all our Lodges.
A lively interest in the history and traditions of Masonry will

Masonry was built upon the foundation stone of equality and

help others to do clear 'thinking and face in a rational way the
great problems of peace and reconstruction.
The history of Masonry might be reviewed in three steps.
The ·first step is that of the early mysteries from which Masonry
sprang; the second, that 'of operative Masonry, actual workers in
stone and nrnrtar; the third is that of Speculative Masonry, the
organized, ~ystematic Masonry of today. Individualism marked
the first step. The novice who learned the early mysteries did so
for selfish purposes, to gain a personal advantage. The second
step was largely materialistic. The idea of mental and moral improvement entered in but it was confined to the Lodge, confined to
the members. In the third and last step altruism controls. We
Masons of today have learned that our responsibilities are not
restricted to the four walls of the Lodge in which we meet; but
that we owe duties to our fellowmen in every walk of life; that
we owe duties of uplift and social service; that as true men and
Masons we must do our part in the great work of making this old
world a better place to live in. This is J,1art of the mission of
Masonry today. It is a mission of education, a mission of brotherhood, a mission of peace.

GENERAL GRAND LODGES
While the formation of a general Grand Lodge might appeal
to some as an ideal, still as a matter of fact it could never materialize. There are certain conditions existing in every ·State
which would prevent such an organization.
There is a need for a National body which will not encroach
upon the functions of the Grand Lodges, but can represent the
Fratern:ty generally when it is necessary for it to act along national lines. Some Masonic "prophets" state that there will never
be occasion for Masonry to act nationally, as there will never be
another war, etc. The leading statesmen of Europe believed the
e.ame thing up to within two weeks of the commencement of war
by Germany. Perhaps the general Masonic "seer" is wiser than
they were or are at the present. We are told that there are thirty
separate wars now raging in the world, and we have no guarantee
that some unexpected cond'.tion might not involve the United
States.
If Masonry is to be a factor in the time of a great crisis it
must be prepared, and have an organization to act as a unit. We
cannot function through . forty-nine different Grand Lodges with
Grand Consistories, Chapters, Commanderies or voluntary Associations. Brother George Wash'.ngton ' said, "In time of peace,
prepare for war." Peace has its national questions as vital to the
existence of our country as war, and they must be handled a great
dt>al more intelligently. We believe that the Masonic Service Association prov:des a reasonable solution of this question.
Illinois:
In the period of reconstruction and readjustment which is taking place, Freemasonry should divorce itself from the old idea of
state rights and commence to plan for a unity of purpose. This
can only be accomplished through some sort of central organization; call it whatever .you may. Before Freemasonry is goin!! to
gain recognition as a world force, it must break down the barriers
of jurisdiction which envelop each Grand Lodge and must subscribe to a general platform of basic principles. This does not
mean the formation of any National Grand Lodge, but it does
mean that there is needed a National Council 'of Administration
which shall formulate a plan to which all the Grand Lodges of the
United States may subscribe, and along which they may work for
the best interests of Freemasonry.

"THE GROTTO"
The chief reason for the organization of other bodies having
as a requirement for admission membership in Masonic Fraternity,
is the failure of the Lodges to interest their members. If the time,
labor and money used in such organizations could be spent in the
work of the Blue Lodge instead of being scattered, the Masonic
Fraternity would perhaps be more practical and instructive.
The remedy for the present state of affairs, we believe, is to
make the Symbolic Degrees so attractive from every viewpoint
that they will not be a recruiting ground for other organizations,
but the place where the members will find their every wish gratified. The millennium may arrive some day.

GROUP INITIATION
We believe that the first degree, from its effect upon the candidate, is the most impressive one in Masonry. The main objection
that can be urged against Group Initiation is the fa'ct that it
perhaps might detract from its solemnity and the effect upon the
novitiate. This is a matter, however, appertaining to the individual
alone. If he comes to the door of the Lodge in the proper frame

individual.
The time saved could be used by the Lodge for "refreshment
and repose."

We believe you are right, my Brother, Masons are "made" only
a.t initiation, and in those old days Masonry consisted of only one

can see no good reason why the restriction should apply to the First
Degree; 1 if at all, we would like to see it in the Third Degree.
It is the personal opinion of the writer that Lodges should not be
allowed to confer the three degrees of Masonry upon any candidate on
the same night, and that a stated period of not less than thirty days
should exist between each degree. Too many are being rushed through,
not orily in the Subordinate Lodges, but also in the higher degrees.
Making Thir.ty-second Degree Masons within a week or ten days from
the acceptance of the application of the E. A: Degree is absurd.

shekels. Masonry will not lose anything that is worth having if it does

fanfares.

HEALTH
This is one public question in which Masonry could become
actively interested wherein politics could not enter. The statistics
compiled by the United States Government in 'connection with
the National Draft Army were appalling as showing the general
·existence of venereal diseases. In September, 1917, out of every
1000 men drafted 388 of them were afflicted with venereal diseases. In November, 1917, out of every 1000 cases of sickness
182% was due to this cause. It was stated in one of the responsible national weeklies that 25% of the drafted men were inherently defective from the same cause. Surely Masonry has
an opportunity for education here, not only to its individual
members, but also to the general public.
Statistics show that public health improves and infant mortality decreases as education increases.

District of Columbia:
As so many Grand Lodges have legislated on prohibition, it may
be of interest to them and to the craft in general to know that since
the prohibition act went into effect the sale of narcotic drugs in the
United States has increased more than 300 per cent, which was not
unexpected. A Treasury Department report entitled "Traffic in Narcotic Drugs," says, "The order of frequency of addiction, according
to nativity, is as follows: American, Italian, English, Russian, Jewish, French, N egr0es or Chinese, Mexican or Austrian, German or
Canadian." ·
In one day (November 5) the Grand Jury in Washington returned
twenty-eight indictments against alleged "drug fiends," and in New
York thirty-four deaths occurred in a period of fourteen days from
wood a!cohol .which had been used in the illicit manufacture of
whiskey. So our greatest fear, that men having a craving for stimulants would seek insidious drugs as sub'stitutes for their accustomed
beverages, has already been more than realized, for Americans,
hitherto so free from addiction, now head the list. We have warned
against this in these very reports, but very much fear the energetic
"prohibs" will not be convinced until those near and dear to them
have become addicts.
,

Children of Israel were driven out of Egypt because of the leprosy
among them, the result of venereal disease, and after forty years of

in the District of Columbia say that since the Kenyon act, abolishing

before. The girls, the police say, are in · hotels, apartment houses and
elsewhere, touching elbows even with Senators' daughters. They are
in Government offices along with the "war workers," with a chance
not only to ply their cunning, but to corrupt good girls. Good men
hesitate to combat the Pecksniffs who assume the role of "uplift," lest
insu'. ting insinuations be hurled back.

HIGHER DEGREES
The growth of membership in the so-called "higher degrees"
has kept pace with the growth of the Blue Lodges. In some
instan.ces this has been at their expense. While we do not think
it is within the province of the Blue Lodge to formally recognize
the existence of other Masonic bodies, or to legislate as to whether
the members should join them or not, we do believe that if it
were possible for the York and Scottish Rite to make a rule that
six months or a year must elapse between the time a man becomes
a Ma~ter Mason until he is eligible to join them it would result
in vast good to all concerned. This practice has been adopted
in some Jurisdictions and the effect is that the only one who has
suffered is the applicant who is doing the rush act. If such a time
limitation could be arranged by mutual consent or otherwise, it
would prevent the Blue Lodge from becoming largely a recruiting
ground and make th• higher degrees desirable for some other
purpose than the mere wearing of an additional emblem.

The most important period to a candidate is that period of
study and reflection in which he has opportunity, undisturbed, to
assimilate those sublime lessons taught him upon entering into the
Masonic life. Without study and thought, he cannot assimilate.
Without assimilation, he cannot grow in Masonic stature. It has
been a common spectacle, growing more and more apparent with
passing years, to see newly initiated Masons being importuned to
seek other rites and ceremonies without having had time to become
acquainted with even the rudiments of the sublime lessons placed
before them for study as Entered Apprentices, Fellowcrafts and
Master Masons. The whole drama of life· as such is placed before
them. It may be elaborated upon, but never increased in scope.
There has apparently developed between the York and Scottish Rites an undignified solicitation of. material, using the Lodge
rooms of Masonry as a recruiting-ground, frequently not even
waiting until the candidates are raised to the sublime degree of
a Master Mason before holding up before their eyes a picture of

South Carolina:
We have always maintained that Masons could relieve more
of their less-fortunate Brethren by Private Relief than by Institutional Aid, salaries of employees and the interest lost on the money
sunk in brick and mortar amount to such huge figures. Now
comes the Board of Control of the Masonic Home at Darlington
(we like the name "Darlington," we live in Darlington, S. C.),
with this admission:
"There has been an average of forty-one persons, who have
been admitted to the privileges of the Masonic Home, who have
been maintained by the Board of Control away from Darlington.
This has been done for several reasons. First, that families might
be kept together; second, it has been found in many cases that
an allowance of much less than would maintain the same number
of persons in the Home could be made, to augment their own
earnings, and thus make it cost the Masonic Home much less than
it would to keep them at Darlington; third, in some instances they
have been maintained outside of the Home because of tuberculosis
or some other ailment which makes it unsafe to admit them into
the Home Family."
Brother Hager does not like our plan of helping our less
fortunate Brethren and their dependents, and, inter alia, says thereanent:
"They undoubtedly have a carefully supervised system, but
after reviewing the proceedings of so many Jurisdictions which
are maintaining splendid homes for the aged and indigent as well
as the orphans, we confess that we lean to the Masonic and sentimental idea of caring for dependents."
Yes, in a way, th$ question with us is one of economy, namely,
how we can do the most good with the money on hand. We
don't like to spend it on brick and mortar monuments which cease
to be assets and become liabilities, nor do we spend our money
on salaries. As to "farming out," we don't do that. We let our .
needy Brethreri and their dependents stay right where they tived
before needing help ; we don't take them away from their old
homes and old friends and associations, and shut them up among
total strangers, where everything they do-get up, eat, walk, go to
bed, etc.-must be done at the ringing of a bell. As to which
"side" is "Masonic and sentimental," we are quite willing for each
one to judge for himself. If Brother Hager would prefer to be
thus taken from his· old home and old friends and made to mingle
with strangers under conditions necessarily in force in a home for
aged and unfortunate Brethren like himself, to remaining where
he is now, among old friends and acquaintances, amid familiar
surroundings, made dear by many tender memories, with no one
to kno'o/ that he is an object of charity save the Masonic Trustees
of his Fraternal Benevolent Fund, then, of course, it is his pdvi-

New York:
We do not want and must not elect to membership the unworthy. cowards. R'rafters, trimmers, weaklings, men lacking backbone, floaters with the popular tide no matter whither they may
trend. Direct your Lodge members in passing upon applications
to do their full duty. manfully, bravely, without fear. without favor.
Direct them to scrutinize closely the character of those who seek
to join. Direct them to make exception of no man, howsoever
great. howsoever wealthy, howsoever influential.
Direct them to see to it that no person be permitted to the
rites of Freemasonry who does not measure up to the full standard
of a man. bearing in mind this axiom, that the end of man's destiny
is not to be counted as the best Frenchman, the best Englishman,
or the best American in any other sense than that he is the best
man that his physical. mental and moral faculties can make of him.
Direct them to use caution, investigation, deliberation, in the
privileires accorded them, and to deny no man entrance into the
Order Masonic, be he ever so lowly and humble, so long as his
character is above reproach.
Admonish them further. that after they elect a man they teach
him Freemasonry, not in the sense of mumbling over the ritual
in a half-hearted, unintelligible sort of a way, but in its broadest
and most siirnificant terms. Teach him to be accepted as a Freemason is to be counted as a man possessing noble aspirations and
high ideals.
Teach him to cultivate friendship, morality, brotherly love,
service. truth. These qualities should be brought out in the beginning. The best way to teach them is ever to practice them yourself.

LARGE LODGES
· As Ledges increase their membership, they lose sight of the
ma.1n purpose of our Organ:zation, that is the development and .
entertainment of the individual. This condition might be · overcome either by limiting the size of the Lodge, setting a fixed
period that must elapse between the time that the degrees may
be conferred on an ind'.vidual member, and educating a Worshipful
Master to the viewpoint that his record depends not on the number of candidates that he raises during his term, but rather the
general good that _w ill come to his Lodge by making it a factor
in the daily life of the individual member and the community.
The first limitation might be too drastic in its actual working
out. The second would tend to the formation of new Lodges by
reason of the fact that the work could not be done in a reasonable
length of time. The third should appeal to reason and be exemplified both by precept and example.

MASONIC INSURANCE COMPANIES
Coupling the word Masonic with any business or activity that
has for its object the financial benefit only of individuals is sooner
or later bound to cause criticism and trouble. This is particularly
so in Insurance companies. They must be governed by the same
laws and regulations that apply generally to that class of business.
If they are not properly conducted they fail, which entails hardships on policy holders or stockholders.
It has been truiy aaid that an Insurance Adjuster is one who
stands between the claimant and immediate wealth, and the denial
of a claim or the unethical conduct of the business is bound to
reflect on Masonry generally. The public naturally associates any
commercial activity bearing the name " Masonic" with the
Fraternity.

78

LATIN MASONRY
The ideals and the source of Latin Masonry should not be
judged by our standards. It was born and exists under conditions
that do not prevail in English-speaking countries. Anglo-Saxon
Masonry was originally a convivial and philosophical society, while

MASONIC SERVICE ASSOCIATIQ~
The Masonic Service Association of the United States is now
an assured fact. In this Committee's report last year the matter
was gone into at length. The following is. taken from the first
bulletin of the Association:
The Masonic Service Association represents a joint arid cooperative effort of the member Grand Lodges to mobilize the ideals
and intellect of all for a solution of those problems which are
nation-wide. No better expression of this desire can be found
than the word "Service" incorporated in the title of the. Association.
The Association is founded upon a conception of Freemasonry
as an organization of "BUILDERS": Builders of CharaCter on the
one hand; Builders working upon the Temple of Civilization on the
other. The type of service which it is ambitious to render is
therefore two-fold: Relief for distress, no matter how caused, when
its magnitude is greater than a local calamity; and Edu ca ti on of
our membership, in order that every Mason may do his full part
in helping solve the vexing questions which today harass humanity.
The Association is possessed of no authority over any Grand
Lodge, and it seeks none. Rather is it the purpose to inspire
Masons to develop in their respective Grand Jurisdictions, through
agencies already established, a clearer understanding of what
Masonry is and for what it stands.
I. RELIEF
The By-Laws of the Masonic Service Association contain the
following provision:
"Upon the occurrence of a disaster of greater magnitude than
a local calamity, the Grand Masters of the several member Grand
Jurisdictions within the division in which said disaster may occur,
shall appoint a committee to survey the needs and report forthwith
its findings to the Executive Commission. The Executive Commission shall thereupon take action on the report of said Grand
Masters to the end that necessary funds shall be provided and
properly disbursed."
. ·
In order to expedite the fulfillment of this provision, the following suggestions are herewith offered, to become operative i~­
mediately such a disaster occurs.
A. WAR. In case a .war is declared to which the United States
is a: party, the Executive Commission will meet as a body and
determine what action shall b.e recommended to the Member
Grand Jurisdictions.
B. CALAMITY. The Association having provided that one member of the Executive Commission shall be nominated by the·
Grand Lodges of each Division, it seems ad;visable to recommend that in order to assure prompt action, the Division Commissioner be considered the representative of the Commission.
If the Grand Masters will pursue the following steps when a
calamity occurs. the Commission will do its full part.
I. While the Press dispatches will under normal conditions
bring the calamity to the attention of the Chairman and
acquaint him with the probable need for action, yet the
Grand Master should notify by telegraph
a. The Chairman of the Executive Commission;
b. His Division Commissioner.

H1':1'0 '.U ' ON CORRESPONDENCE

81

2. The Division Commissioner should proceed to t~e scene
of the calamity, if the Grand Master calls upon him.
.
3. The Division Commissioner a,nd the Grand Master will
advise the Chairman of the Commission what funds for
temporary relief will be required, before the survey . o_f .the
situation can be made by the Grand Masters of the D1~1s1on .
4. The Grand Masters will meet at the scene of the · disaster
if possible make their survey, and advise the Commission
of the ste'ps necessary to cover such relief as is agreed

II. EDUCATION
A. The immediate task which the Executive Commission believes
should be accomplished for the education of Masons, has to do
with the fundamental principles of the Fraternity, the Fatherhood of God and the Brotherhood of Man.
We believe that these principles should be developed in a
way to make every Mason realize what there is in Masonry
which should guide him in his relationship to his fellow men .
In other words. we must explain · this divine · Fatherhood and
Brotherhood in terms of civic duty.
B. We shall prepare outlines of talks to be delivered by competent
brethren in the lodges, which will teach these fundamentals.
1. These outlines will provide for the communication of the
simple, basic, and fundamental ideas which brethren facing
the present crises need.
2. In calling the meetings at which! these talks are to be delivered, Worshipful Masters will be expected to urge particularly the presence of those Master Masons who have
heen recently raised.
3. The selection of speakers is to ~ begun on an equally
simple basis. The Grand Master, by and with the advice
of those who' are called into his councils, will endeavor to
find in each county, or in each Masonic District, a man
who is capable of taking these outlines and weaving them
into a simple, comprehensive talk, to be given in as many
of the lodges near his home as possible.
·
4. For meetings in districts, or in the larger cities where this
program is put into effect. the Commission expects to be
able to furnish speakers of more than local repute. · Their
talks. however. will be based on the same outlines. As
demands for this larger service begin to accumulate, the
Commission will arrange for bookings from the office of
the Chairman of the Commission.
,
S. As far as possible, these talks will be given on a volunteer
hasi~. The Commission hopes that thf' Gra;nd Masters will
be able to draft, as speakers, men .of. talent whose usual
vocations prevent their makinl\' a business of Masonic lecturin~. but who, on the other hand, desire to render se.rvice
to the. furtherance of this great cause.

MASONRY: WHAT IT IS
Masonry means to a man just as much as he. puts into it and
just as much as he expects to get out of it. Some join through
curiosity, some to help their business or worldly standing, and

83

Delaware :
Masonry is not an end, but a means. A creed is but an expres~
sion of our faith. When the mind becomes satisfied with the form,
we miss the essence. The symbolism of Masonry is only the
ladder on which our souls may climb. Our symbols are meaningless until they are translated; and there are no words in which to
express them ; they require to be interpreted into deeds and impulses. If our Masonry is real, we cannot confine it to the Lodge
room nor to intercourse among the brethren.
Illinois :
The time has arrived in our Masonic evolution, when Freemasonry can no longer be considered as bound by state rights,
or limited to groups of individuals. To secure proper recognition
of the institution as a vital factor in human activity, there must
be organization and co-ordination. of effort.
.
.
.
In the period of reconstruct10!1 and .readiustment wh1c~ IS
taking place, Freemasonry should divorce Itself from the old idea
of state rights and commence to plan for a unity of purpose. This
can only be accompfished through some sort of central organization; call it whatever you may. Before Freemasonry is going to
gain recognition as a world force, it must break down· the barriers of jurisdiction which envelop each Grand' Lodge and must
subscribe to a general platform of basic principles.
It is now time for the Freemasons of the United States to lay
aside their prejudice, to forget narrow traditions of the past, and
commence to lay the foundation for a great organized' effort which
will make the fraternity a potent facto t in the affairs of the world.
Iowa:
To the average Mason-and he numbers 1,790,000 of the 1,800,000---Masonry, while possessing rare beauties of ritual, is a sealed
book, so far as the understanding of that ritual is concerned! To
him Freemasonry is a fraternity composed of the best fellows on
earth, wide in their sympathies and their humanities, good fellows,
prosperous follows, the kind of fellows w.ho are doing things in
this world, and therefore the right kind to be associated w ith. · To
his mirid, the Society of Freemasons has much in common with
other societies, and sometimes he is inclined to feel that the bene·
fits of some of the others are more certain.
Michigan:
'In social life, it must break down the artificial barrier of caste
and class which divide men and susta in the true and n atural aristocracy of character as against the false and accidental aristocracy
of birth, wealth or position. And it must go to relieve wherever
distress may ··be and the need of man may call.
In political life, it must demand the full and free rights of
the citizen to the equal protection of the laws and require that all

84

REPORT' ON CORRESPONDENCE

the powers of citizenship be wielded to maintain a government
existing for the benefit of the governed.
In religious life, it must demand complete freedom of decent
worship, attended with fair and free discussion that false doctrine
be eliminated.
In educational affairs, it must . preserve the right of the man
to think for himself, and maintain and support free schools and
institutions of learning where the race may be taught and the mind
made keen.
·
In industrial life, it must encourage friendliness and fair dealing. combating on the one hand those movements of terrorism
and destruction, and on the other those policies of oppression and
tyranny which breed hate and malice.
In all phases of human activity, it must sustain energetically
all movements which tend to raise the level of humanity, make
men free, and induce equal companionship and brotherhood and
oppose those which tend to create classes, enslave men's minds or
souls and destroy fraternity.
The record of a busy year follows; constitution of new Lodges
dedi~ations, laying of cornerston~s, and visitations, all advancing
the ideals of the Craft and · drawing the brethren into close communion.

ev~ry organism carries within itself the seeds of its own decay.
This may also be true of organizations and institutions. The germ
that may injure us is no outside germ, however violent it may be,
bnt . qne of our own . making. We shall live or die as we deserve
to live or die, and the world will, in the long run, gauge us pretty
accurately and rate us as we deserve to be rated. No more deadly
danger can menace us, now or at any other time, than carelessness
in the admission of members and failure to rid ourselves of all

save us, nor can we rely on boasts, however well-founded of the
great antiquity of our Institution, or of what it has don~ in the
past, to offset the deadly menace of even a seeming acquiescence
in the acts of unworthy members. The only Masonry that concerns us is t~e. ~fas<;>nry we are now living-the Masonry of today.
Our respons1b1hty hes here and now, and that responsibility concerns _ u~ and will concern, and, to a great extent, influence our

tongue will be more likely to injure us than all our outside enemies, however anxious they may be for our destruction. Our outside enemies are known to µs, and can be effectually met as the

the danger of the poison that may lurk in our own system. · Do
not be carried away by the talk of such, but let us do all we can

New South W ales:
The Grand Master ably expounds the law of "qualifications,"
sayipg in part:
"The qualifications of a candidate are threefold-mental, moral
and physical: mentally, that he be of sound mind, able to fully
comprehend the nature of his obligations and properly to appreciate .the· tenets and principles in which he will be instructed ; morally, that his conduct be virtuous and his character beyond reproach, lest the honor and good repute of our Institution should
suffer by the admission of. the unworthy; physically, that he be
o f 'able body and of limbs whole as a man ought to be.' This
latter is one of the universally recognized landmarks of Freemasonry, and distinguishes our Institution from all o thei;s, and
connects its present speculative with its old-time operative character. The laws of Freemasonry are of two kinds-local and universal. The former, enacted by each Grand Lodge for the government of its members, to be varied or repealed at . the pleasure of
the bodies who originally framed them, while the laws universal
arc those ancient landmarks which are irrevocable and not to be
altered or departed from by any Grand Lodge. This question of
what may constitute physical defect, moreover, is absolutely t h e
prerog.ative of the Grand Master alone, and in this Jurisdiction
the interpretation laid down in 1901 has always been a\iopted, 'that
unless the candidate be fully able to comply, with our rital observances, giving and receiving the signs, etc., .he cannot be admitted
to the Craft.'
·
" I yield to no one in my sympathy with those who .a re physically unfitted and otherwise qualified, but the ancient landmark
stands, and it is not to be removed or changed by any man."

but the one who dwells on duty a·s exacting as necessity in th e
individual life, and who acts when duty calls.

New Zealand:
It is sometimes said that a Mason should always be given
preference by a Mason~that when there is a· contest for some
post between one who is a Mason and one who is not, though the
non-Mason may be the superior in intellect and qualifications for
the position to be filled, still it is the. duty of a Mason who ma:;
have the gift of office to ·give the preference to his brother Mason.
I refuse to subscribe to that doctrine. I believe that every brother
in this hall tonight believes that a man who is placed in any posi. tion of trust, if he desires to be true and faithful to that trust.
must see that the person who is best qualified for the vacant post
gets it, and that it is neither his duty nor his business to prefer
one who belongs to the Craft. If he did so he would be acting
dishonorably, and if there is one thing above all others that a
Mason should be, he' must be an honorable gentleman. Moreover
he need not prate about his honor. You will find as you mov~
through life that there is a tendency on the part of some persons
to consider that honor is a rare quality. I have had some little
experience of humanity, and I hold that the tendency of the greater
part of our race is to be honest. I always look with suspicion
upon the man who boasts about his honor, and would lead you to
believe that he is a superior sort of person, who is not as other
men are. When you come across a man of that type beware of
him, and watch him.
.
'
Another type that you will meet occasionally is the hypocrite,

The following is taken from an article by Brother Frank S.
Land, 32° K. ·c. C. H., published in the "New Age" of September, 1920:
The Order of De Molay for Boys is hardly more than a year
old, yet already it has attracted the attention of Masonic bodies
throughout the country. Perhaps a brief history of the inception
and ·dev_elopment of this remarkable movement will suggest some
of the possibilities inherent in it.
On March 19, 1919, approximately on the anniversary of the
martyrdom of Jacques de Mo lay, though not with the remotest
idea of signalizing the-anniversary in any way, nine boys, the sons
of Ma:son.s, held a meeting at the Scottish Rite Cathedral in Kansas
City, Mo., on invitation of the Social Service Department. Out of
this meeting the Order of De Molay was formally established and
Kansas City Chapter- was organized. Little was thought at that
time that other cities would be interested in its work. Teachings
along the lines of patriotism, good citizenship, clean living, courtesy,
good sonship and similar virtues which adorn the youthful character were inculcated in a general way, but the need of a ritual
which would appeal to the dramatic instinct inherent in youth was
early felt.
Such a ritual was provided by Brother Frank A. Marshall.
editorial writer on the Kansas City Journal, and from that time
the Order has grown with amazing rapidity.
.
At th_e present time the membership in Kansas City Chapter
1s approximately 1,000, and a convocation to be held on July 31
will i~cre'.1-se the number to approximately 1,200. Chapters have
been instituted at Omaha, Neb., under the sponsorship of the
Scottish Rite Bodies of that city ; at Trenton, Mo. under the
sponsorship o~ the York Rite Bodies; and at Kirksville: Mo., under
the sponsorship o"f the York Rite Bodies of that city. Additional
chapters are to be instituted in the next thirty days in Denver,
C~lo .. under the sponso rship of the Scottish Rite Bodies; Kansas
City. :Kans., under the sponsorship of the Scottish Rite Bodies· at
the University of Missouri, under the direction of the York Rite
Bodies at Columbia: and at the· University of Kansas under the
sponsorship of the Scottish Rite Bodies at Lawrence. 'More than
seventy-five cities have made inquiries relative to the movement
and already a Grand Council has been organized and exercise~
national supervision over the Order.
The ritual is composed of two degrees known as the Initiatory
De1rr~e and the De Molay Degree. The ritual lays stress on the
cardinal virtues which encourage boys to live clean healthful and
patriotic lives in all their relations as sons, brothe~s friends and
future citizens, and the o_bligati9ns assumed are such that, if faithfullv observed. cannot fail to raise the boy up into useful and honorable citizenship in the years to come;
Membership is restricted to boys between the ages of sixteen
and twenty, inclusive, of good moral character. Each boy must be
the son of a Freemason or the chum of a1 son. The members ·are
held to a strict ac·countability ton their conduct much stricter it
might he said. than that obtaining within the large'r fraternities. Any
tendency on the part. of a member to neglect his school work-for
a great number o f its members are in school-is checked summarily.

Wisconsin:
·
Th G and Master was asked by someone to lend his sanction
for a p~op~s;.tiop to amend the constitution of the state so . as to

101

make school attendance at the public schools compulsory and to
abolish all parochial and private schools. Matters of this nature
are entirely foreign to the Masonic institutions. A campaign along
this line would cause bitter strife and work to the prejudice of the
Masonic institution.
In discussing"the public schools of the land,. Brother Pettigrew
(South Dakota) said:
·
"I believe that the time is coming when we should take a stand
against the narrow bigotry of the parochial school. And I want
to say to you that it is my belief that it is a fit s ubj ect for consideration in a Masonic Lodge, and I want to say further that it
is time . the Mas_o ns of every Subordinate Lodge in this state knew
who were running the public schools in their towns. And I want
to go a bit further and ·say that it is time the Masons of this
country were considering and understanding what is being taught
in the public schools."
The subject was considered of such importance that it was
referred to a special committee, who, in reporting, said in part:
" We believe that every boy and girl in America should attend
the public schools until he or she shall have completed a comprehensive common school education. And we believe that all instruction in the American common schools should be given in the English language."
The discussion of this subject comes perilously near the consideration of political topics. Nevertheless, no o ne can doubt that
a republic cannot exist where the great mass of its citizenship is
ignorant. A great degree of intelligence and education is essential as a foundation up on which to base a democracy. The t endency of the public school is to broaden and enlarge the vision
of its student body. The parochial school is n•cessarily restricted
and founded upon bigotry.
QUESTIONNAIRES
That the average application required from "a profane" to a
Lodge does not call for sufficient data to enable the Lodge generally to get an idea as to the qualifications of the applicant is
evidenced by the adoption of questionnaire forms by several jurisdictions. Some of the questions asked in these are not relevant
or proper and others are entirely out of order.
We particularly commend the letter used by the Worshipful
Master of the Lodges of Michigan. We also refer to one adopted
by Mexico which was published last year in our report on page
eleven.

Virginia:
Here is another argument in favor of our rule forbidding investigating committees on petitioners:
Some years ·ago this Grand Lodge (Nevada) ad?pted a fC!rm
of petition for degrees, on which were endorsed certam categorical

REPO.RT ON CORRESPONDENCE

105

que.s tions to be answered in writing by the committee of investigation. I have found committees are making returns without
answerin~ ~hese. q.uestions, and it is my opin_ion, the requirement
works d1stmct miury to the Craft. Committeemen hesitate to
return an unfavorable report in writing, and petitions are reported
on as favorable and the applicant rejected. The matter has been
of such frequent occurrence as to justify attention. I believe the
Craft would benefit by committees reporting direct to the Master
of the Lodge. I recommend that committees of investigation on
petitions for degrees or membership report secretly to the Master
of the Lodge, who shall announce after the final reading of the
petition before the ballot is to be taken. that the report of the
committee is "favorable" or is "unfavorable" or is "divided" as t he
case may be.
. Perfunctory rep<?rts are the usual thing, and they are a poor
reliance at best. Ot course. an untavorable one is equivalent tr•
stating that one, at least, of the committee votes a black ball.
Wisconsin:
Where "bulletins" of this nature (giving names) are sent
thro~gh the m!lils to all the members some of them are pretty
certam to ._fall mto hands for whom they were not intended. In
our own little community of two thousand inhabitants we have
four persons named, "W. H. Thomas." Two are members of our
L<?dge and two are profanes. The danger from making use of
this means of disseminating information is obvious. But why use
an:>'. method? The member, who habitually attends the communications of his Lodge, does not need to be told who is petitioning
for the degrees. He will know by having been in attendance. It
ts the stay-at-home member, who is too indolent or too indifferent
to attend to whom the appeal is made by such means. If such
member receives such a "Trestle Board" and he has no objection
to those whose names are listed he still remains away; but if he
has a. personal ~rudge or spite to satisfy, he attends on th~t 01;1e
occasion and reiects one who perhaps is more worthy and who
would make a better member than he is himself. Why gratify this
class of. members by enabling them to get in their work with the
least possible expenditure of time and energy on their part?'
RELIGION
Any attempt to limit or prescribe the religious opinions or
views of an individual member should have no place in Masonry.
"How good and how pleasant it would be" if, in place of attempting this, we would revert to the Ancient Charge, reading as follows:
. "But though in ancient times Masons were charged in every
country to be of the religion of that country or nati~n, whatever
it was, yet it is now thought more expedient only to oblige them
to that religion in which all men agree, leaving their particular
opinions to themselves; that is, to be good men and true, or men
of honor and honesty, by whatever denominations or persuasions
they may be distinguished."
If we would remember and follow this, utterances and arguments that produce nothing but discord or bad feeling would soon
disappear,

Alabama:
"Declaration of Masonic Faith as to God and the Holy Bible."
A We believe in God, that He is the Father of us all and
that He is the Creator of Heaven and Earth and all things therein.
We believe as we teach, that we should reverence and adore Him
and implor~ His aid in all our laudable undertakings, and este.em
Him as the Chief Good.
B. We believe, as we teach, that no atheist ca~ be made a
Mason, and that no one should be made a Mason without a profession of belief in God.
C. We cannot affiliate, Masonically, with one who denies the
existence of God.
D. We believe that the! Holy Bible, . th.e First Great . Light in
Masonry is more than a symbol. We believe, as we teach, that
the Holy . Bible, sometimes in o~,r work c~l.led ~.h~ "Ho~y S~rip­
tures," and sometimes called the Holy Wntmgs, 1s th~ mestt.mable gift of God to man· that Masonry has accepted this grac10us
and divine gift as containing an exl?ression of ~od'~ Will, and
that its precepts are the rule and guide to our faith m God, and
our unerring guide in the discharge of our duties to God, our
.neighbor and ourselves.
E. We believe that God and . the Holy Bible are essential
to Masonry.

Iowa:
We very much regret that any such action was. taken. (Referring to Alabama's Declaration of Faith.) Such a procedure
comes da,n gerously near forcing the local Lodges to subscribe to
a creed. We wonder what the Grand Lodge proposes to do m
those cases where Lodges composed of men of independent thought
refuse to act upon such a communication.
It is just as if the Grand Lodge were making a n effort to get
each local Lodge to enter. into a written contract to be. religious.
It is very much like insisting that they should enter into a solemn
covenant w hich not only comprises an entire page of printed matter, but is subdivided into five distinct heads, and it is also required
that the covenant be under seal. It is like harking back to the
hard and rigid rules of N ew England Puritanism and from this
it is but a short step to something far more drastic in t he way of
religious exactions. To us the whole business smacks of a certain
Pharis'e eism on the part of its promoters and is very suggestive
of an effort to parade one's religion before the eyes of men. It
runs counter to the broad universality of Masonry which is ever
for breadth and liberty in matters such as these and never for
narrowness. It suggests the opening' wedge of a process of re-·
ligious persecution. What a pity it is that the brethren of Alabama
cannot take their religion for granted, but must thus protest it in
a solemn writing under seal. Nothing is ever gained in the cause
of pure religion and unde filed by the effort to make it compulsory.

South Carolina:
The prayer beginning "Our Father which art in heaven,"
referred tb by Brother Jenks, is very, very erroneously called the
"Lord's Prayer," meaning thereby the prayer of Jesus Christ. The
real "Lord's Prayer," that is, the Prayer of Jesus Christ, is to be
found in the 17th Chapter of St. John. The prayer referred to
by Brother Jenks is one of the oldest prayers to Our Father we
know of, and has been in constant use by the Jewish people, almost
word for word, from their earliest known history.
When His Disciples came to Christ asking Him to teach them
how to pray, He rebuked them by giving them the prayer they
and their forefathers had used from time immemorial. We consider this rebuke one of the strongest the Master ever gave to
His disciples. Thus the Mason, be he Jew or Gentile, Mohammedan or Parsee, Buddhist or Brahmin, can pray without offense
in the hearing of his brethren of whatever creed to "Our Father
which art in heaven."
RITUAL
In this day and age men are concerned with the vital affairs
of life. There was undoubtedly a time when ritualistic work had
its place, and a certain charm, but we must realize that the old
order of affairs is passing away. A certain amount of ritualistic
work is necessary and proficiency should be insisted upon, but
wh~n it becomes the sole object of a Lodge, it can have nothing
other than a bad effect.
We believe that it would be a material gain, if our ritual was
rev:sed to the extent of eliminating certain of the monitorial work
and repetit' ons and short:ning other portions of it. The best
ev:dcnce that too much ritualistic work does not appeal to the
avera""e member is the lack of attendance.

Iowa:
What can we say in our defense? Do we want to plead that

We have at times felt that there was great danger of its degenerating into a mere lifeless mechanical ritualism and thus losing
its power to fulfill any great vital function in human life and of
becoming- a society of men who forever theorized about the true,
the beautiful, and the good without doing very much to bring these
into actual effective life among men.

He decided that the degrees could not be conferred on affirmation, without oath. That student of Masonic law, Br.other George

Oregon:
Complying with a petition signed by several Masters, a remarkable resolution' was presented:
"\Vhereas, believing the Masons of Oregon are desirous of
teaching true Masonry, and our attention having been called to
that section of the ritual which refers to the grave, as follows:
'And they buried the body in a grave six feet due East and West,
and six feet perpendicular,' which statement is not true to practical use; nor has the number six any connection whatever with
Masonry, nor to the Mystical Numbers of the Symbolical Degrees
of Masonry, which numbers are three, five and seven; therefore,
be it
"Resolved, that we are in favor of the Grand Lodge striking
out that section of the ritual in which reference is made to the
six-foot grave.
·
"Resolved, further, that we favor the insertion of the following into that section: 'And they· buried the body in a grave seven
feet due East and West, five feet perp·endicular, and three feet
wide.'
"Resolved, further, that this Lodge indorses the above resolution, and recommends that the same be adopted by the Grand

South Carolina:
We sure were astonished to read this paragraph in the Report
of a Special Committee on Ritual :
"Third, the Grand · Master has recommended that this committee be requested to draft and submit a short form of opening
and closing a Lodge when working in the first and second degrees
at the same sessiotl, as in suspending labor in the third degree
while doing work in either of the other degrees. We know of no
Masonic usage or authority of any kind to justify such a practice.
In our opinion no necessity or reason exists to warrant a Lodge
from deviating from the regular form of opening, and closing in
each of the three degrees as now prescribed by the ritual of this
Grand Jurisdiction. We are further of the opinion that the proposed short form is un-Masonic and contrary to the ancient landmarks of Freemasonry, and if, as the Grand Master reports, this
practice is common among the Lodges of this Jurisdiction, it
should be discontinued."
No wonder the above was promptly tabled. I would like very
much to see the American Lodges adopt the particularly short ·
form of passing from one degree to another used in Scotland.
The whole ceremony does not occupy over a minute, and is done
by an exchange of signs and knocks which cannot be explained
here. In Scotland, where I was raised, Masonically and otherwise, a brothei: who visits a Lodge while in session does not require
to ask the Tyler what degree the Lodge 'is open on; nor to consult the Lights, he knows by the difference in time between the
knocks which the Tyler gives. Likewise, the Tyler is not told
the degree the Lodge is working on, he knows by the knocks
given by the Inner Guard, an officer unkn own in the United States,
save perhaps in Pennsylvania.
The ritual, itself, is but the shadow of the cohesive mass of
fundamental truths embraced in Masonic teachings, and to say
that a candidate is proficient and entitled to advancement merely
b.ei;:aµse h e has mentally mastered its language, is to substitute

the shadow for the substance, a nd the forms and cerem onies for

Brother Vanderlieth of Nevada and Brother Michie have

REPflRT ·ON CORRESPONDENCE

Aaron 's beard, as mentione'd in the 133d Psalm. Brother Vanderlieth contends that the word translated "skirts" in the autn1Jrized
version should be "collar," and that therefore Aaron's beard was
of very ordinary longitude. Brother Michie contends that it went
down to the very edge or hem of his priestly robes and probably
· swept the ground, and fortifies his contention by quoting from the
original Hebrew and discussing the Masoretic points. He assures
us he has met three gentlemen, outside of dime museums, who
possessed such facial adornments. We do not wish to enter into
the controversy, but there is one argument that has not been
mentioned. We read in the book of Numbers that Moses took
Aaron's rod, which was of almond wood, and put it in the Tabernacle over night, and when he ·brought it forth in the morning
it ' had budded and then blossomed and brought forth fruit in a
single day. The record does not state, but we have no doubt that
Moses and Aaron had blanched and salted almonds from it for
dinner that day. Now it occurs to ·us that any old duffer who
was so full of virility that the dry . rod he had leaned on would
burst into blossoms and fruit at his touch would be able to produce a crop of whiskers that would be remarkable. No doubt his
beard was a whopper. The question is one of thrilling and vital
interest, especially to Masonry. Does not Anderson, in his book
of constitutions, published in 1723, say that:
"The Israelites, at their leaving Egypt, were a whole kingdom
of Masons, well instructed, under the conduct of their Grand Master Moses, who often marshall'd them intc;> a regular and general
Lodge, while in the Wilderness, and gave them wise Charges,
Orders, &c ?"
·
Aaron must, therefore, have been a Freemason and, as he
became Moses' successor, must have been Grand Master of Masons.
His beard, therefore, became a sort of Masonic landmark which
could not be changed. True, Mackey does not mention it in his
list of landmarks, but doubtlessly this was an oversight on his
part. If our belief in the extreme length of Aaron's beard is to
be thus swept away by some rash innovator we might even doubt
whether Moses was really Grand Master of Masons in the Hebrew
Expeditionary Force,· and where would the matter stor.? We
shudder to think of it, and are thankful to Brother Michie for having put the everlasting kibosh on Brother Vanderlieth's skepticism.

Los Angeles A. & A. S. R. "Bulletin."
Here 'are two interesting sideli~hts on our late and venerated
brother, Theodore Roosevelt, the first reprinted from McClure's
Magazine and from the pen of Brother John J. Leary, Jr., the
second excerpted from the Bulletin of Oriental Consistory, and
signed "E. A. R.":
"'As you know,' he said, turning to me, 'I am a member of
the local Lodge of Masons. You also know, brother, 1 violate no
secret when 1 say that one of the greatest values in Masonry is
that it affords an opportwnity for men in all walks of life to meet
on common ground, where for the time all men are equal and
have one common interest.
"'For example, when I was . President, the Master was Worshipful Brother Doughty, gardener on the estate of one of my
neighbors and a most excellent, public-spirited citizen, with whom
I liked to maintain contact. Clearly I could not call upon him
when 1 came home. It would have embarrassed him; neither could
he, without embarrassment, call on me. In the Lodge it was different. He was over me, though I was President, and it was good
for him and good for me.
.
"'I go to the Lodge, and even the folks who do not belong to
or believe in the Order, rather like it that I should go. They seem
to feel it is part of the eternal fitness of things. Whenever I
return from one of my journeys I always go there to tell of the
Lodges I have visited, in Nairobi, in Africa, in Trinidad, or the
quaint little Lodge I found away up on the Ascension River. They
sort of feel I am their representative to these Lodges, and th.ey
like it. There's a real community of interest.'

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

While very many of the teachings and principles of our Order
were well exemplified in his life and conduct, his renown came to
him entirely through his efforts along other lines and was in no
way due to the things he did as a Mason; and, notwithstanding
the fact that our Craft most highly esteems the qualities of exalted
statesmanship and is glad to count among its members both of
the present and the· past very many great and good men who have
gained fame through their splendid services to our country, we
were early taught that "Masonry regards no man for his worldly
wealth and honors;" and therefore it is that it has not erected
and should not erect monuments in public places to the memory
of men who have gained distinction entirely outside of its service.
Texas:
You do not address me as a Grand Master of Masons, but
when you invite me to call your enterprise to the attention of

hence in this reply I shall assume to represent what I conceive
to be the sentiments of Texas Masons.
To any eulogy of Colonel Roosevelt, the President, the Statesman, the Patriot and the man of letters, I add my hearty ~om­
mendation. His rugged honesty and splendid courage were typical
of the highest standard of Americanism. He deserved well of his
countrymen and received his reward: Beyond this, Colonel Roosevelt was a partisan, and his claim to enduring fame will rest upon
the viewpoint of the future American; certainly there are many
thousand Freemasons. in these United States who heartily disagree
with most of his public policies, and would not care to perpetuate
them in bronze.

1nemoriaJ. ·

THIRD DEGREE LECTURE
If Masonry is to consist of proficiency in coaching lectures by

all means the commitment to memory of a . Third Degree Catechism is in order.
When "traveling in foreign countries" the Catechism of examination is usually perfunctory, unless some good Brother desires
to satisfy his curiosity. There can be no doubt that there is a
great duty imposed upon Masonry at the present time. Learning
of useless set questions will not help it.
The excerpts. under "Quebec, West Australia and Utah" express our ideas.
Illinois:
There is absolutely no argument in favor of requiring candidates to pass an examination in the catechism of the third degree
more than to make the candidate's progres6 through Masonry a
little more burdensome and to exploit the pet projects of Grand
Lecturers. The catechism as now required from candidates is
entirely too long and as a result the examinations passed in
nearly every Lodge are far from satisfactory. Some of the keenest
and brightest men in the business world liave found it next to
impossible to master the long array of irrelevant matter which
they are required to learn in their Masonic progress. This whole
question ought to be solved by the preparation of short, concise•
catechisms embodying those essentials which every Mason ought
to know. It should then follow that every candidate be made to
master these, and pass a satisfactory examination thereon. Every
Masonic Lodge should be penalized which attempts to smuggle
through candidates improperly instructed, and every Master who
conducts an examination behind the ante-room door ought to be
deposed from office.
There are some things in our Masonic system, that every
Mason should know. For instance, how many Masons are acquainted with the five points of fellowship, wherein is to be found
a declaration of Masonic duty?

CONCLUSION
Brother Joseph W. Eggleston, of the Correspondence Committee of Virginia, refused to write a conclusion to one of his
reports, giving as an excuse that it would save some of his associates at the Round Table from the necessity of writing their own.
We are omitting a conclusion to this report, not for the same
reason as Brother Eggleston, but because our ideas and views are
exhausted, or embodied in the report itself. Like "K. C. B.,"
" I THANK YOU."
Yours Sincerely and Fraternally,
JESSE M. WHITED,
Chairman.

AMERICAN FREEMASONRY
The systems of Freemasonry· practiced in the United States
are generally known as the York Rite and the Scottish Rite.
Properly speaking, they should b~ termed the American Rite and
the Scottish Rite, for the one commonly called York is peculiar in
its organized proceedings only to the United States.
·
The American Rite embra:Ce.s the Symbolic, the Capitular, the
Cryptic and the Templar degrees.
The Symbolic degrees are conferred in a Lodge and are the
Entered Apprentice, the Fellow Craft and the Master Mason.
They are called Symbolic because their prominent mode of instruction is by symbols.
The Capitular degrees ~re conferred in a Royal Arch Chapter
and are the Mark Master, the Past Master, the Most Ex~ellent
Master and the Royal Arch~ The supplemental and honorary de- ·
gree of High Priesthood is conferred ..in a . Council of High Priests
upon · those who nave been regularly elected to preside over a
Chapter of Royal Arch Masons~ They ·are' called Ca[>itular because they are conferred in a Chapter, the work "Capitular" meaning "done in a Chapter." ·
·
'·
·
'
The Cryptic degrees are conferred in a Co~ncil. They are the
Royal Master, the Select Master and the Super-Excellent Master.
They are called Cryptic because the word "crypt" means a secret
vault or underground passage.
The Templar degrees are · conferred in a. Commandery and are
the Red Cross, the Temple and the Malta. .The name Knight
Templar comes from the efforts of the Christian Knights to take
the temple at Jerusalem from the ·Mohammedans.
The Scottish Rite embraces the degrees from the 4th to the
33rd, inclusive. In the Southern Jurisdiction. cif the United States
(which includes all territory south of the Ohio· River and west of
the Mississippi River) the organization of the different bodies, and
the degrees conferre1d by them, are: .Lodge of Perfection, 4° to
14°, inclusive; Chapter Rose Croix; 15° to 18°; Council of Kadosh,
19° to 30°; Consisto~y, 31_0 to',32°; Supreme Council, , 33°.
.
In the Northern Jurisdictioi:i (which includes all S.tates north
of the Ohio River and east of the Mississippi River) the degrees
conferred are: L~dge of Perfection, 4° to 14°,. inclusive; Council
Princes of Jerusalem, 15° and 16°; Chapter Rose Croix, 17° and
18°; Consistory, 19° to 32°; Supreme Council, 33°.

GEORGE FREDERICK RODDEN
Grand Master 1920-1921

r. - - - - -

George Frederick Rodden
Grand Master 1920-21.

GEORGE FRJIDERICK RODD.EN, our fifty-fourth Grand Master, is a
native of California, born at Montezuma, Tuolumne County, December
24, 1867. Because his advent into the world was "the night before
Christmas" may in some measure account for the fact that he is
distinguished for that quality of charity that suffereth long and is kind;
not easily provoked, thinketh no evil, but rejoiceth in the truth-for he
is in truth an apostle of sunshine and a be'.iever that there is good in
every man and every woman.
His father was George Rodden, a native of Vern:ont, whose rugged
hills reflected the sturdy manhood of the sons of the Green Mountain
State. The elder Rodden came to California during the gold rush of
1851, and in 1864 he married ·caroline Thornton of Cincinnati, Ohio.
Four children were the fruit of this union-Harry W., George F., Maud
(Van Norman) and Edna · R. (Martin).
George F. in his early boyhood attended the public schools of his
native town, later attending the high schools of San Francisco. He
has the distinction of being the youngest graduate in the history of the
University of California, in which institution he finished his course
of studies in 1887, too young to receive his degree of Doctor of Dental
Surgery, which degree was conferred after he had attained his majority.
Since 1888 he has practit!ed his chosen profession in the city of San
Francis<!o, although his home was and is in the beautiful city of San
Rafael.
In 1910 he was married to Amy Elizabeth Jackson of Chicago,
whose family is of old English stock. The father of Mrs. Rodden was
a famous organist, and the daughter's love for music but naturally
follows. Her grace and charm of manner have endeared her to the
new-made friends of her adopted home, and the family is a real factor
for good in the social life of San Rafael. Two beautiful children rule
the household-Amy Carolyn and George Frederick, Junior. The
young hop_eful is shown on the opposite page, garbed in the regalia of
his illustrious father.
From the date of attaining his majority Brother Rodden has
evinced an active interest in the social and political life of his community and state, an~ although many opportunities for political preferment

GEORGE FREDERICK RODDEN
GranJ Master 1920~1!121

Were offered by admiring friends and neighbors, these were always ·
declined. However, in 1915 he was induced to stand · for the office of
member of the City Council of San Rafael, to which office he was
elected, and in 1919 was chosen to be the Mayor of that municipality,
and filled this responsibility with the dignity and fearless attention to
duty which has characterized his life.
Freemasonry has had a large claim upon the time and thought of
our retiring Grand Master. He was made a Mason in Marin Lodge
No. 191, at San Rafael, receiving his first degree October 8, his second
degree October 12, and his third degree October 19, 1898. He was
elected Master of his Lodge in 1902, and at his first appearance in
Grand Lodge in 1903, was appointed by Grand Master Nutting to serve
as Grand Marshal; and again appointed to this office in 1904. He was
also given the responsible post of Inspector in 1904, which position he
filled in a most active way until his election as Junior Grand Warden
in 1917.
In 1905 he served as a men:ber of the Committee on Returns, and
in 1914 was appointed chairman of that most important adjunct of
Grand Lodge, the Finance Committee, which place he ably filled until
1917.
During his incumbency as Inspector he originated and caused to
be made a real factor in MasOI1ic relief work the scheme of a general
participation by all the brethren of the Jurisdiction in the glorious
effort of educating the members of the Cr;ift to a proper notion of
personal responsibility one to another, and raising a million dollars
for the Endowment Fund of our Masonic Homes-a dream that will
yet come true.
He is a member and was the first High Priest of Marin Chapter
No. 102, R. A. M., and a member of California Commandery of
Knights Templars.
Such in too brief form is the sketch of the life and activities of
our. retiring Grand Master. It is the prayer of the writer that it may
be ma~y, many years before the Finis may be written, and that he may
be spared to his family, and to us, to a green old age.

Seventy-Second Annual Communication
The Most W o~shipful Grand Lodge of Fr~e and Accepted Masons of the jurisdiction of California commenced
its seventy-second Annual Comm unication in Masonic
Temple in the City of San Francisco, on Tuesday, October
11, A. L. 5921, at 10 o'clock a. m.
Prior to the formal opening, Past Master Hugh K.
McKevitt presented to Grand Lodge a complete and beautiful set of jewels and furniture, the gift of our Grand Tiler,
Brother Frank G. Watson. The list presented is as follows:
Bible, square and compass and case, emblem overlaid
with gold, comport and case, ceremonial vessels and case,
three silver water pitchers with silver trays and silver glass
holders and glasses, three golden candlesticks and case,
one ebony baton with mahogany stand, Bible board, board
for Principal Architect, two gold W arden's columns, ceremonial implements and case. Tiler's sword, Grand Sword
Bearer's sword, rods for Deacons and Stewards, six apron
boxes, a particularly fine banner on which was worked the
seal of Grand Lodge, and a large sit~ American flag.
Brother Watson was called in and blushingly accepted
the enthusiastic thanks of his brethren for his timely and
thoughtful gift.

PRAYER

Almighty God! our Heavenly Father, in whom we live and move
and· have our being, we invoke Thy Blessing upon us Thy children
here assembled in Thy Name and Presence. May Thy favor ever
rest upon our Beloved Institution. Guide and direct us aright in all
our deliberations, to the advancement of those principles upon which it
is founded. We offer Thee grateful thanks for the many blessings
vouchsafed to the Fraternity throughout this jurisdiction and for the
harmony that has prevailed during the year past. P our out Thy richest
gifts upon the Grand Master and upon all who bear authority in this
Grand Domain.
·
For ou; nation would we offer our intercession. Endow with Thy
divine wisdom Thy servant the President of the United States, his
cabinet, the Governor of this State, and all others who guide and
shape the affairs of our country. Bring to naught the designs of those
who seek to undermine our lawful government, constitutional liberties
and religious institutions. As the representatives of the nations gather
for the consideration of the limiting of armament on land and sea,
do Thou preside in their council, aid and direct them to a right decision;
and in Thine own good time make wars to cease and world-wide peace
prevail. Finally, we woµld commend to Thy Fatherly care all those
of our brethren in need or distress-the aged, rhe widows and orphans
to whom we are privileged to minister.
Increase in the heart of every Brother Mason within our borders
a sense of obligation to relieve the suffering and to assist the un fortunate.
Fill us with the spirit of true patriotism and enable us ever to
exemplify in our daily lives those Masonic virtues and graces which
shall ~eflect honor upon our Institution and eventually win Thy commendation in the great Day of Award. Amen.
