ADDRESS OF GRAND MASTER
The Grand Master then delivered his Annual Address,
as follows:
Brethren Qf the Grand Lodge:
Our laws decree that upon the second Tuesday of October
of each year ·at the hour of 10 o'clock a. m., the Grand Lodge
of California' shall convene. Obedient to that manda.te, .then, we
are met in this, our seventy-second annual communication, here
to review and pass judgment upon the work that has. bee~ done
in the year now nearing its close; to scru~inize and d.e termme, as
1 as may be the present state of our affairs, and, out of
near Y
•
·
· 't f full
the rich wisdom of the years that are gone, m a spin o
justice, with high hope, steadfa~t pur.pose and abiding f:ith tha~
Almighty God in His heaven will smile upon our efforts, to for
mulate such plans for the future as wi~l bes~ conduce to t?e wellbeing of our Institution and the satisfaction and happiness of
its members.
.
For reasons that must be obvious, the law provides, too,
that before aught else is ·done, the Grand . Master shall .r~port. to
his brethren and lay before them an account of his admm1stratton
of their affairs.
In consonance with that provision I present m~self .b~f.ore
you this morning to give to you the record of th~ year s ~ct1v1t1es;
to outline for you the code of reasonin~ by which certam deductions were drawn or conclusions reached; and to offer fo~ your
consideration those matters which I believe to be . gumai~ and
which have impressed themselves upon me as be.mg adv.1sable
or necessary. I frankly confess, however, that this task _is approached with no little trepidation.
As I review the past in the unsoftened and unsy.mpa~hetic g~are
of the written word-as I contemplate the huge wmdm11ls ag~mst
which my puny lance has tilted and the feeble marks mad~ there~n,
there is forced upon me the feeling that, in the selectt~n . of its
Grand Master, our last Grand Lodge surrendered conviction to
kindness and permitted friendship to become the master over
reason.
There is fear in my mind and a trembling in ~y heart
lest I have proven altogether inadequate to the work mt~usted
to me-lest my poor judgment has mistaken will to do for wisdom
in accomplishment.
If that be not true and you can, in fair conscience, extend
· some small measure of approval, I shall be glad. If, on the other

379

hand, my fears. be well founded-if it be discovered that I was
right when I suspected myself to be wrong-if it becomes necessary for you to disapprove, then must I seek retreat in the deep
covert of your generosity, solace in your charity, and with Stevenson, devote myself to reflection upon the corrections the while
I admire the castigators.
But whatever the aspersions cast upon Grand Lodge, there is
one. subject upon which I believe there can be no debate, no
controversy. That is the splendid condition of Masonry not only
in this, our own Grand Jurisdiction, but throughout the civilized
world. It may be that propinquity has distorted my vision; it
may be that proximity and contact have destroyed the perspective;
it may be that the intensity of my desire has summoned forth
and materialized the phantom of my hopes to delude me. But, as
I stand before you this morning, I am happy in the conviction
that never, since its history began, has Masonry been more robust,
more highly respected or more influential in its appeal, than now.
From all parts of our broad land comes the same glad news.
Men high and mighty in political, social and economic affairs;
men immersed in the practicalities of commerce; professional men
and humble toilers--all are equally eager to march beneath our
standards, to subscribe to our doctrines and to permit their lives
and destinies to be shaped and determined by the precepts of
our Institution.
·
But could it be otherwise?
When we review the recent and immediate history of the
world, with its strife and turmoil; with its social fabric rent and
torn; with the very souls of men poisoned by unworthy passions;
with estab1ished human relationships disturbed or destroyedmust we not conclude that it is but natural-yes, inevitablethat men of character and understanding, of high ideals and lofty
purpose, should seek to ally themselves with an association the
first and most important of whose tenets is Brotherly Love,
and with recognition of their individual responsibility, hail the
opportunity to serve in that Institution which, like some great
ship, is ever moving onward-silently, steadily, irresistibly onward
-bearing its precious burden of kindness and comfort to those
who are afflicted; of sympathy and compassion to those who are
downtrodden, and abundance of fellowship wherewith to re-establish and strengthen the ties of friendship so rudely sundered yet
so vital to the well-being and happiness of humanity?
Adverting to our own Grand Jurisdiction: While in point of
numbers we have scarce reached the magnificent total of initiates
which last year offered, still the results have far exceeded our
most sanguine expectations. Consideration of unstable and de0

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

pressed financial cond.itions would seem to lead to and justify the
thought that there would be a decided falling off in the number
of our petitioners. The facts, however, as deduced from the
Grand Secretary's report, indicate that such suspicion w.ould not
be well founded. As nearly as the figures may be tabulated at
this date, our number of initiates was 9,198; passed, 8,903; raised,
8,822; affiliated, 1,321; restored, 303, and the total membership is
now approximately 85,200.
But, after all, I believe we are all agreed that the number of
candidates is not the first or most important consideration. Quality rather than quantity, character rather than crowd, seems to
be the underlying policy of all our Lodges. Not only are the
qualifications of candidates most carefully scrutinized through the
prescribed processes of investigating committees, l!ut in many instances the Lodges have gone to still greater lengths. A form
0 f petition is often used which, in addition to meeting the stipulated requirements of our Constitution (section 246), invites answers
to many specific questions concerning matters upon which the
Lodge desires to be informed.
Another plan, used most effectively by many Lodges, comp~ehends the appointment by the Master of a special committee
-usually composed of Past Masters-whose function and custom it is to request the pr'esence of the petitioner and by personal contact and observation, as well as ·by interrogation, so
equip themselves that they will be enabled to act in an advisory
capacity; thus throwing up an additional line of defense around
the personnel of the Institution and adding another safeguard
against undesirable affiliations in the Lodges.
This is all very reassuring and gratifying, but mor~ than that,
it is significant, for it indicates clearly the attitude of mind and
heart which the brethren hold toward their Fraternity.
And may I say in passing, that the Grand Master has been
sincerely impressed and profoundly touched by the magnificent
spirit displayed. Wheresoever I have gone-and my year. has·
been very full-there were to be found the same reverence for our
established principles, the same eagerness in proffered service,
recognition of civic and domestic duties and pride in their performance, obedience to the laws of the Fraternity and fealty to its duly
constituted representatives.
But over and above all, the really high light is the close l!ond
of fraternal affection which holds our brethren in such close communion. In whatsoever community one may find himself, there
will be discovered Masonic brethren working and 'playing together
in perfect accord, upholding their Masonic traditions with every

evidence of their exalted appreciation of the relationships that
should exist between them and the parts they should play in the
affairs around them.

380

381

Necrology.
But while we are gathered here this morning, exultant in our
pride and rejoicing in our strength, we must not be unmindful of
the fact that God in His wisdom has chosen to call from our midst
many who have endeared themselves to us, and who, under the impulse of high ideals and worthy purpose, became exemplars of the
best that Masonry teaches.
Could I but follow the bent of my own inclinations, I should
pay tribute to each of them by having his name read in this open
.;ession. But if we should attempt to do full justice to all and
extol their many virtues, it would be to consume the entire time
allotted for this communication. I must, therefore, content myself by referring only to those who have served this Grand Lodge
in official capacity:
John Plaskett Jarman: On May 8, 1921, our Grand Bible Bearer,
John P. Jarman, was summoned to meet his Creator. His very
name was a synonym for all that was noble. Generous, gracious,
sincere, devoted in his attachment to Masonry, unswerving in his
devotion to his family and friends-there was indeed a man. Always responsive to the call of duty, and mindful of the civic responsibilities entailed by good citizenship, he suffered himself to
be elected to and served through many years in unremunerative
and sometimes ungrateful but most important positions in his home
city. His reputation .for integrity was so high, his thinking so
clear, and his judgment so ne;irly infallible, that even those who
opposed him politically had only the highest respect for him, and
rested content in the knowledge that his approval assurec:I the
righteousness of whatsoever cause he chose to espouse. As we
visualize him sitting in his station in the east, with that kindly, everpresent smile playing over his handsome face; as we hear. again
that soft gentle voice, always raised in solicitous inquiry concerning his friends; as we remember his all-embracing, all-pervading
love for humanity at large, it is poignantly brought to us that
here was a man fit to dwell in the "wide house of the world,"
and it is with difficulty that we' refrain from crying out against
the dread decree which took him from us. Having been invited to
do so by his dear wife, I convened Grand Lodge at the city of
San Jose and on May 13th, with all the solemn ceremonies of the
craft, he was laid away.
The great audience that assembled on this occasion was irrefutable evidence of the love that his friends bore for him and

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

the mountains of beautiful flowers which covered his resting place
would seem to have attested the fact that all the city of.his home
sorrowed.
Granville D. Warren: On September 16, 1921, the Grand
Master was inexpressibly shocked and horrified on learning of the
untimely death of his dear friend and co-worker, Granville D.
Warren.
Soon .the dread news was communicated to . other of his
friends, of whom there were legion. Stunned to the very root of
our consciousness, it was with great difficulty that realization came.
Then a ·pall of sorrow settled over us. Our friend of many years,
our companion in all forms of activity, the · useful, the revered
Grand Warren was no more.
It was so easy to recall him as we had seen him but a few
short weeks before, surrounded, as ever, by a large coteries of
laughing friends, with a glad smile for each and a hearty hand
clasp or shoulder pat for the especially favored ones.
It seemed SG easy to remember him in action, as, in the performance of his duty as Inspector, he went among the officers,
praising here, admonishing there. With an ear quick to detect
the slightest departure from the strict letter of the ritual in which
he was so thoroughly versed, with a r\:verence for perfection which
became a distinguishing characteristic, it was difficult to escape
his vigilance or create excuses which would satisfy.
But when corrections were necessary, they were made with
such gentle firmness that they carried with them no sting of
resentment, no germ of discord.
Capable and strong, unselfish and self-effacing, he commanded
the respect and love of his myriad friends. Surely his name should
be writ large upon the scroll, for Masonry and the world in which
he lived owe a great debt of gratitude.
Otir hearts go out to his stricken family in loving sympath '·
E . E. Knepper: Some years ago, during the convocation of ·
Grand Lodge, I was delighted and surprised to receive a most cordial greeting from one, whom I, while serving as Master of my
mother lodge, initiated into the mysteries of our craft. Shortly
thereafter, and much to the regret of the brethren who had become
sincerely attached to 'him during his short stay among us, he
chose to obey a call to distant parts and passed beyond our ken.
The meeting in Grand Lodge revived old memories and sentiments; since which time, whenever our paths have crossed, we
have enjoyed delightful hours together.

Imagine my dismay when I received a brief letter, under date
of November 22, 1920, from Brother W. E. Hanna, Secretary of
Monrovia Lodge No. 308, announcing the death and interment of
the friend referred to, Brother E . E. Knepper, who had affiliated
with Monrovia Lodge and become Inspector of the 62d Masonic
District.
My personal relations with him were not such as to bring me
into contact with the more intimate side of his life, but the brethren
of his district, more fortunate, speak of him in terms of highest
praise.
At the time the summons came, he was Assistant Superintendent of Schools in Los Angeles County. His clean, straight upstanding manhood, broad vision and warm colorful personality
had won for him the confidence and esteem, not only of his professional and fraternal brethren, but of all the lay world around
him.
Surely the loss of such men is a grievous one; and even the
most discerning minds must be baffled in the effort to discover
the promptings in God's immutable law.
It is in the mind of the Grand Master to request Grand Lodge
to pass resolutions ' of esteem and regret that these beloved friends
have been t~ken, and to direct our Grand Secretary to send copies
of such resolutions to their bereaved families, with the thought
and in the hope that the dark days will be, in some small measure,
brightened thereby.
I have thought it well, · too, to set aside some few hours of
this Communication that we, desisting from all business, may foregather and pay solemn tribute to their memories. I therefore conjure you, my brethren, to assemble here on Thursday morning a~
11 o'clock, with prayer on your lips a nd love and gratitude in your
hearts, that we may, with appropriate exerci~es, manifest our love
for and appreciation of those who have been taken from us.

Because the roster of Masonry is replete with the names of
famous men, it might be assumed, logically, that to add another
. would occasion but little comment. Familiarity often engenders
indifference. But try as we will to hold steadfast to the principle
of democracy and to the landmark that, in Masonry, all men are
upon a level plane, we cannot avoid being a bit jubilant and proud
when a man, who, by his virtues and ability, has won for himself
universal respect, admiration and international fame, evidences
his faith in us by desiring affiliation. On Saturday evening, August
13, a great body of Masons ,(many coming from dista nt places)
assembled at Santa Rosa, there to witness or participate in "the

achievement, foremost of his craft in all the world, he that night
gave us a lesson in those qualities of modesty and humility which
distinguish the truly great, and which should be of such splendid
value to all who would profit thereby. The Grand Master was
honored with an invitation. which he was more than pleased to
accept.

Obedient to the mandate of Grand Lodge, the Grand Secretary and I attended, as guests, the annual meeting of the Masonic
Service Association of the United States, held at ·st. Louis, Mo.,
November 9, 10 and 11, 1920. The purpose of our visit was to
learn at first hand all that we could concerning the hopes, plans
and aspirations of that body of splendid men and Masons; and
having satisfied ourselves upon those matters, to determine so
nearly as our judgment would allow, in what manner and to what
extent they might be adjusted to the needs of California. Realizing that open minds were prerequisite to fair, impartial conclusions, we endeavored to put preconceived notions out of our
heads and to approach our mission in a spirit of even justice. We
were welcome to the forum with all courtesy and consideration,
and with t.he assurance from the · chairman, Brother Melvin M.
Johnson, Past Grand Master of Massachusetts, that jill privileges
(except the voting privilege) were ours.
For two days we listened to reports and statements, a recital
of the activities of the year, expressions of satisfaction and dissatisfaction over what had and had not been done, and finally an
exposition of future plans.
Aside from intense admir:ation for the ability and sincerity
of purpose of the brethren engaged, the impressions which we carried away were absolutely negative. We could not but feel that
something was desired-something great, something mighty, something altruistic, . something that would redound to the good of mankind-but just what that something was, was not( speaking in
mildest terms), convincingly clear. The method of accomplishment was equally vague.
The plan which had reached
nearest to the point of crystallization, was a relief plan which,
in the judgment of Brother Whicher and your Grand Master

carried with it too much detail. We, who have experienced,
know full well that where relief is required, prompt action
is demanded. I know that I speak your minds when I say that
where calamity has befallen or suffering exists, California believes
that relief should be disbursed immediately and without quibble,
and details, if any, cared for afterward. Wherefore, I cannot feel
that this Grand Jurisdiction can be in accord with the plan of
r"elief which the Masonic Service Association has evolved. The
expense of maintaining and operating the association (figures set

In the early months of the year I received the following letter from
the Most Worshipful Andrew L. Randell, Grand Master of Texas:

"My Dear Brother Rodden:
"I enclose a copy of the supplemental report of the Committ~e on Foreign Correspondence, adopted by the Grand Lodge
of Texas at its meeting last month, which is self-explanatory.
The adoption of this report was not a hasty action as a
result of the idea of some individual, but came after a great
deal of thought and consultation upon the part of a number
of leaders in this jurisdiction and after repeated interviews
with brethren of both Grand Lodges in the City of Mexico.
"This Grand jurisdiction has heretofore extended recognition to the York Grand Lodge of Mexico, the regularity of
whicli, as you probably know, has been repeatedly attacked by
the Grand Lodge Vallee de Mexico. Some jurisdictions in the
United States have recognized one of these grand bodies,
others have recognized the other, and still others have ex-

388

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

tended recognition to neither. Besides these grand bodies with
conflicting claims, there are other grand bodies in the Republic
of Mexico claiming the right to recognition.
"We in Texas have given a great deal of careful thought
to conditions existing in Mexico, and we have reached the
unanimous conclusion that now is the accepted time· for
Masonry and for all other organizations looking to the uplifting and advaru:ement of that people to move forward to hi~h:r
and more secure ground. The President of the Republic is
not only friendly to Masonry and other institutions of similar
aims, but he is unfriendly to all those interests which are
inimical to the principles for which Masonry stands. A number
of his Cabinet members are reported to be Masons.
"In our judgment, the conditions in Mexico are more
favorable than ever before in the history of that war-torn
Republic, and the success or failure of all organizations which
~tand for civic and religious 1iberty during the next few years
will determine the conditions in Mexico for a generation or
more to come. The regular and proper activities of such organizations sorely need a united and active recognition and
support from ·the United States.
"Masonry in M·exico has not made the greatest progress
in r~cent years, because of the condition of affair: in that government, yet the qrder has lived, and to a certam extent has
grown, and AII}erican Masons on the ground are now of t~e
unanimous opinion, as far as we have been able to ascertain
their views, that the harmonizing of differences, if possible, and
a united backing from American grand jurisdictions, will enable
Masonry in Mexico to rapidly assume its due proportion of'
membership and influence.
"With these thoughts and ends in view, the Grand Lodge
of Texas took the action set forth in the inclosed resolution.
It was the hope of the Committee and of the Grand Lodge that
the representatives of other Grand Lodges in different section~
of the country would see fit to co-operate with the Gran~
Master of Texas and his Committee in making an investigation
on the ground which would be so thorough and complete and
so clearly set f~rth all the facts involved, that Mexican M~son:y
could be united in its work and American Masonry united m
its recognition. We felt, however, that we should official~
request the co-operation of the Grand Masters .and th~ Grand
Lodges of the border States, which are more directly mvol;ed
and more closely in touch with Mexican conditions. I am tak~ng
this up with the Grand Masters of Arizona and New Mexico,

in the hope that by prompt correspondence we may be able to
unite upon some plan of work together and some definite time
at which to make a visit to the City of Mexico, which will be
absolutely essential to a complete investigation.
" Please let me have your ideas and suggestions as to the time
to make the trip, the scope the investigation should take, the
methods to be used in making it, etc., and also be kind enough
to send me copies of data and reports that may have been
made to your ... Grand Lodge, and of any action which your
Grand Lodge may have taken in this matter. If you have any
personal views outside of these, an expression of them will be
greatly appreciated.
"I trust that I may hear from you as promptly as possible,
for the reason that at the best, a good deal of time will be
required to work out the whole matter of arrangements, ancl
I sincerely hope that there may be nothing whatever in the way
of your complete co-operation.
"It was my pleasure to meet you in St. ·Louis last November,
and I regret that I did not have opportunity for a real good
chat with you. I am wondering what impressions you have
received or what conclusions you have reached in reference
to the Masonic Service Association. Possibly I may have the
pleasure of seeing you again in Washington at the meeting of
the George Washington Memorial Association on February
21st.

In this connection I feel that I should say to you that the appearance of this Commission was viewed with suspicion by the representatives of the York Grand Lodge. There had been printed, and more or
less generally circulated, a pamphlet written by Past Grand Master
Seamon of the York Grand Lodge in which it was stated that "the
object of this investigation (by the Texas Commission) is not to
upbuild Ancient Craft Masonry, but to help the Ancient and Accepted
Scottish Rite to build up that organization in Mexico"; and that the
resolution adopted by the Grand Lodge of Texas withdrawing recognition of the York Grand Lodge of Mexico and providing for an investigation "represented only the wishes of some members of the Scottish
Rite who just happened to be .influential in the Grand Lodge of Texas."
It was furthermore directly charged that the investigation was "to be
made by men who are now 33rd degree men, or who expect to receive
that degree at an early date."
Of course this was very unfortunate; particularly in view of the
fact that there was at the time the inquiry was commenced, and perhaps
even yet is, a very strong suspicion that what had been done in Texas
was at the behest and solely in the interest of prominent Scottish Rite
Masons who had been expelled from the York Grand Lodge. These
charges did not emanate from some irresponsible person, but from ·.a
Past Grand Master. Furthermore Brother Seamon is a man widely
known, not only in Mexico but in this country as well, as an earnest,
zealous Mason ·and particularly well informed concerning the history of
Masonry in Mexico and qualified by a long residence therein to speak
with authority concerning the conditions. In this particular instance of
course his zeal outran his discretion; and his judgment had been swayed
by his prejudice.
I may her7 say to you that there is no member of the Texas Commission who could be more desirous than am I of being able to recognize as regular Masons the men who have been expelled by the York
Grand Lodge. Until I met them in Mexico, I did not personally know
them as did some of the members of the Commission; but I had heard
them very highly spoken· of by intimate friends of mine, and personal
:kquaintance confirmed the opinion of them I had thus formed. The
desire to see · the condition in Mexico so changed that we might hold
fraternal communication with, and regard as our brethren, Americans
of their character and standing, was therefore a very natural one; but
I am sure that there is no member of that Commission who would not
readily and willingly subordinate his desire to his. conception of right
and justice., The personnel of the Commission should be a guarantee
of this. Grand Master Randell's reputation for ability, integrity and
sincerity is not confined to the State of Texas; and no one who knows
him will believe that he was influenced by any unworthy motive in the
selection of his Commission.

The Grand· Master of the York Grand Lodge, M. W. Ernest

Although it is probable that the result of our visit will have rendered it unnecessary, I nevertheless deem it proper to premise my report
of what is proposed for the future by a statement of existing conditions.
For a proper understanding of the situation as it exists today and

Insofar at least as this concerns the Grand Lodge of California,
no good purpose would be subserved by referring to the condition of
Masonry in Mexico prior to the year 1892.
In that year the Grand Lodge of California received a proposition
from the Body generally known as the "Gran Dieta" of Mexico to
enter into a treaty of fri endship. From the report of the Committee
on Jurisprudence it appeared that the Grand Dieta was organized i:s
1890; that it then had under its obedience 17 of the Grand Lodges and
320 subordinate lodges of the Republic of Mexico; that it had adopted
a constitution; and that it had also adopted a decree or order prohibiting any subordinate lodge under its jurisdiction or obedience from conferring the so-called Scottish Rite . Degrees in Masonry. Upon the
recommendation of the Committee action was deferred; but in 1898 rec-

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

ognition was granted the Gran Dieta upon the request of Brother Alexander K. ·coney, the Mexican Consul General at the City of San Francisco, who at the time was the Master of La Parfaite Union.
The Gran Dieta at its inception was a central Grand Lodge. Its
original constitution was subsequently changed so that it became in
effect a confederation of the symbolic Grand Lodges and practically an
alliance against the Supreme Council of the Scottish Rite in Mexico. In
1901 without one dissenting vote it was fo~mally dissolved, and the
Grand Bodies composing it were "returned the office of representation
before foreign Masonic Powers which they had voluntarily conferred"
upon the central Body.
Among the Grand Bodies of which the Gran Dieta was composed
was the "Gran Logia Valle de Mexico"; and in the year 1902 recognition was accorded that Grand Body by the Grand ,Lodge of California. The claim of the Valle de Mexico to control Symbolic Masonry
in Mexico was not, however, undisputed. There was in existence a
Body known as the "Gran Logia Santos Degollado"; but in 1905,
largely through the efforts of Grand Master J. 0. Mordough of the
Grand Lodge Valle de Mexico the Grand Lodge Santos Degollado
. <:eased its labors, and the lodges under its obedience surrendered their
charters and accepted charters issued to them by the Grand Lodge
Valle de Mexico. Thereafter and until the year 1910 there was a temporary cessation of the internecine strife in which Masonry in Mexico
had been so long involved.
As the situation is described by Brother Cecil C. Freston in the
pamphlet written by him and addressed to Brother Oliver D. Street,
the Chairman of the Foreign Correspondence Committee of the Grand
Lodge of Alabama : "There existed a reasonable condition of harmony
between the lodges which ~as perhaps due in no small degree to the
fact that with the development of the resources of the Republic through
the fnvestment of fabulous sums of foreign capital Mexican Masonry
became in closer contact with both English and American Masonry.
Nevertheless at the yearly sessions of the Grand Lodge there was
always more or less friction." This pamphlet of Brother Freston's, by .
the way, is about the only fair, calm, dispassionate review of the ••separation" which occurred in 1910 that I have seen; and I am sending
you a copy in order that you may be advised of the details to which
for obvious reasons I make no reference.
Viewed in the light of the history of Masonry in Mexico, the
schism which occurred in 1910 is not so extraordinary as it would
otherwise appear. The English speaking ·Lodges had grown in number
and influence. Many of the Mexican Lodges were, as they say, "en
suefio"-as we would describe it, they had become dormant. The English speaking Masons had been trained in Symbolic Masonry as taught
and practiced in the United States of America, Canada and England,

while the Mexican brethren had been trained to a greater or less
degree under the influence of Scottisli Rite Masonry. What seemed to
Mexican Masons to be eminently right and proper in the conduct of
their lodges was looked upon with doubt and apprehension by their
English and American brethren. In a sense Mexican Masonry was a
reflection of the political history of the Nation. The divergent idea8
and opinions entertained were to a great extent the result of racial
differences which could be neither reconciled nor overcome. The disinclination of the Mexican brethren to submit to constituted authority
and to abide by the will of the majority was no less evident in the
Lodge than out of it. On the other hand, from what I have been told
by men who passed through those stormy times which preceded the
secession of the Mexican brethren in 1910, I am not prepared to say
that the Mexican brethren were the only ones unmindful of the spirit
in which Masons should express their difference!; of opinion.

The acrimony which it appears characterized many of the debates

those who had been trained in Masonry as we under stand it, than
in their Mexican brethren for whom might be pleaded in extenuation
not only lack of experience in democratic institutions, but that fervid
temperament common to all Latin peoples.
If I were to analyze the real cause of the difficulties which c~l­
minated in 1910, I would say that it was the racial characteristic of the
Mexican brethren to which I have referred. They had not become
imbued with that spirit of democracy which impels the Anglo Saxon
to patiently submit to what we know as "majority rule." The trouble
arose over the adoption of certain amendments to the Constitution and

25 chartered Lodges. All the Lodges represented of course participated

The five seceding chartered Lodges, together with the two under

subsequently, on the 23rd day of June, 1910, without notice to any of
the other Lodges, held a meeting and declared themselves to be the

which had been working under dispensation. This is the Body which
is today known as the Valle de Mexico.
After the secession of the Lodges just referred to, there remained
on the roster of the Grand Lodge Valle de Mexico from which they
had seceded 16 American Lodges and 2 Mexican Lodges. This Gra.nd
Body at its next annul\! Communication in 1911 changed its name from
that of "Gran Logia Valle de Mexico A. L. y A. M." to "York Grand
Lodge of Mexico F. & A. M.", and as such is today fraternally recognized by twenty-nine of the American Grand Lodges and by the Grand
Lodges of England, Ireland, Manitoba, New Brunswick, New South
Wales, Philippine Is'.ands, San Salvador, Scotland, South Australia,
Tasmania and Victoria. The York Grand Lodge does not at this time
recognize any other Grand Body in the Republic of Mexico.
.In view of the fact that, in attempting to justify the action of the

matter.
For the most part, the objections are highly technical in their

constitution designed to force the Mexican brethren out of the Grand
Lodge."
The fact that the Constitution which had been adopted in 1900 was
not suited to, the changed conditions had long been recognized. There
had been various amendments adopted from time to time, and in 1906
a committee was appointed "to revise the constitution and other laws
of the Grand Lodge." Nothing definite was accomplished apparently
until 1909, when Brother Moorhead was elected Grand Master. P. G. M.
Ernest Tudor Craig in referring to this matter says: "Brother Moorhead worked hard and faithfully. He took as his stand'ards New York,
Pennsylvania, Texas, and New ' Mexico combined with a careful study

of that of the Grand Lodge of England; but many others were studied
for points best suited to our needs. . . . After his death, at Brother
Reynoso's request, he then being Acting Grand Master, I went to the
room where Brother Moorhead had passed away and, picking up his
pencil, sheets and notes, faithfully transcribed on the typewriter all
that he had written. With this ~ompleted, at my request, Brother Reynos? appointed a committee consisting of Brothers Mordough, Young,
Waite and, I think,. Lynde-Lockwood, and myself. We carefully went
over every clause, meeting constantly, night after night for weeks. , . ,
The whole work of submitting the new constitution was done strictly
in accordance with the requirements of the old constitution. Printed
copies in Spanish and English were submitted to each Lodge. The
votes were carefully counted and recorded and to the very oest of our
ability everything was done masonically, properly and in order, and
the count was properly reported to the Grand Lodge."

During the controversy which has raged during the last few

Grand Warden. It is extremely unlikely that he would have been

Not only as Deputy Grand Master, but as a Past Grand Warden

In any event, as I have said in view of all the circumstances,

There is only one other question raised to which I deem any
reference necessary. At the time the name was changed to York
Grand Lodge, English was adopted as the official language, but
provision was made permitting the two Mexican Lodges which had
remained loyal to continue to work in the Spanish language; and
the Grand Secretary was directed to correspond with . those Lodges
in Spanish.
The argument advanceq in support of the objection to the use
of the English language is that it will preclude Mexicans from
becoming Masons unless they are able to speak English. The
fallacy of such an argument becomes at once apparent wlien it is
remembered that there are now Spanish speaking Lodges composed
of Mexicans under the Jurisdiction of the York Grand Lodge, and
that there is nothing to preclude that Body from authorizing any
Lodge to work in Spanish, or in any other language.
The original provision of the Constitution read as follows:
"Sec. 2. '.L'he Jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge is over all
regular Lodges working the York ritual and all F. & A. Masons
within the limits of the United States of Mexico, and the official language shall be English."
Because of the fact that that phraseology might be construed
as claiming jurisdiction over all Masons, irrespective of the Rite
practiced, which of course was never the intention, that Section was
subsequently amended to read as follows:
"Sec. 2. The York Rite will be employed in this Jur:sdiction,
and the official language of the Grand Lodge will be English."
While Olle may question the wisdom of such legislation, or even
its propriety, there can be certainly no doubt of the right of a
sovereign Grand Lodge to adopt as its official language that which

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

it deems best suited for its purposes. It must be confessed that
the use by a Grand Lodge of a language other than that of the
country in which it is located is unusual; but the entire situation in
Mexico is unusual and extraordinary.
· ·
While I have not herein referred to all the objections which
have been urged against the regular.ity of the York Grand Lodge,
there is none I think which I have not carefully examined; and
while I would not unqualifiedly approve every one of its acts (and
all that it has done) I unreservedly express the opinion that that
Grand Body is well entitled to the recognition heretofore by the
Grand Lodge of California extended it tactily under its present
name, and formally when it was known as the Gran Logia Valle
de Mexico. So much for what I have termed the legal aspect of
the situation.
·
Notwithstanding what .occurred at the Annual Communication
of the Valle de Mexico in 1910, the period commencing about that
time and continuing until the latter part of 1919 was perhaps, all
things considered, the most harmonious in the whole history of
Masonry in the Republic of Mexico. Within ·a short time such feeling as had been engendered at the time of the secession completely
disappeared, and there were two Grand· Bodies each of which was
pursuing the even tenor of its way. It appears that there was even
an attempt made to enter into some rort of an agreement, under
the terms of which the York Grand Lodge would control the York
Rite working exclusively in English while the Valle de Mexico
would continue to work the Scottish Rite degrees in Spanish; and
while no formal treaty was ever made, there . was apparently a
sort ·of tacit understanding to this effect, and no complaint was
heard. The York Grand Lodge of Mexico was very generally recognized by the American Jurisdictions, and the members of the
Valle de Mexico were apparently not very greatly concerned
whether or not they obtained that recognition which the American
brethren so craved. The Scottish Rite Bodies accepted as members
Americans belonging to the York Grand Lodge, and Mexicans
belonging to the Valle de Mexico; and apparently made no dis.tine-·
tion between them. Bro. Seamon describes the situation as follows:
"The Mexicans who were fond of the Scottish Rite met together
with some English speaking members of the.Scottish Rite who were
prominent in the Shrine and Commandery and a few in the Chapter
of Royal Arch Masons, and the members of the Ancient Craft
Masonic Lodges met together with a few Mexicans who liked the
ideals of Ancient Craft Masonry and spoke English. The English
speaking Masons saw that it was wisest for them to keep their
own ideals and permit the Mexicans to run their Scottish Rite
Bodies in their own way. . For nine years peace prevailed. A few

Americans very closely identified in business relations with Mexica11s, and some who I believe had intermarried into good Mexican
families, associated more with the Scottish Rite Bodies and very
seldom took part with the Ancient Craft Masons. I understand
that some of the Mexicans objected to Americans coming into their
Scottish Rite Bodies but I have not followed up this matter, as
it was none of my business and I sympathized with the Mexicans in
their desire to rule their own Scottish Rite organizations. The
separation was found to result in good, and in spite of the revolutionary conditions in Mexico during all the past ten years Masonry
prospered and there was the normal, variable, activity in the
Mexican Scottish Rite Bodies."
The condition, it is true, was an anomalous one ; but neverthe·
less apparently very satisfiictory. At. all events the Americ;an
Masons were united, and the members of their Lodges received such
recognition from the American Jurisdictions as was accorded the
members of .any Lodge located in the Republic of Mexico.
Today, unhappily, the situation is far differe nt. Instead of
peace .and harmony there is discord and confusion. I am now
referring only to the condition in the City of Mexico. Digressing
for the mom.ent I may say that in Tampico, which I visited at the
request of Grand Master Nicklos, the condition is on..: in which
every American Mason may justly take p.ride.
In Tampico the York Rite Masons have a Lodge of about 230
members and have just completed a magnificent Temple costing
about $125,000. The utmost harmony prevails and they are doing
a wonderful work not only for their own brethren, but for sojourn- .
ing Masons. To the latter the Lo~ge means no less than it ·does to
its own members-perhaps more; because it is the one place to which
clean-living, right-thinking young men from the Oil Fields can go
when in Tampico, and where they are certain to find the association
they seek.
Here in Tampico is exhibited the real spirit of Masonry. It is
only fair to say, however, that it may be that the same spirit would
be found among the "rank and file" in the City of Mexico if it were .
not submerged in the vortex of hate which seems to have engulfed
their leaders, and which has divided the English speaking Masons
into two contending factions. Indeed the real quarrel, as I view it,
jg not betiween Mexicans and Americans, but between two groups of
Americans. One of these American groups, it is true, is now allied
with the Mexicans; but only, it is clear, by force of circumstances.
The woes of their Mexican brethren, it seemed to me, are but an
incident of their own quarrel. The situation furnishes another
instance of the truth of the old adage "Politics makes st~ange bed

fellows';" because curiously enough in this gro11p are men who are

difficult to remember just who was "we" and who "they." It would

was thus prepared a fertile field for any seed of discord. There

I regret that I am compelled to say that there is a very general
belief, shared by brethren of both the York Grand Lodge and the
Valle de Mexico, that the condition which now prevails is due
primarily to the part played by one of our own brethren of whom
complaint was made last year, but who I still believe was actuated
by only the best of motives.
It appears that Bro. Forbes visited Mexico in the year 1919;
and it is said that on his arrival he announced that he had been
commissioned by the Sovereign Grand Commander of the Scottish
Rite of the Southern Jurisdiction of the United States of America
to investigate the condition of Masonry in the Republic of Mexico.
To thoroughly understand just what occurred and to appreciate
the effect of such an announcement, it must be remembered that
Masonry in Mexico is of Scottish Rite origin; and that the history
of the Valle de Mexico is the record of an unceasing conflict with
the Supreme Council of the Scottish Rite in Mexico for the control
of Symbolic Masonry.
Although the Supreme Council long ago formally renounced
any claim to the control of the first three degrees, there are still
Scottish Rite Masons, it is said, who contend that the regularity
or irregularity of a Grand Lodge and the Subordinate Lodges under
it is to be determined by the recognition or non-recognition of it
by the Supreme Council. This contention is cited as the reason for
the desire upon the part of the Supreme Council for "Treaties of
Friendship" with Symbolic Grand Lodges; and the Valle de Mexico
as it existed prior to 1910 had consistently refused to enter into
any such treaty. The Ancient Craft Masons looked with suspicion

upon anything which even by the widest stretch of imagination might
be construed as the indication of an attempt to question the absolute
sovereignty of the Symbolic Grand Lodge. On the other hand, at
the time of the secession, the Supreme Council recognized the
seceders as the legal Valle de Mexico and entered into a Treaty
with them; and in a Treaty made between the Valle de Mexico
and the Grand Lodge of Vera Cruz had been named as the Arbitrator of any dispute that might arise thereunder.
As a maher of fact, it is by no means certain that Bro. Forbes
had the authority it is said he claimed to have. In any event insofar
as the present situation is concerned it is immaterial whether he did
or did not have any authority from anybody. All that is material is
what he said and what was done.
·
It would not be fair to Bro. Forbes to here set forth the statements he is said to have made in private conversations with brethren who appeared before the Commission; because he has had no
opportunity to deny or explain them. Conceding that the witnesses
w~re absolutely honest and truthful, there is always to be remembered the fact that it is extremely difficult after any lapse of time
to correctly repeat conversations, and particularly if they occurred
during a stress of passion or excitement. Furthermore the really
important thing is not what he actually said, but the result thereof;
because he is not on trial, and reference is made to him only as a
factor in bringing about the present condition.
There is no doubt that the impression obtained by those with
whom he talked is that he would be able to, and would obtain
recognition' for the Supreme Council of the Scottish Rite of' Mexico
if that Body would declare the York Grand Lodge irregular and
clandestine. It is also certain that he publicly stated to members of
lodges in obedience to the York Grand Lodge of Mexico that they
were irregular and clandestine Masons, and that they could be
legitimatized only by joining with the Valle de Mexico which was
the only legitimate Grand Lodge; and. that he promised them that
if they would render a nominal obedience to the Valle de Mexico,
that Grand Body would enter into some sort of an arrangement
whereby there would be no interference with English speaking
Masons, and that the Grand Lodge Val!e de Mexico would change
fr~m the Scottish Rite to the York Rite ritual.
Whether or not any promises were actually made by Bro.
Forbes to the Supreme Council, the fact remains that the Supreme
Council did issue an edict or balaustre declaring the York Grand
:C-odge and its members irregular and clandestine, and proclaimmg the Valle de Mexico as a legitimate Grand Lodge. Copies of
this balaustre were sent to the members of all the York Rite lodges

The occurrences just related of course created an iQtense feeling. Indeed I da"ubt that even in the most troubulous times through
which Masonry in Mexico has passed there was ever presented a
more deplorable situation than was thus created among the leaders

liberal Mexican gentlemen whom it was my good fortu ne to meet,
and whose names I do not at the moment recall, they could establish such social relations between the best citizens of Mexico and
our own people residing there as would undoubtedly result to the
ultimate benefit of both Nations..

No one, unfamiliar with the details involved can have a
just conception of the measure and extent of their' devotion and
sacrifice. I do know that whatsoever they do is regarded by them
as a privilege. I do know that theirs is a labor of love, and their
full compensation lies in the knowledge that to them is given
op~ortunity to dispel the shadows which lie across the path down
which our old folks are traveling, and' to bring happiness and
fair promise into the lives of our little ones. We are very
proud of them, and proud of the work they are doing for us. It
has been my privilege on numerous occasions to meet and confer
with them in San Francisco, L os Angeles and at the Homes.
Consequently, feel myself competent to assert that neve r since
their establishment, have our Homes been more thoroughly or
carefully administered.
We find in Section 41 of our Constitution a provision which
requires the Trustees to set aside one-half of the moneys received for the maintainance of the Homes and one-half for permanent improvement. I cannot believe that to be other than
an unnecessary stricture upon the flexib ility of the funds and one
which may bring conditions to seriously handicap. It is easily
conceivable that there may come a time when there will be a
large amount in one fund and a small amount in the other, yet
the needs of the Institution would require that conditions be
reversed. A resolution will be introduced asking Grand Lodge
to remove this needless restriction and permitting the Board to
use the funds as necessities require. I believe t hat should be
done.
One cannot speak, either, in too high praise of the internal
operating staff. Our Superintendents, Brothers Hartman and
Spencer, have peculiar adaptability for their chosen work, and in
all they do ere competent and sustained by a spirit of exalted
humanitarianism. That is easily true of our Matrons and their
invaluable assistants. It would seem that the mere fact that these
good people have chosen to devote their talents and energies to

During the more or less extensive building operations at Covina
there were of necessity many men employed. Owing to differences of opinion which arose and acrimonious discussions which
follow.ed, a spirit of discord and rebellion was engendered. This
finally resulted in the preferment of charges in our Covina Lodge
against Brother Spencer. The affair was of such serious nature
as reflecting upon the reputation of the Fraternity, that my at·
tention was immediately engaged. Complicating matters still further, one misguided brother, a· Past Master of Covina Lodge,
publisher of a local . newspaper, made copy of the text of the
charges, and the next morning an open-mouthed community was
regaled by a recital of the entire transaction. The course of
action to be pursued in the premises was very clear. I immediately deputized the Inspector of the Sixty-second District and
instructed him to make a most searching inquiry and discover
all that he could conce.rning the matter. May I say now, and
with a spirit of pride, that if ever man was faithful to his trust
in the performance of duty, that man was Inspector Frank M.
Beardsley. Forsaking his own interests, he devoted himself for
almost two weeks to the fulfillment of his mission. Driving
~bout in his machine, accompanied ·by a stenographer, he inter~iewed all interested parties and was indefatigable in his efforts
to uncover the truth. Promptly, upon the conclusion of his labors,
he compiled and filed with the Grand Master a report covering
three hundred and twenty-six pages of typewritten testimony. With
the information thus obtained the Board of Trustees was armed
to investigate in its own behalf. The entire Board met in a session covering several days; examined witnesses under the kind
surveillance of Past Grand Master Weller, and finally submitted
;i report of its proceedings. The summary of the findings of the
Trustees was, "We have carefully considered the charges made
against you and have concluded that the said charges are unfounded,
that they are probably the result of gossip emanating from former
employees who have been heretofore discharged for cause."
Had this written Finis across the face of things, .I would have
been glad, but I could not feel that I would be justified in failing
to take cognizance of the inexcusable violation of Masonic law on
the part of the brother who, although a Past Master and supposedly

As to their ability, there can be no question. Incidentally,
let me add, that my observations brought the conclusion · that
they are of that type whose ambitions will not permit them to ·
rest content with anything less than perfection either in themselves
or their officers. Consequently, a high' degree of excellence in the
ritualistic work is noticeable throughout the jurisdiction.
Last year, in his report, the Grand Master presented to Grand
Lodge a plan which· contemplated a change in our present system
to the end that in place of' an Inspector having immediate .charge
of a district, there should be an officer, with title of District
Deputy Grand Master, whose functions should be the same as
those of the present Inspectors, except so far as the ritual is concerned, and to represent the Grand Master. The Grand Lecturer
then to select and appoint various officers to be known as Deputy
Grand Lecturers ; they to teach and supervise the ritualistic work
and examine officers.
With an idea that the practicability of the plan could be best
determined by experience, I took it upon myself to follow insofar
as possible, within the law, and authorized the Inspectors of a
few districts where the work had. been impeded by the difficulties
of travel or communication, to appoint some few competent men
to supervise the esoteric work, the Inspect or to be general supervisor and check up the results. Invariably the reports have been
most gratifying. Wherever the above plan has been inaugurated,
more men have been enlisted in service, new ambitions have been
stirred, and the ritualistic work ha s improved by reason of the
immediate and ever-present personal supervision.

I do hope, brethren of the Grand Lodge, that you will give
sincere consideration to this matter. in all its details. I do hope
that, with your breadth of vision and generous disposition, you
will be enabled to see, in this project, a big constructive work which
intrigues your attention and justifies your support. The Grand
Master has not permitted the use of any part of the contingent
fund allowed at our last session for the above purpose, for he
felt that the plans had not developed to a point which would
justify him in so doing. It, therefore, remains intact.
Inspectors
When I essay to speak to . you about Inspectors I feel constrained to preface what I have to say by craving you1" kind
indulgence, for I fear that I have become a bit "dotty" on the
subject. And so would you, my brethren, if you had had my
opportunity to be of them and with them; to analyze their
worth as men a nd have disclosed their fervency, their zeal and
their devoted attachment to service in behalf of our institution.
Almost always, wheresoever I have visited about the state,
arrangements for my comfort, convenience and pleasure have been
perfected by the Inspectors, and so completely as to leave nothing
to be desired, nothing with which fault could be found. If the
fates, in the perso n of the Grand Lecturer, decreed that I should
participate in the esoteric work, in the larger centers, there have
I found the entire corps of Inspectors, ready and eager to assist.
Their personal relationships, too, were so delightful. There
was such a wonderful "esprit de corps." No small jealousiesne petulance that one was to occupy a conspicuous and important
office, the while another, perforce, must content himself with a
minor and inconspicuous one. But always a perfect harmony
and good fellowship. Sincere delight in the other fellow's praiseworthy accompllshment-good natured raillery at some unfortunate who had been guilty of a temporary lapse.

the chameleon, they soon took on the color of t heir surroundings,

disputes reflected upon the fraternity.' Again, many ardent supporters of Masonry, in the belief and conviction that by so doing

Clandestine Masonry
During the year the R.'.W.'.Brother Burke was approached
by representatives of a body known as the "American Masonic
Federation" with a view toward reconcilement. It w as definitely
stated that their lodges in California were out of h armony with
their Supreme Grand Lodge, a nd wished t o divorce themselves
from it. The Grand Master of the "Provincial Grand L odge of
California," a Mr. P. J. Wilkie, offered to have resolutio ns introduced into that body, looking toward the desired end, and practically guaranteed their passage, but only upon condit ion that the
Grand Lodge of California, F. & A. M., would' take care of the seceding Lodges or, in other words, absorb them into its organization. He called attention to the fact, too, that in the event of
our failure to act promptly in the mater and bring about the desired
coalition, there ' was the terrifying alternative of finding ourselves
face to face with a strong competition that would seriously impair o~r health.
While I was visiting in Los A ngeles during the month pf
June and immediately prior to the Communication of their Provincial Grand Lodge, several attempts were made by representatives
to confer with me. I refused to see them, but sent them word that
there was absolutely nothing about which we could confer. That
if they desired as individuals to affiliate with the Masonic Fraternity there was one way, and only one, by which tha t might be
accomplished: by restoring themselves to proper status, by renunciation of their present allegiance, and then by following the course
prescribed for all others.

Unfounded Rumors
In our capacity as Masons, we should observe the same laws
and be controlled by the same rules of conduct as govern us as
men. There is a natural predilection in most of us for a nice juicy
bit of scandal, and there is nothing that we like better than to
take the other fellow arourtd the corner, to pour into his ear some
vivid little tale, taking a thance, of cour6e, that it be true.
I feel that one' could not receive a more salutary bit of advice than "Guard well your tongue."
Upon numerous occasions, .good brethren have come to nie
.with statements that sundry business houses held decided antipathies against us and refused to employ any one wearing our
emblems. I have gone to considerable trouble in investigating
these charges, sometimes through dependable agents, sometimes
devoting my own time. Invariably I have found them to be but
vague rumors, having no foundation in fact. I believed it necessary ~o call this matter to your attention, brethren, as serious
injury might be done to reputable people and certainly the dissemination of that which we are not certain is. true reflects unfavorably
upon us.
Unworthy Use of Ballot

I can not forbear speaking of it. Very frequentl y we find that
to be the genesis of great discord in the Lodges. It breeds an
ill which is difficult, by reason of the laws and processes involved;
to cure. Generally easy of diagnosis, it is most difficult to correct.
I have received numerous complaints that the action of some
bro'ther was seriously militating against the harmony and wellbeing of the Lodge. I am constrained to believe that there are
some who, in all honesty, feel that the ballot is a righteous weapon

Organizations Demanding Masonic Affiliation as Prerequisite to
Membership
One of the great problems confronting us, and difficulties besetting us, is the mushroom organization which requires Masonic
affiliation as prerequisite to membership. Wrong in its conception,
questionable in its activities, and disastrous in its consequences,
it may not longer be disregarded; it may not be lightly considered,
but must be looked upon with what seriousness the extent of the
menace demands.
All over our broad land they are coming into being. E very
day brings forth a new one. Primarily they are supposedl'y estab-

424

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

lished for the purpose of providing the recreation and diversion
which the dignity and decorum of our lodgerooms will not permit,
or for the creation of an additional bond which will inspire mutual
assistance-or in plainer language, "boosting one another." They
serve as a lure to the lighter-minded and frequently become the
impulse prompting the type of man to whom that sort of thing
appeals to seek membership with us. Their interjection into
various communities has engendered bitter opposition from those
who give Masonry a high place in their lives, and have developed
schisms which have seriously endangered the harmony of theretofore harmonious bodies. Their work is carried on in a spirit of
buffoonery, and ever and- always, in public print and advertising,
do they pridefully proclaim their relationship to the great Masonic
fraternity.
There can be but one result if that sort of thing is permitted
to continue. The good name of the fraternity is endangered, its
ideals will be shattered. There will be dissension and dissatisfaction and shame where pride should ride high. A wise Master
wrote me some time ago, telling me of a brother, not a member of
his own Lodge, who had requested the privilege of the floor that
he might solicit membership for a club which he was forming.
Permission was denied on the grounds that the Master was not
satisfied that the project had the sanction of the Grand Lodge.
His letter requested my views and had incorporated a copy of
these sections of the by-laws of the proposed organization: Said
by-laws predicated in Section A-Organized to promote a stronger
fraternal relation among Master Masons and their families. Section B- To discuss and take action upon any subjects or matter
that is of vital interest to two or more members of this organization. Membership in the organization is limited to Master Masons in good standing in a Lodge recognized by the Grand Lodge
of ~he State of California, and it appears further that a pledge
of secrecy, both as to the proceedings had within the club and
the names of the members thereof, is required. The penalty of
the obligation is:
"Under a penalty of expulsion from this club and having charges preferred against me in my Blue Lodge."
I acknowledged the Master's letter with the following response:

"March 29th, 1921.
"Dear Brother French :
"Adverting to your favor of the 21st instant, requesting
my opinion as to the right of Evergreen Lodge to contribute
from its funds the sum of $1,500 towards the building of a
Community Hospital in your city-I must answer that the
Lodge can not do so. Section 88 and 88c leave no room for
doubt as to the correctness of this decision. Further, the Lodge
has no right to donate the stock which had come into its possession by deed of gift and must make every effort to have it
returned. That stock had become a part of the treasury of the
institution, and, as such, could not be given away except for
Masonically legal purposes. The brethren seem to forget that
Lodge funds are trust funds and must be so considered and
guarded.
"I fully realize the embarassment and difficulties which
this interpretation will engender and I regret its necessity,
but there is no alternative.
"With kindest personal regards, I am
"Sincerely yours,
"(Signed) Grand Master."

Public School Week
If there had been no higher or more worth"y impulse than the
splendid success which attended and magnificent results which
followed Grand Master Adam's inspired Proclamation, setting aside
one week of our year for devoted service in the cause of our
Public Schools, a repetition of that activity would have been jus-

.

~~

But the success of last year's effort was not the only thought
I had in mind when I concluded that there should be another week
set aside during this year.
. I was impelled by the profound conviction that, as worthy
citizens of this great Republic, as children of those who gave their
all th"at it might be firmly established as heirs to this, the greatest
treasure that ever descended to a race of people, it was our duty
and our pride to support it and its institution with all the intelligence which we could command, and all the fervor of g.-atdu,l
souls.
Therefore, I took it upon myself to issue the following:
"September 19, 1921.
"PROCLAMATION.

"Dear Brethren:
"There can be no good Mason who does not love his country and its institutions.
"His love must be of that practical, unselfish variety which
impels service in its behalf to the utmost C?f his capacityyea, even to the point of sacrifice, when necessary.
"The most important element in any country is the men
of that country; and that which develops high character in its
citizenry, wields the greates influence for good and must be
looked upon and accepted as the most valuable among its i~sti­
tµtions.
"We Masons have devoutly believed and held that, fundam~ritally, the greatest contributing force towards the happin~ss
of our people and the well being of our nation is our common
school system of education.
"In our public schools the minds of the generation that
is tq come-the generation that is to assume the burden and
responsibility of the affairs of our country-are shaped and
moulded.
''There our youth is taught the qualifications necessary to
respected maturity; there does it become impregnated with
those ideals which shape its attitude with respect to home and

433

in public; there is developed the spirit of love of God, country and fellow which was first inspired at its mother's knee;
there "does it become imbued with all those graces of heart
and mind so vital to the well being of our glorious America.
"Believing, then, that as Masons and men, we can best
practice our art and demonstrate our citizenship by attesting
our friendship for and belief in and, by all means in our power,
giving encouragement to such an institution;
"We-George Frederick Rodden-Grand Master of Masons
in the jurisdiction of California, have designated and set apart
the first week of October, 1921, as Public Schools' Week and we
request and direct all subordinate Lodges in this Grand Jurisdiction to forego their customary work, so far as that may be
lawful, and with heart and tongue join in promoting the welfare of our Public Schook
"G!lORGt F. Ronn!lN, Grand Master."
Visitations
I have always held fast to the idea ·that a Grand Master, like
any other executive, must study the problem which confronts him,
and having determined a course of procedure which would seem
to him most effective, hew close to the line.
With that thought in mind, I have chosen to go among my
brethren as an apostle of the spirit of Masonry.
I have tried with what little power I possess, to point out
to them its beauty, its wonders and its worth, feeling, I hope not
illogically, that if I could but exalt it in their minds and in their
hearts to that high plane where it so rightfully belongs, if I .could
but glorify it and make them happy in its service, there would
lie the greatest accomplishment.
So I have traveled back and forth, hither and yon.
One cannot say how successful he may have been, but I do
know that if their pleasure even approximated the joy that was
mine, then are we fortunate indeed.
I may not impose upon your patience or your time by giving
a detailed recital of the extent of my visits (the account will appear in its proper place in the proceedings), but I would have
you to know that wherever and whenever it has been possible, I
have answered the call.
And what a privilege it has been.
The unive~sal kindness of the brethren, their splendid hospitality, the eager acceptance of what little I had to offer and

434

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

their charity for my shortcomings, have made an inerasible impression upon me.
Surely if one failed )n response to the nobility of ·such men,
then in truth must his body encircle a heart -of clay and his soul
be muted by thoughts inglorious.
In Appreciation
At the beginning of my term of office, I felt a natural timidity
lest I had undertaken more than I could accomplish. Nor was
that fear dispelled until the reflection came that all around me
were men, capable, conscientious and e.xperienced men, who would
willingly assist whenever I found myself in deep waters.
And all have met that mental prophecy.
Never have I been disappointed;
Witqout reluctance, without hesitation, my lightest wish has
been observed; the most serious commission accepted.
· 1 wish I might attest the depth of my appreciation by calling
them each by name and·givini you a detailed recital of all that
has been done. But that, of course, may not be. I must content
myself by speaking only of the few who have been so closely
with me ,and upon whose time .and talents I have most impos<'•l.
It has been necessary, upon several occasions, for me L\'.l cail
upon the R.'.W.'.Deputy Grand Master, Brother Burke, not on!y
to perform the duties incident to his office, but for other and
alien duties, as well.

I need not tell you, my brethren, you who know him so wel!,
how. thoroughly, how competently, and how willingly he has complied with every request or what splendid .service he has rendered
the fraternity.
Our R.'.W.'.Senior Grand Warden, Brother Sherman, too, by
his sage counsel, his words of encouqi.gement and smiling response to every call, has put you and me under a debt oi everlasting gratitude and the R.'.W.'.Junior Grand Warde!l, Brother
Crites, has been ready at all times to sacrifice his time and ex·
tensive business interests upon the altar of duty. He has traveled
long distances under trying conditions in order that the Grand
Master might be relieved of a responsibility or freed for some
more convc!nient service.
Brothers Adams, Whicher and Baker-words ·cannot tell a ll
they have meant to me.
No lab~r has been too arduous, no sacrifice too great.

Delicate, courteous, with a wlsdom that passed all understanding, with a patience divine, they have been veritable towers
of strength. To these good brethren I extend my profou~d
thanks. I can only say to them that if in future my poor service
will be of any value to them, I am theirs to command.
During the year dispensations have been granted for various
purposes-organization of Lodges, etc. Lodges have been instituted and constituted, halls have been dedicated and cornerstones
laid, all of which will appear in the Grand Secretary's report.
A petition was received for a dispensation to establish a Lodge
in the city of Venice. It was in proper form and strongly supported, but was protested by the nearest Lodge. The fact inspired
an investigation covering several months. I finally concluded
that, under · conditions prevailing, the proposed Lodge would subserve no good purpose and denied the petition.
Which brings me properly to my
Conclusion
Wherein I can say in all truth and in all sincerity that you
have made my year of service as Grand Master, a year of such joy
as has come into the lives of but few men.
You have showered me with riches of your friendship and devotion and have called forth from me a response of fraternal love
that knows no limitations.
I can only feel and with the poet say:
"The riddle _of the world is understood
Only by him who feels that God is Good.
As only he can feel who makes his love
The ladder of his faith, and climbs above
On the rounds of his best instincts."

REPORT OF GRAND SECRETARY
To the M. W. Grand Lodge of California:
I have the honor to present herewith my fourteenth annual report of
the transactions of the Grand Secretary's office for the fiscal year ending July 31, 1,921, together with a detailed account of aU moneys received
and disbursed within the year. I also append an account of receipts
since the close of the fiscal year to and including October, 1921, and
all unfinished business of Grand Lodge:
Masonic Homes Revenues.
1. The practical working of the provisions of Section 41 of the
Constitution, providing for a substantial contribution for the benefit of
the Masonic Homes from all petitioners for the degrees 1 is now assured;
and I am proud to caU attention to the fact that for the year just ended,
the members of our Lodges have actuaUy saved for the Lodge treasuries
more than $54,000 which, had it not been for the present provision,
would necessarily have been paid by the members through their Lodges
for the support of the Homes. This saving to members was accomplished by the reduction last fall of the per capita tax from one doUar
to thirty-five cents. So far as I a~ advised, no petitioner lias objected
to paying twenty doUars for the benefit of the Homes; on the contrary,
reports are that petitioners are proud to be participants in the maintenance of these visible monuments to relief, and to be, in fact and in
deed, serviceable to their less fortunate feUows, their widows and
orphans.

It is to be noted that a few Lodges do not yet understand that the
twenty-doUar contribution from petitioner s is no part of Lodge funds
and no part of the fee fixed for the degrees; and it is hoped that
Masters will fuUy inform themselves with respect to this matter and
instruct their Secretaries accordingly. The special receipt to be delivered to initiates immediately after receiving the first degree is overlooked in some Lodges, and Inspectors are desired to report all such
delinquencies to the Masters.
Membership.
2. At tqe close of our last Annual Communication there were four
hundred chartered Lodges on our registry, with a membership of
76,873. The gain for the year just closed is less than the previous year,
being 8,315 net. The membership as of July 31, plus the newly-formed
Lodges, is now 85,181.

Duplicate Charter Issued

5. The hall of Imperial Lodge No. 390 was destroyed by fire on
the night of September 19, 1921, nearly all furnishings and books and
charter being lost. A duplicate charter was issued September 22, a~
of the original date.

443

6. T he matter of conferring degrees by courtesy is still a problem
that is difficult of proper solution. Our Lodges, like Lodges in all
English-speaking jurisdictions, are · congested with degree work, and
while they delight in extending favors to our sister jurisdictions, yet
fr_equently requests come at times when it is impossible to grant prompt
response. Our Lodges have requested one hundred and ninety-three
degrees to be conferred by Lodges of other jurisdictions in the year
past, and Lodges of other jurisdictions have been accorded the favor
of work to the number of twelve hundred and eighty"six degrees,
without fee. Ordinarily all this work would have been a pleasure-as
it is always a pleasure for California Lodges to grant favors to their
Eastern brethren-but it so happens that ninety per cent of all requests
are for degree work to be conferred at San Francisco, Los Angeles,
San Diego, San Pedro and Vallejo. I commend this subject to your
serious consideration.
Constitution and Ceremonies

7. Nearly ten thousand copies of the Constitution and Ceremonies
were sold last yea r for distribution, as required by law, to those who
had received t1'e tliird degree. The edition last printed will be
exhausted before the end of October, and I desire definite inst ructions
with respect to the contents to be included in the next edition. I
respectfully suggest, and recommend, that all Regulations be omitted
therefrom. T he Constitution (section 228) defines a Regulation to be
any resolution, edict, law or ordinance of any kind, other than the
Constitution, which Grand Lodge may adopt. I further recommend
that all Regulations be r eferred to a committee for careful scrutiny
and revision if need be; that such committee be directed to report to
the Grand Master within six months, and that upon the approval of
the report by the Grand Master and the Chairman of the Committee
on Jurisprudence, the Regulations be printed and sold to members
of the Craft at a price to be fixed by the Committee on Accounts.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Special Communications of Grand Lodge
12. Grand Lodge was conven~d in special commumcatlon by
order of the Grand Master for the purpose and at the times and
places following :
October 22, 1920, R. W. Arthur S. Crites, Junior Grand Warden,
convened Grand Lodge and laid the corner stone of the high school
at Hanford.
October 30, 1920, R. W. Samuel E. Burke, Deputy Grand Master,
convened Grand Lodge and laid the corner stone of the Union high
school at Moorpark.
November 4, 1920, R. \V. Arthur S. Crites convened Grand Lodge
at Turlock and laid the corner stone of the new Masonic hall at that
city.
February 17, 1921, R. W. Arthur S. Crites dedicated the new
Masonic hall at Fellows.
April 30, 1921, the Grand Master convened Grand Lodge and laid
the corner stone of the Grammar school at Hollister.
May 2, 1921, the Grand Master convened Grand Lodge at Atascadero
and laid the corner stone of the Union high school at that place.
May 4, 1921, the Grand Master convened Grand Lodge at Corcoran
and laid the corner stone of the new high school.
May 13, the Grand Master convened Grand Lodge at the city of
San J ose and conducted the solemn funeral ritualistic services over
the mortal remains of our Grand Bible Bearer, John P. Jarman.
May 14, 1921, R. W. Samuel E. Burke convened Grand Lodge at
Ho'.lywood and laid the corner stone of the new Masonic hall at that
city.
June 3, 1921, the Grand Master convened Grand Lodge at Lincoln
and laid the corner stone of the Civic Auditorium at that city.
June 4, 1921, the Grand Master convened Grand Lodge at .Yuba
City and laid the corner stone of the Live Oak High school near
that city.
August 6, 1921, the Grand Master convened. Grand Lodge and
laid the corner stone of the new Masonic hall at that city.
September 7, 1921, the Grand Mastei; convened Grand Lodge at
Sacramento and laid the corner stone of the new building for the
ChJmber of Commerce.
September 27, 1921, the Grand Master convened Grand Lodge at
Turlock and with solemn ceremony dedicated the new Masonic hall
at that city.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON GRAND MASTER'S
ADDRESS
Brother Henrf'E. Verble presented the following report:
To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:
Your committee to which was referred the Grand Master's
Address, and the annual report of the Grand Secretary, has had th.e
same under consideration, and respectfully reports thereon as follows:
I
Grand Master's Address
We have read with earnest approval the account rendered by
the Most Worshipful Grand Master with respect to his stewardship
of the affairs of the Fraternity during the Masonic year now closing. The matters touched upon in the address indicate clearly
that a vast volume of work has fallen upon the Grand Master and
that it has received his most energetic attention.
You who have had the privilege and pleasure of meeting our
Most Worshipful Grand Master as he has traveled over the jurisdiction know and appreciate how untiring have been his efforts to
build into the Craft that true fraternal spirit that we are sometimes prone to neglect. To know him is t o love him. And your
Committee feels that the personal touch which .he has endeavored
to give to the Craft has proven of inestimable value.
Your Committee desires to express, for itself and for this
Grand Lodge, full appreciation of the devoted service which our
Most Worshipful Grand Master has rendered to t he Craft. We
find his address replete with observations and recommendations of
large and lasting value, and sincerely commend the same to the
th oughtful considerat_ion of our brethren throughout the jurisdiction.
