$25,663.59

The inventory of assets, consisting of envelopes, bulletins, blanks,
three typewriters and an addressograph, listed at $5,801.15. .
The report of the Executive Committee showed an expense account
for last year of two cents per capita for the membership of the 37
Grand Jurisdictions belonging. (California's tax for last year would
have been $1,340.00, or six per cent of the total cost.) One member
jurisdiction represented at the St. Louis meeting stated that two cents
per capita was objected to by his Grand E,odge, and yet it is proposed
to fix the tax at five cents per capita, which would mean this year for
California a payment of more than $4,200.00. A permanent Secretary
has now been employed, at presumably a salary befitting the position,
with permanent headquarters at the city of Washington, D. C.
The general purpose of the Association is a "joint and co-operative
effort of the member Grand Lodges to mobilize the ideals and intellect
of all for a solution of those problems which are nation-wide." The
type of service which it is ambitious to render is two-fold: "Relief for
distress, no matter how caused, when its magnitude is greater than
local calamity; and education of our membership, in order that every
Mason may do his full part in helping solve the vexing questions which
today harass humanity."
All this of course is commendable, but the detail of the plan is
not in our humble judgment to be commended. Take the scheme for
relief for an instance; The by-laws o.f the Association provide t!iat
"Upon the occurrence of a disaster· of greater magnitude than a local
calamity, the Grand Masters of the several · member Grand Jurisdictions
within the division in which said disaster may occur, shall appoint a
committee to survey the needs and report forthwith its findings to the
Executive Commission. The Executive Committee shall thereupon
take action on the report of said Grand Masters to the encf that necessary funds shall be provided and properly disbursed."
California Masons, who experienced the glorious and immediate
relief sent from all parts of the world at the time of the destruction of

463

the cities of San Francisco and Santa Rosa by earthquake and fire in
1906, and which relief was so urgently needed, will hardly assent to the
imposition of any circumlocution such as is proposed by the Association.
We know the joy and the beauty of voluntary and immediate response
to need, and like many other jurisdictions, we always take cognizance of
the great calamities that occur at times outside our confines by promptly
telegraphing assistance, fully trusting the afflicted brethren to do what
ought to be done, without the intervention or investigation of any outside committee or commission. We are sure this Grand Lod~e will
not approve the proposed scheme of relief.

In the matter of Masonic education proposed by the Association,
we can heartily indorse it as a proper Masonic work, but one that can
be handled by the several jurisdictions and by Masonic publications at
less cost than will be entailed by the Association and fully as effectively.
As is usual in any assemblage, much interesting oratory was
indulged in, and the brethren expressed their views frankly, but with
a diversity of sentiment which indicated to us that it would be a difficult matter for the association to frame a code of laws acceptable to
the craft. All through the many addresses the dominant thought
seemed· to be that the Masons of the United States should get together
and operate as a unit. But there was lack of unanimity, so far as the
speeches indicated, as to just what line of operation should be pursued.
Several eloquent brethren expressed the notion that we 'aught to "swat"
the Pope; others· that we as Masons should take an active part in
politics and see that none but Masons should be elected to public
office; one frankly questioned the practicability of the organization.
However, a considerable sentiment appeared to be that the Association
should confine its activities to an endeavor to inspire Masons to develop
in their respective Grand Jurisdictions, through agencies already established, a clearer understanding of what Masonry is and for what it
stands-and if the Association would hold to this broad proposition we
could commend it to your favorable consideration, with certain reservations, to wit: That the Association eliminate from its by.laws and
scheme of organization everything except the proposition to invite an
annual or biennial gathering of representatives of the several Grand
Lodges for the sole purpose of getting in close personal touch, to
exchange ideas, to encourage jurisdictions to devote time and energy
to education along lines of civic endeavor and personal righteousness;
to not attempt any cumbersome and impractical plan of general work
or to formulate any definite programme-our idea being that the representatives should get, by personal contact, the viewpoints of the
others and to stimulate each other to go back home "".'ith renewed hope
and renewed faith that the real mission of Masonry is not to advertise

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRA:ND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

our benefactions, but ro teach our novitiates to be law-abiding, loyal
citizens, alive to all matters political, social and moral, that tend to
stability in government and decency in the home. All this to be without
dues or fees except possibly the expense of sending a representative to·
such conference.
We recommend that this Grand Lodge do not join the Masonic
Service Association, as at present organized.
GEORGE F. RovmlN,
Grand Master.

I have visited most of the districts throughout the jurisdiction,
and have held schools of instruction, both day and night sessions.
These schools have all been well attended by the officers and many
members who were interested in the work, all keen in their desire
to perfect themselves in the ritual. I have also given instruction
to officers and brethren in my office from time to time, and often
at the Masonic Club.
The work accomplished by the Most Worshipful Grand Master
in his visitations during the year has been of great benefit to the
Craft. He has visited almost every District and has conferred
degrees at most of the meetings. The appreciation of the brethren
was evinced by the large attendance at the meetings, and the
splendid and impressive manner in which the Grand Master per- ·
formed this work will surely result in much good.

REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER
To .the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of Califor11,ia:

Never before has there been such an enormous growth of the
fraternity as we have had during the two years past. Twenty new
Lodges have been formed this year-the same number last year.
The formation of these Lodges has · to some extent relieved the
vast amount of work which has confr<:>nted many of the Lodges.
The net gain, however, is bU;t slightly less than last year. Quite
a number of Lodges have adopted a policy to not endeavor to keep
up with the petitions offered, but have simply made th.e candidates
wait a time with patience,, and have followed a suggestion made
not to confer more than three firsts or seconds and only one third
degree at· any one meeting. This has given the Lodges time for .
educational and social enU:rtainments, which policy has also' increased the attendance and has resulted in much benefit to the
officers and members, as well as getting away from the so-called
degree mill, that many of the Lodges have resorted to in their
efforts to keep up with the petitions presented. Hence it would
seem that the best solution to relieve this excess of work is the
f.ormation of new Lodges. The really true fraternal spirit prevails
to a far greater extent in the small Lodge than is possi-ble in the
larger ones, the former giving more opportunity for the members
to become acquainred' with one another.

Condition of Lodges
I have received reports from all the Inspectors, and they report
the Lodges under their guidance to be prosperous and the general
condition o f the Lodges is good, and doing effective work. Most
of these are in splendid financial condition. A large majority have
worked out a regular educational program each month, which has
been of much benefit to all concerned and has stimulated interest
and increase in attendance.

It has been my pleasure to accompany the Most Worshipful
Grand Master on many of his visits throughout the State. He has
·visited most of the districts. Many of these were joint meetings.
At quite a few of these visits the Grand Master conferred the third
degree in his own inimitable manner, bringing out the hidden
beauties of the ritual, which was much enjoyed and highly instructive to all, by the perfect and splendid exemplification of the work
conferred, and which was followed by his interesting, progressive,
spiritual . and moral ideals, impressed in his addresses, pointing out
the duties that we as Masons should practice in our daily lives.
All of which was greatly enjoyed and enthusiastically received by
the brethren. Many of these visits were to Lodges that had never
before had the honor of receiving a visit from a Grand Master.
Among this number was Western Star No. 2, at Shasta. Many
years ago this was a busy, thriving community, but now almost
qeserted. The brethren came from great distances to attend the
meeting.
Deaths of Inspectors
It is with much regret and sorrow that I report the loss and
death of Brother John P. Jarman, Brother Granville D. Warren
and Brother Edmund E. Knepper, all of whom had served this
Grand Lodge faithfully and well as Inspectors for many years.
The fraternity and the communities in which they lived have sustained a great loss.

REPORT OF TRUSTEES OF MASONIC HOMES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge ofi_ California:
Your Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California submits herewith its annual report for the fiscal year ending July 31, 1921,
and incidental matters up to and including September 17, 1921 :
Immediately after the close of the annual communication of Grand
Lodge in October, 1920, your Board met and organized by re-electing
Brother Charles M. Wollenberg as President, and Brother James B.
Gist as Vice President. The Board as now constituted consists of the
following members: Charles M. Wollenberg, whose term will expire
in 1922; James B. Gist, whose term will expire in 1923; Charles G.
Johnson whose term expires October, 1921; Robie E. Dill, whose term
· will expire in 1924; and the Deputy Grand Master, and Senior and
Junior Grand Wardens, together with the Grand Treas~rer and Grand
Secretary as ex officio Treasurer and Secretary r.espect1vely: Brother
Dill became a member by appointment of the Grand Master, m November, 1920, Vice E. B. Spencer, term expired. ·
Six regular meetings were held in the year and weekly conference
meetings were held in Los Angeles and San Francisco.
In accordance with the authority granted by Grand Lodge last year,
your Trustees on November 6, 1920, appointed Brother E. B. Spencer
as Superintendent of the Home at Covina. Brother Spencer had been
for many years a hard-working and zealous member of the Board of
Trustees, and during the years of his incumbency had given much
valuable time and thought to the affairs of the children. He was the
logical appointee to take the active management of the Covina Home,
and we believed his tenure as Superintendent would be marked by
continuing this institution as one of the great agencies for child welfare
in America.
·
.
It later appeared to Brother Spencer that his private business would
suffer more than we could reasonably ask if he should continue to
devote his entire time to the affairs of the Home as Superintendent, and
on September 17, 1921, he presented hi~ resignation, in the following
letter:
·
"Covina, California, Sept. 17, 1921.
"Board of Trustees, Masonic Homes of California.
"Gentlemen:
"In · closing my report for the year's record of activities at our
Covina Home I find much pleasure in the fact that we are now enjoying many fea~ures long desired but not established. The Vocational
Building for Boys, the Domestic Science Cottage for Girls, the extensive
playground equipment, the boys club room, the girls music roon; and
the beautiful operation of our self-government plan places our children
in a situation for general development that is probably not equaled in
a home of this character in the country.

473

"I feel that I have had a most active part in accomplishing this
result. It has been attended, however, with much effort and much
sacrifice. It has met with much praise . and our management has
received the strongest approval of those most familiar with the work
and most competent to judge. It has not been without criticism. The
detail of the work has been trying. The effort to please all has not
been entirely successful, but has takep long hours and much labor. My
personal affairs have suffered. My time has been taken from my family
much more than I anticipated.
"For this reason and for the reason that all the real needs for the ·
most successful operation of the Home hav~ been met, I beg to tender
you my resignation as Superintendent of the Covina Home, to take
effect at your convenience. Permit me to thank all members of your
Board for the kind association and p!easant labors together in the
interests of the most interesting and deserving family of happy and
healthy children in the world, let me assure you of my heartiest cooperation in your good work, and if I may at any time be of service
to you by counsel or otherwise, consider me always at your command.
"Fraternally yours,
E. B. SPENCER."
The resignation was reluctantly accepted; but at the earnest solicitation of the Board, Brother Spencer was prevailed upon to continue as
Superintendent until the end of the year.

MATRONS AT DE;coTO AND COVI N A

On October 15, 1920, the resignation of Mrs. Maude E. Miller as
Matron at the Covina Home was received and accepted. Mrs. Miller
had been associated with the Home for eight years. She was dearly
loved by all the children, and her services were highly appreciated by
the Trustees. Ill-health, however, demanded that she relinquish her
duties there, and she was reluctantly permitted to retir e. She will carry
with her in whatever field she may be the best wishes of every member
of the Board, and the prayers of the children that she may be restored
to full health.
On July 1st, 1921, Miss Sallie Daingerfield resigned her position
as Matron at Decoto, for the purpose of engaging in school work-a
work she had long cherished. She had proved to be an excellent
Matron, and the Trustees released her only because the change appeared
to be for her benefit. H er successor was found in Mrs. Minnie Richardson ( Ma5onic affiliation being King Solomon's Lodge No. 260.)
CARI( OF THI( BODILY AFFLICTl(D

One of the most difficult problems that confronts your Trustees is
in the matter of applications from Lodges. in behalf of men· and women
who are afflicted with bodily disease that necessitates constant personal
attendance and medical care. These cases, as a rule, are particularly
needy and frequently are the most deserving of assistance at the hands of
the fraternity. They cannot be cared for at the Decoto Home, as the

476

PROCEEDINGS OF THEl

hospital there is not large enough to care for others than residents who
may become ill after admission to the Home. The Trustees, during
the past year, have assisted several Lodges to find suitable accommodattions for their helpless dependents, and in some instances have assisted
in a financial way, in accordance with the authority granted the Board
last year by Grand Lodge.
LIBRARY

The library at the Docoto Home is enjoyed by most of the residents,
and while the shelves are well filled, there have been few recent contributions of books. We call the attention of our brethren that it is
not only works on philosophy and Masonry tha.t are enjoyed by the
men and women at the Home. A good novel, a love story, or a thrilling
book of adventure has the effect for a time at least to bring back to the
aged ones dreams of youth-splendid dreams of "auld lang syne" that
are gone forever to them, but nevertheless that make for sunshine in
the hearts of those whose suns are nearly set. Therefore, we ask that
brethren will kindly remember the Home library and send books which
they have most enjoyed.

Trustees, to provide for the maintenance of the Homes and for such
improvements as are then in progress or contemplated for the immediate future, the surplus shall be by them allocated to the Endowment
Fund."
The purpose of this change is to enable us to use for building purposes all funds not needed for maintenance. At present, under the provisions of section 41, we must allocate one-half of the fund received to
maintenance and one-half to building. Any surplus in either fund goes
to the Endowment Fund. If there is a deficit in one fund and a surplus
in the other, we can not now apply the surplus to wipe out the deficit
but must appeal to Grand Lodge for financial assistance.
We believe that the adoption of this amendment will hasten the
time when we can come to Grand 'Lodge with a recommendation that
the fifty-cent 'Building Fund tax be repealed, thus reducing the burden
on the Lodges.
We are also recommending that the per capita tax on the Lodges
be twenty-five cents, a reduction of ten cents over last year. This makes
a total reduction of seventy-five cents in the eighteen months the new
law has been in force.

The building program at Decoto will call for about $250,000, and
this amount will be in the Building Fund hy the time it is needed.
Covina will need additional buildings for the children next year, as
we are rapidly reaching the limit of the present accomodations. fo
order that we may meet this condition we recommend that subdivision
1st of s~ction 41 of the Constitution be changed to read as follows:
"1st. For every degree it shall have conferred during the year, the
sum of one dollar; and in addition thereto, the sum of $20.00 for the
use and benefit of the Masonic Homes of California, for every candidate
of its own Lodge upon whom it shall have conferred the first degree
and for every member elected for affiliation. upon a dimit, or cer.tificate
of standing or withdrawal, from a Lodge of a jurisdiction other than
California. The contributions for the use and benefit of the Masonic
Homes shall be by the Lodge collected from the petitioners at the
time of ·the receipt of their petitions and transmitted to the Grand
Secretary on the first day of November, February, May, and August
of each year; no remittance shall be made for account of any petitioner
until he shall have received the first degree; and immediately upon
receipt thereof the Grand Secretary shall pay the same over to the
Grand Treasurer to be by him held subject to the order of the Trustees
for the use and benefit of the Homes. When the amount thus collected
and so held shall be more than sufficient, in the judgment of the

PRINTING 01' SUMMARIZED RiPORT

Recognizing the value of publicity, and believing that the members
of the fraternity are entitled to be fully informed with regard to the
work of the Homes, we would recommend that a . condensed summary
of this report be printed, together with the regulations for admission,
and illustrated with views of both Homes, and that said report be
distributed to each member of the Fraternity.
REQUEST THAT BRl(THRl(N VI SIT THI\ HOMl(S

It is the desire e.nd hope of the Board that every member in attendance at Grand Lodge will visit the Decoto Home before returning
to their respective Lodges. Only in that way may the brethren personally know of the work being done for our dependent brethren and their
widows and mothers. We feel sure that if every Mason in California
could visit the Homes, talk to the residents, greet their brethren there,
their widows and mothers, they would enthusiastically spread the word
throughout the jurisdiction that we have in the two Homes real monuments to the Masonic doctrine of relief ; and still ·more important, that
the visitors would return to their homes with · a high resolve to
encourage those who have been specially blessed with ·large, fortunes, to
devote a part thereof to the maintenance and further improvements of'
the Masonic Homes of California.

COMMENDATION

We feel that we cannot close this report without calling attention
to the cheerful response Past Grand Masters Adams and Weller always
have made when the Board has needed legal advice. Hardly a week
goes by but some question arises or legal papers require to be drawn,
and without hesitancy we have handed the work over to one of these
good brethren. This work has always been done without fee or co~t
of any kind to the Homes. Brothers Warren E. Libby, John W. Gwilt
and other good attorneys have also rendered appreciated services without
fee, for which we extend our thanks.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GENERAL CONDITIONS AT DECOTO HOME
During the past year there have been admitted to the Home
22 men and 13 women; 25 have passed to their last reward. There
are now at the Home 87 men and 59 women.
Every room in the women's department is now occupied, and
as admissions can only be made as vacancies occur, the need for
additional room is most urgent to provide for those now on the
waiting list. ·
The health of the Home has been good with the exception of
th.ose who are becoming infirm and helpless. Increased accommodations are also needed at the Coleman Hospital. It was originally
built for 15 beds and is now caring for 11 men and 12 women.
A number of the Brethren continue to contribute to the welfare of the Home by their services in performing light duties of
various kinds in keeping with their strength.
The women residents attend to the making, mending and marking of hoitsehold .linen and have taken charge of not only their own
rooms but also th.e halls, stairways, wash rooms and other parts of
the main building and annex. They also assist in work con~ected
with the dining rooms and at the hospital.
Special attention is paid to the social features of the Home and
all the residents are afforded all the diversion necessary.
Many entertainments have been given for the pleasure and
benefit of the members of the family by Lodges, members of Lodges
and t~eir ladies. All holidays have been observed with appropriate
exercises.
The following is a list of those· who have contributed to our
enjoyment.

visited the Home.

COVINA HOME-SUPERINTENDENT'S REPORT.
Board of Trustees,
M asonic Homes of California.

The increasing demands of the Covina Home necessitated the
creation of the office of Superintendent, to bring into practical operation
the many departments of this work in the thorough manner that the
high ideals of Masonry 'should require. Having been requested by
your Board to accept this responsibility, I have endeavored to perform
the duties of the office to my best judgment, and I am encouraged to
believe that the results accomp!ished justify the pride the Fraternity
displays in our Home, and merits the approval so generously exprP.sseo
by many friends and Masons most familiar with the work and most
competent to judge. My fullest compensation, however, is the gratitt;de
and sincere appreciation of the children who strive so earnestly to
reach the highest mental and, physical standards. The result 0f their
efforts, and the satisfactory co-operation of our patient matrons and
assistants, is best shown in the reports of Doctors Faber and Ritter
in their examinations made by the Department of Pediatrics of
Stanford University, which they will report to your Board.
Organization-Best results are obtained by a systematic use of
our time. Waste of time or material destroys efficiency and discourages
industry. The more quickly necessary duties are performed the more
time is .conserved for diversions. H appiness is derived from satisfac.
tion in labor as well as in the pleasant hours of diversion. Our aim
is happiness in occupation as well as diversions; therefore an organiza·
tion of departments, with none overlapping, has stimulated a healthy
competition among members of our staff, as well as our appreciative
children. Our staff is organized as follows .:
Edward B. Spencer
Dr. W . P. Magan
Dr. J . M. Dunsmoor
Dr. Warren Gill
Prof. Geo. M. Hargrave
Hanora A. Douglas

Superintend~nt
Home Physician
Consulting Physician and Surgeon
Chief of Dental Work
Physical and Manual Training
Matron

Immediately on assuming direct charge of the H ome, new filing
cabinets were installed ; and all records of children, including copies
of applications, family. history, and the charts showing the physical and
mental surveys of Stanford University were segregated by Lodges.
In future all correspondence, health reports, school records or other
information will be carefully kept in these files for the benefit of the
child or Lodge, as well as our own record of the child's care.

504

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Under the direction of Doctors Magan and Dunsmoor, physicians,
and Dr. Gill, dentist, we followed every recommendation made by Dr.
Faber; and the Matron, Housemothers and others, under the direction
of the Superintendent, followed faithfully with most pleasing resuits
the recommendations of Dr. Arthur J. Ritter. Our internal management has been changed to a marked degree. We have endeavored to
eliminate every feature or form of institutional methods, and give the
home spirit in actual practice in all domestic details. The children
enjoy these changes, and they have demontrated by their interest in
our new features that with proper cooperation the plan is most
practical.
A Self Government plan actually in operation has proven a most
constructive feature of our work. Our plan takes the form of our
National Government in a legislative way, but places the executive
in the hands of committees. The "House" is composed of children
in the fourth to the seventh grades inclusive. The "Senate" is formed
by children of the eighth grade and High School. _The Matron,
assistaut matron, and House Mothers form the Cabinet, and the
Superintendent is the directing head. This will at once be termed
semi-seli-goverpment by those experienced in the work. We will
admit ·that to the extent of the advisory cabinet and executive officer,
but the children through their committees actually put into operation
the resolutions of the Bodies of their Congress. '.J'he failure of selfgovernment in chi!dren is the lack of executive ability, judgme~t and
initiative. This semi-self-government, if you choose to so designate
it, with instructors as counsellors, makes the plan a practical one,
and the results in inspiring interest in the government of the Home,
and pride in establishing high standards for their perso~al conduct,
is gratifying. It solves many disciplinary problems and stimulates the
principles ·of good citizenship in the child mind.
As a part of our educational work I feel I should mention here
that our work has been made more pleasant and more fruitful of good
results by the insta'.lation of some very practical interior improvements
by some of our generous friends in the Fraternity. Brothei: Joseph
E. Hinds of Corona Lodge, Pasadena, fitted up a beautiful music
room at much expense in the girls' dormitory building. Walls were
beautifully painted in mottled tints, a stage constructed with curtains
and lighting effects, and hardwood floors built in for instruction in
classic dancing.
The Patrons Association of the Eastern Star of Los Angeles and
Orange counties furnished a club room for boys in a ~ost el_aborate
way. Lockers were installed for sport costumes, hikmg suits and
drill uniforms as well as card tables, games and other diversions for
the active-minded boy who demands intelligent indoor recreation.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The past year has also witnessed the expenditure of nearly $5000.00
in playgrounds and equipment. The child needs play. Recreation, is a
physical and mental necessity. Whether or not all may approve of
this expenditure of money, we are ready to report we have derived
most satisfactory results from well directed p'.ay. with these scientifically designed forms of playground equipment. Let us here acknowledge our debt of gratitude to the Grand Court of the Order of
Amaranth through the efforts of their wonderful Grand Matron, Dr.
Flora Smith of Kingsburg, and the general Masons composing the
"Masonic Players" under the direction of their enthusiastic and capable
leader, .Brother Jesse Whited, for much of this equipment. Our hours
are so .arranged that each child receives a certain amount of outdoor
diversion. Generally they all like it, and are eager for games of competitive skill and physical action, but we have occasionally the book- · ·
worm or semi-anemic who requires urging.
Many minor improvements have been made to aid the operation
of detail work or add conveniences or privileges which should properly
be mentioned. A barber shop has been constructed in the half basement of the boys' building. Mizpah and Hollywood Lodges supplied
good barber chairs, and Brothers Greer and Pitman of these Lodges
furnished an electric hair clipper and other tools. A playroom for
small boys too young for school, and others during unpleasant
weather, has been partitioned off and lockers for playthings built in.
A series of portable tables and benches .has been provided for the
comfort of visiting Lodges who come from a distance and desire
lunching accommodations. South Gate Lodge is now constructing a
large awning that will provide a most comfortable feature for outdoor
meetings. This is circular in form and built around the steel flagpole in front of the group of buildings. Lockers and store rooms ·
have been provided for playground apparatus, tennis nets, basket ball,
base ball volley ball outfits, etc. A grand stand is now being constructed ~n the base· ball field, the gift of Fresno Pyramid of Sciots.
A small blacksmith shop with forge a:nd suitable equipment has saved
much in time, money and convenience. A new milk house .was · a
pleasing improvement. Wheeled containers for garbage and waste
removes the unpleasant part of this work for the boys. Incinerators
at the rear of each building makes easy work for little fell~ws to
keep the yards clean. Curbs built on .roa~ways keep playgrounds and
gardens free from carlessness of drivers. Many, many other ~uch
features are installed to keep the lesson of system, economy of time,
and neatness before the young and impressionable mind.

housing and care of our family. First, we must mention the Manual

The general appearance of the property has been greatly benefited

property line and kept in order by our own men. New shrubbery and
roses have been set out in places before left bare. Roadways have

Old trees, and useless or unprofitable trees, have been removed from
the orchard area and fruit trees planted. An unsightly ravine always
used as a dumping ground for neighbors and others has been partially
filled and set to orange trees which fills out our lines to even dimensions. For particulars of our farm improvement, I refer you to the
attached report of our farmer which may be interesting to those
desiring this detail.
The question is frequently asked, "How are the children supplied
with personal funds or spending money, such as enjoyed by the child
in the private family?" This is nicely cared for by our merit system
which compensates through the medium of prizes for efficiency neatness, effort, thoughtfulness and voluntary 'service. This year,' being
one of much new work, the boys were given first opportunity to do
work that '\\'.Ould ordinarily be done by employed workmen. Digging
tree holes, grading terraces, roadways and playgrounds, setting shrubbery, helping with fencing, etc., all brought them amounts in proportion
to the cost if done outside. Boys share in these extra amounts, ~nd
enjoy additional privileges, who care for chickens, pigs, bees, garden,
lawn or special work that occurs from time to time. Merit prizes are
given for industry each six months. A display of useful articles is
opened up like a fair and the number of •articles shown ·at such times
is surprising. The girls filled an exhibition space 22 x 44 with garments,
needlework, and handwork. Boys displayed many models of "auto-

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

508

mobiles", furniture, rollers, etc. Each entry received some prize.
Swimming, diving and hiking priZ'es are awarded generously, all which
stimulate effort with beginners. Care is used to provide prizes for a
variety of effort, so that none may be without encouragement in
some line.
Moneys are frequently left by visitors. No child accepts a "tip"
for a service, but the visitor is permitted to contribute to a "Treat
Fund" in which all participate. Visiting Lodges some .times leave a
collection and Chapters frequently donate a dollar to each child for
spending money. This fund amounted this last year to over $300.00,
and gave the children about '$4.00 each spending money.
Some children receive small amounts of money from parents or
their Lodges, some earn money caring for grounds, or work at school.
These funds go to their private account. Each child is given opportunities to earn so their private accounts are nearly equal in amount
and no embarrassment is suffered. High School children are given
a small allowance to meet little emergencies, and to take part in all
l>chool activities. This is charged to school expense from our maintenance fi,md. Each child also has a savings account in the bank.
This is added to by their own earniilgs and certain Lodges, Chapters,
the Grotto and others contribute equally to each child about Christmas
time. Friends frequently send amounts for the Easter trip to Baldy,
Thanksgiving treat or for their Beach season. These amounts go to
the Children's Self-Government organization and many p!easant outings
are provided.

In closing my report I desire to express my great pleasure in
serving yon the past year, and I have enjoyed participating in the
privilege of bringing these many new advantages to our de~erving
children. I have done this for the great love I personally cherish for
them all and my compensation is their appreciation of my efforts.
Now th~t my dream of ''.a beautiful perfect and complete whole" in
'the way of equipment is realized, I am requesting you to relieve me
of further responsibility in the detail of the work. A new S11perintende.n t can now step into a systematic organization of well trained
children without our good work suffering any inconvenience from the
change. You have my strongest good will, and 'if I may be of service
at any time to you or your new Superintendent, in counsel or otherwise, consider me always at your command.
Fraternally submitted,
E. B. SPENCER, Superintendent.

COVINA-RESIDENT PHYSICIAN'S REPORT
In making this report I will only endeavor to cover those things

that pertain more or less directly to the health of the children.
In a general way the children are more free from disease than
those of the ordinary institution, or I might say even the surrounding
community, for they have a regular daily programme which they follow
and which involves proper exercise, an abundance of fresh air, good
wholesome food and kind and competent supervision and care by the
Superintendent and house mothers.
As to the diet, their menu consists of an abundance of plain,
wholesome and nourishing food. Special attention is given from time
to time to their diet and where one child requires special attention
to his diet this is looked after and the patient kept under observation
till he is set aright. Fresh vegetables and fruits in season are served
daily and I find no combinations of left-overs served at the tables or
on the trays.
An inspection of the hygienic surroundings and observation from
time to time shows them to be without fault. The sleeping quarters
consist of small wards, provided with at least one full window for
each bed, thus giving sufficient air and light for the occupants. The
wards are kept spotlessly clean and each child is taught to make his
own bed. The lavatories consist of sprays, washbowls and toilets
where the children take daily baths, etc. Each child has his own
towel, hairbrush, etc., and locker. Up-to-date playgrounds and a large
swimming pool are other features that add to the health and pleasure
of the kiddies. The children are examined from time to time for any
communicable disease that they may have, so that proper steps may
be taken i~ the matter of isolation, etc., that the other children may
not be exposed.
The Home provides proper and necessary facilities for manual
training for the children. This is very advantageous · in that it fits the
boy or girl with a trade or occupation, by means of which he may make
his livlihood when he grows up, is discharged from the Home, and
thrown on his own resources. It also helps to keep him in good
physical condition thus rendering him less susceptible to the diseases or
infections with which he may come in contact.
As stated in the beginning of this report the amount of sickness
in the Home is at the lowest possible figure. This is due largely to
the hygienic surroundings, proper diet, the out-of-door life which all
the children enjoy and last but not least, the kind and conscientious
care given by those in charge. I believe that Mr. Spencer and his

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

co-workers deserve the credit for the fact that in the past three years
there have been no deaths at the Home. This to my mind is evidence
• of successful preventive mea~ures.

COVINA-DENTIST'S REPORT
Upon being given the privilege of serving our children at Covina
m the care of their teeth, I called together my brethern of Wilshire
Lodge in the dental profession, and on April second we made a
complete survey of the seventy-seven children in the H~me at that
time. The work indicated was placed upon charts made for each child.
It was a most agreeable surprise to find their mouths in such
good condition. There was no · pathological condition of any note.
Not an abscessed tooth in the entire Home, which is quite remarkable
and very extraordinary. This is probably due to a great extent to the
instruction the children receive, their good care and the plain wholesome food selected for them.
The following work was indicated: 60 cement or temporary fillings
for deciduous teeth, 48 silver or amalgam fillings, 5· gold inlays, 1
porcelain crown, 57 extractions, 12 regulation cases, five of which were
important, and about half .of the children needed prophylaxis.
After charts were made for each child, they were divided into
eight groups, with the· work as nearly equal as possible. A dentist was
then assigned permaner.itly to each group, and he is responsible for
the dental work of his group. These groups are like little dental
families, and. the doctors take a particular interest in t,heir little patients.
The children also take pride in having their own dentist, and each
one thinks his dentist is the best.
The operating is. done mostly in the splendidly equipped operating
room at the Home. Some of the work is done jn the dentist's office
in Los Angeles.

COVINA-SCHOOL REPORT
Your Superintendent, our good Brother Spencer has invited me
to join him in his report of the past fiscal year, and to make you
familiar with advantages offered to the school of which your
children are a part. The teachers of both the High School and
Grammar School speak in terms of praise of the Masonic . Home
children. They reflect their Home training in their courteous bearing,
their neatness in personal appearance and their active interest in all
the elements of school life. They occupy a prominent place in our
student body. Their intelligence is noticeably above the average and
they are chosen as class or student body officers frequently by the
popular vote of students.
The Covina Union High School opened the 1921-22 session with
an enrollment of 3'10 students, and a faculty composed of 19 teachers.·
The course of study embraces all the subjects of an up-to-date high
school, and offers studies that prepare any boy or girl to take up
such courses as Agriculture, Architecture, Chemistry, Commerce,
bentistry, Engineering, Forestry, Household Science, Journalism, Law,
Medicine, Music, Art, Pharmacy, and entrance to any college.
The school offers courses in both metal and wood shop. The
metal work includes forge, lathes and auto mechanics. This year the
wood shop is giving, in addition to the regular wood work, reed and
upholstering furniture. The commercial department offers work in
general office practice, such as posting and filing. The department is
well equipped with adding and posting machines, together with dictaphone and typewriters.

The work is progressing splendidly, and now that vacation is
over, it will soon all be complete. The Doctors will have only occasionally to examine their little dental families to see if they are in need of
repair or new work.

Mention should be made of our unusually well equipped physics
and chemistry laboratories.

This work is done by dentists from Wilshire Lodge No. 445.
They wish the credit, be that what it may, to go to the Lodge and

The school has always been act ive in athletics, sending out teams
in such sports as football, baseball, track, basketball, and tennis.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Interscholastic debate is fostered, and the students are encouraged
to participate in all kinds of forensic work. Each year two or three
plays are given, whereby a large number of students are given privileges
to work out along this line.
Music occupies an important place in the school. Much individual
instruction is given. Any student who has music ability is encouraged
to develop it. Every year a large musical program is given, using
every possible ability in the school.
The social life of the school is almost ideal. The moral conditions
are superb. The school is very democratic; it is like a large family.
The number is not large, so that a student may be personally acquainted
with every student in school.
The Charter Oak Grammar School is a most unusual rural
school.. In fact, it is a rural school with city advantages. It has an
enrollment of 150 children, with a faculty of eight teachers, five
regular and three special instructors. These children have work in
cooking, sewing, manual training, and art under very skillful teachers.
The district is a very·wealthy one, and has just voted bonds for
$50,000 with which to erect a modern cement building, which will
be well lighted, heated and ventilated. This will complete the conditions at Charter Oak, making it one of the ideal situations and
surroundings for school facilities in the state.
The school has for its principal a most capable woman in Miss
Clara Thompson. She devotes her whole life to the school, and the
children all like her and willingly follow her instruction.

COVINA-REPORT ON MANUAL TRAINING
A report from my department must be one descriptive of future
plans rather than of past work, as I am only beginning my labors·
with you. I must say that in the short time I have worked with
your boys I am wonderfully impressed with their knowledge of
organized effort, their eagerness to acquire profiCiency and their
gentlemanly deportment. It reflects the greatest credit on the management and I am pleased to become a member of the operating staff of
workers with these boys. In the Manual Training department I have
outlined the following as the best type of work for th is Home:
1. Repair work about the buildings, it being a method of teaching
the boys economy and also familiarizes them with factory methods
of assembling furniture.

513

3. Toys, made before Christmas, have a high educational value
.
and also gives to the boy the spirit of 'giving.
4. Reed furniture is fast coming into popularity, and, as the
layout is inexpensive and cost of materials is slight, it is being used in
schools to a large extent at this time. Reed work can be given as
low as the 6th grade with success. Range of projects are from baskets
and reading lamps etc. to ferneries and library tables-, etc.

5. Kite work. For spring work the making and flying of kites
can not be surpassed for popularity and also for its instructive value.
A proposed kite contest will be held where all the boys can compete
in the many events where kites can be used.
In Physical Training I find a receptive spirit for training and a
love of contest among them that greatly aids the instructor.
Organized play is recognized as one of the important parts of a
child's education. It trains him to work with others in a harmonious
manner. These great truths will be the aims of the Physical Training
program for the boys of the Masonic Home. With this in view it is
planned that the boys of the H ome be organized into groups, each
having a leader or captain, in order to make the instruction more
beneficial and helpful.
The Physical Training program will be divided into two divisions.
First: the physical development division which will include posture
training, gymnastic tra"ining such as Indian club drills, tumbling on
the mats, pyramid building, rope climbing, horizontal and parallel bar
work, practice on the overhead ladder, swimming and other work
utilizing the splendid equipment of the H ome. Second: the athletic
division where the boys will be given instruction in the various athletic
games as base ball, track, basket ball, tennis, indood, hand ball and
soccer, and also in Mass games which will train alertness, knowledge
of the rules and judgment, such games as snatch ball, ostrich tag,
prisoner's base, etc. will be used.
Contests of various kinds will be planned between the boys of
the Home and the near by Grammar Schools. These contests will
bring the boy in contact with other boys and will teach him to control
his will giving him self-control, self-reliance, courage and above all he
will be coache.d to go into these games as a true sportsman playing
the game fair no matter what the results may be.

514

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Another phase of the Physical Training program will be the
establishing of good health habits. A strong physique can not be
built up in a cigarette smoker, nor in a body who indulges in any
form of intemperance, and this truth will be brought out in every
part of the work.
The Masonic Home has a very fine physical training equipment
including grounds and apparatus and every effort will be made to give
the boys the full benefit of this.
G1;:o. M. HARGRAVE, Director.
COVINA REPORT ON FARM WORK.
The farm work of the Masonic Home this year has been so ·satisfactory that I feel our report will please Masons of California very
much. I wish they could have a before and after picture of the place
since it has been my privilege to do this work under your able and
courteous direction.
First let me say the grounds and soil are well adapted for the purposes, and satisfactory results are easy with your complete equipment.
The most important improvement of the year I should say was the
. grading and setting out of the citrus and deciduous orchards. About
forty well developed deciduous trees were moved to a location formerly
used as chicken runs, without loss. One hundred sixty-two new Valencias were added to the orange grove, and where new grading permitte<I
planting in an irregular piece near the cottage, a variety of unusual
fruits were planted for table use. New terraces were added to the side
hill vineyard and 235 new grapes were set or replaced. The sloping
ground on the lower area has been set to 184 deciduous trees with a loss
of only six, which have been replaced. These are all doing well. The
area below the sceptic tank has been terraced and set to berries consisting of two rows blackberries, three rows dewberries, two rows raspberries, two .rows loganberries and an irregular area set even with
strawberries. All areas between rows of new trees have been planted
to milo maize and Egyptian com, which produced well. All the alfalfa ·
field was plowed up and reseeded and new pipe placed to give satisfactory irrigation facilities.
· The garden ground has been changed to row the vegetables so that
a slower water flow is used and a much increased space covered. Pressure water has been extended to this tract and propagating beds and
plants are now convenient for use. Aside from this tract we have
squash, pumpkins, melons, etc., on sloping ground, and artichokes, asparagus and tomatoes on the hill ground.
Our livestock is in good shape. We were obliged to dispose of
one horse and secure a new one. We lost a fine cow through an acci-

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

.515

dent. We now have a good heavy team and .a light .horse for single
work. We have five graded Holstein cows; all doing well. One change
is recommended in this herd. We have eleven hogs or pigs which are
easily kerit by our surplus from the garden and waste from the building.
Our chickens are a good strain of white leghorns. We have about two
hundred young hens now doing well. This number will probably be
doubled in the spring. The chicken runs were all rebuilt and houses
furnished to designs given by the Holly Poultry F~rms Co., which supplies us with chicks.
The boys give entire care to the bees and they are doing well. The
boys show intelligence in their care of the pigs and chickens and I
recommend they again try their hand with ducks and rabbits.
The fencing, irrigation lines and roadw.ays which gave us some inconvenience are now in best order and all work well in · the general
system.
The older trees, both lemon and oranges, are doing remarkably
well. Last year all trees were pruned well back, fertilized and some
grade lines changed. The results were shown this year and our fruit
is of the highest grade. We have the "Sunkist Grove" sign awarded
us, which shows the standard of care and product.
Permit me to express my pleasure in performing my part of the
good work entrusted to you and the cordial men composing your
·
Board of Trustees.
Respectfully submitted,
M. G. GRADL£R, Farmer.

In making a report of the past year's work at the Masonic Home
at Covina, I can only say there has been less to do than in past years.
My calls have been for consultation largely, as Dr. Magan of Covina
has kindly and generously met the· needs Ki the ordinary illnesses common to children.
·
·
I was called in consultation with Dr. Magan in the serious illness
of James Keeley and Helen Gilliam and assisted the operation performed on James Keeley. I d.esire to commend Dr. Magan for his skill
and judgment in this case.
·
At the close of school each year, it is my pleasure to call with other
doctors who are specialists in their work, and care for all cases of
adenoids, enlarged tonsils or similar troubles. This year I was assisted
by Dr. Walter L. Crane, Dr. W. Frank Holman, Dr. R. F. Hastreiter,
Dr. Robt. M. Dunsmoor and Dr. Nannie C. Dunsmoor. W e found much
less work to do this year than previous years and the health of the
children most satisfactory.
Respectfully.
J. M. DUNSMOOR, M. D.

VISITATIONS TO COVINA HOME.
The visitations this year by different Lodges and Masonic bodies
were so well distributed and so nicely conducted that no inconvenience
was suffered and much pleasure and benefit derived. This year the
Lodges and individuals sought to entertain the children rather than the
children furnishing "programs" so frequently to crowds of visitors.
Our friends have been kind in words and deeds. Lodges bringing out
shows Saturday have frequently brought their "officers and enjoyed the
evening with the children. Jackie Coogan, Wesley Barry, Bennie Alexander and other child successes have visited personally and entertained
the children. Anne Raymond, the "Health Fairy," gave her lectures
physicians have spoken on health rules and dentists on care of teeth
and business men described their manufacturing plant or shipping interests. Other visits are as follows:
September 9th, 1920. Harbor Chapter No. 174, 0. E . S., conveyed
the children of the Home to Point Firmin, near San Pedro, to a picnic
with suitable observation of Admission Day. A splendid picnic lunch
with many refreshments. was provided, and games in the afternoon were
in generous prizes awarded.
September 19th. South Gate Lodge No. 320 and South Gate Chapter No. 133 visited our family in large numbers. This good Lodge
always takes the children among their numbers for basket lunch and
some provide ice cream and other refreshments for them. They left
with the children a generous amount for their Treat Fund, and a very
large quantity of fru its, jams and jellies for their store room.
September 19. Dr. Flora Smith, Grand Royal Matron of the Amaranth, and her splendid corps of officers paid the children a visit. Dr.
Smith, with· her genial personality, has won the hearts of all the chi!-

dren and is an inspiration both to the members of our large family and
to our staff of assistants who look forward to her pleasant visits. Dr.
Smith offered prizes for a contest for essays on the virtues or emblems
of the Amaranth. She declared every essay a winner and gave each
child a $1.00 bill as a prize.

October 10th. Through the courtesy of Brother F. B. Comfort of
University Lodge, the Golden Bell Quartette gave a musical and entertainment for the children.
October 24th. Moneta Lodge No. 405 came with their families to
view the buildings and Home and entertained the children on the lawn
and grounds with some pleasing numbers.
October 31st. East Gate Lodge No. 290 mingled with the children,
exchanging different features of entertainment and" making the day a ·
most delightful one.
November 4th. About forty-five members of San Diego Lodge No.
35 visited with a committee from West Lake Lodge that they might
have an opportunity to carry back to the Lodges of San Diego their impressions of our good family and the nice Home provided for them by
the Fraternity.
November 7th. Highland Park Lodges No. 382 visited the Home
and entertained the children with some exceptional numbers. They
left a generous supply of fruits, jams and candies.
November 14th. Los Angeles Lodge No. 42, with a committee of
wonderful entertainers, gave the children a day of music and vaudeville entertainment that was wholesome, pleasing and instructive. It
was a day long to be remembered.
November 14th. Ashlar Lodge No. 306 of Colton came over from
their home place in a number of automobiles, all loaded with fruits,
and spent a portion of the day visiting with the children. Brother Andrews, the Master, attempted to look young again, that he might remain.
November 20th. Sister Hammersly, Matron of La Puente Chapter,
and a committee of about twenty of her good members, spent an interesting afternoon with the children and becoming quite well acquainted
with some of our older girls. They left a liberal quantity of fruits,
walnuts and almonds.
November 21st. No more active or generous Lodge exists in the
jurisdiction than Culver City Lodge No. 467. Their whole membership
appears to be entertainers, and their presence with us was like one continuous round of humorous episodes.
·
November 21st. ·several members of Wilshire Chapter No. 329
called at the Home and spent an hour with the children. This good
Chapter is deeply interested in our family and always remembers them
nicely through fruit season.
November 28th. Ramona Lodge No. 457 and Ramona Chapter No.
'J67 called with a musical and entertainment program for the children,

September 19. A most desirable visit was received from Artesia
Chapter No. 253, 0. E. S. Our friends enjoyed the visit with the children and left a generous supply of canned fruits.
September 26th. Miss Italia Anita Garibaldi, granddaughter of
General Garibaldi of Italy, lunched with the children and then gave a
most pleasing address describing conditions in her native country. I:Ier
reference to her distinguished father as a Past Grand Master of Masons
brought forth applause from the children. Brother A. Vignola, who
accompanied Miss Garibaldi, requested and was granted the privilege
of preparing the lunch for the children.
September 26th. Sunset Lodge No. 352 gave the Home a visit. No
special program or reception was arranged as it . was the wish of the
Lodge just to mingle with the children as one family visiting another
Ice cream and cookies ' were served by the Lodge for all.
September 26th. Buena Park Lodge No. 357 and Buena Park
Chapter No. 240 paid their annual visit to the children and left for
them a \>'ery generous donation 'of preserves, fruits and jellies.
September 30th. Silver Trowel Lodge No. 415 visited the Home in
good numbers. As this Lodge meets in the day time and is composed
largely of musicians, theatrical people and others whose vocations
occupy them in the evening, they made their visit in the morning. They
brought with them a good band or orchestra, ran ~ome good moving
pictures and supplied the children with a generous quantity of ice
cream and cake.
October 1st. Dr. Flora Smith again visited the children, bringing
with her about twenty friends and Grand Officers. The children gave
her a reception in the evening which was really a credit to them; and
much enjoyed and appreciated by these Grand Officers.
October 1st. Mizpah Lodge No. 378 visited the children and provided a most interesting and instructive program among their friends
and visitors for the children.
.
October 10th. Wilmington Lodge No. 198 was entertained by the
children in a visit to the Home. Newell Brown, a graduate of the
Home and occupying a responsible position in one of the banks of Los
Angeles, was present and gave a most appropriate address .of welcome

a hand-made quilt and a good quantity of fruits and jams.
December 5th. The "Happy Family Club" of Moneta Chapter
visited the Home under the leadership of Sister· Moore, their Matron.
They left $1.00 each with our children, to be spent according to the
wishes of the child.
December 5th. Ocean Park Chapter No. 245 visited the Home.
As our children had been entertained by this generous Chapter at the
beach, they had many personal acquaintances among their numbers and
enjoyed this return call. Sister Bertha Buchanan deserves much credit
for arranging these outings..
December 5th. Ontario Chapter No. 105 with a good representation of membersl'lip, with Companion R. · D. Newton, the High Priest

December 12th. Highland Park Lodge, generous and enthusiastic,

usual hearty welcomes from the children on their visit to the Home.
December 20th. Columbia Chapter No. 247 of Sawtelle, California,
visited the children, and Sister Stella Waggoner presented a Masonic
Tyler's sword to the Home.
December 20th. Jasmine Chapter, 0. E. S., of Azusa has never
missed a visit to the children the Sunday before Christmas for twelve
years. The children always look forward to their packages of homemade candies.
.
December 23rd. The members of Glen Chapter of Glendora are
certainly qualifying themselves as a good neighbor and call frequently
at the Home. · This was an official visit from the Chapter.
December 31st. Fullerton Lodge No. 339 has been so frequent a
visitor to the Home ·that the children like them as neighbors, and. can·
call many of them by name: Fullerton walnuts are used in generous
quantities, as both the Lodge and Chapter supply us with them every
season.
January 16th. A number of members of Redlands Lodge and Redlands Chapter, under the leadership of our good friend, Brother J. H.
Logie, paid us a pleasant visit.
.
January 23rd. The Scottish Rite Bodies of Los Angeles are always
thoughtful of the children and provide them many diversions, but had
not visited as a body to meet the children in their own Home. On this

visit the members attended in large numbers and furnished the childr<!n
a highly instructive and entertaining program the entire afternoon.
Our friends seemed to appreciate the opportunity of mingling with the
children and learning how their little friends were caring for their own
Home.
February 13th. Visit of officers of Grand Council in ceremony of
turning over the first shovelful of earth for the construction of the
Domestic Science Cottage.
February 19th. The official visit of Effie Easton, Grand Matron of
the Eastern Star, and Grand Patron Roy Musser, with many other
Grand Officers and Matrons and Patrons of Southern California. T his
reception was conducted entirely by the children and was one of the
feature occasions of the year.
March 20th. Members and their families of East Gate Chapter .
gave the children one of their usual cordial visits and left a great many
very thoughtful presents for the dormitory rooms of our older girls.
This Chapter is very practical and very thoughtful in their assistance
to our children.
March 27th. Annual Easter trip to Camp Baldy and neighboring
points of interest. This year forty-nine of the children selected for
their physical endurance made the four-day hike with the average of
eight miles per day. They enjoyed the heavy snows of the mountains
and every moment of the trip was one of happiness and thorough appreciation. Funds from treat fund and from friends supplied unusual
refreshments and the Camp Baldy Company extended us every courtesy.
April 10th. Members of the Jinnistan Grotto Patrol with their
families gave the children a good visit presenting the boys a good baseball outfit and giving some good pictures.
April 12th. Grand Officers of the Amaranth under the leadership
of Dr. Flora Smith held a cerem·o ny of dedication of the playground
equipment given to the children by this worthy order. A beautiful
ceremony accompanied by musical numbers arranged for the occasion
added much to the beautiful settihg of the presentation of this generous
gift. The Fraternity is much indebted not only for the material evidence of the good will of the several courts of the Amaranth, but for
the good spirit they entertain toward the Home and the love they display for our children. Dr. Smith is truly a woman of wonderful personality and magnetism, and her interest in our children is deeply appreciated by every member of our big family and those entrusted with their
care.
April 24th. About fifty members of Lancaster Lodge visited the
Home and brought with them a good supply of the healthful products
of the fertile Antelope Valley.

April 24th. University Lodge No. 394, with Wilson's Jazz Orchestra and the inimitable Chester Conklin with a three-reel comedy of his

from the Home to that city and gave them a wonderful drive over this
beautiful section. The Eastern Star gave them a delicious luncheon,
and in the afternoon the children were guests of Redlands Masons at
the Pageant, which was given to celebrate the evolution of this wonderful section from the desert to the rose.
May 1st. Southland Chapter of Pasadena entertained the children
with a May party in the summer house. Each child receive<l a pretty
hand-made May basket filled with choice fruits and candies.
May 7th. The Matrons and Patrons Association of 1920 0. E . S.
met at the Home. The Patrons formally dedicated the clubroom which
they have furnished for the boys. The evening was il most enjoyable
one and the boys showed due appreciation to the Patrons for the handsome manner in which their club room was equipped.
May 8th. It has been a custom for the past four years for Unity
Lodge of Glendale, in conjunction with other Masonic Bodies of that
city, to celebrate Mothers' Day at the Home. Each family acts as
mother to some child in the Home for that day. Basket lunches wrre
served on our lawn and suitable entertainment provided for children
and E'.Uests. Each child receives a box of candy with his name burned
011 rhe box, and Brother Henry always supplies each child and guest
with a bottle of soda.
May 15th. The San Pedro bodies of Masonry, with their ladies and
families, always set apart a . day for a visit with the children. They
are a good, live, active bunch of Masons, and the children anticipate
their visit with much pleasure.
May 29th. Ocean Park Lodge No. 369 visited the Home and provided musical and other numbers for the entertainment of the children.
After a visit through the buildings and grounds they gave the childn:n
a treat to ice cream and drinks.
June 2nd. Rising Light Lodge and Chapter of Huntington Park
came in good numbers and enjoyed the afternoon at the Home. Our
gymnasium room was opened up and some very entertaining numbers
given for the children. They presentM the girls with tennis racquets
and balls for their new court.
June 4th. The officers and members of the 53rd Masonic District,
under the directing hand of Brother D. J . Reese, held a meeting of
their association in the boys' clubroom, after which they visited the
several departments of the Home, and indulged in some active gam~;
with the children.

June 5th. Corona Lodge No. 324 of Pasadena called at the H ome
with many of their ladies, and enjoyed being guests of our children
for an afternoon.
June 11th. Through the generous and valued efforts of the Catalin:;
Circle Club, which is composed of Masons of Avalon on Catalina I sland,
about fifty of the older children of the Home were given a two-day trip
from the Home at Covina to Catalina and return. Every feature and
concession on this magic isle were turned over to the children, and they
were not permitted to make the expenditure of the moneys given to
them by other friends as pocket change for this trip. The Masons of
Avalon are deserving of every encouragement in their work, the highest praise for the relief work they have been doing, and for their
thoughtfulness in providing this wonderful trip fo r these children.
June 19th. West Lake Chapter, Eastern Star, again visited tht
children. This time for the purpose of presenting each child $1.00,
which they termed a "foolish dollar,'' that they could spend in any way
they chose while at the beach. After exchanging features of entertainment the visitors went over buildings and grounds.
June 19th. Evergreen Lodge and Ungava Chapter of Riverside
visited the Home, entertained the children and then presented the children's self-government organization $50.00 for use at the beach. T his
was overlooked at the beach season and r emains in their treasurr.

the Home to be their guests at the Temple in Azusa on this evening.
The members of the Chapter called for the children in autos, gave them
a real banquet at the Temple, then assembled in the Lodge room, where
felicitations were exchanged, the members of the Chapter rendering
an excellent program and the children conferring a degree of their
"Builders 1Club."
June 24th. Our Grand Master Brother George F . Rodden and
Brother Thomas J. Baker and others visited the Home and exchanged
greetings with the children.
July 27th. On this date our children took their annual trip to
Balboa, where they remained until September 6th, enj oying a delightful summer season and operating under their self-government organization, which usually prevails at the beach.
August 20th. The Matrons and P atrons Association of the Eastern Star under the direction of Brother R. B. Lafontaine held a day
of outdoor sports in the childrens' camp at Balboa. Prizes to the
value of $50.00 were given in the swimming and diving events.
August 21 st. Los Angeles. P yramid of Sciots No. 30 brought their

DONATIONS TO COVINA HOME.

It is pleasing beyond measure to witness the favors extended
by Lodges, Chapters and Masonic bodies to our children. It is
more like neighbors exchanging courtesies. The attitude of bestowing a charity to dependents is seldom noticed. The spirit of equality
and mutual greetings between visitors and children is so evident
when visits are made and things are left (listed as donations) for
the pleasure of the children.
Many Lodges and Chapters were very generous this year.
Whittier Lodge generously contributed nearly $300.00 to furnishing the little girls' playroom, and Los Angeles Lodge No. 42 furnished rugs for the same room. Pasadena Commandery furnished
dressers for Girls room and settees for Boys clubroom. East Bay
Matrons Association of Oakland were busy all year; Long Beach,
Luceme, Harbor, Jasmine and other Chapters gave their annual
Christmas boxes with individual presents to each child. And so we
might go on, but the following list shows how generously the
children were remembered. Our Matrons have attempted to keep
the list in an accurate manner, but if an error is found we hope we
may be pardoned, as the list is fortunately a long one and some
confusion in names and Lodges will occur.

MASONIC HOMES OF CALIFORNIA
RULtS FOR ADMISSION.

The Masonic Homes. of California, incorporated, are maintained
by the _members of Lodges holding obedience to the Grand Lodge
of Free and Accepted Masons of the Jurisdiction of California,
and are conducted by authority of the Grand Lodge through a
Board of Trustees. They are supported by direct appropriations
from Grand Lodge by funds which are derived from (1) per capita
dues from Lodges, fixed annually ; (2) the sum of twenty dollars
from each petitioner for initiation and from each applicant for
membersh!p from another Jurisdiction; and (3) from bequests, g ifts
and donat10ns.
.The Home for the adults is located near Decoto, Alameda
county, and the Home for children is located near Covina, Los
Angeles county.
. Those eligible for admission are : Master Masons who have for
at least three years prior to application been members in good
standing of a Lodge in this Jurisdiction ; the wife of a Master
Mason who is eligible to the H ome; the widow of a Master Mason
who at the time of his death was eligible for admission to the

548

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

549 .

Home; the mother of a Master Mason who was eligible for admis. sion at the time of his death, or who if living is incapable of caring
· for her; a dependent normal child over the age of four years and
under the age of fourteen years, provided its father was eligible for
admission to the Home at the time of his death. The child of a
living father who is eligible to admission to the Home, may also be
admitted i~ circumstances justify it. Likewise a child who may be
dependent upon a graiidfather who is eligible for admission to the
Home, may in the discretion of the Board, be admitted.

Adult residents of the Home may be given leave of absence, on
application to the Superintendent, for a period of not to exceed three
months in any one year, for the purpose of visiting friends, or to
seek employment. Lodges will be held responsible for any such
absentees until their return to the Home.

A hospital is maintained at the Decoto Home for the proper
care of residents who may require hospital treatment; but applicants for admission who, at the time of such application, are unable
to care for themselves at toilet and at table, to dress and undress
themselves alone and unattended, will not be admitted to the
Home, but may be by the Trustees placed in institutions organized
and operated for the care of such physically incapacitated applicants, on such terms as may be agreed upon by and between
the Trustees and the Lodge of which the applicant is a member.

All residents, adult and minor, must cheerfully perform such
labor and duties as the Superintendent or Matron may assign.

The Home being designed for worthy and dependent Masons,
their wives, widows, mothers and minor children, the eligibility of
applicants for admission must be certified by a committee of the
Lodge making application and passed upon by the Board of
Trustees; and all adult persons who may be admitted as residents
must assign all their property, real and personal, and any income to
the Homes as a condition precedent to admission. In case any
resident having transferred to the Home any funds or property,
shall withdraw from the Home, or shall be discharged therefrom
for cause, the Trustees shall withold from any funds or property
assigned to the Homes by the applicant a reasonable sum per month
for the time said resident has lived at the ·Home, and the remainder,
if any, of said funds and property shall be returned by the Trustees
to said resident upon such withdrawal or discharge.
A part of the consideration of the acceptance of an application
from a Lodge fpr the admission of any person to the Home shall
be an agreement on the part of such Lodge to keep such person
decently and properly clothed while a resident of the Home, 'to
receive back such resident and relieve the Home of any further
care or responsibility at the request of the Board of Trustees, and
to pay the necessary funeral expenses in case of death of the
applicant while a resident of the Home.
All accepted applicants must be provided with transportation ·
and proper attendance (if necessary) to the Home or other place
p.rovided, by the Lodge making the application. They must also be
provided with at least two complete changes of clothing,

In cases of persistent insurbordination, intemperance, insanity,
or contraction of contagious or infectious disease on the part of
any adult resident, or of incorrigibility on the part of any child, the
Trustees may return such person to the custody of the Lodge.

The Board of Trustees will endeavor to keep all children
admitted to the Home until they become self-sustaining; the Board
may consent to the binding out of children, when deemed for the
best interest of any child, to any trade, or place them in any proper
school or employment.
Each Lodge in the Jurisdiction shall be entitled to have maintained at the Home for adults, without charge two residents and
one additional for each three hundred members or fraction thereof
in excess of three hundred. For each resident in addition to such
quota a monthly fee will be charged, the amount to be fixed from
time to time by the Board of Trustees. The number of children
from any Lodge is not restricted.
The Board of Trustees may admit to the Home Masons, their
wives, widows, mothers and children, not covered by these regulations, when in the sound judgment of the Board the circumstances
presented justify such admissions.
All applications must be made upon blanks to be procured from
the Secretary of the Board of Trustees, which blanks when filled
shall embrace a full statement of the applicant's financial, mental
and moral condition, and a statement by a competent medical
examiner, together with the report of the investigating committee.
of the Lodge; and the application, when signed by the Master and
Secretary, shall be forwarded to the Secretary of the Masonic
Homes of California, Masonic Temple, San Francisco, California.

The report was adopted as presented, except that recommendations 1 and 3 were referred to the Committee on
Finance, and recommendation 2 was referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence.

A MENTAL AND PHYSICAL SURVEY
OF THll

ilaanutr ijomt f nr <lt4ilbrtu at aintriua. <ltnliforuht
By ARTHUR JoHN RlTTllR, Lecturer on; Mental Deficiency
and
HAROLD K. FABllR, M. D.
Associate Professor of Medicine and
Executive Head of the Department of Pediatrics
From
Department of Pediatrics of Stanford
University Medical School.

October 10, 1921.
LELAND STANFORD JUNIOR UNIVERSITY
SAN FRANCISCO, CALIFORNIA, October 11, 1921.
Dr. George F. Rodden,
Grand Master of Masons.
Dear Sir :
.
We have the honor to submit herewith a report of the mental and
physical survey of the children at the Masonic Home for Children at
Covina, California, made by us during the second and third weeks
of September, 1921.
Very truly yours,
HAROLD K. F ABllR.
ARTHUR J. RITTllR.
The annual mental and physical survey of the Masonic Home for
. Children at Covina was made by your examiners this year during
the second and third weeks of September. The methods of examination
were, like those of preceding years, as thorough as it was possible to
make them but the methods employed were in general the same as
previously used. It is thus possible to make a direct comparison
between the findings of this year and those of preceding years and to
check clos~ly the mental and physical progress made by the children
who had been in the home since June of last year or longer.
Physical Examination
The general impression left on the observer after a careful physical
examination of all the children was that they were distinctly above

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

551

the average in height, weight, muscular development and posture. T he '
comparison of the records of those children who were ·at the home in
June of 1920 shows that the average gain for the fifteen months was
2.9 inches in height and 13.l pounds in weight. The gain in height
is extraordinary since the accepted standard of growth, even through
the most rapid periods of normal growth, is considerably less than
this. It is a common observation that children who gain rapidly in
height tend to fall considerably below normal weight, and it is therefore especially noteworthy that these children maintained and in .
many instances actually improved in nutrition during a period of
unusually rapid growth in height. In musculature the progress of
the children who have had the benefit of the Home for six months
or more was also found to be extraordinarily good, the result unquestionably of the physical training and development so intelligently
and thoroughly directed by the Superintendent, Mr. Spencer. A
much smaller percentage of the children showed faulty posture
than last year and in practically all instances the defects found
were slight or negligible. The condition of the teeth of the
children was found to be excellent, a point which should be
singled out for high praise. It was quite evident that instruction in
the proper use of the tooth brush has been thoroughly given and that
decay has been promptly dealt with. The few cases of enlarged tonsils
occurred in children who had been but a short time in the Home.
In the examination of the lungs, heart, abdomen, genitals,. joints and
bones a very few abnormalities were noted which will be presented
later in a detailed report, but in general it may be said that in these
points as in others the condition of the children was excellent. A
number of instances · of moderate degree of fiat foot was noted and
it is recommended that the study of this situation, with a recommendation for suitable shoes, be made by an orthopaedic surgeon.
Of the physical condition of these children it may be said Jhat
this is far above the average of our general population. When such
a condition is evident it always means one thing, namely, intelligent,
conscientious and thorough personal supervision. We strongly feel
that in the case of the Masonic Home at Covina, the high stand.a rd of
physical excellence is the direct result of the unremi tting attention
and care given the cihldren by the Superintendent, Mr. Edward B.
Spencer.
In conclusion, the food and general sanitation of the Home was
inspected, both being found to have improved over the high standards
observed last year. The cooking is good, the food palatable, abundant
and properly balanced. An abundance of vegetables, meat, milk and
butter fats is afforded by the diet. Certain recommendations made
last year in regard to the wash basins have been carried out. The
building was found to be neat and the wash rooms and toilets very clean.

The 3 remaining are below school age. The mental examinations

of Case No. 127 B. P. who has a rather low mentality, and who should

Case No. 121 S. V. who came from a distant mountain district,

due to isolation and lack of opportunities.
