has proven to be such, and was returned to the lodge, which is providing for the child a suitable home.
It is strongly recommended that Case No. 3 be placed on a farm.
This suggestion was made in the 1920 report. This boy has intellectually matured, and he himself suggested that he be permitted to go to
work. With the exception of those few who are still fee!ing the
effects of their former environment, the conduct and behavior of the
children is excellent.
It was stated that the Masonic child is the leader in both Grammar

District Superintendent, Mr. Ben. S. Milliken, whose report has
been submitted separately.

BIOGRAPHY OF GRAND MASTER
Brother Leo Bruck submitted the following:
Whereas, Grand Lodge causes to be published a record of the
Proceedings of each Annual Communication; and .
Whereas, These records form the history of this Grand Lodge,
which records become more valuable as the years roll on; and
Whereas, Said Proceedings also contain a half-tone portrait of
the Grand Master printed on its firs't page; therefore be it
Resolved, That the Grand Secretary be instructed to cause a
short biographical sketch of the life of the Grand Master to be
printed on the page opposite the half-tone portrait, said sketch not
to exceed one page.

Referred to the Committee on Finance; which Committee reported recommending that the resolution do pass.
Grand Lodge concurred.

587

Committee reported, recommending that section 155 be
amended to read as follows :
Sec. ·155. A candidate elected to receive the three degrees in
a Lodge in this Jurisdiction, or a candidate elected to receive all or
any of the degrees in a Lodge in another Jurisdiction recognized
as regular by this Grand Lodge, may receive the second or third
degree, or both, but not the first, in another Lodge upon the request of the Lodge in which he was elected. If the request be
made by a Lodge of another Jurisdiction, it shall be transmitted
through the Grand Master or Grand Secretary of that Jurisdiction
· to the Grand Master or Grand Secretary of this Jurisdiction. No
petition, reference, ballot or fee shall be required in the ·Lodge
conferring any degree upon the request of another Lodge, and the
candidate will be a member of the requesting Lodge. An Entered
Apprentice or Fellow Craft may, after receiving a waiver of Jurisdiction from his Lodge, petition another Lodge for the remaining
degrees or degree, accompanying it with the fees required therefor.

The recommendation was concurred in and section 155
of the Constitution was amended as set out above by
unanimous vote. (Effective January 1, 1922.)

ANNUAL OR.A,TION

Brother Harvey D. Loveland, Grand Orator, Past
Master of San Francisco Lodge No. 360, delivered his Annual Oration, as follows: .
Most Worshipful Grand Master, ·
and Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
Preliminary to what I shall say at this time, may I not repeat my
response to the Most Worshipful Grand Master's courteous inquiry as
to the duties of the Grand Orator? As by the regulations provided,
I answered that his duties were to "Deliver at each annual commnuication an address to the Grand Lodge upon matters appertaining to the
Craft, and to deliver such other addresses as may be desired."
I indulge the hope that my remarks upon this occasion will square
with the first part of that definition, while as to the rest, I respectfully
report that I have accompanied the Most Worshipful Grand Master, and
other Grand Officers, at different times, and the Right Worshipful
Deputy Grand Master upon one important occasion, in addition to which
I have visited and lectured to nearly four score Lodges during my
year as Grand Orator, and I would be doing violence to my feelings; my
brethren, if I did not bear witness _to you, whose servant I am, to the
depth and sincerity of the welco_me extended to me, not as I fondly
believe for myself, but as your representative. The enjoyment and fra~
ternal reciprocations of those hours I shall ever reflect upon with deepest
sensibility.
My brethren, another cycle has been completed, another milestone
erected in our fraternal lives, and again we are assembled in the fitness of time, in the fellowship of our great Institution, and in the providence of God, to discharge our duty by the proper and orderly conduct
'Of the affairs of this Grand body, as such service finds expression in the
usual review, consideration and approval of faithful performance of duty
by our chosen representatives.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

589

The thought that comes to my mind at this moment is not what I
am going to say, or how well or how ill I may say it, but rather, ho~
will you receive it? In other words, can I bring your hearts and minds
into harmony with mine, or mine in touch with yours, that we may
sympathetically and understandingly think and speak of some of those
things concerning which the brethren of the Mystic Tie have a common,
sacred and an abiding interest?
Such will be my endeavor. I could not wi~h that the field of thought
to which I am properly limited today had been less ably covered in the
past, as that would be to deny to you and to me the pleasant recollections
born of having listened to or read the beautiful, scholarly and appropriate grand orations of the past; but I would indeed, my brethren, that
I could feel ass_ured of interesting you as these eloquent exponents of
thought upon the subject of our noble science have interested me. But
as their devotion to our g~eat Institution was expressed in service to
emulate, not to copy but to emulate a Bledsoe, a Nieto, a Burke, a
Webster, an Adams, a Victor, a Waste, or a Boynton, and others who
preceded them, is the proudest compliment I can pay them.
Beautifully has the poet expressed the sentiments of service"There are valiant hearts, there are spirits brave,
There are souls that are ,warm a_nd true;
Then give to the world the best that you have,
And the best will come back to you."
In harmony with that idea I shall try, first, to give you my best
-thought upon the subject of Freemasonry as a science as it fin ds expression in our daily lives; and, second, from the principles thus developed
to deduce some of the pure and holy lessons taught by it, and to comment briefly thereon, especially upon the analogy between the Operative
Art and the Speculative Science.
Keenly do I realize that in speaking to this text upon this occasio~
and in this presence, I am indeed an heir of Alexander, for whom no
worlds are left to conquer.
The genesis, the history, the philosophy, the romance and the beauty
of the moral, ethical and spiritual worth and excellence of our noble
science have been the subject of thoughtful consideration and eloquent
discussion by members of the craft in whose shadow and at whose feet
I could well sit as a learner. But if it seem idle or presumptuous for
me to try to say anything new or interesting upon a subject involving
consideration and analysis of those eternal truths upon which civilization and the progress of our race depend-truths .that were old when the
world was young, truths upon which this great Institution is predicated,
let me say, my brethren, that it is because of association with you and

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

others like you in this "Aristocracy or True Republic of Human Effort
for Good," which is what Freemasonry really is, that I find courage to
submit these thoughts, born of that association.
·
The subject is old, old but ever new, and my apology if such be
necessary, must be for the manner of presenting it rather than that the
theme is inappropriate or untimely.
In passing I want to say that in my judgment, many of us as
Masons are too prone to emphasize the importance of such fellowship
in our Institution as finds expression in payment of dues, wearing an
emblem, and semi-occasional visits to our Lodge, and too little disposed
to seek for the enjoyment and happiness which are always to be found
by the thoughtful mind in the contemplation of the desirable consequences resulting from recognition and observance of the teachings and
tenets of Masonry.
Believing this, it will be my endeavor. to present to you some
thoughts, the consideration of which will lead us to the contemplation
of things no less beautiful and interesting, because their appeal is to
the heart and mind by which we bridge the centuries of the past and
learn the story of the ages that the great founder of our Institution,
chosen of God to erect a Temple to His holy name, spake words of
wisdom when he said:
"There is n_othing new under lhe sun."
The cooing of a babe at it's mothers breast was heard ere civilization was born, but is dear to the mother who hears it today as she clasps
to her breast the evidence that through suffering she has earned the
greatest of all crowns, the crown of motherhood. So too, that which I
shall say may have been said before. My words may awake in your
minds remembrances of something you have heard or read and, perchance, thought beautiful; or hearing now for the first time, find interesting.
My object will have been attained and my hope realized if a few
moments of enjoyment ar~ added to your lives and I can feel that I
have helped us all to find:
"Songs in sunshine,
Tongues in trees,
Books in running brooks,
Sermons in stones
And good in everything."
Briefly then as to fe'.lowship in this great Institution and the obligation laid upon those who have knelt at its altars and taken upon
themselves its vows of service, as well as its honors of membership ;
Masonry is an art of such compass and extent that a knowledge
of its mysteries is attained only by degrees.

By much instruction and assiduous application are advances made.
Every step is progres_sive and brings to us new light and understanding
of which are born higher ideals, nobler aspirations and purer lives.
Preston, one of the greatest writers upon Masonic subjects says:
"According to the progress we make, we limit or extend our inquiries
and in proportion to our capacity we attain to a less or greater degre~
of perfection."

590

•

591

To be thoroughly instructed in the lectures, familiar with the ceremonies and proficient in the degrees of Masonry is, or should be the
ambition of all who stand within the sacred portals of its temple. 'But
this very inclination, laudable as it is, prompts a more rapid progress
through its forms than is consistent with a clear and adequate comprehension of its prin<;iples. This results in but a superficial, or at best,
only a theoretical and speculative knowledge of its sublime arcana and
by failing to absorb the beautiful lessons taught by its symbols' and
allegories, and enjoined by its rules, we do not live in its influence or
exhibit its effects. Satisfied with the shadow, we fail to find the substance and rest in the means without attaining the end.
Well has it been said that "he who understands the application of
the various tools and implement~ of the craft is thereby prepared for
every go9d work; but only he who uses and applies them to intellectual,
moral and social edification is the workman who need not be ashamed."
Therefore, our desire should not be merely to arrive at perfection
in the lectures and proficiency in the degrees but to enter into the spirit
of the solemn rites of our Institution, and learn the full import of its
interesting symbols that we may be perfect in the application of its
principles, in the possession of the virtues it demands, and in the discharge of the duties it enjoins.
As to the claim that Speculative Masonry is a Science: Science is
defined as: "Knowledge classified and made available in work in life
or in a search for truth."
'
'
Accepting this brief but beautiful definition, how completely it
justifies the claim that Freemasonry is a science. I would paraphrase
it and say it is the science of life, or of living as the Supreme Grand
Architect of the Universe intended man should live, as a free man,
free in all that the term implies, and rich in that freedom because of
having earned instead of inheriting it.
Someone has said that: "Life is made up of effort and results
and that the strength of the effort is the measure of the result."
If this be true, and I doubt if any will be found to question it it
inevitably follows that correlated unity of action in preparation for,
and co-operation in effort will be reflected in results or accomplishments.
Thus is presented the first maxim or established truth of Freemasonry, the strength of harmony, which is the shibboleth of our Institution.

GRAND LODG E OF CAL IFORNIA

592

593

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

By its recognition we are enabled to overcome all obstacles in our search
for truth and light, and in it we recognize the ~w of the Universe.
Under the operation of that law, the numberless spheres which
·compose this and other solar systems, roll on and ever on through the
vast immensity of limitless space, each an individual unit, yet each
a part of a perfect whole. Without that law suns would roll. on suns,
and systems, systems crush, and mighty chaos, appropriately called the
"insanity of nature's forces," arch enemy of heaven's first law, would
prevail.
Order prevents this dire result, and natural forces, working in
their accustomed manner and under "that supreme intelligence which
prevails all nature,'' finding expression in the law of cause and consequence, disclose certain truths and make apparent certain principles
which are generalized under the term science; in other words, as above
quoted : "Knowledge classified and made available in work, in life,
or in a search for truth."
Science is a comprehensive term, as its definition implies. There
is the science of many things : Mathematics is the science of numbers
and space : Geometry is that branch of mathematics that treats of the
measurements of lines, angles, surfaces and solids. Hence Operative
Masonry is an applied physical science in that through it knowledge,
classified and made available in work, is developed.
Speculative Masonry is a metaphysical science proC:ucing knowledge
classified and made available in the study of life and the search for
truth.
The analogy between Operative and Speculative Masonry, the use
of symbolism and allegory in explanation of that 'analogy and the
beautiful moral, ethical and spiritual lessons drawn therefrom, offer to
our initiates an ever increasingly interesting study of life and of the
high destiny of man, as the teachings and tenets of our Institution are
portrayed by our ritual.
The more noble and glorious purposes to which the working tools
of the Operative Art are theoretically applied in our Speculative
Science, are told in the beautiful allegory "The Search for Light."
All that the past has taught us, all that the present means to us, all
that the future has in store for us, is told in that sublimely beautiful
allegorical and symbolical interpretation of Speculative Masonry. The
search for light is a search for truth, for truth is the light of knowledge
as error is the darkness of ignorance.
Dante with soul attuned to the music of the spheres, plead for
human pr~gress when he wrote: "Give the world light and the people
will take care of the rest."

Our own Quaker, poet and scholar, Whittier, lover of truth and
justice, for the sake of justice and truth says: "Truth should be the
first lesson of the child and the last aspiration of manhood. * • * *
It is the sovereign good of human nature."
And so these ideas, born of the noble uses to which the working
tools of Operative Masonry are put, and of the results obtained, have
their correspondence in the thought life of Speculative Masonry, and
in the i_ndividual experience of its members.
More time than is available upon this occasion would be required
to do more than to refer briefly to some of the beautiful lessons presented by our noble science to the thoughtful mind.
From the time when, uninfluenced by friends or acquaintances,
and moved solely by a desire to avail himself of the teachings of an
Institution for which he feels a profound respect, and in a condition
of helplessness, which bears eloquent witness to his faith and trust in
those with whom he seeks to associate, the candidate alarms our outer
door, to the moment when he receives the right hand of fellowship
from the Master of his Lodge, a faithful picture of life, with its
strength and its weakness, its hopes and its fears its failures and its
successes, its sunshine and its shadows, is portray~d and presented 'by
allegory, symbolism and precept, and through all of the beautiful and
interesting drama is found the urge and influence to high ideals, noble
aspirations and worthy accomplishments, the realization of which finds
expression in perfect manhood and virtuous, well ordered lives. Hence
such teachings have become an active force for good in our civilization.
W hat greater good could parents wish for their sons than that
their lives and characters should be moulded upon and express the
beauty of thought and conduct of which the perfect ashlar is our Masonic
symbol? Or, more comprehensively, what more could be asked in
the interest of civilization and the moral, ethical and spiritual progress
of our race, than that man live as members of this great Order are
taught to live, "meeting upon the level, acting by the plumb and parting
I
upon the square?"
Omar Khayam, the Persian poet and philosopher, said of the Koran,
the Mohammedan ~ible: "Burn the libraries; their value is found in
this book."
With greater truth and logic the brethren of the Mystic Tie
could say : "Accept and live by the teachings and tenets of Freema~onry, and do away with legislatures and courts that make and
enforce the lawful requirements of society unde'r conditions incident
to our complex civilization.

There are beautiful thoughts beautifully expressed, of man in his
revelation and duty to God, to his fellowman, and to himself, in the
Koran, just as there are in the Vegas of India,_ the Zenda-Vesta. of
Persia, the Sagas of Scandinavia, the Hebrew Scriptures and the Bible
of the Christians. All these sacred writings, sacred to the people
and civilizations whose religious thought they express, admonish, reprove and urge along moral, ethical and spiritual lines, but, with the
exceptions of the Hebrew Scriptures and the New Testament, t~ey
express these sentiments of guidance and direction with greatly varym~
degree of reference to and dependence upon the sense of moral respons1~
bility to a spiritual Deity, looking to preparation for a future state.
The religion of Buddha, founded about six hundred years before the
Christian era began, which has so many adherents in China, Japan,
Siam Thibet Burmah Ceylon and other Eastern countries, is founded
upon' correc; and vi;tuous conduct, not as a mea~s of reac~ing _a
fuller richer life in a future existence, but to avoid sorrow m this
life ~nd to reach "Nirvanll" or perfect rest. Some of his expressions
ris: to sublime heights of moral beauty, but his teachings are all too
barren of reference to One Supreme Being to whom conscience is
responsible. In other words, he proclaims the brotherhood of man
but does not reveal the fatherhood of God.
Buddhism therefore like the materialism of Confucius, has failed
to keep step ~ith higher' religious thought because it failed to teach its
adherents the necessity for moral, ethical and spiritual accomplishment,
and responsibility therefor. Just as an arch is complete when the
keystone has locked its parts and unified its elements of strength, so
faith and good works, the necessary requirements of religious life, when
crowned by the keystone of continued well-doing, not to avoid sorrow
and trial in this life, but in obedience to Divine command and in preparation for life eternal, form the arch of perfect life.
The claim that Freemasonry is a science, the science of proper
relationship to God and to our fellowman, is proven by the fact that
its every urge and influence is toward higher and better ideals, purer
and nobler living. In other words, it seeks to insure that each. of its
members be not less a man than God and nature intended he should
be, without fear and above reproach.
It does not claim to be a religion, yet the eternal truths underlying
religion, pure and undefiled, are basic and fundamental to our noble
science. It demands of its initiates, before being admitted to its fellowship, the same belief in God, the Suprem~ Grand Architect o_f .the
Universe, that is demanded by the church of him who professes rehg1on,
before the sacred rites of baptism are administered; and of its members although without sacrament, the same purity of life and conduct
as the church requires of its communicants. In fact our ceremonies, by

595

which good men and true, who knock at our door and are found worthy,
are admitted to membership in our Institution, may well be compared to
the baptismal rites by which religious fellowship is established.
·
Science and Religion, so long seemingly irreconcilable in principles
and teachings, are now recognized as two paths leading to the same
goal.
No longer are these two great lines of thought considered antagonistic or even divergent. Religion may be defined as acceptance of
truth revealed as the will and wisdom of Deity; Science as a search
for truth, the handmaiden and supporter of religion in that by investigation and demonstration it proves much that is claimed by
religious precepts, and by explanation satisfies doubt and skepticism.
The Decalogue, the foundation upon which rests one of the oldest,
if not the oldest revealed religion, seeks to rule or govern by prohibition
or command, yet the wisdom and justice. which find expression in the
ten commandments are easily susceptible of scientific demonstration.
The Golden Rule, for which the world waited .for unnumbered centuries, can be shown scientifically to be "best boon to mortals given"
in that its observance establishes justice and equity for all to the
advantage of all.
What better definition of Freemasonry can be found than the
words of Bishop Wilson applied to culture, which after all is like Freemasonry, a search for tru.th, "To make reason and the will of God
prevail," he says. How perfectly it describes the aim and object of the
teachings and tenets of our Institution ; a search for truth, a search
for that upon which civilization, ~he progress of our race, aye the
orderly existence of things physical and metaphysical depend.
Sir Francis Bacon, admittedly one of the deepest thinkers of the
past, thus describes the result of the search for truth in analyzing
science and religion: "A little science inclineth man's mind to atheism, but depth in phiolsophy bringeth men's minds about to religion."
Surely the spirit of prophecy, which in all ages has helped the finite
mind of man to discover the beauties of the unseen, inspired the philosopher as he thus proclaimed the bands that wedded science and religion.
Creatures of · circumstances, born of education and environment, as
we all are, thinking men of all ages have striven for the light of truth.
Barham Mirza, the Hindu philosopher, compares that striving to following the flight of a bird. "Truth," he says, "is a bird that flies so
fast the eye of man cannot follow it, and so high that it is lost to
sight in the skies. But now and then one of its feathers falls, and
when it t.ouches the earth it becomes a prophet 6uch as Mahomet or
Moses." In other words, a teacher.

And so we reach the briefest possible definition of the science of
Freemasonry, "Knowledge of Truth." With that knowledge comes the
realization that God is truth and light and goodness and beauty, and
preeminently God is lov·e, as these are the elements and attributes of
love.
That iove is within us, over us, around about us. It is seen in the
beauty of the violet, and the fragrance of the rose ; in the glorious
tints of our gorgeous sunsets, and in the grace and loveliness of
woman; it is heard in the "Songs of birds and in the roar of the cataract; in the roll of the thunder and in the cooing lullaby of the
mother to the babe at her· breast; it burst forth into living beauty under
the chisel of Phideas and the brushes 'of Raphael and Angelo, and
from the pens of Shakespeare and Milton. He who creates beauty,
who promotes virtue, who unselfishly strives for the good of his fellowman, is an exponent of Truth and in thought and deed, if not . in
membership, a believer in the teachings and tenets of our great Institution.
Remembering the definition of science, that it is "Knowledge classified and made available in life, in work and in a search for truth," are
we not amply justified in our claim that Speculative Masonry is a
science. It is knowledge classified and made available in the activities
of life. Hence the conclusion is inevitable that it is a science, the

Someone has said that life is comparable to a rail~oad of whi~h
we ourselves have built the road bed of our own experience and ~aid
the rails on which we are pushing our engines ahead to larger realizations or backward to failure and defeat. Difficultie~, or even temporary

Somewhere the sun is shining, and confidence, patience and decision

599

Let us know then "that the highest lesson in life is not to live in
the present or in the future, but in the eternal.''
The old mystic Boehm declares that "He to whom time is as
eternity and eternity as time, is free," an aphorism worth remembering.
Strikingly are the pure and holy lessons taught by our ritual told
in the injunction, "Let your light so shine before men." In this, the
will of the Master finds expression as it does at times in the language
of parables, but the inference is plain.
The light which we are exhorted to "let shine" is the sentiment of
love and friendship expressed ln unselfish helpfulness.
To complete the analogy from which this lesson is drawn, we
must have ·some standard of comparison, something with which to contrast this light, the radiance ·of which we are bidden to disseminate, to
the end that our efforts may be seen of men and glory be given to Him
who orders all things well. That standard of comparison is sunshine.
Comparable to the life-giving, life-sustaining effect of sunshine in the
physical world, is that of friendship, faith and trust in the metaphysical,
or in man's association with his fellowman.
To be surrounded. by friends, to associate with those whose confidence we reciprocally enjoy, develops the best there is in us. We
grow and expand in those qualities of heart and mind which have
enabled us to command and deserve the esteem of our associates.
Equally important is the fact that if we deserve and -enjoy love and
confidence, we naturally exhale or throw off and create an atmosphere
of faith and trust, and the world is better for our having lived .in it.
Even the Master when He came to earth, preferred to be called the
"Friend.'' Friendship is the mirror of the soul, reflecting the strength
and the weakness of man. It is pregnant, with self-creative force,
and we should never forget that t he world gives to us just what we
give to the world ; a smile for a smile, a frown for a frown. Around
our sacred altars of 'friendship we assemble, bringing our votive offerings to that temple erected 'in the hearts of the brethren of the Mystic
Tie, the cornerstone whereof is virtue supported by wisdom, strength
and beauty. There, undisturbed by the urge of selfishness, or the call
of ambition, we keep alive upon those altars the sacred fires of Faith,
Hope and Charity and of Brotherly Love, Relief and Truth. T his is
the heritage which has come down to us, hoary with age, · ripe with the
wisdom of the passing years and rich in the glorious realization that
true happiness is found in unselfish effort to enliven the kindly sensi~
bil_ities of human nature, and to promote the eqdearing civilities of
social intercourse, and upon us is laid the sacred obligation of transmitting that heritage, pure and undefiled, to those who will come after
us.

Just as there are periods when we are denied the blessing of sunshine, so, in the march of human events, individuals, states and nations
are called upon at times to stand within the shadows born of · selfish
greed, unholy passion or unworthy ambition. But such periods are
transitory, and as they are caused by disregard of right and truth, and
justice, so they can be terminated by the exercise of these virtues; and
never before in the history of civilization has there been so world-wide,
so universal a demand for the recognition of human rights and human
liberty by the final banishment of that arch enemy of the progress of our
race, the first and worst of the four dread horsemen of the Apocalypse,
the appearance of which creates conditions which invite and presage the
coming of the other three.
The greatest issue ever presented to the civilized world is demanding attention. To the eternal credit of our country and of themselves,
be it remembered that two of our Chief Magistrates, one at least of
whom is a member of this great Institution, have striven to bestow
upon world civilization the blessing of universal peace. Our sympathies
and our prayers are with President Harding and his capable Secretary of
State in their noble efforts. No Moses climbing Sinai's height to
receive instructions from the Infinite ever brought greater blessing to
earth; no plumed knight of the golden age of chivalry, who strove for
the redemption of the Holy Sepulcher, or sought for the Holy Grail,
.e ver had nobler quest; and may their efforts be crowned by the realization of Tennys<?n's dream, told in the prophetic words:
"When war drums beat no longer,
And battle flags are furled;
In the Parliament of Nations,
The Congress of the World."

REPORTS OF COMMITTEE ON JURISPRUD~NCE
The Committee on Jurisprudence presented the following reports relative to .the Decisions of the Grand Master:
Decisions
To the M:. w.\ Grand Lodge of' California:
We have had under consideration ~he ~ecisions of the Most
Worshipful Grand Master as reported m his address, and report

thereon as follows:
1 Dedsion 1 presents the following facts: The Master of a
Lodg.e, at a stated meeting of the Lodge, refused to allow a reso-

603

The Grand Master ruled that the Master of the Lodge should
have allowed the Lodge to consider the resolution.
We are satisfied that the conclusion of the Grand Master was
correct. We do not rest our conclusion entirely on the formal
language prescribed as the preliminary to the actual closing ceremonies, further than to say that the language immediately following, "If not, we will proceed to close," clearly enough shows,
as the Grand Master says, that the process of closing had not yet
commenced. In other words, the Lodge was still fully open when
the resolution was offered. The only possible legal objection to
· the consideration of the resolution at the time it was offered was
that possibly, in view of Article XII of the Uniform Code of
By-laws prescribed by the Grand Lodge for our Lodges, it could
· not be considered after the order of tusiness specified in that
Article had been concluded. The Article provides that "the regular
order of business at every stated meeting· of this Lodge shall be
as follows:

1.
·2.
3.
4.
5.
6.

Reading of the minutes.
Repo s of Committees.
Balloti g.
Recepti n of petitions.
Miscell eous and unfinished business.
Conferri g of degrees.

This, so far as appears, is the only provision of our law relative to the matt here involved. It is not necessary here to consider whether th s Article was designed to lay down a hard and
fast ru.le which u der no circumstances could be departed from by
a Lodge. It doe not more at most than to prescribe the regular
order in which usiness shall be transacted at a stated meeting.
The resolutio here fell under the 5th, and, except for the conferring of degr es, the last subdivision of the Article, viz.: " Miscellaneous atid unfinished business." The minutes show that no
degree / as conferred at that meeting, so that insofar as the order
.of-business was concerned, it came up in the Qrder prescribed by
the Article. And, as stated by the Grand Master, the formal question by the Master prescribed by our ritual, "Has any brother

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

604

anything," etc., implies a common acceptation of the practice of
considering at that time any miscellaneous and unfinished business
that may be suggested.
We conclude, therefore, that inasmuch as the closing ceremonies had not commenced at the time the resolution was offered,
the resolution was in order, and should have been submitted t.o
the Lodge for consideration.
The Grand Master was right in so ruling.

Adopted.
2. This decision related to certain transactions on the part of
Evergreen Lodge No. 259, with relation to the gift of certain
shares of stock of the value of $1,000 owned by the Lodge to a
community hospital, and the proposed payment to such hospital
of $1,500 in consideration of a promise on the part of the hospital
to "dedicate a room" with an inscription therein as to "the donor,"
and to allow the Lodge to occupy the same for a Mason when not
otherwise occupied, charging only a hal.f rate therefore in such.
until such time as the other half-rate amounts,in the aggregate to
the full sum of $2,500, being an amount equal to the $1,000 stock
donated and the $1,500 paid.
We are informed that this matter has been completely closed
and that the case is practically a moot case.
Insofar as the Grand Master ruled that the gift of the stock
was in violation of our law, his decision was undoubtedly correct.
Insofar as the proposed expenditure of $1,500 was in substance a
donation or gift to the community hospital, it was forbidden by
our law. We think it should be stated, however, that there is nothing in our law precluding a reasonable contract by a Lodge for
hospital accommodations, involving the expenditure by the Lodge
of money for such accommodations even though the same be paid
in advance. We certainly do not consider the proposed arrangement here a wise arrangement financially.

Adopted.

. 4. Decision 4 was made in a case where a ballot upon a petition for the degrees disclosed a single cube. No second ballot
was taken, as is required by our law in such a case. The Master
should at once, without disclosing the result, have ordered a second ballot for the purpose of correcting a possible mistake, without permitting any discussion before the second ballot. (Section
104, Const.) Because members who were not present at the time
of the first ballot had entered the Lodge room, it was concluded
that no second ballot could be had, and by unanimous vote of the
Lodge a dispensation for a re-ballot was thereupon asked.
•
The Grand Master very properly held that the coming in of
members absent at the first ballot should not have been allowed to
interfere :Vith the taki~g of a second ballot as required by our law,
but that inasmuch as 1t had accomplished that improper result a
re-ballot under dispensation was "the simplest and most just w~y"
to obviate the effect of the error.
We recommend that the decision be approved.

Adopted.

in receiving two pet1t10ns for degrees. Upon the material facts
stated in the decision, viz. : that the petitioners tived throughout
the greater part of the year within the Jurisdiction of the complaining Lodge, and had been for years registered voters of communities within such Jurisdiction, we are of opinion that the

A man may establish his residence away from his family if he

(Sec. 95e, Const.)

Petition of · Eden Lodge for Concurrent Jurisdiction

To the M.< w:.Grand Lodge of California:
Eden Lodge No. 113 requests the adoption of a resoluti~n
granting it " concurrent" jurisdiction with the Lodges of the city
of Oakland over all the territory over which the Lodges of such
city now have jurisdiction. The application is accompanied b?' certificates showing the consent of all the Lodges of the city of
Oakland. The application has been approved by the Grand Master.
We regret to be compelled to report that there is no authority
under our law as it now stands for conferring such concurrent •
jurisdiction. The construction of section 92a of our Constituti~n ·
is definitely settled by our decision rendered in the year 1919 m
the case of San Fernando Lodge No. 343, where we held that "the
Grand Master correctly concluded that under our existing law the
Lodge could not be given concurrent jurisdiction with the Lodges
of the city of Los Angeles over territory within the legal bounds
of the city of Los Angeles." (Proc. 1919, p. 574.)
What Eden Lodge No. 113 really wants is jurisdiction over
the territory it lost by reason of · its annexation to the city of
Oakland. Its situation in this respect is the same as was that of
San Fernando Lodge No. 343, and its remedy is to ask for a resolution giving it exclusive jurisdiction over that territory. If not~ce
of such an application had been given to the Lodges of the city
of Oakland, we might 11ow consider the application. But no such
application was made, the application asking and the Oakland
Lodges consenting only to a resolution giving concurrent jurisdiction.
We are of opinion that the present application must, if we
adhere to our law, be disapproved.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC
EDUCATION
To the M:. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Masonic Education is pleased respectfully
to report that much genuine progress has been made along the
lines which were prescribed by this Grand Lodge at its last Communication. The work of this Committee is essentially pioneer in
· its character; for that reason it is necessarily slow in development.
Because of that fact, your Committee has at all times strenuously
endeavored to avoid proposing or countenancing that which might
subject to unwarranted criticism the program approved by Grand
Lodge.
If conditions which have been beyond the power of the Committee to control have rendered it impossible to report as large a
measure of progress as might have been desired, it has been due
in part to the determination to avoid any action which well-meaning
men might justly construe as too radical a departure from the tra•
ditions of the Craft.
In those communities where there has existed the clearest
understanding on the part of the officers and' members of constituent Lodges regarding the purposes of the committee, and the
scope within which its actions have nece ssarily been confined, there
has been the fullest co-operation. In such localities there has

610

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

been evinced an aroused interest in the far-reaching effect of the
educational program, as reflected by an increased attendance in
the Lodges, better Lodge management, and a more intelligent conception and performance of Masoni.c responsibility.
Owing to the dis-similarity of conditions and needs throughout
this Grand Jurisdiction it has been quite impossible to formulate
a hard and fast program which would be uniformly adaptable. It
has been found that to quite a degree self-determination by each
Lodge must be the rule. This conclusion applies to topics as well
as to speakers.
Regarding both topics and speakers; your committee can not
assume responsibility for all speakers who have appeared before
Lodges. It has, however, always stressed the absolute necessity
of avoiding controversial and partisan questions which might cause
distress to those holding contrary opinions. 'J:he fact has ever
been emphasized that it has never been the purpose of Grand
Lodge, nor has it been the intention of this committee to lend
itself to any subtle p~opaganda. The endeavor has always been
made to impress the importance of the avoidance of action by
i.odges along any particular lines. The supreme effort in the work
has been to disseminate information of an accurate, dependable
character and particularly to inspire our members to make a practical application of Masonic principles and truths to individual and
civic life. If that inspiration could be obtained through a lecture
on Masonic history, philosophy, or symbolism, or through a discussion of human welfare problems and the outstanding· needs of
the day, this committee has always been, willing and ready to cooperate to the best of its ability.
To weigh or measure the far-reaching influence of the educational work would be quite an impossible task. Its value is cumulative and cannot be determined in the same mann~r one would
estimate the worth of a material commodity. One of the important
phases of the activity of the committee has been that dealing with
the consideration of more efficient Lodge management, with espe.
cial reference to effective methods concerning our accessions.' As
a result of such discussions, valuable assistance has · been rendered ..
Our appreciation is due the Inspectors who, in addition to
their numerous duties and responsibilities, have unselfishly supported the work.
To obtain first-hand information regarding the progress and.
effectiveness of the educational work and to receive suggestions
to form a basis for a further development of the educational program, the General Chairman of this committee, with the approval
9f the M.'.W.'.Grand Master, called a conference in ea~h of the four

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

611

districts of this Grand Jurisdiction. On August 20th, he attended
a conference af Sacramento of the Masters and Wardens of the
Northern District. On August 27th, he attended a conference at
San Francisco of the Masters and Wardens of the Bay Counties
District. On September 10th, he attended a conference at Visalia
of the Masters and Wardens of the Central District. On September 23rd, he attended a· conference in Los Angeles, of the Masters
and Wardens of the Southern District. These four conferences
were marked by a splendid spirit of enthusiasm and a determination to carry on the work with greater vigor than ever before.
As an evidence· of the keen interest taken in the educational work
several of the Masters and Wardens in one district drove a distanc~
of 125 miles to attend the gathering. At another conference officers of the Lodges came a distance of 250 miles.
At each conference a full and free discussion was had of the
pressing needs of the Lodges along Masonic educational lines.
The desire was everywhere manifested to find a vigorous, practical
application of Masonic principles to the life of today. Not too
much value can be placed on the inspiring influence of confer.e nces
as indicated. . It proves conclusively the necessity for the officers
of Lodges in a given district to meet together, think a~d plan
together for broader and more efficient methods in carrying on
Masonic activities.
As a result of the conferences held in the several districts
the. following deductions have been made representing the composite views of the officers of many Lodges.
1. It is clearly apparent that some plan must be evolved
immediately to send speakers to the Lodges in outlying commu. nities, where the pleasure and profit of hearing well-informed
brethren is an infrequent occurrence. This phase of the work well
merits the most careful consideration of this Grand Lodge.
2. Individual Lodges in many of the outlying districts cannot
afford to pay the necessary . traveling expenses for bringing speakers from a long distance. Adequate financial provision should be
made by Grand Lodge to solve that phase of the problem and
care for· their needs.
3. A consistent effort should be made to hold group meetings
of the Lodges within a reasonable distance of each other to hear
well qualified Masonic speakers.
4. The value of Officers' Associations is again einpha·sized in
building a better Masonic community spirit, not alone in rural districts, but in the larger centers as well.
5. Outlines of Masonic talks should be prepared by the committee, that speakers may be developed in each and every Lodge,

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

612

The proper administration of the duties of this committee
necessarily entails a vast amount of labor. Considering the large
territorial dimensions of the State and that the general chairman
of th~ committee ought to ~isit the several centers for the purpose
of attending personally to the organization of the work, and also
that at all times there are many details demanding attention, we
feel that the time is fast approaching when it will become necessary
for this Grand Lodge to employ a capable executive, under an
adequate salary, who would be required to devote his entire time
to the development of educational work.
While the .time may not now be ripe for this plan wt; feel
that in the near future its adoption will become imperative if full
scope is to be given to the growth of Masonic educational work,
and we therefore recommend such step to the thoughtful consideration of the Grand "Lodge.
Your Committee desires to make the following recommendations:
1. That the present form of organizatioll of this Committee
be continued.
2. That the organization of Officers' Associations be continued.
3. That means to meet the needs of outlying Lodges be given
immediate attention.
4. That speakers' boards be formed in each of the districts.
5. That the policy of holding group meetings of Lodges in
the interest of educational work be encouraged.
6. That an adequate appropriation be made for the work of
this committee.

It will be readily noted that we have made the smallest showing since the campaign to build up the Endowment Fund was
instituted. However, we feel that our brethren are obtaining a
more thorough knowledge of what we are accomplishing in the
Homes through the medium of the moving picture films, which
were exhibited in the Lodge rooms of the subordinate Lodges of
this Jurisdiction.
As advised in last year's report, the pictures of the Orphans'
Home at Covina were take.n by the Robert Brunton Studios of
Hollywood, the present officers of which are members of the
Fraternity, who made no charge for the work performed. The
pictures of the Home for the elderly at Decoto were under the
direction of the Trustees of the Masonic Homes. These pictures
were arranged so as to give our brethren an intimate knowledge
of the equipment of the Homes and an insight into the lives of
the occupants.

620

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Brother J. M. Whited, in charge of the films in the northern
part of the State, detailed Brother W. R. Gibson to display them
in the north, while Brother Howard S. Tracy handl~d the films in
the southern part. Both brethren displayed a marked aptitude for
this work, presenting the pictures in an attractive way and giving
brief talks which created considerable interest and enthusiasm.
· We received a number of letters from different brethren expressing their appreciation and pleasure in obtaining a clear and
well defined impression of just what is being accomplished in our
magnificent Masonic Homes. Many expressed surprise over the
fact that the elderly and the• orphans were being so well cared for,
having heretofore had no conception of the scope and breadth of
our work and of how splendidly we are equipped.
Extracts from a number of the letters read as follows:
"The pictures are surely fine, and they were appreciatively and gratefully received and warmly applauded. It
is quite conservative to say that nine out of every ten in
the audience last night left the hall with first-hand knowledge that was absolutely new to them. Such seeds so
sown are certain- to grow and to ultimately bear fruit, as
well as yield present and immediate returns financially."
"I am writing to express my sincere gratitude and
profound appreciation for the visit of Captain Tracy with
the pictures of the Homes at Decoto and Covina. I am
sure my Lodge and the community join me in the assurance
that they were superlatively edifying and instructive as
well as entertaining. They surely deserve all the support
the Fraternity can give them. I congratulate you, also,
upon the selection of such a capable and versatile brother
as Captain Tracy. His brief remarks accompanying the
pictures were peculiarly proper and comprehensive."
"The pictures that were shown of the Masonic Homes
at Decoto and Covina were very interesting and instructive,
and every one present was very enthusiastic. Very few·
of us had any idea that our aged brothers and sisters, and
our orphans were being so well cared for, nor had we any
conception that our Homes were so splendid, both as to
buildings and equipment. Much favorable comment was
made on Brother Gibson's fine talk on the homes anl pictures, and the spirit in which Brother Gibson and the
pictures were received will have a lasting effect."

For· the past two years the Endowment Committee has recommended to the Grand Lodge that they definitely determine whether
or not it is advisable to raise an Endowment Fund, and if it be
advi!able, then an active, energetic drive or campaign be instituted
until the goal is reached.
The Endowment Fund has made a rather unsatisfacto~y showing during the past two years, and your Committee feels that unless
there is a spirit of co-operation and determination by the members
of the Grand Lodge to reach the goal outlined some years since,
and if the interest is only to be half-hearted, then it is a recommendation of the Committee that it should be made clear, by vote
of the Grand Lodge, that no further efforts be made.
While this same thought has been presented twice before, no
action ·has been taken and it is the unanimous request of your
Committee that Grand Lodge now definitely determine the plans
for the future.

John Plaskett Jarman

. Past Grand Master Keesling spoke as follows :
I believe it cannot be gainsaid that in addition to the symbols
and ritual of the Fraternity, every ceremonial requirement serves
its very important purpose or purposes. The direct purpose of
the fun~ral service is to offer up the last sad tribute of our affection. This we readily understand in the case of those with whom
we may be acquainted; .it perhaps bec;,mes more perfunctory so far
as that feature is concerned, but nevertheless still a Masonic duty,
in the cases of those who may be strangers-but the other purpose
is ever present. A memorial service similarly fulfills the require~
ments of this other purpose, and on this other purpose I will primarily dwell.
·
The potential thinkers are many. The voluntary thinkers are
few. The Masonic system instructs and inspires thought and
action. Why the potential thinkers are many and the voluntary
thinkers are few, may afford cause for speculation. It is a fact,
nevertheless, and causes concern as we consider the demands of
our particular form of government. Ours is the problem of
prompting thought. One would believe that there are sufficient
everyday warnings to produce the result, but practice demonstrates
that it is not so. Even the simplest duties remain unperformed.
Ordinarily, something terrific, something awesome, something spectacular, Something heroic, is required. You know what is necessary to awaken consciousness.
We place a stress on the funeral service. Some uninformed
people know only that the Masonic Fraternity insures a decent
burial. Indeed, the Fraternity carefully safe-guards that ·attention
to the strange brother. Aside from the fact that it is the charitable
thing to do, even in such a case there remains, the other purpose.
Men proceed to their studies for the purpose of uninterrupted
thought. They approach the sanctuary so that, undefiled by the
material activities about them, th~y may clearly perform their de-

626

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

votions. For the time occupied by the funeral service we are
removed from the material things of life, and, in the presence of
death, are prompted to give consideration to the spiritual, and we
search the innermost recesses as we take a mental inventory.
Circumstances impel us to visualize the rew~rd of a virtuous
and well spent life. The memorial service is not unlike.
Today, in this asylum, which for the time being has become
a sanctuary for the purpose of doing honor to those whom we are
privileged to honor, we naturally eliminate the worldly and enter
into that which is spiritual. The cere'mony of itself must produce
that result.
It is emphasized by the character of him whom we honor.
John Plaskett Jarman was born in England, January 27th, 1849,
and came to this country when he was seventeen years old. He
resided in California and in Santa Clara county since 1866. He
was initiated in San Jose Lodge No. 10, August 17th, 1885 ; passed
August 31st, and raised September 29th, 1885. He served as Senior
Deacon during the years 1886, 1887 and 1888, as Junior Watden in
1889, and as Master in 1890 a.n d 1891. He again served as Senior
Deacon in the years 1893, 1894 and 1898, and as Master in 1906.
He was Inspector of his district from 1910 to 1920. He was Grand
Bible Bearer of the Grand Lodge from 1914 to 1921, and at the
time of his death was serving in that capacity. In addition to this
Masonic service, which was well performed, he served, with great
honor to himself and the Fraternity, as a Trustee of t he public
schools of the c.ity of San Jose for many years. He died May 8,
1921.
In departing hence he left the other members of his family,
consisting of the splendid woman who was his life companion, a .
son, Albert H. Jarman, an honorable member of the legal profession of this city, two daughters, Kate Williams and Edith Jarman,
true to the type of the honorable man who was their father.
As I awakened to the responsibility of saying something of
my friend and brother worthy to be recorded, I was traveling the
same road taken by John Burroughs on ·his last journey, and as I
gazed forth on the fields and scenes ~o much belov ed by him I
recalled his last words, in effect: "How far am I from home?"
What a splendid index to the worth of the man ! Great as was his
achievement in the scientific world, even greater was he in the
appreciation of home. Animals and ignorant humans will fight for
their abiding place. But a profound understanding of the requisites
of protection of home and insuring the liberty and pursuit of happiness of those therein, free from attack, by proper discharge of
duty to family and society, is the virtue of a good and substantial
citizen. Our brother had that virtue. His conduct throughout

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

627

life constantly exemplified it. The love of his family, the respect
of his neighbor and that of his business associates, testify to it.
His service to the Fraternity, to the. community, to the unfortunate,
was marked by sacrifice generously bestowed.
"And the Voice that was soft er t han silence said,
'Lo, it is I, be not afraid !
In many climes without avail,
Thou hast spent thy life for t he Holy Grail;
Behold, it is here-this cup which thou
Didst fill at the stieamlet for me, full now;
Thjs crust is my body broken for thee,
This water His blood that died on the tree;
The Holy Supper is kept, indeed,
In whatso we share with another's need:
Not what we give, but what we shareFor the gift without the giver is bare;
Who gives himself with his alms feeds three,
Himself, his hungering neighbor, and me.' "-Lowell.

•

In my iife he stands as an inspiration for honorable conduct
His was of the unspoken influence, which c~mmanded my attentio~
to things Masonic.
He was truly a successful man.
"The talent of success is nothing more than doing
what you can do well, and doing well whatever you
do without a thought of fame. If it comes at a ll,
it will come because it is deserved, not because
it is squght after."-Longfellow.
What he did he did well ; he did it without a thought of fame
or rew~rd. Dollars and cents were not his objective. But he was
rewarded, and wha t a splendid thing it is to know that it was not
a reward reserved until he had gone to the great beyond. It was
evidenced by the respect and esteem, and love, of those· who knew
him. Nothing he did did he begrudge. Cheerfulness marked his
conduct. His advice was sought; it was cheerfully given; it was
good. He was soft of voice, sweet of temperament and firm in
righteousness. He was fearless in the cause, loyal in his friendship
ever considerate and unselfish. He was a God-fearing man.
'
And so his life must inspire desire to correct our errors fuller
appreciation of proper Fraternal int ercourse, and unselfish ; ervice.
Laws are necessary to govern conduct. No law was necessary to
prescribe his. ~ondu.ct. . With such character of citizenship, only
law! of admtn1stration would be necessary. This mild-mannered
man achieved real success.

Granville Dexter Warren

Past Grand Master W ebstei- addressed Grand Lodge
as follows:
Gran~.ille Dexter Warren, Past Master of Brooklyn Lodge, lnsp~c­
tor of one of the large and important districts in this Grand Junsdiction for so many years that he came to be affectionately referred to
as the Dean of Masonic Inspectors in Alameda county: 1t is with a
pr<Jfound sense of personal p'rivilege that I undertake to. pay tribu~e
to the memory of this beloved brother, though I might wish that this
duty and privilege had been committed to the charge of one able more
eloquently than myself to portray his many virtues and express our
appreciation of his life and character.
One of the many and various services rendered to Masonry by
Brother Warren, the outstanding and distinctive one was as Inspector.
He and I assun:ed the work of Inspectors in Alameda county at the
same time, and at a time, too, when the work of inspection had not
been so thoroughly organized as it has since become under the management of our t>eloved Grand Lecturer ; so that it was necessary for
us to in a measure, pioneer the work of inspection at that early date;
~nd shall not forget the patience, courtesy, ability and tact with which
Brother Warren attacked the problems attending this work. To him,
his work as Inspector was not done when he guided his Lodges correctly through the ritualistic work and the conduct of their business,
but he had so large a human interest that he entered into the personal
problems of the members of the Lodges under his jurisdiction in many
cases. And it .was no uncommon thing for him to be consulted upon
the most intimate personal problen:s of his brethren. It was my privilege working with him in the adjoining district, to know many of such
inst;nces and one could not fail to be impressed with the ready
sympath; and intense brotherly feeling of Brother Warren in all these
ministrations; modest, unassuming, yet forceful and kindly, he went
about his daily duties with characteristic energy and efficiency. One
thing which I might say was almost a hobby of his, was the ce~enting
of closer fraternal relations between the Lodges of his district and
county. He had no use for mock protestations of fraternal ism; but
always, as he did himself, expected his brethren to practice what they
preached, and had very little patience with jealousy between Lodges.
No man whom I ever met could more justly be said to have attained
spiritual freedom; that freedom which has been defined somewhere in
Masonry as free.dom from prepossessions, prejudices and errors, or
that mental equipoise which neither priest nor potentate can disturb or
bend to his dictation.
·
'·

i

While Brother Warr en was no worshi-pper at the shrine of tradition, and did not consider himself bound to customs and observances
merely because of their age, on the other hand, he steered his course as
a man and a Mason far from the other extreme of dangerous radicalism; a well-balanced man and Mason. While we have ' been deprived
of his bodily presence, his spirit, his influence and his inspiration are
still with us to guide, to cheer, to inspire. And we know, and say with
profound appreciation, that the impress of that noble character has been
left ineffaceably for good upon the community in which he lived, and
the fraternity in which he labored so long and faithfully.
To Granville Dexter Warren, then, this tribute : the good man;
upright citizen; true Mason; master of the Light, and devoted friend.

Edmund Elnathan Knepper

.Brother ~obert L. Wood of Lexington Lodge No. ·104,
delivered the following, prepared by Brother Frank A.
Nance, of Monrovia Lodge No. 308, who was unavoidably
absent:
On November 19th, 1920, at Monrovia, California, the spirit of our
beloved brother, Edmund Elnathan Knepper, passed on to its reward.
Always a leader and earnest worker in every organization with which
he was identified, his going was a great personal shock to his hundreds
of friends and associates in church, club, school and lodge. The death
· of no other citizen in many years has occasioned such general sorrow
in t~at c01_nmunity as did the loss of brother Knepper, and on the day
of his burial all the schools and business houses suspended their activities out of respect for his honored memory.
Born at Henry City, Illinois, on February 4th, 1871, of a family of
scholars, Brother Knepper early determined to follow educational
~ork, and after grad11ation from Stanford University he entered upon
his career as a teacher at Lewiston, Idaho. After a few years he
moved to San Rafael, California, and later to Monrovia where he
became City Superintendent of Schools, which. post he 'filled with
marke.d success until chosen to serve Los Angeles County as Assistant
s.upermtendent of Schools. In this important office his work was of the
h1g?est order. T~oroughly trained in school supervision, tactful,
patient and possessing rare judgment, his influence touched the lives .
of thousands and his conscientious labor set a record mark for efficiency in his department.
As a citizen, B'rother Knepper exert~d a wide influence in the moral

~ocial and political life of the community. He was identified with eve~
movement for the benefit of his fellows, and was never known to

630

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

neglect a civic duty that fell to his lot. His patriotism and devotion
to his country during a great war deserve special praise. Disqualified
for military service, to his great regret, he gave untiring assistance to
the various war work organizations and cut his personal expenditures
to a minimum that by this sacrifice he might give greater aid to assist
in financing the war.
'The home life of our beloved brother was beautiful. For rr.any
years he was the sole support of his family, to whom he · was the
incarnation of a!l that is good in man.
Ed. Knepper was a true gentleman. Wherever one could meet him
he would be received in a kindly, courteous manner that was at once
delightful and assur.ing. His manner inspired confidence and his
excellent judgment generously aided all who sought his counsel. His
personality and exemplary conduct had an excellent influence upon the
young men of the community, in whose welfare he took the deepest
interest.
Although his loss is keenly felt as an educator, as trustee of the
Presbyterian church, as a director of the Granite club and as a patriotic,
upstanding American citizen, his guiding hand is probably more sadly
missed in the affairs of the 62nd Masonic District of which he was
Inspector.
Brother Knepper was a member of the Masonic order for twenty
years. He was initiated a tr.ember of Nez Perce Lodge No. 10 of
Lewiston, J:daho, August 17, 1901, passed to the degree of Fellowcrait
one week later, and raised as a Master Mason on August 31st, having
taken the three degrees in two weeks, his. uncle, Grand Secretary of
the State of Idaho,· conferring the degrees. On November 10th, 1907,
Brother Knepper became a member of Monrovia Lodge No. 308 by
affiliation and served as Master of that Lodge during the year 1910.
As Master his rare good judgment and personal charm endeared him
to the craft, and his untiring assistance at . all times during his ten
years as Past Master made him invaluable to the officers and members
of Monrovia Lodge. He was a 32° member of the Scottish Rite Bodies
of the Los Angeles ConsistOTy and a member of Al Maliekah Temple
of the Shrine.
On account of his peculiar fitness and his loyal devotion to our
Institution he was appointed Inspector of the 62nd District about a
year before his death. During this brief period, by consistent and
conscientious effort, he brought up the work of the seven Lodges of
the district to a higher degree of proficiency than they had known for
several years. In this work his kindly personality and generous wisdom
won the love and respect of all the brethren with whom he came into
personal touch, and his influence still remains as an inspiration to all
who had the good fortune of being associated with him.

To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:
It is with pleasure that your Committee on Returns has to
report that the returns and dues from the several Lodges for the
year ending July 31st, 1921, were, for the most part, presented very
promptly and most of them were correct. It is the returns that are
late in arriving, and those that are incorrect, that are annoying
to our Grand Secretary.
· It is the duty of a Master of a Lodge to see that the returns
and dues from his Lodge are forwarded promptly to the Grand
Secretary.
With the exception of Westwood Lodge, U. D. at Westwood,
·
and Benjamin Franklin Lodge, at Los Angeles, all the L9dges of
the Jurisdiction have sent in their returns and are included in the
Grand Secretary's report.

of Master Mason (8,831) this year is not as large as last year, it
shows that the Lodges have been very active. F.rom personal
observation, and from reliable reports, it n;iay be stated that the

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CHARTERS
To the M:. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committ~e on Charters has had under consideration the
petitions for charters of the following Lodges, for the formation and
opening of which dispensations were issued within the past Masonic
year :
Harbor Lodge, at Richmond.
Point Lodge, at Richmond.
Cupertino Lodge, at Cupertino.
Mt. Olive Lodge, at Los Angeles.
El Segundo Lodge, at El Segundo.
Cahuenga Lodge, at Hollywood, Los Angeles.
Fremont Lodge at ·Oakland.
Lebanon Lodge, at San Francisco.
Capital City Lodge, at ·Sacramento.
Stockton Lodge, at Stockton.
Your Committee has examined the dispensations, by-laws and
books of record of said Lodges, has found the same to meet the requirements of the Constitution, and therefore recommends that a
charter issue to each of them, numbered respectively as follows :
Harbor Lodge No. 502, at Richmond.
Point Lodge No. 503, at Richmond.
Cupertino Lodge No. 510, at Cupertino.
Mount Olive Lodge No. 506, at Los Angeles.
El Segundo Lodge No. 507, at El Segundo.
Cahuenga Lodge No. 513, at Los Angeles (Hollywood) .
Fremont Lodge No. 497, at Oakland.
Lebanon Lodge No. 495, at San Francisco.
Capital City Lodge No. 499, at Sacramento.
Stockton Lodge No. 498, at Stockton.
Your Committee has also had under consideration the petitions for
charters of the following Lodges, to which dispensations were issued ·
during the past Masonic year:
Benjamin Franklin Lodge, at Los Angeles.
Joppa Lodge, at San Joaquin.
With reference to Benjamin Franklin Lodge, your Committee finds
all books and records in satisfactory condition, with the exception that
the by-laws, M heretofore reported by the Committee on By-Laws of ·
Lodges, have not been signed by the charter members. Your Committee. recommends that . a charter issue to said lodge, ~o be designated
and numbered Benjamin Franklin Lcidge No. 509, at Los Angeles, but

that said Lodge be required to secure the signatures of its charter
members to the by-laws as a prerequisite to the constitution of the
Lodge.
With reference to Joppa Lodge, your Committee finds all books
and records in proper form, with the exception of certain omissions in
the by-laws heretofore noted in the report of the Committee. on By-La~s
of Lodges. Your Committee recomrr:ends that a charter issue to said
Lodge to be designated and numbered Joppa Lodge No. 508, at San
Joaquin, but that said Lodge be required to correct its by-laws prior
to its constitution.
Your Committee has also had under consideration the petitions for
charters 'of the following Lodges to which dispensations were issued
within the past Masonic year:
Sunnyvale Lodge, at Sunnyvale.
Silver Cord Lodge, at Santa Ana.
Palms Lodge, at Palms.
Seaside Lodge, at Long Beach.
Roosevelt Lodge, at San Francisco.
Westwood Lodge, at Westwood.
We find that the minute books of these lodges are deficient; that
sorr:e of them have failed to record the minutes of their preliminary
meetings · that some have failed to enter their dispensations and bylaws and . that some have failed to enter their financial statements.
Exa~ination discloses, however, that the requisite proceedings were
taken in all cases and that the cimission.s from the record books were
due to the inexperience of new Secretaries. The delegates of each qf
these Lodges having agreed that the minutes will be promptly corrected
to meet the r equirements of the Constitution, your Committee recommends that charters be issued to the foregoing Lodges, to be designated
and numbered as follows:
Sunnyvale Lodge No. 511, at Sunnyvale.
Silver Cord Lodge No. 505, at Santa Ana.
Palms Lodge No. 512, at Palms.
Seaside Lodge No. 504, at Long Beach.
Roosevelt Lodge No. 500, ~t San Francisco.
Westwood Lodge No. 501, at Westwood.
Your Corr:mittee has also considered the petition of Riverdale
Lodge, at Riverdale, heretofore opened under dispensat~on, for a charter and finds that the minutes of the Lodge are deficient. The delega;e of said Lodge has promised that the minutes will be put in proper
condition forthwith. Your Committee therefore recommends that a
charter issue to said Lodge, to be designated and numbered Riverdale
Lodge No. 496, at Riverdale. Having learned that the Junior Warden

nominated by said Lodge to serve under charter has failed to perfect

REPORTS OF COMMITTEE ON POLICY AND

Masonic Club at University of California

To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on General Policy and Purposes, to which was
referred that portion of the Grand Master's report relating to the
Masonic Club at the University of California, has had the same under
consideration, and to meet the need, your Committee recommends :
First: That the Grand Lodge of California hereby approves of
the erection of a suitable clubhouse near the campus of the University
of California for the use of Master Masons, and sons and daughters
of Masons at the University.
Second:. That the Grand Lodge give its consent to a statewide
appeal among Masons for the necessary funds to erect and equip such
a building.
Third: That the Grand Lodge hereby authorize the formation of
.a corporation, or association for the purpose of holding title to the
necessary property, and to administer the business affairs of the organization, the plan of such organization to be approved by the Grand
Master, and provided, always, that the Grand Lodge shall have at
least one representative, to be designated by the Grand Master, on
such board.

Adopted.
Recognition of York Grand Lodge

To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on General Policy and Purposes have had under
consideration the matter of Masonry in Mexico, as set forth in the
report of the Most Worshipful Grand Master, supplemented by the

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

report of Past Grand Master Charles Albert Adams, who was delegated
by the Grand Master to represent him in an examination on the
ground of the conditions presently surrounding Masonry in Mexico.
At the outset, we desire to commend the foresight and wisdom of
the Grand Master in delegating the personal investigation of this
subject to Past Grand Master Adams; secondly, we are greatly indebted
to the latter gentleman for his illuminating and comprehensive report,
, and feel that the subject has been most thoroughly and ably covered.
We therefore heartily concur in the recommendations contained in that
report. We therefore offer the following resolutions and recommend
their adoption:
Whereas, This Grand Lodge, at the Annual Communication of
1902, extended fraternal recognition to the "Grand Lodge of A. F. &
A. M. Valle de Mexico"; and
Whereas, It now satisfactorily appears, after thorough inquiry and
investigation, that the Grand Lodge Valle de Mexico, to which recognition was so extended, changed its name in 1911, and ever since has
been, and now is, known as the "York Grand Lodge of Mexico F. &
A. M."; and that there is no reason why that recognition should be
, withdrawn; Now, therefore, be it
Resolved, That the Grand Lodge of California, being fully advised
of all the facts and circumstances, hereby formally extends fraternal
recognition to the York Grand Lodge of Mexico F. & A. M., of which
M.'. W.'. Ernest J. Nicklos is Grand Master; and that the Grand Master
of Masons in California, when so requested, arrange for an interchange of fraternal representatives ; and be it further
Resolved, That the Grand Lodge of California does hereby express
the hope that a solution may be found for the problems now confronting Ancient Craft Masonry in the Republic of Mexico, and that harmony may be restored; and commending the fraternal spirit which
prompted the Grand Master of the York Grand Lodge and .his brethren
to adopt the suggestions and recommendations of the Texas Commission
for a merger with the Grand Lodge Valle de Mexico, and confirming
the assurance given at that time by the representative of the Grand.
Master of Masons in California, together with the Texas Commission
and the Grand Master of Louisiana. Be it further
Resolved, That in the event of a merger of the York Grand Lodge
of Mexico· with the Grand Lodge Valle de Mexico and the organization
thereby of a new Grand Lodge in the Republic of Mexico, the fraternal
recognition hereby extended the York Grand Lodge of Mexico be
deemed to be extended the new Grand Lodge so formed, under whatever
name it may be known. ·

Past Masters of Island Lodges
Your Committee on General Policy and Purposes has had under
consideration the request heretofore made that the Past Masters of
Lodge le Progres de l'Oceanie who served as Masters thereof prior to
the time a charter was issued to said Lodge by the Grand Lodge, and
the Past Masters of Pacific Lodge who served as Masters thereof prior
to the time a charter was issued to said Lodge under the name of
Honolulu Lodge No. 409, and who are now members of said respective
Lodges, be given the status of Past Masters of this Grand Lodge and
your Committee is of the opinion that the request should be granted.
The Past Masters of Lodge Maui, now Maui No. 472, were accorded
the status of Past Masters of this Grand Lodge and the situation of
the Past Masters of old Pacific and old Le Progres de l'Oceanie are
quite analogous, and their desires in this respect are laudable and
reasonable.
Your Committee therefore recommends that the following resolution be adopted :
Resolved, That the title of Past Master as defined in our Constitution shall apply to all the Past Masters of Honolulu Lodge No. 409 and
Le Progres de l'Oceanie Lodge No. 371 who served said respective
Lodges as Masters prior to the time the said Lodges became subordinate
of this Grand Jurisdiction and that all such Past Masters shall hereafter be entitled to all the rights and privileges of this Jurisdiction
under our Constitution.

Adopted.
Expenditures for Refreshments
Your Committee on General Policy and Purposes has had under
consideration the amendment to the Constitution proposed by Reginald
W . Clapp, affecting the provisions relative to the 20 per cent of the
total revenue of a Lodge available for purposes of refreshment and
the promotion of fraternal intercourse. The object sought to be accom-

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

652

plished by the change in our laws, proposed by Brother Clapp, is to
enable a Lodge to base its expenditures within the limitation of 20 per
cent of the gross revenue, upon the revenues of the current year rather
than those of the preceding year.
The amount of money proper to be expended for refreshments
and the promotion of fraternal intercourse varies from year to year.
There appears to be no good reason why a Lodge should not be permitted to expend a definite proportion of its revenues, for those purposes
without reference to the amount of revenue received by it at some
previous time.
Your Committee therefore recommends that Section 89 of the
Constitution be amended to read as follows:
Section 89. Excepting, however, that the Lodge n:ay expend 20
per cent of its total revenue for purposes of refreshments and the
promotion of Fraternal intercourse.

Adopted, and section 89 amended as above by. unanimous vote.

Dual Membership

Masonic Education

Your Committee on General Purposes and Policy, to which was
referred the resolution calling for the amendment of section 157 of
the Constitution to permit dual membership, begs leave to report as
follows:
The subject of dual membership is one which deserves very careful
investigation and mature consideration. There are many good reasons
in our judgment why dual membership should be permitted, and there
are at the same time objections of more or less validity which may be
urged against the introduction of this new policy in our law and policy.
As at present advised your Committee is favorable to the establishment of the dual membership system, but until it has made further
investigation and given a greater consideration to the question it is
not prepared to make any recommendation to the Grand Lodge on the
subject. Your Committee believes that the interests of the craft would
be better served if consideration of this matter by the Grand Lodge was ·
postponed for one year, and it therefore recommends that the subject
be postponed until the next Annual Communication of this Grand
Lodge.

Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has had under
consideration the interesting report of the Committee on Masonic
Education, and after a careful examination of the same feel constrained
to say that the general plan of Masonic education now in operation is
both practical and workable, for the r.eport of the Committee on Education shows progress. And therefore, r:eiterating our unswerving faith in
the prime importance of Masonic education and our earnest desire· to
see that work carried on energetically, we recommend the adoption of
the suggestions numbered 1 and 2 of the report, namely, (1) That the
present form of organization of the Committee be continued. (2) That
the organization of Officers' Associations be continued.

Adopted.
