Consideration of Grand Master's Address
Your Committee on General Policy and Purposes has had under
consideration those portions of the Grand -Master's address dealing
with
I. Private concerns;
2. Clandestine Masonry;
3. Organizations demanding Masonic affiliation.
Use of Word "Masonic" in Business
l. As to the first, your Committee notes with approval and hearty
comrr:endation the efforts the Gra.nd Master has made through his
letter to the Craft to insure that all the brethren should have a clear
idea of the exact nature of these organizations, no matter by what
name they go. In this connection and supplemental to his original
report, the Grand Master reported notification in writing by one such
organization, which had been in business for twenty-:;ix years, of its
intention to change its name and drop the objectionable word "Masonic"
from its title, and that initial steps to that end had already been taken
by that organization.
In this connection, also, your Committee is advised by the officers
of another organization using the word "Masonic" in its title, under
the advice of eminent legal and Masonic counsel, not connected with or
employed by this organization, that they were entirely within the law
of this Grand Lodge in so using the word "Masonic," yet, nevertheless,
by reason of the fact that misapprehensions have arisen and much
criticism has been directed against them, they have decided to change
the name of the organization and eliminate the word "Masonic" from
the title thereof, in the hope that such action will ren:ove any further
misapprehension and misunderstanding by any member of the Craft.

Adopted.

Status of Adult Daughters of Masons

I

The attention of your Committee on General Policy and Purposes has been directed to the fact th'a t the daughter of a Master
Mason has been treated as such (regardless of her age) as to general relief; but that general rule has not been applied so as to admit
an adult daughter of a Master Mason to our Homes.
This matter was referred to this Committee at our last annual
communication, but was deferred pending investigation and is now
before us for final consideration . Brother Leo Bruck has conducted an exhaustive correspondence with other grand jurisdictions
and has submitted the voluminous results of the same to your Committee.
Without deeming it necessary to go into the merits, it is the
sense of the Committee that whatever rule of construction is
adopted, should be uniform in its application, and since we now
extend general relief to adult orphan daughters of Master Masons,
we believe that the Trustees of our Homes should admit such
orphans in proper cases to the benefits of the Home, and we therefore recommend the modification of the present rules of admission
to the Home so as to accomplish this result.

Boards of Relief
Your Committee has received and carefully checked the reports
of the Boards of Relief of San Francisco, Los Angeles, Oakland,
Sacramento, San Diego, San Bernardino and Honolulu: The~e
reports show that the splendid work of relief so long earned on m
this grand jurisdiction, has continued during the. past year. T~e

behalf of distressed Masons far beyond the conception of the
average member, and we heartily commend their work. Your

In connection with the Boards of Relief in ' San Francisco, Los
Angel1ts, San Diego and · San Bernardino, employment bureaua have

Francis Drake Lodge
Your Committee has had under consideration the request of Francis
Drake Lodge No. 376, for reimbursement for funds expended for the
support of Mrs. Charlotte Nass. It appears from the correspondence
that Mrs. Nass is the widow of a deceased Mason who was a member
of Fortitude Lodge No. 19 of Brooklyn, New York. Mrs.. Nass is
more than 80 years of age, and is in a helpless condition, which required
that she be placed in a home where she could receive constant care.
She is at present in the home of Anna. Henry, 3136 Fruitvale avenue,
Oakland, and the expense of maintaining Mrs. Nass in this home is
$80.00 per month. Fortitude Lodge has practically declined to assist
in the support of Mrs. Nass.
We recommend, first, that the case be turned over to the Board of
Relief of Oakland, and that they be requested to take up the care of
Mrs. Nass, and that Francis Drake Lodge be relieved from further
responsibility. Second, that we recommend Francis Drake Lodge · to
turn over all the correspondence to our Grand Secretary, that he
communicate with the Grand Secretary of New York, and see if some
assistance and reimbursement cannot be had from Fortitude Lodge.
We further recommend that the amount heretofore expended by
Francis Drake Lodge, namely, $310.00, be returned to it. We therefore
uffer the following resolution and recommend its adoption:
Resolved, That the sum of $310.00 be and is hereby appropriated
from the funds of this Grand Lodge to reimburse Francis Drake Lodge
for the amount expended in the support of Mrs. Nass.

Adopted.

· Berkeley Lodge
Your Committee has had before it the claim of Berke!ey Lodge No.
363, for reimbursement of the sum of $275.00. It appears that George
Uttley, a member of Confidence Lodge No. 203, of Castroville, di'ed
in May, 1920, leaving a widow who is a helpless invalid and requiring
the attention of a nurse. Berkeley Lodge has been handling the case
and so far has expended several hundred dollars. It has been able to
collect from friends and distant relatives all but the sum of $275.00.
It appears that Confidence Lodge consists of 28 members and the Lodge
is unable to reimburse Berkeley Lodge. We therefore offer the follow. ing resolution and recomrr.end its adoption :
Resolved, That the sum of $275.00 be appropriated from the funds
of this Grand Lodge to reimburse Berkeley Lodge No. 363, for the
moneys expended in the assistance of Mrs. George Uttley, for the
account of Confidence Lodge No. 203 of this Jurisdiction.

Adopted.

fro.m said Lodge in 1919. We recommend that tjle request be granted,
and therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption:
·Resolved, That the sum of $1.90 be appropriated from the funds of
this Grand Lodge to reimburse North Star Lodge No. 91, for refund
of overpaid Grand Lodge dues.

Adopted.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON GRAND LECTURER'S
REPORT
To the M.'.W.'.Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee to which was referred the report of the Grand
Lecturer, begs leave to present the following report :
We commend the faithfulness and zeal which our beloved brother,
v:. w:. Grand Lecturer Thomas }. Baker, has e•er shown in the .
performance of the arduous duties pertaining to his office, and congratulate him and his corps of Inspectors on the high standard of efficiency
now attained throughout this Jurisdiction in the various Lodges. His
willingness, his courtesy, and his kindness have endeared him to our
entire membership.
We concur in his suggestion that the formation of additional
Lodges, rather than the building up of our merr:bership in Lodges of
great size, gives opportunity for our members to become better
acquainted and to practice the true fraternal spirit both inside and
outside of the Lodge room. We rejoice with him in the formation of
the twenty such new Lodges during the past year.
The tribute which the Grand Lecturer pays to the several Inspectors, and the credit which he ascribes to them for the good condition
of the Lodges in their several districts may be well deserved, and
undoubtedly is, but we are more than ever impressed with the fact that,
after all, the high standard our Lodges have attained and the care
with which the work is universally conducted, is due in the last analysis
to our beloved Grand Lecturer, Thomas J. Baker.
THEODORE M. WRIGHT,
FRANK

B. DRAKE,

Committee.

Adopted.

Past Grand Master Charles Albert Adams was app~inted
Master of Ceremonies, and the officers-elect and appointed,

Burke a beautiful ebony gavel, mounted with silver, the
gift of his brethren of Sunset Lodge.
Past Grand Master Frank M. Angellotti then, in a happy
speech, and as a life-long frien'd and neighbor, prese.nted to
the retiring Grand Master a consol phonograph with records and a tea wagon.
The retiring Grand Master, in the felicitous manner in
which he excels, delivered the Charles Albert Adams button-badge to his successor.

seventy-second annual Grand Lodge was closed m Ample

REPORT
OF THE

Committee on Correspondence
OCTOBER, 1921 .
By JESSE M. WHITED

To the .M ost Worshipful Grand Master, Officers, Members of the
Grand Lodge of Californ~a, and Brethren of this Jurisdiction:
~

I submit my third report on Foreign Correspondence.
The general topics of interest in the various Proceedings are:
(1) The tendency of the various Grand Lodges to take action
against the "higher degrees" and miscellaneous organizations.
(2) The enormous growth of the Fraternity, and the reason
therefor.
·
(3) The attempt to find some means to overcome the danger
due to that increase.
(4) An effort to devise some way to make Lodges something
other than "degree mills."
(5) The continuation of Masonic education and establishing
new plans in Jurisdictions that have not yet given this matter
attention.
(6) The part that Masonry must play in the affairs of the
day, and particularly the Public School question.
Some Grand Lodges have gone so far as to pass resolutions
endorsing the "Smith-Towner Bill." From a theoretical standpoint
this may be contrary to an Ancient Landmark (?) but we can not
help but feel that it is a step in the right direction. General resolutions endorsing a theoretical question or the sentiment thereof,
without taking a positive position, are about as effective as resoluting in favor of the spirit of the Ten Commandments or the Declaration of Independence.
The proceedings of Nova Scotia, Nevada, Maine, Pennsylvania,
Vermont and Utah have been received too late for reviewing and
including the valuable part thereof in this report. They all contain
most interesting and valuable material.

2

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

Acknowledgment is again made of the obligation we are under
to the Secretaries of the several Grand Bodies and Grand Lodges of
the United States, the Editors of Masonic publications and other
writers, whose replies to. questionnaries have materially added to
whatever value this report may have.
ADVERTISING
The association of· the words "Mason" or "Masonic" with
enterprises established or promoted for private gain, cannot be too
strongly condemned. The average member, naturally assumes that
they are operated for the benefit of the Fraternity, and consequently
feels duty bound to patronize them. A number of the States have
made it an offense to use the word "Mason" or "Masonic" in cases
of this kind, and the soone'r the rest of the Jurisdictions fall in
line the better it will be.
There is also too much advertising of the private doings of the
Fraternity, but as we are living in a "progressive age," we are perhaps_ but following the natural trend of affairs.

banking institutions of San Juan," to use the woi;ds o~ grand S.ecretary J. G. Torres. In a little more than a year, its ongmal capital
has been multiplied nine times ov('!r, its deposits excee~ $150,000,

the legal rate of interest; it has encouraged thrift and sav1~g; it has

to make our Fraternity a tool for selfish ends whether such effort
comes from a sneaky politicaJ party· or from an organization which
is doing unselfish and effective uplift work. In either case, the

Florida:
He reported a peculiar case of an appeal for aid, the like of
which we have never heretofore heard. A man who was a member
of a Lodge in Texas skillfully composed a letter and mailed one to
all of the 900 Lodges in Texas, certifying that the writer was
afflicted with tuberculosis, that he had been promised complete
restoration by a physician after he had spent two years in a certain
climate, in the West, and requesting of the Lodge a loan of $15 to
assist him in making the change and living during the time required.
It was agreed that if he recovered he was to return the money as
a loan, but in case he lost his life, the loan was to be considered
a donation. Enclosed with each letter was a certificate from a
physician that the applicant was a Master Mason, that he was
inclined to believe that the case was curable, and the assistance was
asked to enable him to 1 be restored to health. The appeal was
without authority, and the Grand Master commenced an investigation. It was found that if all of the Lodges appealed to made him
the loan it would amount to over $13,000. It was also discovered
that the man was not suffering with an acute case of tuberculosis
but was working at his daily employment and receiving good
wages. He was a heavy drinker and it was only while drunk that
he lost any time. Charges were preferred and the man expelled.
Illinois:
Many protests have come to the grand master from lodges.
and brethren concerning soliciting for so-called Masonic insurance.
At a recent session of this Grand Lodge, it was specifically decided
that insurance of all kinds is prohibited. Insurance is a business
whether it be called Masonic or otherwise. The mere fact that an
insurance company will accept Masons only, does not exempt it
from the prohibition· in the law as referred to above. The only
business permitted in the law is "the printing or publication of
Masonic books, papers, or periodicals, or the manufacture and sale
of Masonic supplies." The Masonic papers are thus favored because of their value to the craft.
The specific question involved at this time is whether publishing in the Masonic press the advertisements of foreign insurance
companies bearing the name of "Masonic" is a violation of the
law. These organizations have the legal right to do business in
Illinois, if they comply with the regulations of the insurance department of the state. We are of the opinion, however, that the
Grand Lodge has complete jurisdiction over the individual Mason.
It can prohibit him from being a party to an:Y business in violation of Masonic law. Any insurance assuming to be Masonic is
illegal under the laws of this Grand Lodge.
We are of the opinion that the publication by a Masonic newspaper of advertisements of insurance or other business enterprises,

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

bearing the name of "Mason" or "Masonic," is contrary to the
spirit of the sections quoted. The rea~ons will readily appear. The
representative of a so-called Masonic insurance company can go
into the Lodge rooms with a copy of a Masonic publication and
solicit the business of Masons who are led to believe that because
the advertisement appears in a Masonic paper that it is fostered,
supported and authorized by the Grand Lodge of Illinois.
It is impossible for the Grand Lodge or individual Masons to
know the character of those corporations organized under the laws
of other states.
·
We therefore hold, that the law contained in Sections 716 and
717 would subject the publishers of Masonic papers to discipline
by their )odges.
Your committee regrets that it may seem to hold against the
business transactions of our Masonic papers. However, in construing the law we must do so from its meaning, and from the
spirit of the Craft.
ATTENDANCE
There is a letter on file in one of the minute books of Virginia
written in the early part of the Eighteenth Century complaining that
the brethren spent their time in the anteroom with "Jachin" and
"Boaz." That was the respective designations of two demijohns
of good Jamaica Rum and Holland. Gin. Brethren of the Revolutionary period certainly enjoyed privileges that are forbidden to
us now.
Owing to the vast amount of degree work that has been, and
still is, being carried on, the average member finds little to attract
him to the regular meetings, and statistics show that even at the
best the Lodge life of the average member is not more than seven
years. The remedy for this is in the hands of th Worshipful
Master, and the attendance at meetings must depend upon his
ability to provide entertainment and instruction' outside of mere
ritualistic work. We believe that Lodges should devote more time
to the social side of our organization, but as the average Master
is prone to measure his success by the number of degrees conferred,
the remedy will undoubtedly have to come from the Grand Lodge
itself. This can be done by shortening the ritual, and setting a time ·
limit between the conferring of each degree on an individual. '
Every Grand Master is fertile in ideas along this lin.e but none
of them have been able to do' any thing practical to solve the
question.

Mexico:
It is the country newspaper which really interests a man. After
reading the big dailies with their world-wide news, he turns with
a sigh of content to his own little home town, one-sheet paper, and
there he reads all the home news. ·How Miss So-and-So spent the
night with Miss This and That and had a most enjoyable visit; and
John, who came home fr.om the war with medals .on his breas.t,
was received by the village band and escorted up main street to his
home, where his aged parents were waiting to receive him, etc., etc.
· As we said, it is the same with our Annual Communication.
We want to know what this Lodge is doing, and that one, and we
want to meet all our old friends, and slap backs and clasp hands,
glad indeed to meet those from whom perhaps we have not heard
from in a whole year.

As a rule the neophyte, after ·havin~ been, as a rule, given the
degrees, with greater or less care, as time permits, is left to shift
for himself. After the first glamour has worn off, he finds little to
attract his attention and gradually he ceases to attend. For him
the Lodge becomes simply a place in which candidates are nightly
passed through certain ceremonies and that is all. We know of
many fair-sized Lodges of 150 to 200 members, where the attendance is certainly on an average not over ten per cent. Does not
this point the moral, if not adorn the tale?
Mississippi:
Before entering upon his address proper the Grand Master
proceeds to lecture the delegates to the Grand Lodge relative to
their duty. He states that while subordinate Lodges pay the expenses of their representatives to the Grand Lodge sessions, often
they fail entirely to get any benefit themselves, and, of course, fail
to carry any information back home to the brethren, who are thus
taxed without any returns.
My Brother, this applies to Mississippi also. Many delegates
are sent to the Grand Lo'dge who spend' very little time in the
lodge room; and who, as soon as they arrive, begin to figure on
getting a leave of absence to return home. They are always careful, however, to arrange matters so they can draw their mileage
an.i per diem.
New Mexico:
Under this head the Grand Ma.ster wisely says:
.
"In general, I find our Lodges in good, healthy condition. My
observation in conjunction with the reports of the District Deputy
Grand Masters is that the attendance is not what it should be. I
do not mean . to imply that non-attendants are not good Masons;
nevertheless, I am convinced that this is partly due to our officers,
who, for various reasons, do not make the meetings attractive
enough, disregard the importance of punctuality in meeting, and
do not exemplify our work properly. There seems to prevail only
the desire to get through with the meeting in record-breaking time,
and this, coupled with a vei:y scant knowledge of our laws, is not
conducive to bring about a good attendance."

New York:
I have no desire to criticize in the least degree the work of the
past, but I do say that our Masonic Fraternity has been far too
much occupied with what we call "making Masons." How often
do we hear our Lodges spoken of as "degree mills" and their work
as "grinding out degrees!" Is there not altogether too much of
truth· in this reproach? Two statements have been so commonly
made in Masonic circles that I know you must all have heard
them, namely, that there are as many unaffiliated Masons in this
state as there are in good standing, and that the average Masonic
life of our brothers is about seven years. Whether these statements
are altogether correct is immaterial. Certainly there are numbers
of men everywhere who, having received their degrees and attended
a few communications, appear to lose all interest in our work and
practically drop out of sight. What is the cause of this condition?
Are these brethren disappointed in what they have received? Have
they come to the conclusion that if Freemasonry consists only in
working over and over the same degrees there is nothing in it for
them? Did they join solely out of curiosity, expecting something
entirely different from what they received? Is there too much
repetition of ritual? l confess that I do not know! But whatever
the reason, the facts remain that many drop out and that the
average Masonic life in this state is far too short. Do not these
facts force us to the conclusion that we are not interesting and
holding our members as we should? What is the remedy? Of
that I shall speak later. But I do not see how the Fraternity can
continue to thrive unless. it faces squarely this condition and makes
whatever effort is necessary to overcome it.
South Carolina:
Brother Edward P. Hufferd, Grand Orator, Connecticut, delivered a brief address on the "Universality of Masonry," asking
the question and not satisfactorily answering it, "If Masonry is so
universal, why are lodge meetings so poorly attended?" One great
reason, we believe, is because the officers of lodges do not familiarize themselves with the ritual, so are unable to confer the degrees
in an interesting and intelligent manner.
Texas:
I had the pleasure of being present on this occasion and assisted in conferring the degree upon this candidate, which was done
at the conclusion of a meeting unique in its character, in that the
Lodge was opened in the Master Mason's degree, in the Masonic
Temple, at 2 o'clock a. m., and remained in continuous session
throughout the day, the officers serving in relays, and conferring
more than thirty degrees during the session. There were in attendance teams from several of the neighboring Lodges, who
served alterna~ely in conferring the degrees, and in each instance
these Brethren acquitted themselves with credit and distinction.
Virginia:
I wish there was a law in Masonry whereby a Brother might
be cited to appear and show cause why he should not be suspended
for non-attendance at the stated communications of his Lodge.
So many men apply, are made Masons and pay their annual dues
from year to year and never show their faces inside the Lodge

room, and expect to reap all the benefits of Freemasonry. After

West Australia:
Why not see that every candidate, when taking his third degree, purchases, or is presented with, a Volume of the Local Proceedings? Where the proceedings of other Lodges are reviewed
the information from a Masonic point of view is invaluable-especially is this so in the volume we have before us, and we know of
no other better medium to whet one's appetite for more.
It is freely acknowledged that many a worthy Mason becomes
an inactive member of the Craft through having to witness ceremonies only year in and year out. The Masters have the remedy
in their own hands, and can make the gatherings informative and
instructional by using the digests in the proceedings for the education of Lodge .members. Those who wish to dip deeper will find
the libraries open whenever they desire.

Texas: A remarlcable feature of his (Grand Master). address
is that he does not report having made any decisions.
From this it would appear that the Grand Master of Masons in
California does not report all the silly questions which he is asked
to answer and calls his answers "decisions."
For instance, if he is asked if a blind man, or a man with both
legs cut off, is suitable material for the degrees of Masonry, he
does not call it a "decision." Pity that some other Grand Masters
do not follow his example.

Masonic Service Association, and many other subjects are discussed
by him, .with. liberal quotations from the Proceedings of the various
Grand Lodges.
His report is both interesting and instructive. .

CATHOLICISM
As stated in our previous reports, we believe that Masonry, as
an organization, has no quarrel with the Roman Catholic Church, as
a religion. Any movement'founded on intolerance cannot succeed.
Unfortunately, the radicals on both sides are considered by the

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

general public as spokesmen for the respective organizations and
attract more attention than they properly should. If we will devote
our activities to doing good because it is right, and pay less attention to what the opposition is doing, we have nothing to fear.
Actions speak plainer than words.

are fighting for nourishment. The propaganda of sending money abroad
'may be judge<l ·by observing who gains in the settling of war.

Alabama:
No Mason with a correct understanding of Masonry could think
of warring against the Catholic' Church as a religion. Masonry fights
only Catholicism's presumptous claim to tempora land political power
and in resistance of the unprovoked war it has been making for near
two hundred years upon Masonry.
District of Columbia:
There is reference in the proceedings to fight with the Roman
Hierarchy. We have from the first been on the defensive. We have
Roman Masons among us, and good ones at that, who never hear in
the Lodges an intolerant word. But turn to the Cannon Law of the
Church of Rome and you will find all politics-the power of the Holy
See to depose kings, princes and potentates, to take from them their
municipalities and distribute them according to his sweet will among
his faithful; to absolve men from their oaths as well as deprive them
of their possessions. The cannons are not on lines of religion, superstition nor sorcery, but political domination.
Turn to the books of that famous author, Bishop Ligouri, Catholic
Cyclopedia, Vol. I, and you will find that he makes every priest greater
than the Blessed Virgin, because she raised Christ but once, while any
priest ·can raise Him when he chooses. These are the outrageous and
blasphemous edicts the French Masons would not subscribe to, and
is probably why the holy fathers dubbed them atheists, which so many
gullible American Masons sided in with.

We have not, however, seen anything in the last year, to diminish
our fear of Romanism. To replenish an army there must be one-half

ban and the native-born requirements have been abolished in our army.
The Hungarian, Polish, Irish, Austrian and Portuguese immigrants
are accepted on landing, enlisted and encamped, where they are taught
English at government expense. How long will it take to Romanize
the army? Every last one of these Roman recruits owe first allegiance
to a foreign Prince.

Mississippi:
Brother Darling (Vermont) seems violently opposed to the Masonic
Service Association. He deplores the controversy between Masonry
and the Roman Catholic Church, and while he disclaims holding any
brief for the church, yet his argument seems to be in justifications of the
attitude of the church rather than of Masonry. In the opinion of this
humble scribe, Mnsonry would never have resented any attack, made
by the church or any other organization, on the institution per se; but
the insiduous advances, looking to entrenchment in governmental
affairs, and the persistent and growing efforts to annihilate our Public
School system, are direct attacks upon the basic principles of Freemasonry. The Institution of Freemasonry has always stood by the
Constitution of our country, and for the integity of her Institutions;
and that power or influence that would attempt to lay violent hands
on these, should receive the condemnation of Masons. Freemasonry
stands for intelligence and enlightenment; and any encroachment upon
our Public School system, by a power that loves darkness rather than
light, and whose material and financial interest is advanced by keeping
its votaries in darkness, must encounter opposition of our great
Fraternity.
Most Worshipful Brother Oliver Lee McKay presented the following Resolutions which were, on motion, unanimously adopted:
Whereas, The Knights of Columbus has recently submitted to the
American Legion a proposition to make use of the sum of six million
dollars of the war chest fund allotted to that organization for the
building of a memorial auditorium to be known as the "Knights of
Columbus Hall," under the auspices of the American Legion; and
Whereas, The war chest fund was created by the American Government, during the stress of war with foreign nations and at a time
when three millions of our boys were in France and Belgium, and was
contributed largely by those who were not members of, or affiliated
by rela:tionship or otherwise, with the membership of the Knights of
Columbus; and

18

Whereas, The war chest fund was created for the relief of our
boys serving in the American Army at home ancl abroad and not for
the purpose of building auditoriums for the glorification of any Fraternal, Religious or Political organization; and
·
Whereas, The American Legion has declined to accept the money
tendered, for purposes above set forth, unless all restrictions as to its
disposition were withdrawn; therefore,
Be It Resolved: That the Grand Lodge of Masons of Mississippi
in annual Communication assembled, heartily applauds and endorses
the action of the American Legion ,and puts itself on record as strenuously objecting to the disposition of any part of the war chest fund,
no matter in whose custody it may be, except in carrying out the purposes for which it was created, namely, the industrial and vocational
education of our disabled soldiers, who offered their lives upon the
altar of sacrifice, and the children and dependents of such.

Vermont:
We carry no brief for the Roman Catholic Church, but any movement on the part of Masons or any association among Masons which
seeks to get into any controversy with that church is an injury to
Masonry and outside the purposes of the Order. There is probably
something in the confessional of the church and some of the so-called
secrets of Masonry which render it best that ·a good Roman Catholic
should not become a member of the Masonic Fraternity, either from
the standpoint of the church or of Masonry, and there the matter
should drop. Masonry is not seeking to make recruits from the Roman
Catholic Church, and the Roman Catholic Church does not want ·its
members to be Masons. While Masonry does not solicit members on
the one hand, on the other the spirit of Masonry is deeply religious and
we have no quarrel with the religion of others ; neither are we to forget
that the Protestant and the Roman Catholic Churches sprang from a
common origin and are both Christian institutions. There is altogether
too much groundless emotion on this question.
Virginia:
We think the Grand Master was needlessly uneasy on account of
Romanism. True, as individuals we are all aware of the priestly
antagonism to our organization, but some of us do not fear it in the
least, for either America or Freemasonry. The Menace did and the
New Age is now doing us harm, for controversy is just what the priests
want. For hundreds of years Rome has been making the very same
fight against human liberty and human enlightenment, and yet their
power is less today than ever before. Even their extensive advertising
through the very creditable work of the Knights of Columbus in the
war does not seem to have deterred young men from seeking our

Instead of a Foreign Correspondence (Vermont) report, but called

because it has nothing to do with us or we with it. For ages the fulminations of the Popes and Cardinals against our Institution have in

us give it to them.
Under all the enthusiasm poured out in that movement, we plainly
read between the lines a hysterical desire to compete for general favor
with the Knights of Columbus. We do not envy them the credit they so
richly earned by good works in France, and for the reason that their
activities were out of place and too evidently for public applause, as
ours would equally have been. That sort of mission is a duty of the
Red Cross and to a lesser degree of the Salvation Army and Y. M. C. A.
Masonry's mission in the world is of a totally . different character.
Even were this not true, the desire to spend vast sums for a junket
after the fighting and hardships were things of the past, was childish
desire for notoriety which should be beneath our dignity, and of no
possible use.
Under the head of "The George Washington National Memorial

"The organization of this Association, however, has aroused considerable opposition in anti-Masonic quarters. Open expression of this

"Present conditions tend to make it soon incumbent on Catholic

To use the French idiom, "It is to laugh." For more than a ·

his letters did say that he had nothing to do with and had not been
present in any of the English Lodges for years. At this time the
English Lodges in America were under the ban, they being Tory and
disloyal in membership. The Grand Lodge of Virginia, of which he was
a member, refused to recognize any but the "Ancient York" Masonry,

Their ritualistic proficiency is very nearly perfect, and they are at home
in all of the several stations. They may, perhaps, work with such speed
that they do not give proper expression or interpretation to the ritual
but they are regular "bears" for work and .many Masters have cause to
bless them for aid when badly needed. These men are called "rounders."
They will work uncomplainingly for the long a~ternoon with no reward
in sight other than a Lodge supper and a cigar or two. They are
emphati~ally not the "knife and fork brigade," meaning members who
. arrive just in time for the supper but who are too busy to s~ay for the
evening work. These men are really .good Masons, as their work or
business is such that they are free during the day or who are not compelled to labor daily, and most of them are memb~rs w~o have an
abiding love for Masonic work. Nearly every Master m Chicago knows
these "rounders." They are a bunch ?f good fellows, b~t it is. do1;1btful
if they receive credit commensurate with the value of their service m the
cause of Masonry.

New Hampshire:
This is the thirteenth successive report which I have been permitted to perpetrate. The number is by no means looked upon by me
as being an unlucky one. Rather than that, I deem it a piece of good ·
luck. To be sure, it has meant that much of labor has been involved.
But what of that? It means, most of all, that I have been the one man
in all New Hampshire who has been permitted to absorb from its very
source, the great things of our. world-wide fraternity. It means that
I have been kept in a splendid Masonic atmosphere all the time. It
means that I have been in personal touch with marked Masonic
devotees, the world around. It means that I have had the opportunity,
as a contributor, to add my mite to the whole, no matter how great my
failure. What better luck than that could one expect? The law of
compensation surely bobs up and rewards every correspondent. Fortune
came my way when the official hand drafted me for this service. ·

DECISIONS
There is no doubt but what the time of the Grand Master is
with answering a lot of fool questions that could
easily be solved by reference to the written law. It is easier of
course to ask for an opinion than to solve the question yourself.
You also have a "come back" on your advisor. The Grand Lodge
is largely responsible for this, as the policy is to legislate for every
possible question that has or may arise. This condition exists not
only in Masonic government, but also in our National, State and
local affairs. We could with great advantage follow the English
method and allow the Lodges to govern themselves more, and let
the Grand Lodge concern itself only with matters of general policy.

Illinois:
One of the most hopeful signs of .the times as indicated by the
proceedings of the various Grand Lodges is a disposition to stabilize existing laws . During the year there have been very few decisions on the part of the Grand Masters, and such as have been
presented have in · a large measure related to the interpretation of
local laws, and, so far as the writer has been able to discern, no
· startling nor alarming decisions have been made by any Grand
Master, nor has there been any disposition on the part of anyone
to deviate from the established rules and conditions of the Society.
One of the greatest needs in the Masonic world today is less tinkering with existing rules and regulations. While the amendment
habit has been by no means conquered, yet there is a very strong
disposition on the part of all Grand Lqdges to correct their books
of statutes as far as possible and then to let them alone. It is predicted that the time is not far distant when a decision of a Grand
Master will be a very rare thing, because the laws, the rules and
regulations of the society will become so well understood that
there will be no necessity for any Grand Lodge official putting an
interpretation upon them, other than that which is implied in the
law itself.

DEGREE WORK
One of the most important questions before · the Fraternity
today is the vast amount of degree work that is being done. Lodges
have practically ceased to perform any other function. Various
remedies have been suggested, but no Grand Lodge has yet been
able to lay down a rule that offers a solution of this troublesome
question.
Well p~id Secretaries, large stipendiary lists and expensive
Temples have been · some of the contributing causes to the desire
and necessity of Lodges having a large membership. We believe
that if a membership limit was fixed beyond which a Lodge could
not go, and they be allowed to confer degrees only on a certain
fixed number thereafter during a year, it would aid in solving the
question. It would tend to the formation of new Lodges. Less
commercialism and more education should be the policy.

Idaho:
We believe it is the deliberate judgment of this Grand Lodge
that the time limit between the reception of the petition and the
ballot should never be set aside. We are strongly of the conviction that the desire to hurry men through the degrees of Masonry
is born of a misguided ambition. When a man applies for the degrees of Masonry, is elected, initiated, passed and raised, this
period should be made one of the impressive times of his life and
any short cut that detracts from the occasion is unfortunate.' All
such practices as shortening the time, and curtailing the degree
work, have a tendency to commercialize the institution,' and cheapen
it in the estimation of the candidate.

growth of Masonry. - Our doors are throngeq by thousands of candidates seeking admission. From Maine to California, from Minnesota to Texas, conditions are the same. Lodges have become

Lodge dues is another matter which claimed his attention.

Canada:
I have been called on to rule that an organization called "The
Eastern Star," whose membership is composed of women, the
relatives of Masons, and whkh have also attached to each of their
lodges a few Masons as patrons, is clandestine. I decline to rule,
as I know nothing about the Order, and have been assured by
some of the male patrons that the Order does not claim to be
Masonic. However, in the proceedings of the Board of General
Purposes of the Grand Lodge of England I find the following:
"The Board's attention is being increasingly drawn to sedulous
endeavors which are being made by certain bodies unrecognized as
Masons by the United Grand Lodge of England, to induce Freemasons to join their assemblies. As all such bodies which admit
women to membership are clandestine and irregular, it is necessary
to caution Brethren against being inadvertently led to violate their
obligations by becoming members of them or attending their meetings. Grand Lodge, nine years since, approved the action of the
Board in suspending from all Masonic ri~hts and privileges two
Brethren who had contumaciously failed to explain the grave Masonic irregularity to which attention is now again called, and it is
earnestly hoped that no occasion will arise for having again to
institllte disciplinary prnceedings of a like kind."

Massachusetts:
I am told that wives often view our Order with distrust,' because
there are secrets belonging to it that their husbands do not permit
them to know. I have found little serious conjugal trouble on this
account, but if there are any here who have; let me read the oldfashioned words of a historian. Perhaps he belonged to this
Lodge; I don't know. He is an old-fashioned writer, and he uses
old-fashioned language. He says:
"The good Mason in his family is high without severity; condescending, without meanness. His commands are gentle; indeed
his wishes are commands, for all are equally ready to make him
happy. To his wife, he is a tender husband, not a usurping lord.
To his children, he is a kind and providential father, not a domineering tyrant. To his servants, he is both friend and employer.
His home, whether a cottage or a palace, is, while he is present,
the habitation of peace. When there, he leaves it with reluctance.
When absent, his return is expected with great avidity."
That sounds pretty good. If all t h is were generally k nown and
believed, and if we Masons lived up to it, the first question a young
lady would a sk a young man proposing marriage would be, ''Are
you a Mason? If so-yes."

EDUCATION-MASONIC
From the replies to the Questionnaires sent the various Grand
Secretaries, as well as from the proceedings themselves, it appears
that there is a demand for "more light." We do not think that the
Masonic Lodge is perfonnlng all of its functions unless it includes
in its work enlightenment on our origin, history and traditions.
Under this head we would also include education on the great
questions of the day which are vital to our Country. This does not
mean that a Lodge should assume a definite position or resolve for

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

37

or against any course of action as regards particular questions. If
in our daily life, in our ante-rooms and at our Clubs we can discuss
these matters without strife, it certainly seems that we should be
able to do so when within a tiled Lodge.
Alberta:
When a Brother becomes a Master Mason our duty towards
him has just begun. He should be taught what Freemasonry really
is and what are its qims. Most Initiates are hungry for such teaching. Our Lodge officers, chosen from all walks of life, have seldom
the time to study ways and means other than by "Work" to teach
the fundamental principles of the Craft and supplement the ritual.
One of the functions of our Lodges of instruction should be to
provide the necessary information a·nd suggest methods. We must
apply methods which will be interpretative to the "Work" and
of our history, our organization and form of government. We
must translate in mo'tlern terms that work brought down to us
through the centuries so that its usefulness may be the better revealed. To accomplish this requires that men charged with this
promulgation should be trained and educated Masons, schooled
in the lore and customs of the Craft and possessing a vision of the
world's problems. They must be able to so visualize Masonic
principles that the Brethren may learn Freemasonry's solutions of
these problems.
District of Columbia:
The Grand Lodge of Washington has a committee on Masonic
research and education, which recommended a standing committee
whose duties shall be as follows:
1. The committee shall, on request, furnish speakers on Masonic and kindred subjects of Lodges, and for community meetings

2. The committee shall cause to be published, or printed, and
circulated such addresses as are delivered under the direction of
said committee as may be determined upon.
3. The committee shall provide for a circulating 1ibrary of Masonic literature, and shall specify rules governing the same.
4. The committee shall invite and conduct correspondence with
Lodges, or members thereof, . concerning Masonic subjects.
In other words, it is an effort to make the Lodges attractive,
and if it succeeds there will be a diminution of members in the
Grotto, the Clubs, the Shrine, and maybe the Chapters.

The study side of Freemasonry, put into effect in Iowa seven
or eight years ago, has spread to California, Indiana, Maryland,
New Jersey, North Dakota, Texas and Utah.
The Iowa plan embraces a standing Committee on Masonic
Research, the special function of which is to promote the study
side of Masonry. At the last communication of the Grand Lodge,
Iowa provided for a bureau of Masonic speakers and lecturers as
a part of the plan. By means of the large library of the Grand
Lodge at Cedar Rapids and the twenty circulating libraries, Iowa
has begun a remarkable work, and in their views of physical qualifications and intellectual Masonry. Iowa Masons have taken a
great step forward toward a great future for Masonry;
California has a Committee on Masonic Education which provides speakers for such Lodges as desire to hear-and the demand
is greater than can be filled-with the result that the attendance
is increased materially and a better interest manifested throughout
the Jurisdiction. "We find," says Grand Secretary John Whicher,
" that our Brethren are fed up on the ritual and that they want to
know something, not only of Masonry, but want information on
all current topics of the day."
Indiana Masons have a standin,g Committee on the Study Side
of Masonry, which, from time to time, sends out to the subordinate
Lodges selected printed matter, which, in the judgment of the
committee, will be of interest to the Craft. These a.r ticles are read
at special meetings of the Lodges, and after the reading an informal
discussion held, which usually results in two or three subjects being
assigned to certain members of the Lodge to be reported upon at
a future meeting. The results of the meeting are reported back to
the general committee and filed for future guidance. The plan, on
the whole, Is reported t o have been very satisfactory.
New Jersey, while holding in abeyance the plan of a Grand
L odge library, has devised methods for having published, in leaflet
form, from time to time, Masonic history of special interest, literature explaining the symbolic meaning of the degrees, and extracts
from lectures on Masonic subjects. These are to be forwarded to
the Worshipful Masters of th e Lodges with th e request that they
have copies printed and sent out with their regular no.t ices to
members.

South Dakota:
To the writer it appears that in the present juncture of world
affairs it is important that we take knowledge of the facts of human
nature, and without sacrificing anything of the high purposes and
aspirations of Masonry, seek for ways and means of accommodating tbe Masonic institution to the life and experience of the average man. We will fin d him interested, and perforce, deeply so, in
his present day problem. He is surrounded on every hand by glaring evidence that men get on in the world paying no heed to the
square, the level o r the plumb. The appeal of Masonry that will
offset the Impressions upon the mind of the young man observing
th ese things, lies not in the facts of its history, or in its symbolism,
alone, but in the human touch of heart to heart brotherhood. After
all said and done it is important first to "know th yself," and
next that the "proper study of mankind is man."

GRAND OFFICERS
Our Grand Master stated, after traveling through his Jurisdiction, that he found fifty percent of the Fraternity did not know
who the Grand Master was, and the other fifty percent didn' seem
to care very much. Custom has limited, except in certain States, the
term of office of the Grand Master to one year, but there is no
gainsaying the fact that the Jurisdictions which continue the Grand
Master in office for at least two years have produced men who have

Maryland: ·
"I want to state now, at the very beginning of my term, that I feel

Wisconsin:
One of the first things a Grand Master, on being elected to. office
thinks he must do, is to revolutionize the aims, and ourposes of the
Craft in order that Masonry may be "doing something." No one would
contend that the church does not do anything. It is not building navies,
equipping armies, manning ships, boring tunnels or conducting vast
enterprises, but its teachings reach every city, every hamlet, every
home, and nearly every human being in civilization, and have transformed mankind from savages to civilized human beings, practicing
charity and revering God. The work of Masonry is of the same general
nature. It does not undertake to perform every good work · that any
enthusiast may suggest in order that something may be done. Its aim
is to hold · before humanity high ideals and by constant teaching of
them to make mankind better, wiser and consequently happier. These
are the things that are rea!ly worth while.
"THE GROTTO"
"The Grotto" still seems to be in disfavor in certain States.
There is a growing tendency to legislate against organizations
having membership in the Masonic Fraternity as a basis for eligibility to join. "The Grotto," being one of the newest arrivals in
the fraternal world, is naturally the first to come under the ban.

Illinois:
From different points in the state complaints have come to me
regarding outside organizations drawing their members exclusively from
the Masonic Fraternity. By connecting the word "Mason" or "Masonic"
with their activities impression was left upon the public that these
organizations were part' of the Masonic institution. In advertising
public demonstrations so much of the circus and cheap show variety was
given as to bring ridicule and reproach upon Masonry. Having their
stunts and shows in Masonic temples cast odium upon the Craft. It
became necessary to call attention to Masons to this condition. Consequently under date of November 8, 1919, I sent a letter to each Lodge
and ordered it to be read at three separate stated meetings. At the same
time I took this up with Jesse K. Seeright at Pittsburgh, Pa., Grand
Monarch of the Grotto of the United States. Very promptly he replied .
deploring the cause of complaint. He says ''I know from the tone of
your letter that you had ample cause to send out the letter." Following
this on December 30, Grand Monarch Seeright issueq an edict to all
Grottoes forbidding the actions a.pout which complaint was m<;1de. I
especially appreciate the prompt action and proper spirit shown by the
Grand Monarch and am convinced that local organizations were ignorant of what they did.

I~

I believe this great numerical increase in our Fraternity comes at
a most opportune time, because now, during these strenous days of
unrest, disquietude and dangerous agitation, more than ever before,
is the world in need of every moral and intell~ctual force that tends

devotees in this country alone, constitutes one of the gravest of the
moral and intellectual forces in the United States, and by persistent
and united effort can wield a mighty influence in the interests of good
citizenship and of good government.
It has within itself an unlimited power for the betterment of many
existing conditions and the key to its possibilities is education and
enlightenment. Let us teach and spread broadcast the great moral
precepts of our institution; let us stand as a unit for our free public
school system and guard and p.rotect it against every assailant; let
us teach that service and sacrifice are two of the most commendable
characteristics in the universe; let us practice and teach loyalty,
devotion and patriotism to our flag and our country; and above all let
us emphasize our faith and belief in the Fatherhood of God and the
Brotherhood of Man.
Illinois:
One of the principle subjects which has engaged the attention of
nearly every Grand Master as judged from the Proceedings reviewed
relates to the tremendous increase in membership which the Craft has
enjoyed during the past two or three years. Many Grand Masters
have speculated upon this wonderful addition to the membership of our
Lodges but no ove seems to have been able to ascertain the direct
cause as to why so many men, both young and old, have sought the
privileges of the Fraternity. Among the reasons assigned are the
influence of the war, the fact that a large number of men are beginning
to realize that Freemasonry is really worth while and the general law of
the survival of the fittest. As to whether or not this increase is to be
permanent no one seems to be able to arrive at a definite opinion. It
is believed, however, that while the crest of the great wave has been
reached, yet it wi11 be several years before Freemasonry will drop back
to the ordinary methods of pro'cedure, particularly in this respect.

Georgia:
The great increase has swept through Lodge room doors without

·
With the exception of several optimistic Grand Masters, the flood
of applications is viewed with much alarm. The comparative value of
t}uantity and quality is being weighed in the balance and for the greater
part it is being discovered that Masons are b!!tter than members; that
men need Masonry more than Masonry needs men. The Fraternity is
struggling to forget the disregard of principles during the war and settle
again upon the foundation of our fathers. We raised no protest when
applicants, called to arms, suddenly found a desire to become Masons
and were railroaded through, but even though· we may be branded as
guilty of treason by our own Brethren, we are of the emphatic opinion
that it is better to put a little sand on the rapid-transit tracks and slow
up a bit.
Students and leaders of Masonic thought are considering as never
before that Masonry is more than a phonographic recital of ritualismthat the Blue Lodge is not just a stepping stone for the so-called higher
bodies and the Shrine.

to the Mason, those associations which unite himlielf and his fellows

all but an exceedingly small percentage of its meml>ers. The Lodge
grows unwieldly; its members indifferent. Hence proposals that such
Lodges should be broken up, and that a limit of membership should

Nebraska:
We have had a wonderful growth during the past Masonic year.
Four thousand three hundred candidates were raised to the sublime
degree of a Master Mason. How many Master Masons have been made,
no one knows. The amount of work which has been done by some
Lodges has been really appalling, and has left little time for the social
and deductional side of Masonry. The ritualistic side has predominated
and much remains to be done in our Lodges, not merely repeating to
our candidates our beautiful lessons, but to impress our members, new
and old, that Masonry is an actual living vital force which if properly
applied will do much toward solving many of the trying problems of
the day. In that way its real aims and purposes can be accomplished
and Masonry maintain the exalted position it has ever held and will
·always hold.
I am not pessimistic over the outlook. The material we have
wekomed to our arms is the flower of the land, and they come to us
for light and if we but give it to them, the future of Masonry and
America is in safe ha11es. We have taken the responsibility and it rests
upon you and me to see that every candidate raised becomes a credit
to Masonry and a real brother to each of us and to humanity.
New Mexico:

political prospects. But whatever the cause, it forebodes danger. ·
Are we drifting towards the Rocks of Danger? Time only can tell.

HIGHER DEGREES
At present there is a tendency to legislate against the
"Higher Degrees." There is no question but members are rushed
from the Blue Lodge into the other branches without giving them
opportunity to become acquainted with the teachings of the first
three degrees. While a time limit could be set, as has been done in
several States, still the question arises, "What, at the present time
is the Blue Lodge doing for a new member after he has b.e en
'raised' to maintain his enthusiasm and interest."
Unfortunately the witnessing of the conferring of degrees is
about all that he gets. When the Lodge ceases to be a degree mill,
and gives its members the advantages they now secure by belonging
to the "Higher Bodies," just so soon will the Blue Lodge perform its
proper function and -the existing condition of affairs be remedied.
British Columbia:
With the modesty for which the "higher bodies" are noted, the
Grand Master of Knights Templar of Wyoming requested the Grand
Master to prevent the Annual Communication of Grand Lodge from
clashing with the Triennial Conclave of Knights Templar to be held
in Philadelphia. The Grand Master realized that he had no authority
to postpone "or to attempt to change" the time of meeting of Grand
Lodge, but suggested that if no one turned up at the proper time, he
could call an "adjourned meeting" of Grand Lodge. Being of an

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

present time is to be deplored, as it does in a very great sense destroy
the favorable impression created in the minds of candidates who enter
our brotherh0od. Masonry should steer clear of commercialism. There
is or ought to be a marked distinction between members and money,
between monuments in the hearts of men and monuments of stone.
Any man who seeks the mysteries of Ancient Craft Masonry
through curiosity, for personal advantage or gain, with fun or frivolous
things of any kind the goal of his ambition, should be rejected. There
are those who sign a petition with some of these things in view, but
are rescued from this unworthy thought somewhere along the line of
travel, and they that so start and are not so rescued will never be
benefitted thereby and will be a positive injury to the Craft.
We require a man to ponder over and study each degree for at
least twenty-eight days before be can be advanced; however, it frequently happens that before he has received the first three degrees,
sometimes, before or soon after he has presented his petition, he is
solicited for what by some is termed the "higher degrees" and possibly within a few days afte he has received the degree of Master
Mason he has had -conferred upon him many additional degrees, and
then on to the feast of fun so much enjoyed while traveling over the
hot sands of the desert. Of course the~e things are not our business,
strictly speaking; however, in justice to the mother organization such
practices should not be permitted by organizations basing their membership on members of the Ancient Craft. .
·
. It is especially to be remembered, my Brethren, that there is rio
place in Masonry for anything frivolous. Beginning with the conversation between the candidate and the Brethren whom he requests to
sign his petition,-on the street, in the parlor or ante-room, anywhere
you meet him, especially in the preparation room where he first gets a
glimpse or suggestion of the future, the greeting should ever be cordial,
dignified and earnest. Nothing frivolous should be indulged. He then
approaches the threshold of Masonry in the . proper spirit and in the
right kind of environment. When he knocks on the door for admis.sion he is all expectant, he is serious as he should be. Thep when he
declares that he puts his trust in that God whom we as Masons rever- ·
ence and serve, he is prepared to travel to the East in due time, to be
raised to the sublime degree of a Master Mason, and to fully embra:e
the belief in the immortality of the soul.
Let every man, after arriving at the years of mature judgment,
without suggestion or environment directmg his mind, of his own
free will and accord, petition for the degrees. Exercise Masonic
unselfishness, care and prudence in accepting his petition, and then
confer the degrees upon him in that dignified, impressive way that
appeals to his intelligence, to his manly ideas and to his very soul.
Impress upon him in the degree of. Entered Apprentice the teachings,
the beauties and the service expected of a Mason,-in the degree of
Fellow Craft, impress upon him the lessons that open up a study of
the world and all things therein contained and make him feel at
the end of this degree that he is in a holy place. And in the Third
Degree fully impress upon him that honorable conduct, courageous
action, unwavering virtue, tried and true, are essentials to a pass-port
to the realms of eternal life. Let all the work be done with that distinct
deliberation, that the candidate of average intelligence gets every word
and every lesson intended. Thus we make better men and better
Masons.

New Mexico:
When it becomes necessary for a Grand Master to say, "Unless
over•zealous and fanatical members of so-called higher bodies can be
curbed, it may become necessary to invoke disciplinarian measures to
safeguard the Ancient Craft," we must admit that we have a problem
that calls for solution. However, we are inclined to the opinion that
while the "higher bodies" may be barred from the Lodge room, the
best way to cope with the situation will be to make the first three
degrees so attractive that the higher degrees will look less alluring.
It is true, however, that many join the Blue Lodge simply because they
want to be Shriners and their first impression has been made by attending the "circus" which the Shriners put on at the time of their initiation.
Let us forbid solicitation until after we have seasoned material in the
first three degrees, but at the same time let us give more attention to
the beauties of the first three degrees and solicitation will become less
popular and effective.
North Carolina:
Coming back to our own Order, we find that Masons are not
satisfied with the divme truths inculcated in the symbolic de15rees; but
they wish to wear the purple of the so-called "higher bodies." The
Arabic Fez, coupled with the foolish stree~ parade, brings more joy to
the modern Mason than all the beauties of the third obligation; and
the resurrection of the body pales into insignificance when compared
to the alcoho!ic elevation of the soul. And although we are taught that
it is decidedly unmasonic to solicit candidates, yet we find a large
number of those "elevated" gentry going about the State with petitions
in their pockets, openly and notoriously begging men to join; and I
have no hesitancy in asserting that ninety per cent of the Knights
Templars, Shriners and 32d degree Sc.Qttish Rite Masons are unable
to repeat the obligation of the Master's Degree as it is taught by the
Grand Lecturers, I know that this statement will be challenged; but I
stand ready for the test.
I have taken all of these degrees. I have worn a Fez and witnessed
pranks that made me ashamed of the Order. I have worn the uniform
of a Knight Templar and sat in the Consistory of the Thirty-second
Degree. I am not here to condemn these orders or to claim that there
is no virtue in them. They are all good in their way; but I do claim
that Masons should learn their letters before they attempt to read, and
that nobility of character should be measured, not by the number of
degrees you have taken; but by the manner in which you e"emplify
those degrees to the world at large. No man enjoys more than I do
tne motion picture show and the stage; but for the unadulterated
principles of the Craft, give me the old fashioned Mason, who has
heard of these things, but never sought them, who believes in the
fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man as the mud sill of
Masonry; who extends the hand of true friendship, unadorned by the
gauntlet of the Templar ; who . bows his head in the presence of his
Maker, free from Fez or other ornament; and who does not believe
that a uniform will gain him a pass-port into the gates of the Great
Beyond. We are getting away from the ancient fandmarks; and it
may be well for us to remember that Masonry, after all, is now and

Virginia:
We have long held that Masonry would gain limitlessly if all the
bodies except Lodges and Royal Arch Chapters could be abolished. But
how? There is a harmful sore spot in the breast of many a noble
Mason because of this aristocracy in what should be a perfect Brotherhood. We see evidences oi it every day in those who cannot, in
justice to their loved ones, afford these expensive side Degrees, and
now and then in a few who could stand the expense but fear that they
would not be considered congenial.
It seems to be an evil without a remedy.
Of course that Shrine temptation is the chief cause of the trouble
alluded to, and of another more serious still. There are men who join
us simply for Shrine membership. This is a hard accusation, but
there is truth in it. Personally we wish the Shrine would throw open
its doors also to Knights of Pythias and Odd Fellows. It would work
to our advantage.

As we have often said in these reviews, let's keep our Masonry,
Masonry. Brother Street this time made a long report on A, A. S. R.
bodies recognized by the Southern Jurisdiction of the United States.
What Alabama Masonry has to do wit it is a puzzle. The Rite is a
separate and distinct organization, based on Masonry, but in no real
sense a part of it. Its degrees are side degrees, beautiful in parts and
containing much of scholarship and Eastern lore, whether all authentic
or not we do not know, nor pretend to say. In any case Grand Lodges
are composed of the representatives of thousands who know nothing of
the Rite and those representatives have no right to take offa:ial action
on the subject. Brother Street's personal . position is another matter
and his own business, but it should not prejudice Alabama Masons
against the York Grand Lodge of Mexico as it seems to do. He
reviewed that Grand Lodge although not recognized and does the square
thing, as follows:
* * * * * *
If our Masonry is to become anything else than that Brotherhood
under that Fatherhood, we want none of it anymore. We may as well
speak frankly here as elsewhere, and we regard it as a duty to speak
frankly, because we plainly see either ruin, or else a separation into two
factions just in front of American Masonry. This writer is a member
of the Consistory and wishes it well. Still nothing can absolve us from
our duty and allegiance to our old mother, the York Rite. It is a
pity there are two Rites, we need but one. An egg is full; nothing can
be added to its contents. Equally is it true that nothing can be added
to Symbolic Masonry, nor can it be improved upon, try who will. One
of its chief foundation-stones is the perfect equality of its self-governing
membership, as is by no means true of the Scottish Rite. The latter
is under control of a governing body called the Supreme Council. The
rank and fife have no word in their selection and no knowledge of what
they do. '!'hey are not even informed as to their lavish expenditure of
funds raised from fees. This all powerful oligarchy is as irresponsible

as was the German Empire before Democracy overthrew it. One of
their late moves towards imperialism is their denial that Masonry can
legitimately use the term York Rite. Descent from a center at York
has been claimed since 1738. This claim is too well established for

Washington:
The time has come when, in the judgment of thi5 Committee, some
action should be taken by this Grand Lodge to limit the use of its
degrees as a basis for membership" in other organizations. In the large
centers few if any Master Masons are permitted to stop at that point
and obtain any adequate knowledge of the C,raft, its history, purposes
and regulations, before they are solicited to "advance." Indeed in many
cases they are solicited and their applications are written and signed
for some of the so-called "higher bodies". before they have completed
their Blue Lodge Degrees. Clubs, societies and other organizations
organize "teams" to exemplify the Degrees as representing these other
societies, and are advertised as a star attraction to gather a large
attendance. As a usual thing -these teams are through the minute they
have conferred the second section of the Third Degree, and the candidate sees a dozen hear the lecture where there had formerly been a
hundred.
What can a candidate think of the sincerity of those who preach the
wondrous beauty of the Blue Lodge until he begins to take the degrees
and then hears nothing from them except the wonders which are yet to
come?
Of cQurse, we are to blame because we do not protect these new
J.fasons. Perhaps we do not purposely degrade them or detract from
them, but we do not positively exalt them. If we continue to permit
our degrees to be merely a vehicle to carry the initiate on to the "real
thing," we have no reason · to complain at his lack of appreciation of
them.
Your Committee therefore feels that it is the positive duty of this
Grand Lodge to protect the dignity, solemnity and importance of her
degrees and the obligations upon which they are based; and he
recommends that it be made a Masonic offense in this jurisdiction to
solicit or propose a Master Mason for membership in any organizaticin
for which that standing is a qualification until such person shall have
been a Master Mason for a period not less than one year.
West Virginia:

thorough sympathy and accord with both York Rite and Scottish Rite
Masonry, for each Rite teaches beautiful and sublime lessons, but
fundamentally there are no higher degrees than the three degrees of
Ancient Craft Masonry, and we need to impress upon the Brethren the
n ecessity of not only mastering these degrees, but also having them

Grand Master of the State. When Chancellor Livingston rose tc.
perform the part of the program assigned to him, it was found that
no Bible had been provided. From the Fedenl Hall, on Walt
Street, where the inauguration of the first President of the Republic
took place, to the meeting rooms of St. John's Lodge was only a
few stef s. General Morton went quickly and brought the altar
Bible o the Lodge, with its cushion of crimson velvet. Upon this
Masonic Bible the first President was sworn. After repeating the
oath of office, he bowed reverently and kissed the page of the
sacred Book on which his right hand had rested. There was a
moment of profound silence. Then Chancellor Livingston exclaimed solemnly and with loud voice, "Long live George Washington, President of the United States!" The tension with which
the assembled multitude of people had followed the simple ceremonies of the inauguration was released. A thousand voices joined
in the acclamation as with one voice, "Long live George Wash-·
ington !" The President thereupon proceeded to the Senate Chamber to deliver his first address as Chief Magistrate of the free and
independent Union of States.
The Bible used on this occasion was returned to the Lodge, in
whose possession it has remained to this day. The pages on which
the hand of George Washington had rested and which received
the imprint of his reverent kiss have been skilfully mounted with
transparent silk to preserve them from defacement. The pages
are those of Genesis, Chapter 49.
The Bible bears the publication date of 1767. It was presented
to the Lodge by Jonathan Hampton, on November 28, 1775, the
night on which he was elected an installed as Master. The cover
bears in gold lettering this inscription: "God shall establish. St.
Joh n's Lodge constituted 5757. Burnt down 8th March, 5770; rebuilt and opened November 28, 5770; officers then presiding: Jonathan Hampton. Master; William Butler, Senior Warden; Isaac
Heron, Junior Warden."
On a page inserted after the inauguration of the firs.t President
w e read these beautifully engrossed words:
"On this sacred volume, on the 30th day of April, A. L. 5789,
in the City of New York, was administered to George W ashnigton,
the first President of the United States of America, the oath to
support the Constitution of the United States. This important ceremony was performed by the Most Worshipful Grand Master of
Free and Accepted Masons of the State of New York, the Honorable Robert R. Livingston, Chancellor of the State."
INVESTIGATION OF CANDIDATES
There is too great a laxity in the investigation of candidates,
due to the fact that the committee does or will not properly perform
its duty. In some of the Jurisdictions Lodges have made it a
practice to investigate a petitioner informally by having him appear
before a Committee of Past Masters and Officers of the Lodge.
If he passes their scrutiny satisfactorily, his petition is received and
regularly presented the usual committee appointed and another
investigation made. This is a custom that could well be introduced

Perhaps our greatest obligation at the present time is that of
protecting the Fraternity from the admission of the unworthy, and
especially from those who are unmindful of their duties to God,
their country, and humanity at large; and who cannot or do not
understand· what true citizenship and fraternal fellowship mean.
While the inner door of our tiled Lodges should ever swing wide
open for the reception of the worthy and well-qualified, it should
as readily close tightly against those whose curiosity or ambitions
do not square with those ideals so frequently_. set before us in all
our Masonic teachings.. Let Freemasonry continue to be a benefi·

abiding faith in humanity, and an uncon9ue;a,ble hop~ for t?e fu!ure
· prosperity of the world. And may we mdividually, m lovmg kmdness, press ever onward in the great cause of universal truth and

God, ever remembering that "In His Court of High Chancery, the
rules of right and not of might will be strictly enforced against
those who have taken unjustly, wealth, rank, influence, reputation
or affection." And, "the God of love and peace will delight to dwell
with and bless us."

The Investigating Committee in ·the Lodge is, unquestionably,
the most important committee in the Lodge, but the system of investigating candidates is in most cases entirely too lose. I have
known men to be initiated, passed and raised_ in a Lodge, who, at
the time they filed their applications, were absolutely unknown to
anyone in the Lodge; even proposer and ·seconder had never seen
them. I have known a man to be introduced a petitioner to a
Lodge so that he could sign his application five minutes after. As
long as that looseness in taking in members prevails, some of the
men that we are taking in are going to do us great injury,
N ew Jersey:
Much has been said-by some-of the enemies of Masonry.
Undoubtedly we have many such-organized and individualthough they are showing their inability to do us real harm. The
enemy we should most fear is the enemy in our own ranks, the
man who, by his conduct, brings criticism and obloquy on our
Fraternity; and we must remember ~hat all such-and it is useless
to deny that they exist-have been proposed for membership by
two Masons, investigated by three other Masons, and finally admitted to membership by a clear ballot. It has been said that

.
The mission of Masonry is too sacred a matter in the light of
.
the present day need to longer allow the approaches to its memberships to be obscured or unnecessarily veiled to the applicant. Masonry is too generally judged by the deportment of its members
to longer risk affiliation on the part of any but good men and true.
The seven letters of Masonry are symbols and when translated they form the seven letters of Service. The word Service.
is but a symbol of our duties, obligations and responsibilities, and
when measured by the rule of human relationships they become the
pass-words to the hidden mysteries of a life of perfect happiness.
Not infrequently our committees bring in favorable reports .
based on an investigat\on of the most perfunctory nature and the
candidate is elected on simply hearsay evidence. What an attractive opportunity this system presents to the man with selfish or
ulterior motives. Evidence is at hand to support the contention
that men no higher in type than the Communists of the Russian
International have attempted to enter our ranks and in instances
have probably succeeded and for what purpose? In the name of
Liberty: In the name of all that we hold most sacred: Shall we
be indifferent to this menace?
We are awake to the situation in all its phases here in Memphis. Already in most of our Blue Lodges a special Inquisitorial
and Educational · Commission has been appointed by their ;videawake Masters.
This commission meets an evening or two preceding the stated
meeting and with the investigating committee's reports in hand it
is required that e.a ch applicant appear before them individually.
These commissions, composed of highly intelligent and zealous
men, then inquire very diligently into the candidate's motives in
applying for membership, his conception .of Civic duty and his
viewpoint regarding education. The applicant is then instructed
in some of the fundamentals of the Society's relation to the affairs
of men in terms of service.
Wnile the above plan is somewhat of a departure from cummon
practice and cqmparatively recent in its origin, the innovation has
more than demonstrated its usefulness. Careful consideration by
all Lodges is recommended.

MISCELLANEOUS ORGANIZATIONS
There · are undoubtedly too many organizations having as a
prerequisite for joining membership in the Masonic Fraternity. As
there is no need for them, and a number are started simply to boost
certain individuals or for financial gain, they cannot, by reason of
this fact, expect to survive. The present situation appears to be
analogous to that which existed in Fr.ance during the Eighteenth
Century when there were over two hundred side degrees or orders
connected with the general Masonic organization in that country.
In time they all died out, and we look for that to be the result from
the present condition of affairs.

MASONIC EDUCATION
The proposition of educating the membership of the Fraternity
throughout the various Jurisdictions still continues to be a problem.
A number of States are following the program outlined by the
Masonic Service Association while others are working along ideas
of their own.
The following replies to a questionnaire sent to the various
Grand Secretaries show the extent of the activities along this line:
Arizona: Active membership in Masonic Service Association
of the United States.
. Floridl!-: V:f e ~ave a Committee on Work who hold four schools
of mstructio,n 1!1 different. parts of the. State each year, besides a·
number of district conventions and special meetings.
Idaho: The way has been cleared for a practical ·organization
at the next ·meeting of Grand Lodge.
Louisiana:

Nova Scotia: Several paJJers read and distributed under the
auspices of the Nova Scotia Lodge of Research.

other Masonic subjects.
·

NEGROES ,
The position of the Negro in Masonry is a unique one. It
does not appear that it will ever be possible that American Jurisdictions will admit them fellowship along the same lines as English
or French Masonry. It does, however,. afford a topic of discussion
for our Southern brethren.
