PAST MASTER'S DEGREE
While a number of States have recognized the degree of Past
Master, we can see no objection to a "Past Grand Master's Degree,"
provided the members eligible to the same want it. As Past Grand
Masters usually compose the Committees of the ·various Grand
Lodges, it would appear that they have sufficient opportunity for
association in that manner rather than by a separate degree.
Florida:
For a number of years we have had in Florida, a little ceremony wnich is conferred upon the Grand Master elect, the regular
installation ceremony being interrupted and the officer elect being
taken to a proper. place where the Past Grand Masters present
would confer upon him the "Secrets of the Chair" and were supposed to give him certain instruction in the modes of recognition
by which he could make himself known as a Past Grand Master.
Not having any regular ritual for this ceremony, and owing to
the death of two or three of our Senior Past Grands who generally
officiated in the conferring of the degree, it has somewhat fallen
into disuse.
Being informed that such a ceremony was almost entirely unknown among the American Grand Lodges, a communication was
addressed to the Grand Secretary of each Grand Jurisdiction in the
United States asking if they. had in their Grand Lodge any cere-

-

.

In nearly all of the States, they report that at one time they
did have a Past Master's degree, but that they abandoned that
many years ago, but no Past Grand Master's degree.
In Kansas, t hey report that they abandoned the Past Grand
Master's degree or ceremony, but that they have a Past Master's
degree which is conferred upon Masters of Lodges at the time of
their installation and that a very impressive ceremony is carried
out for which their Grand Lecturer has prepared a ritual.
From Massachusetts, the oldest Grand Jurisdiction in the
United States, they report that they have no Past Grand Master's
degree and never have had.
From Maryland, the Grand Master reports that they have no
Past Grand Master's degree or ceremony, and that no one seems
to have any recollection that there ever was one. He reminds us
that the late Grand Master, Brother T . J. Shy.rock, served for more
than twenty-five years as Grand Master and if there ever was such
a degree it passed into disuse . .
The Grand Secretary of Nevada tells us that they have no
Past Grand Master's degree, but the Lodges use the Past Grand
Master's degree in their installation ceremony.
South Carolina:
Referring to the Past Master's degree he (P. G. M. of Illinois)
says, "The subject is passed by this writer for the reason that he
· does not consider it worth discussion." When we consider that
this degree is conferred in fifty English-speaking Grand Jurisdictions and not recognized in only t wenty, we think it is worth dis-

all limbs and members.

~ital to us as Citizens and as Masons. The time is rapidly approachmg when Masonry must do something to justify its continued existence, and ~e believe that one of . the means toward accomplishing

mnash the Sacred Calf (.w perhaps it's now Bull) of Precedent and
do some thing practical for our Brethren.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

We hasten here and now, and for all time, to declare with all
the steadfastness of our mind and soul that we stand squarely on
the Landmarks, which our Grand Lodge says no man can change;
but we do contend that Freemasonry, resting on these same Landmarks, without changing one Egglestonian jot or tittle, can meet
and aid in conquering a situation which needs ~he thoughts, prayers
and actions of America,n Masons.
The education that is being urged for American Masons is as
American Masonic education, having as its threefold purpose the
conservation of the republic, the co-operation of pure citizenship
and the Americanization of the people. Conse,rve, co-operate and
Americanize is the call to our 2,000,000 Masons-American Masons
-who can carry on to fulfillment our highest principle and ideal.
It is thoroughly proper, it is highly Masonic that we stand for
and fight for ths highest form of government; that we seek to preserve the principles for which our forefathers fought and died;
that we urge and secure one people, one nation and one flag; that
we "Americanize."
Idaho:
Masonry has much more of interest in the future than is found
either in the present or in the past. What _the fraternity has done
and is doing is of course full of interest, but when we look to its
future, when we see its possibilities for becoming the greatest,
the mightiest of all world powers, then it becomes positively inspiring.
What Masonry has done and is doing is perhaps to ;i:e extent disappointing. Many Brethren throughout the land feel that
the Fraternity has not risen to its greatest opportunities; in fact,
there is a feeling among some of its most devoted members that
we are to some extent standing still and resting too much on the
past history of our ancient order. The great question naturally
arises among our profound thinkers as to what Masonry can do to
awaken from that lethargic condition into which it has occasionally
drifted.
Masonic education is the keynote of today and the bringing
of this subject into right relations so as to make it a living force
is occuping the attention of many Grand Lodges at this time.
Idaho must not lag in the. great w<;irk before us.

of our educational institutions without being subjected to advice
through the Masonic Fraternity.

RELIGION
As Masonry does not concern itself with religion, and is not a
religion itself, any effort to introduce that topic into our work oiproceedings cannot have other than a bad effect. We presume it
will continue to be a · matter of debate "until time shall be no
more." All of us like to play with edged tools.
Alabama:
There are those perfectly h onest Brethren who, if they could,
would n ot only require this .belief but belief in every doctrine anq
statement of the Bible as well as in every orthodox teaching of
Christianity.
·

*

*

*

*

*

•

Some Grand Lodges have added to these requirements a belief
in the Christian religion. We can see nothing to prevent a Grand
Lodge some day requiring a declaration of a belief in "foreordiria.:
tion" or "free moral agency." It is certainly an innovation in the
body of Masonry to exact a belief in immortality.

Many of our Americ!J-n Masons do not understan? ~hat ..in
Continental Lodges the Bible is not upon the Altar, but 1t is lying
on the Master'~ pedestal, as is also the case in some of the Eng·
lish·speaking Lodges. It has been decided in Massachusetts, af.ter
an exhaustive examination of the law and precedent, that according

is placed upon the Altar. It will be readily understood that the
Sacred Book of the Law includes th e Koran, the Veda, th e Pentateuch, the Scruti, as well as the Bible.
' Referring to the question o f the use of the Holy Bible on the
Altar in English and American Lodges, we no.te in t he ~ast Proceedings of the Grand Lodge of England that 1t was decided that
the provincial Grand Lodge of India could initiate candidates
without ipterference with religion , and laid down the rule, "He
need not cease to be a Mohammedan, Buddhist, Hindu, Jew, Christian or any other denomination."
The Grand Registrar of the Grand Lodge of England stated,
"It is not a question of the Bible being on the Altar," it is "The
Volume of the · Sa cred L aw." Among the· Christians it is the Old
and New Testament combined. Among th e J ews, it is the Old
Testament alone. Among the Mohammedans, it is the K oran.
During the latter part of 1875, there was considerable stir
among the Craft L odges in India, as ta the propriety of the use
of the Koran in Masonic Lodges under English Constitutions.
Considerable cor respondence was h ad with the Gra nd Lodge of
England, in L ondon, which brought Ol!t the. fact ?f t he initiation
of the King of O udh, a Mohammedan, in Friendship L odge No. 6,
in London, on April 14, 1836. At t he initiatory ceremonies, a volume of the Koran was u sed. The book had been furnished by
the Grand Master, and the candidate was obligated upon it by
·t he Grand Master of the Lodge, who was an English clergyman.
This stopped further discussion, and it was settled in the Grand
Lodge of England and her colonies, that it was proper to obligate
all candidates upon that particular book which they held to be
most sacred, and contains the wotk of De'ity. All of th is has been
accepted and acknowledged as correct and right by the Grand
Lodge of Scotland, and the annual appointment of Grand Shastii
Bearer, Grand Veda, Bearer, Grand K oran Bearer, Grand Bible
Bearer, etc., has been regularly made.

CONCLUSION
Our ideas and views having been fully given in the report itself,
we omit a conclusion other than to borrow from Cor~espondent
Bro. JOSEPH M. LOWNDES, of Wyoming, the following:
There ain't no use kicking, brother,
What's all this holler about;
Because some poor correspondent
Has taken up the scissors route.
He is writing for his Craft,
So cut out your little whine;
They may like his way the best,
Better say, "Doing fine."
Do you remember what we're taught,
Seems to me I hear it clear,
As the Master to me said,
"Cheek to cheek or mouth to ear."
The thing to do is to curb your pen,
Kind words, be they yours or mine,
Will make more friends for you and me,
As we'll be, "feeling fine."
I use the scissors where ere I can;
They help to shorten the day,
And to the Craft they give the words,
What the other fellow had to say.
You can call it fazy, indolent and such,
But three-fourths of the forty-nine
At the Round-Table, to the scissors
Do say, "cutting fine."
Yours sincerely and fratei:'-nally,
JESSE M. WHITED,
Chairman.

AMERICAN FREEMASONRY
The systems of Freemasonry practiced in the United States
are generally known as the York Rite and the Scottish Rite.
Properly speaking', they should be termed the American Rite and
the Scottish Rite, for .the one commonly called York is peculiar in
its organized proceedings only to the United States.
The American Rite embraces the Symbolic, the Capitular, the
Cryptic and the Templar degrees.
The Symbolic degrees are conferred in a Lodge and are the
Entered Apprentice, the Fellow Craft and the Master Mason. They
are called Symbolic because their prominent mode of instruction
is by symbols.
The Capitular degrees are conferred in a Royal Arch Chapter
and are the Mark Master, the Past Master, the Most Excellent
Master and the Royal Arch . The supplemental and honorary degr.ees of High Priesthood is conferred in a Council of High Priests
upon those• who have been regularly elected to preside over a
Chapter of Royal Arch Masons. They are called Capitular because
they are conferred in a Chapter, the word "Capitular" meaning
"done in a Chapt er."
The Cryptic degrees are conferred in a Council. They are the
Royal Master, the Select Master and the Super-Excellent Master.
They are called Cryptic because the word "crypt" means a secret
vault or underground passage.
The Templar degrees are conferred in a Commandery and are
the Red Cross, the Temple and the Malta. The name Knight
Templar comes from the efforts of the Christian Knights to take
the · temple at Jerusalem from the Mohammedans.
The Scottish Rite embraces the degrees from the 4th to the
33rd, inclusive. In the Southern Jurisdiction of the United States
(which includes all territory south of the Ohio River and west of
the Mississippi River) the organization of the different bodies, and
the degrees conferred by them are: Lodge of Perfection, 4 ° to
14', inclusive; Chapter Rose Croix, 15' to 18°; Council of Kadosh,
19' to 30'; Consistory, 31' to 32°; Supreme Council, 33°.
In the Northern Jurisdiction (which includes all States north
of the Ohio River and east of the Mississippi River) the degrees
conferred are: Lodge of Perfection, 4 • to 14 •, inclusive; Council
Princes of Jerusalem, 15° and 16°; Chapter Rose Croix, 17° and
18°; Consistory, 19° to 32°; Supreme Council, 33°.

MEMBERSHIP TABLES.
The tables following, showing! the membership, net gain or net' loss,
and totals, are prepared not only for the Information of the members In
our own Grand Jurisdiction. but likewise for the Craft at large and others
interested. •
We believe there should be a sort of mutual understanding among
the writers of the Reports on Correspondence-that the work of preparing
these tables be left to some one of the writers and thereby relieve any
others from the laborious task of compiling a corresponding report.
The preparation of such statistical tables requires much labor and
the Grand Secretaries and Grand Recorders should endeavor, as far as
possible, in compiling their data for the printed Proceedings, to Include
information needed in preparing these figures, such as a plain showing
of the membership the previous year, the present membership, the net
gain or net loss, the number of c hartered bodies on the rolls the previous
year, number revoked or surrendered, number chartered, and the present
number on their rolls. This Is a simple statement, easily prepared, but
of ines timable value to the one who prepares such tables a s are herewith
submitted.
The writer of this report Is ready to receive any nominations and
is perfectly willing to relinquish the work In favor of any brother who
desires to compile these figures.
ALBERT K. WILSON,
Committee.
